items.title: ‘Its sheer madness is unparalleled’: inside the production design of I Love Boosters
paragraphs: Boots Riley's absurdist crime comedy I Love Boosters is far from conventional. From its stunning movie posters to its action-packed trailer, it's not a movie that comes quietly. Following a group of shoplifters as they face off against fashion mogul Christie Smith, the film soon spirals into a surreal science fiction body horror with some slicing social commentary for good measure.

But such an eccentric story needs immersive production design to match – that's where Christopher Glass comes in. To understand the meticulous practical effects process behind I Love Boosters and more, I sat down with Christopher to uncover the intricate artistry of production design and the evolution of the industry.

Christopher Glass is an Art Director Guild (ADG) Award-winning and Gold Cannes Lion-winning Production Designer whose work spans feature films, television, and commercials. Known for creating visually ambitious, emotionally resonant worlds - he has collaborated with some of the most influential directors working in film and advertising today.

I think beyond the obvious technological changes that have happened in the last 25 years (iPhones, iPads, Motion Capture/LED Volumes, real-time rendering and now AI) the largest conditions that have changed in the industry are economic.

The decentralization of film work from a Los Angeles hub to being scattered all over the world, chasing the latest tax rebate; the creation of IP-obsessed streaming platforms with tech companies swallowing traditional studios via ever larger mergers and acquisitions have created an environment where there is less work in general.

When there is work, it tends to be less creative and completely risk-averse. There is a focus on collecting libraries of “content” versus actually having an interest in making great films, TV shows or commercials. That’s why movies like “I Love Boosters” and what NEON and A24 are doing is much needed today.

In an ideal world, film companies would break away from these monstrous corporations and return to smaller autonomous studios, run by people who truly care about telling unique and compelling stories.

I think miniatures and forced perspective are my favorite practical effects, overlooked not only by audiences but also by filmmakers themselves. Filmmakers sometimes don’t know or realize these are great options for getting tangible effects in camera.

People tend to think miniatures have to be small buildings and cars. I have used 70% scale miniature “backings” to eliminate the need for LED walls or traditional translight backings. You get parallax when you move the camera. You can dress or light up windows how you want and change everything in modular ways. You can design sets with forced perspective to make things look further away or more expansive. These are techniques that have been around for over 100 years.

We used miniatures on “I Love Boosters” in a different way. Almost the entire third act is a combination of full-scale and 1/6th and 1/12th scale miniatures. We have stop-motion characters running across moving vehicles, down streets and alleys. It was an intentional choice for the handmade look.

In fact, when we were shooting, our Director Boots Riley thought some of the miniature shots started looking too real and told the folks at Blind Beagle FX (the miniature company run by Christopher Warren) to make them look more “miniature.”

I have a few favorite projects for varying reasons. “I Love Boosters” stands out for sure. Its sheer madness and creativity are unparalleled for me. I also really loved doing the battlefield war sets for “12 Strong” – which was a completely different experience – and “The Jungle Book” will always be a special film for me. I learned a hell of a lot from that and really loved the people I worked with.

Hands down, the Apple short film directed by Spike Jonze starring FKA Twigs called “Welcome Home.” Every detail, from the lighting, camera, props, actor choreography, music cues, and artwork, was subject to complicated practical effects and moving set pieces.

As an example, we built the apartment twice. One was “normal” and unmoving. The other one was the magic trick set where everything moved and stretched. Each moving piece affected the next, like a domino effect.
HomePod — Welcome Home by Spike Jonze — Apple - YouTube

One time Spike asked me to move the coffee table about 4 inches in one direction. I had to explain to him that the metal table, with a spring-loaded stretching magazine was attached to the stretching rug, and both were bolted into moving tracks underneath the floor connected to levers hidden just out of view of the perpendicularly moving walls at the end of the room… So it wouldn’t be easy.

Everything in that set depended on precise placement, choreography and movement. Every pattern and texture of fabric had to be precisely made and printed to achieve the “pixel” stretching effect throughout. The umbrella on a stand, a bike and a lamp had to be meticulously sculpted to be extruded by movement.

The large moving wall actually hovered on air bearings and was timed to the music. The hallway was made of ribbons stretched with so much tension, it bent the original steel frame and had to be rebuilt before shooting. The list goes on and on. Nothing was easy about that project. I thought it was the end of my career, and it was all going to go down in flames. But to my pleasant surprise, we won a Gold Cannes Lion for Film Craft.
Coming in close second for most difficult was “I Love Boosters!”

Natalie Fear is Creative Bloq's staff writer. With an eye for trending topics and a passion for internet culture, she brings you the latest in art and design news. Natalie also runs Creative Bloq’s 5 Questions series, spotlighting diverse talent across the creative industries. Outside of work, she loves all things literature and music (although she’s partial to a spot of TikTok brain rot).

items.title: Who could be behind the Binance hack and what we know so far
paragraphs: Binance, the world's largest crypto exchange, has been hit by what is believed to be the largest crypto hack ever at $6.3bn (£4.7bn).
Crypto is a type of digital asset which does not exist physically like cash or coins. Instead, people use digital wallets on their smartphones or computers to access and manage it.
Richard Teng, Binance's co-chief executive officer, said it is working with the authorities to work out what has happened and it will cover all losses.
Binance is the world's largest cryptocurrency exchange by trading volume, where people can buy, sell and trade digital currencies, like Bitcoin, as well as deposit and withdraw them.
It was founded in China in 2017 and has hundreds of millions of registered users worldwide.
The exchange has come under scrutiny over the past few years - notably in 2023, when its then-chief executive, Changpeng Zhao, resigned after pleading guilty to money laundering violations.
Last year, a lawsuit in the US accused the company of helping send millions of dollars to US-designated terrorist organisations.
In 2024, the company said it has more than $160bn in assets.
The hack happened to Binance's global centralised exchange, Binance.com.
Binance.us, which provides trading services specifically for US residents, said it has not been affected by the issue.
In a statement, Teng said: "Our initial investigation suggests this security incident may have started with a compromised DevOps engineer's laptop.
"That gave an attacker access to a service container, where they submitted unauthorised withdrawal transactions."
He said the hack "was not a simple 'one-click' action" but a "more complex attack process".

Raghu Nandakumara, vice president of industry strategy at cybersecurity platform Illumio, said this could mean an engineer was "talked into taking a test" and malware - malicious software – "landed on their laptop while they did it".
Because the laptop already had sufficient security privileges, Nandakumara said early reports suggest it became "the attacker's route straight into production, and from there to the wallets".

"You can build a vault with mathematical firewalls, but if the individual holding the keys can be duped, the vault is opened," said Dr Clive Summerfield, head of FARx, a biometrics in AI security company.
Binance co-chief executive officer Richard Teng speaks at a conference
It is not yet known who is behind the attack, but some analytics firms have pointed to North Korea - though this has not been confirmed.

AI-powered investigations company TRM Labs said in a report several elements of the Binance attack resembled earlier incidents linked to the territory, including a $1.5bn (£1.1bn) hack on the ByBit exchange in 2025.
These previous attacks have been linked to a cluster of cyber-criminals accused of working directly for the regime called the Lazarus Group - also known as TraderTraitor.
North Korean foreign policy expert Dr Edward Howell, from the University of Oxford, has told the BBC that Pyongyang "has a long history of using cyber warfare to extract cash".
Howell said North Korea "basically has a state-run cyber warfare agency", which it uses "to fund its weapons of mass destruction programmes" and as a "slush fund" for its leader Kim Jong Un's regime.
Howell added that as of the current day "about 40 – 50% of North Korea's weapons of mass destruction programmes are funded by cyber and crypto-currency warfare".
North Korea has always denied any involvement in these attacks; Binance has not directly responded to BBC queries about the incident's potential links to the area.
In his earlier statement, Teng said Binance users' funds are safe and, as a precaution, all deposits and withdrawals had been temporarily suspended.
He said the firm would cover all losses from its emergency reserve set up for such situations, and make up the rest with company funds.
Binance said it had been working with partners to freeze the affected assets, with around $3bn reportedly located so far.
"We are still on track towards the expected timeline to resume the withdrawal service in 45 hours," it said.
Users from other crypto platforms have also been warned to be wary of hackers seeking to exploit the situation.

Marijus Briedis, NordVPN's chief technology officer, said people should be on the lookout for things such as "an email claiming your funds are at risk", "a fake support account offering help" or "a message urging you to move your cryptocurrency to a 'safe' wallet".
"Check updates through the Binance app or a website address you already trust," he said.
"Avoid links in unsolicited messages, and never give anyone your password, verification codes or wallet recovery phrase."
Binance.us said it had not been affected by the issue
Jennifer Craven, an international commercial fraud expert at the law firm Pinsent Masons, said the repercussions of the hack could "extend well beyond Binance".
"More broadly, the incident exposes the fragility of parts of the crypto ecosystem," she said.
"If a platform as sophisticated as Binance can suffer a serious attack, regulators will inevitably ask what that means for smaller, less mature platforms and currencies."
She said the attack would likely accelerate scrutiny of how the sector protects both its infrastructure and its customers.

Although there is no evidence yet that AI was used in this attack, it fits into a much wider concern in the financial industry of whether AI agents could potentially identify weaknesses in software and work out how to exploit them much faster than human hackers.
The Bank of England has warned, external this could leave institutions struggling to fix vulnerabilities before attackers take advantage of them.
Crypto has become an increasingly popular way of investing and transferring money online, partly because, unlike traditional currencies, it is not controlled by central banks or governments.
This makes it popular for people who think decentralisation can bring financial freedom.
But it also makes it extremely volatile, with it rising and falling in value at the whim of buyers and sellers.
According to Solcard, a crypto-funded prepaid payment and virtual card platform, somewhere between 560 million and 741 million people own crypto worldwide in 2026.

items.title: Binance hackers stole $6.3 billion in record-breaking crypto heist
paragraphs: Binance has disclosed that $6.3 billion worth of crypto funds have been stolen from the platform, in what’s believed to be the biggest cryptocurrency hack on record. In a series of updates posted to X, the crypto exchange said that user funds are safe, and that around $3 billion of the impacted assets have been frozen so far.

Binance has publicly committed to covering any losses resulting from the hack. The company has an emergency reserve fund of around $1.3 billion (at last valuation) to protect user assets in these situations, and said it has also reserved over $6.34 billion of company funds to cover this incident — $5 billion of which is “already held in the exact token assets that were impacted.”

“Our initial investigation suggested that the security incident may have involved a compromised laptop, however our subsequent investigation has uncovered additional points of breach,” Binance reported on X. “This was a complex attack, and we are doing all we can in coordination with law enforcement to resolve it.”

The company shared details about the compromised laptop that belongs to one of its DevOps engineers in a prior update, saying it allowed an attacker to access a service container and submit unauthorized withdrawal transactions. Deposits and withdrawals have been suspended in response to the hack, and the affected address has had its authorization revoked.

“To be clear: the attacker did not simply use one engineer’s permissions, and this was not a single ‘one-click’ action. It involved a more complex attack process,” Binance co-CEO Richard Teng said on X. “Our investigation has not attributed responsibility to any individual. So far, we have found no evidence of any wallet private key leak.”

Binance may not be pointing fingers at who’s behind the attack, but blockchain analysis firms TRM and Chainalysis both attribute it to TraderTraitor, a North Korean cybercrime hacking group that has a history of stealing funds from cryptocurrency exchanges. This is the largest known cryptocurrency heist in history — four times higher than the previous record, when $1.46 billion was stolen from Bybit last year — and according to TRM, most of the theft occurred over a period of just 20 minutes.

This isn’t the first time Binance has been hacked, having suffered a previous security breach in 2019 in which $40 million worth of crypto assets (valued at the time) were stolen. The latest hack comes as cases of large-scale crypto theft are escalating, however, after several heists were disclosed by crypto companies in September. There are also new concerns around how AI tools can be used maliciously against the industry, with OpenAI reporting earlier this month that one of its models managed to swipe fake crypto on an Ethereum test network it didn’t have access to.

“This is an extraordinary hack, for its size and for the response... Few financial systems have ever shown a theft of this scale,” TRM chief policy officer Ari Redbord said in a statement to Sky News. “The theft shows how exposed the system is to sophisticated attackers moving at a speed we have never seen.”

items.title: From Bitcoin to Binance: Crypto terms and what they mean
paragraphs: From the rapidly rising and falling values of Bitcoin to high-profile heists like the hacking of Binance, the world of cryptocurrencies is often in the headlines.
The world's biggest crypto exchange said hackers had gained access to $6.3bn (£4.7bn) worth of digital assets, and while it has frozen about half, many remained in the hands of the thieves.
These stories are full of specialist language that people outside the industry struggle to understand.
So if you're unsure what the blockchain or a crypto echange or even a cryptocurrency itself are, here are some key terms and what they mean.
While many may struggle with the finer points of crypto, pretty much everyone has heard of its most famous product: Bitcoin. But what actually is it?
Bitcoin is a cryptocurrency, which is to say a type of digital currency. Unlike traditional currencies, Bitcoin is not controlled by centralised financial institutions.

This makes it popular for people who think decentralisation can bring financial freedom, but it also makes it extremely volatile with it rising and falling in value at the whim of Bitcoin buyers and sellers.
Donald Trump has pledged to make the US the "crypto capital of the world" - backtracking on his previous claim that Bitcoin was a "scam".
Its price topped a much-awaited threshold of $100,000 in December 2024, then rose to $120,000 in July 2025 as US politicians prepared to debate bills to regulate digital assets.

In October 2025, Bitcoin hit an all-time high of around $126,000, buoyed by a continued wave of institutional investment and positive market sentiment. But it has been known to plummet in value just as quickly as it spikes.
In early February 2026, its price dipped below $65,000 to effectively wipe out gains achieved under President Trump.
Against the backdrop of these frequent price fluctuations, speculation continues about the true identity of Bitcoin's mysterious inventor known only as Satoshi Nakamoto.
Brit says he is not elusive Bitcoin creator named by New York Times
Seven wild moments from the turbulent story of Bitcoin

Blockchain is the technology underpinning all cryptocurrencies, and many related products like non-fungible tokens (NFTs). In essence, it is a virtual spreadsheet on which all the buying and selling of crypto is recorded. They are arranged in blocks linked together in a giant chain - hence the name.
Every cryptocurrency transaction is individually recorded onto the blockchain by a huge network of volunteers verifying its authenticity by using computer programmes.

The incentive to do this for Bitcoin's network is that the first person to validate transactions is rewarded in Bitcoin. This potentially lucrative process, known as mining, is also controversial because of the incredible amount of energy, external used as people the world over race to be the first to successfully update the blockchain.
Are cryptocurrencies the future of money?
A crypto exchange is the digital platform where investors can buy, sell and trade cryptocurrencies.

Similar to traditional investing, a crypto exchange acts as a brokerage where people can transfer traditional money, like pounds or dollars, in exchange for cryptocurrencies like Bitcoin or Ethereum. Most transactions are accompanied by fees.
Binance is the world's biggest, which is part of what makes the hack so monumental.
A crypto wallet is a place where investors hold their cryptocurrency. There are two types, a hot wallet and a cold wallet.
Hot wallets are connected to the internet, and thus more accessible for quick transfers and easy access.
Cold wallets are physical devices like specially designed USB sticks that store crypto offline typically for safer and longer term storage.
Man told he can't recover £598m of Bitcoin from landfill site

ETFs are portfolios that let investors bet on multiple assets without having to buy any themselves. Traded on stock exchanges like shares, their value depends on how the overall portfolio performs in real time. They can comprise a combination of gold and silver bullion, for example, or a mix of shares in both technology and insurance companies.
A spot Bitcoin ETF buys the cryptocurrency directly, "on the spot", at its current price, throughout the day.

While some ETFs already contained Bitcoin indirectly, the US approved several spot Bitcoin ETFs in January 2024. This allowed new investors, such as investment management firms like Blackrock and Fidelity, to enter the speculative world of Bitcoin without having to worry about digital wallets or navigating crypto exchanges.
How big banks are becoming 'Bitcoin whales'
Meme coins are a form of cryptocurrency used for fun and speculation.
They are typically created to capitalise on social media trends or viral memes - such as for internet-famous pygmy hippo Moo Deng.
But meme coins are heavily criticised for their speculative nature and the risk involved for investors, as they often have little prospect of accumulating value over time.

They can also be susceptible to "rug pulls" - where promoters of a cryptocurrency draw in buyers to raise the price of their coin, only to stop trading activity and make off with the money raised from sales.
Some celebrities have faced backlash after launching meme coins.
'A mockery': Trump's meme-coin sparks anger in crypto world
Online star Hawk Tuah girl faces crypto coin criticism
"Stable" is the key word here - this cryptocurrency differs from others as it is intends to be less volatile in value.

This typically works by the price being linked to an existing asset, for instance currencies like the US dollar or pound sterling, which in theory should make them more stable in price than cryptocurrencies that are not backed by assets.

Stablecoins themselves are usually controlled by companies that provide them, with transactions recorded on digital ledgers. While held up by some as the future of finance, high profile price collapses of stablecoins have alerted regulators to risks for investors and prompted scrutiny over their supposed stability.
Cryptocurrency firm Terraform, behind the crashed TerraUSD and Luna tokens, files for bankruptcy
XRP is a cryptocurrency used by a platform called the XRP Ledger. It was created by the co-founders of financial services company Ripple Labs in 2012 as a cheaper, faster alternative to Bitcoin.
The cryptocurrency has a fixed supply of 100 billion coins, which were created when it launched. Much of it is held by Ripple and periodically released into circulation.

Unlike cryptocurrencies such as Bitcoin, transactions made using XRP are verified through consensus - whereby the majority of validators on its peer-to-peer network must agree whether or not a transaction is valid before it is added to its blockchain.

This has been credited with allowing many transactions to take place simultaneously, at high speed and low cost - making it appealing to financial institutions or for processes like cross-border payments. But as with other cryptocurrencies, XRP has received regulatory scrutiny and seen sudden, sharp declines in value.

items.title: Olaver unveils multi-purpose Laneway Studio with "lantern-like" glass-block facade
paragraphs: In the garden of a Melbourne family home, a facade of glass blocks set within recycled white brick and a concrete band beam tops this two-storey studio by Australian architecture practice Olaver.

Olaver designed Laneway Studio to appear as a “beautiful object” reflecting light into the garden in the day and glowing like a lantern at night. The multi-purpose building was designed in response to the growing needs of the family of five, offering a practical alternative to renovating the existing home.
It houses a study-cum-guest-room with an en-suite and terrace on the first floor and an open-plan living area below, fitted with concealed laundry facilities and a bar.
The new studio block was constructed behind the main house and its newly configured garden, designed by landscape architect Penny Starr to include a pool and areas of planted foliage.
Large glass-panelled sliding doors leading into the garden from both the house and studio create a seamless flow between the interior and exterior living spaces.
Another sliding door on the opposing wall of the studio, made from oak with a steel-clad exterior, connects the studio’s living space with the titular laneway behind the property.

“With large sliding doors on opposing walls, the ground floor can open right through, so it works as an extension of the garden and pool terrace to the laneway rather than a closed room”, Olaver director Emlyn Olaver told Dezeen.
“Open, the space feels far bigger than its footprint, and the family can spread across the house, the pool and the studio as one connected space when entertaining”, she continued.

Inside, the ground floor was designed to be minimal and open-plan to ensure its multi-functionality. It features neutral terrazzo flooring throughout. Oak cabinetry conceals storage, laundry facilities and a TV nook and frames a central bar area with a stainless-steel sink and surround.
“We wanted the studio to be calm, with joinery doing the heavy lifting so each space can change roles without feeling cluttered”, Olaver explained.

“Every space had to do more than one job; a laundry, a living room or a bar depending on the day. That flexibility also gives the building a longer life, because the family’s needs will keep changing as the kids grow up, move out and come back.”
On the first floor’s east-facing wall, overlooking the garden, a facade of glass blocks was installed above a concrete band beam to bypass planning restrictions on the use of conventional windows.

The glass-block facade brings in soft morning light while offering privacy to the first-floor interior and, viewed from the garden and house, transforms the studio into a “glowing lantern” at night, Olaver said.

The first-floor interiors were also designed to be multi-functional, comprising a combined study and guest bedroom with an en-suite and small roof terrace. Red wraparound tiling in the bathroom is echoed by red panelling in the nook of the foldable bed, itself concealed behind more oak joinery when not in use.

“The new studio’s interiors echo the existing home’s rich but calm textures,” Olaver said. “Natural materials and tactile elements exist in both spaces, but the studio is slightly more playful in its approach.”
The project tasked Olaver with extending the home of a family rapidly outgrowing their existing space.

“In Melbourne, the usual answer is yet another extension that eats into the backyard,” she said. “Laneway Studio goes the other way, keeping the garden at the centre of the site and showing how a well-designed studio can add flexibility and density to an existing lot.”
More studio developments recently featured on Dezeen include a Camber Sands studio made using waste materials and a green-tiled studio in a London garden.

items.title: Footage of Seoul crush to be removed from Call of Duty after backlash
paragraphs: Video clips showing the aftermath of a deadly crush in Seoul will be removed from the latest Call of Duty game after an angry reaction from victims' families.
Real life news coverage of the 2022 disaster which killed almost 160 people was included in an opening scene of Modern Warfare 4 to illustrate a fictional invasion from North Korea.
Bereaved families said they were "appalled" to see the footage - which included people being removed on stretchers, body bags on the street and resuscitation efforts - repurposed for the game.
Activision, which makes Call of Duty, has since apologised and confirmed it would be removed in the game's next update on 12 November.
The crush happened in the narrow alleys of Seoul's Itaewon district when more than 100,000 people went to the area to celebrate Halloween four years ago.
The streets became so tightly packed that people could not move and some were unable to breathe.

In a statement on Thursday, the families of those who died said the disaster "was a tragedy that caused hundreds of casualties, and citizens who took part in the rescue or witnessed it have suffered from trauma until now".

"We cannot help but be appalled that the chaotic and desperate scene, in which many citizens at the site performed CPR to save one another and victims lay on the freezing street, was used to create a scene in a game.
"Using such an event as material for a game made for entertainment is in itself highly inappropriate and senseless."

Activision confirmed it had used real news coverage of the disaster "to establish the game's fictional narrative" but insisted it had "not intended to reference or trivialise the Itaewon disaster or any other real-world tragedy in any way, shape or form".
Confirming on Friday that the footage would be removed in a statement, the company offered its condolences and apologised to the bereaved families and victims who have been hurt by this incident.
The decision was welcomed by the 10.29 Itaewon Disaster Bereaved Families Association, however the group told the BBC they had not received a direct apology from Activision.
Modern Warfare 4, which was released last week, had already faced criticism for basing the game on North Korea invading South Korea, as the two countries have been technically at war for decades.
Fighting stopped in the Korean War in 1953, but the two countries never signed a peace treaty and conflict is a very real worry in that part of the world.
At the launch of the game, Call of Duty's chief marketing officer, Tyler Bahl, told BBC Newsbeat: "We have to understand this is entertainment".

items.title: Streeting denies 'kicking can down the road' in defence spending row
paragraphs: Defence Secretary Wes Streeting has denied "kicking the can down the road" over how much the UK spends on defence.
The government has faced criticism for not setting out a pathway at Wednesday's Budget to hit its target of spending 3% of GDP on defence by 2030.
Streeting is at odds with MPs on the Commons defence committee over the issue.
It comes as Chancellor John Healey and Streeting announce that foreign firms which are awarded defence contracts of more than £50m will need to invest an equal value back into the UK.
Under the new investment rules, described as an "offset strategy", these companies will need to spend an equivalent amount on British factories, jobs and training.

The Ministry of Defence will apply the rules on a "case-by-case" basis from April 2027, the government said. Healey and Streeting will unveil the policy on a visit to UK defence contractor BAE's shipbuilding site in Glasgow later.
Countries including Poland, Norway and the Netherlands have mandated similar rules to "boost the economic benefit from defence procurement", the government said.
While ministers hope the rules increase investment in Britain's defence industry, they appear designed to do so in a politically palatable way rather than committing to spending cuts.

Tan Dhesi, Labour chair of the cross-party Commons defence committee, said on Wednesday that decisions had been "kicked into the long grass" to next year's government spending review, rather than announced in the Budget.
He warned that without building capabilities now, "we risk leaving ourselves seriously vulnerable in the event of a major conflict".
Streeting hit back at these comments as "unfair" and "unfounded".
Speaking on Thursday, Dhesi said the committee stands by its criticism.
"We had hoped to see that the chancellor would set out a precise pathway to spend 3% of GDP on defence by 2030," Dhesi told BBC Radio 4's Today programme.
"But instead some of those key decisions on defence have lamentably been delayed until next year's spending review."
He praised the government for plugging a £4.7bn hole in the Defence Investment Plan in the Budget, through asking government departments to cut their capital budgets by 1%.
Responding on Thursday, Streeting told Today: "I like Tan very much, he's a friend and I respect him, but I strongly disagree with him.
"And I don't think the charge he makes of delaying or kicking the can down the road stacks up against the extra money that is already going into defence and the capability we're funding right now."

Streeting told BBC Breakfast the new rules, aiming to create "bang for the British buck", would help achieve this target given increasing defence spending "does come at a cost to the country and other things we'd like to spend money on".
He said waiting for the spending review, which does not have a fixed date and could come in the second half of 2027, was "the right thing to do" so ministers can look at "spending in the round".
He added that the UK was ready to deal with hostile threats, but "we're not where we'd want to be".
"There's no sugarcoating the fact that our Armed Forces were under-invested in for more than a decade," he told Breakfast.
Defence analysts have questioned the government's ability to deliver on its 2030 target and the Nato-wide target of 3.5% by 2035. UK defence spending is at an estimated 2.6% of GDP this year.
Some estimates have suggested the government will need to spend an additional £10bn annually to reach its targets.
Tory leader Kemi Badenoch said on Wednesday that Healey "failed his own test" by not setting out a "plan for 3%".
Healey resigned as then-Prime Minister Sir Keir Starmer's defence secretary in June over not spending enough on defence.

In the Budget, Healey said the UK was negotiating with Finland, Poland and the Netherlands to set up an international bank - the Multilateral Defence Mechanism - to boost defence investment and joint procurement.
But Conservative shadow defence secretary James Cartlidge said this amounted to "turning to borrowing at a time when the national debt is over £3 trillion".
"The answer is not more borrowing – it's to cut welfare to fund defence," he said.

items.title: Prominent Russian newspaper shuts down under pressure from authorities
paragraphs: The paper said that over time six journalists connected with the paper were killed for "fulfilling their professional and civic duty." Those reporters include Anna Politkovskaya, who was shot dead in the stairwell of her apartment block 20 years ago this month. Among the subjects she had reported on were the wars in Chechnya.

In the statement announcing its closure, Novaya Gazeta launched a stinging attack on the Russian authorities, claiming the newspaper was the victim of a "coordinated act" and blaming "the repressive state apparatus".
"Human rights and freedoms have been eliminated in the country and their protection has been equated to a crime," the statement said.
"The courts have been destroyed along with the law. Having personal convictions is now state treason."
Since Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, the pressure on independent journalism and independent Russian journalists has been growing.

Soon after the start of what the Kremlin calls the so-called "special military operation", new laws were adopted in Russia. Their aim: to punish dissent and silence criticism of the war and of those in power.
Novaya Gazeta itself and its staff had been facing a multitude of problems.

The authorities had already revoked the newspaper's licence and blocked access to its website. Several of its journalists and contributors had been designated "foreign agents", a label often used by the Russian authorities to punish critics.
Earlier this year there was a police search of the editorial office. A veteran investigative journalist, Oleg Roldugin, was arrested and charged with "unlawful access to computerised information".
In connection with the case, the newspaper's editor-in-chief, Sergei Sokolov, was recently taken in for police questioning and his home was searched.
Despite increasing pressure, Novaya Gazeta had managed to continue operating, albeit in a reduced form.
Loyal readers used virtual private networks to circumvent official blocking of the website and access content. But the loss of its licence and other restrictions dealt a major blow.

One of the founders of Novaya Gazeta in the 1990s - and for many years its chief editor - was journalist Dmitry Muratov, external. In 2021, Muratov was awarded the Nobel Peace Prize for efforts "to safeguard freedom of expression, which is a precondition for democracy and lasting peace".
The award didn't stop the authorities from declaring him a "foreign agent" in 2023.
At the offices of Novaya Gazeta, they've already started packing.
The end of this newspaper is very much the end of an era.
In an increasingly authoritarian Russia, it's also a sign of the times.

items.title: Binance flags 'potential security issue,' says approximately $6.3 billion impacted
paragraphs: FILE - The Binance logo is seen on a smartphone, Feb. 28, 2023, in Marple Township, Pa. Matt Slocum/AP hide caption

LOS ANGELES — Binance, the world's largest cryptocurrency exchange, said Thursday it's investigating reports of a potential security issue as its founder said the incident "does look like a hack on Binance." The company said late Thursday the estimated total impact was at more than $6 billion, which could be one of the most significant of such security incidents on record.

It wasn't immediately clear the extent of the damage hackers might have been able to cause, and Binance had not explicitly confirmed that funds had been pilfered. The company said its teams are "working around the clock" to resolve the issue.
"Rest assured that user funds are completely safe," a Binance spokesperson said in a statement.

"Our security teams are reviewing all relevant information with urgency, and we will provide updates through official Binance channels as soon as we have verified information," the statement continued.

The company wrote on its X account that the estimated total impact sat at around $6.3 billion. It said it has worked with blockchain partners to freeze affected assets, with roughly $3 billion frozen on-chain so far.

"Binance's initial investigation suggests that the security incident may involve a compromised DevOps engineer's laptop, which allowed an attacker to gain access to a service container and submit unauthorized withdrawal transactions," the company wrote.
"We have found no evidence of any wallet private key leak," it added.
Binance said it will share more technical details once the investigation is complete and when the facts are "fully verified."

"Our teams work closely with law enforcement, issuers, blockchain intelligence firms and industry partners to trace and freeze additional assets," the company wrote in a separate post earlier Thursday.
Binance also said all deposits and withdrawals are temporarily suspended while it conducts security checks, freezes funds and works with law enforcement.
Stablecoin providers Tether and Circle each said they froze funds Thursday in response to the incident.

Jeremy Allaire, co-founder and CEO of Circle, wrote on X that the company had frozen the equivalent of more than $800 million in currency associated with the incident "in coordination with law enforcement." Tether CEO Paolo Ardoino said on X that the company froze the equivalent of more than $1.5 billion in currency related to "a potential Binance exchange hack."
The price of bitcoin dropped 3.2% Thursday evening to under $79,000.

Binance was founded in 2017 by Changpeng Zhao, who in 2023 pleaded guilty to a felony related to his failure to prevent money laundering on the platform and stepped down as CEO. President Donald Trump pardoned him in 2025.

Zhao posted on X on Thursday that "User funds are safe!" but added that the incident "does look like a hack on Binance." He added that while he doesn't manage Binance anymore, "as a shareholder, I expect all user funds will be fully covered."

Zhao was released from prison last year after being sentenced for violating the Bank Secrecy Act. He was the first person ever sentenced to prison time for violations of that law, which requires U.S. financial institutions to know who their customers are, to monitor transactions and to file reports of suspicious activity. Prosecutors said no one had ever violated the regulations to the extent Zhao did. Zhao and Binance have been key supporters of some of the Trump family's crypto enterprises.

items.title: Alaska's Senate race faces claims of spoiler candidate. And, Hegseth ousts Army general
paragraphs: Good morning. You're reading the Up First newsletter. Subscribe here to get it delivered to your inbox, and listen to the Up First podcast for all the news you need to start your day.

It is the final stretch before Election Day on Tuesday and candidates are making final campaign stops and delivering closing arguments. President Trump has been campaigning for at-risk Republicans, but he has abruptly switched to virtual rallies.
A person walks past a voting sign at the East Point Library on Tuesday, the first day of early voting, in Atlanta. Megan Varner/Getty Images hide caption

Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth has dismissed Army Lt. Gen. Brett Sylvia, who oversaw planning at the Pentagon. Sylvia was also part of the Joint Chiefs of Staff. His removal comes as the U.S. and Israel prepare for a new potential round of attacks against Iran. Although Sylvia held a senior position in strategy, planning and policy, he was not directly involved in day-to-day operations regarding the Iran conflict.

Thousands of military veterans with VA-backed mortgages have faced higher interest rates and monthly payments since last year, after the Trump administration shut down a key part of the VA's home loan program. Before it was shut down, the Veterans Affairs Servicing Purchase (VASP) program, created under the Biden administration, helped tens of thousands of veterans who had fallen behind on their payments by rolling missed payments into a new, low-interest mortgage. The mortgage industry and housing groups warned the administration not to kill the program without first creating a viable replacement. Without one, vets had to modify loans at higher interest rates. An NPR investigation found that more than 15,000 veterans experienced monthly payment increases of at least $150 after their loans were modified due to financial hardship. More than 700 veterans saw their payments rise by $1,000 or more.
by Rob Stein, NPR's science desk correspondent and senior editor

I've been doing stories about the organ transplantation system for decades. One of the most fundamental guiding ethical principles in organ donation has long been the "dead donor rule." That rule, stated simply, says: Organs should only be retrieved for transplants from a person who is dead, and death should never be accelerated to try to boost the chances their organs will be usable. To make sure that's the case, there's long been a strict firewall between the doctors and nurses trying to save patients in the hospital, and the organ retrieval teams standing by to try to procure their organs.

But over the years, I've heard many stories from family members who nevertheless felt pressured to donate their loved one's organs. So when I got a tip that the Organ Procurement & Transplantation Network, which runs the nation's organ system, was planning to relax that firewall, I instantly knew that was a big story.

I rushed to confirm the documentation that the network's board of directors had indeed endorsed the change, which would go into effect Nov. 18. I then reached out to bioethicists and others for their reaction to this major change. The revision was part of a set of new policies designed to boost donations and improve patient safety. Those changes were spurred by disturbing revelations about mistakes, including patients literally being wheeled into the operating room to remove their organs when they were still alive. Some of the changes were praised as improving safety. But many bioethicists and even some transplant surgeons and patient and organ donation advocates say relaxing the firewall between care and organ retrieval teams is dangerous. The fear is it could lead to families and caregivers discontinuing treatment too soon, and deepening distrust in the organ donation system.
I explored what these rule changes will mean for organ donors. You can read about it here.

items.title: Beijing Queer film festival cancelled after harassment from authorities
paragraphs: Beijing’s annual independent queer film festival has been cancelled after what is understood to have been a campaign of sustained harassment from authorities.
Beijing Queer film festival, which was due to begin on Friday in China’s capital, is one of the country’s oldest independent film festivals.

In a statement posted on Instagram late on Thursday, the organisers said: “We regret to inform you that the Love Queer Film Week … has been cancelled. We sincerely apologise for any inconvenience and disappointment that the cancellation of this event may cause to those who planned to participate or had been looking forward to the film week.”
Police had increased pressure on the festival through repeated phone calls in recent weeks, it is understood.

Founded in 2001 by a group of Peking University students, the festival grew to become the only film festival in mainland China to offer a public forum for films and discussions exploring LGBTQ+ issues.

The Chinese authorities have grown increasingly intolerant of open discussion of feminist or LGBTQ+ issues. Film festivals in particular attract particular scrutiny because they provide an opportunity to platform narratives that sit outside the Communist party’s worldview.

Beijing Independent film festival, China’s most prominent independent film festival, was closed down in 2014 after the authorities detained the founders and shut off the electricity supply to the venue. Last year, an independent Chinese film festival that was due to be held in New York was cancelled after harassment from the Chinese authorities, an incident which raised concern about transnational repression.

Maya Wang, the deputy Asia director for Human Rights Watch, said: “The Chinese government under Xi has been relentlessly tightening social and ideological control, and so any activities outside of those sanctioned by the party-state are subjected to intensifying scrutiny and often also official harassment.

“The authorities have put more pressure on what little is left of China’s civil society, as well as the LGBT communities and independent film-makers. A queer film festival basically faces all of these overlapping pressures.”
Hongwei Bao, a professor of Chinese studies at the University of St Andrews who focuses on LGBT issues, said that the festival was “a beacon for LGBT resilience” in China.
“The shutdown of the Love Queer Cinema Week has a chilling affect on the Chinese queer community,” Bao said.

In June this year, screenings of films with LGBTQ+ themes that were scheduled to be held in Beijing during Pride month at the Institut Français, a French cultural centre, were cancelled because of police harassment.

Despite the increased pressure, Beijing Queer film festival remains a popular event. Several international film-makers whose work had been selected for the festival had travelled to China to participate. Last year, the festival received 200 volunteer applications, four times the number received in 2024.
Beijing’s public security bureau could not be reached for comment.

items.title: The two most interesting risks to Anthropic
paragraphs: You're reading a newsletter from The Indicator from Planet Money. Once a week, we curate our favorite stories and insights on business, finance, economics and why they matter. Subscribe here to get it in your inbox every Friday.

A TILE GAME is giving a boost to Chinese factories. Our very own Jennifer Pak reported that Chinese manufacturers have not had the easiest few years with U.S. tariffs and the war in Iran pushing up costs. Well, the aged game of Mahjong is giving them a surprising boost. That's because it's having a moment in the U.S. and some entrepreneurial citizens in China are enjoying the benefits. Mahjong sets can sell for like $300-$400 in the States … and want to know how much they cost to make? ~$30. One businessman said he used to make the game primarily for Chinese consumers. Now, every set is exported to the U.S.
People playing the centuries-old game Mahjong in San Francisco, California. Justin Sullivan/Getty Images North America hide caption
Justin Sullivan/Getty Images North America

What to Know: Anthropic gave the world 94 pages of risks to its business (slash the entire AI economy) in its IPO prospectus aka the S-1. It wouldn't be Anthropic if they didn't discuss the "existential risks" to humanity and society several times. And isn't that an important risk to disclose? Another that stood out: the AI boom has a glaring point of failure. The majority of advanced semiconductor manufacturing is concentrated in one place, Taiwan, and if anything were to happen there, it could disrupt the entire AI economy. Think earthquake, Chinese military action, blockades. But I want to focus on a different risk, because it is FASCINATING!
Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei has persistently raised the safety concerns of AI. Kevin Dietsch/Getty Images North America hide caption

Committing to the past at a premium: Anthropic is worried about aging out of the tech that's powering its AI, while paying the same prices. What does that mean?! AI companies have to lock into pricey contracts for all sorts of softwares, hardware, data center, and squadrons of GPUs. But technology is advancing quickly right now. New GPUs, for example, could come along that can do the same amount of work for way less money. Then Anthropic is stuck like CHUMPS in a contract paying a premium for old hardware, while some competitors may be doing more for less.

What To Know: Microsoft offered buyouts to 60,000 employees, roughly a quarter of its staff this week. And doesn't that sound better than "Microsoft laid off 60,000 employees this week"?? Skydance ALSO offered a buyout to employees on Monday, though it's not clear how many would be eligible. And here at NPR, we've been a fan of the term buyout too. So what's the real difference in offering a buyout versus just laying off staffers?

The difference: Morale? Morale. There's something about a "mega-layoff" that doesn't inspire worker confidence. A "buyout" not so much. Really? Ok, I guess. The WSJ reported the focus in C-suite land is on the ratio of employees to AI agents inside companies. Companies have to find ways to pay for the ever-increasing costs of AI … and you know … actual human workers expect to be paid.

Andy Challenger, Chief Revenue Officer of Challenger, Gray & Christmas, a consulting firm, told the Journal that it can help staffers emotionally by making it a little easier to let go. It also tends to motivate older staffers to retire a little bit early, which may be the company's goal.

If you HAVEN'T listened: I never thought I'd yearn for the days when the internet felt wholesome. Where you could go to blogs and random sites and make friends across the world. Well, more than half of internet traffic now comes from non-humans, aka bots. They're pouring into the digital veins of the World Wide Web, ignoring a lot of ads, generating all kinds of comments, nonsense and what have you. One interesting takeaway: this shift from human-to-bot traffic changes the business model of the internet. If humans let bots do their shopping for them, then ads suddenly become less useful. And if ads don't pay out for websites, then who pays for them?

If you HAVE listened: Writer and researcher Erin Kissane says she believes Dead Internet Theory came out of a human impulse to "create speculative fiction versions" of real-life societal change that scares us. As a reminder, Dead Internet Theory is the idea that the internet becomes just bots talking to other bots.They're pouring into the digital veins of the World Wide Web, ignoring a lot of ads, generating all kinds of comments, nonsense and what have you. One interesting takeaway: this shift from human-to-bot traffic changes the business model of the internet. If humans let bots do their shopping for them, then ads suddenly become less useful. And if ads don't pay out for websites, then who pays for them?
