"I didn't have expectations because every game is a different game and I just wanted to do my best, but I guess my aim was to raise awareness of stammering.
"I had people reach out about how I'd helped them, I had mums reach out about their kids and how it's helped them... it was just good to educate others."
Alex Oleksy hopes the faithful will come out victorious
Series three's Alex Oleksy originally hails from Scotland, but lives in Whitby.
Although he admits the traitors are "playing it really well" this season, Oleksy is a true faithful and hopes they can defeat the traitors.
"James Acaster is such a reluctant traitor! We've seen all different kinds of traitors, but I don't think we've seen one that played quite like James."
Oleksy, 32, watched the show with his mother-in-law before signing up, and expected to "breeze right through it and win the money".
"I don't think I expected it to be quite so mentally taxing... it turns you so paranoid, it's unreal," he said.
"Everything is heightened; you're making friendships in the blink of an eye, you're deciding who your allies are...everything is just so heightened.
"It's like having a pot on the boil and as soon as these factors come into play, you're just constantly bubbling over."
He does caveat that by saying how much he loved being part of the show and how much it "taught him" about himself.
Oleksy was eventually banished by his fellow players, and says by that point, he was "desperate for a moment of vindication".
"I couldn't wait to get up there and be like, 'haha, told you'."
The final of Celebrity Traitors will air on BBC One at 20:00 GMT, and while many people will be glued to their sofas, venues across the region are hosting dedicated watch parties.
Headrow House in Leeds is hosting a screening of the final, as well as a repeat of the semi-final for those who missed it on Thursday, from 18:00.
The event is ticketed but free to attend.
Two Thirds Beer Co in Sheffield is also showing the final.
Owner Ben Stubbs said: "We're all huge fans of The Traitors here, and we actually showed the final of the last series earlier this year.
"We weren't quite sure what to expect, but the response was brilliant."

items.title: Hazardous driving conditions for Friday as fog warning issued by Met Office
paragraphs: Thick fog has formed on Friday morning across parts of the United Kingdom which could lead to hazardous driving conditions.
The Met Office has issued a yellow severe weather warning for fog from Lincolnshire, the East Midlands, the Home Counties into parts of Greater London.
Fog will be dense in places with visibility below 100 metres at times and it will be most extensive and disruptive during the morning rush hour.
It will slowly begin to thin, lift and clear later this morning but in some rural spots in eastern England it may not clear until this afternoon.
Met Office severe weather warning for fog issued on Friday morning
Early morning mist and fog patches on Saturday may lift into low cloud, which could hang around all day.
Some areas will fare better with some spells of sunshine with many areas staying dry.
The exception to this theme will be north-west Scotland, where a weak weather front will bring thicker cloud and rain for a time.
Temperatures will be close to average and will be overall, similar to recent days.
By Sunday this dying weather front will bring some thicker cloud to Wales and central England threatening a few patches of light rain or drizzle, but not much.
The rest of the UK will have a dry day on Sunday with variable cloud and some spells of sunshine at times.
With drier weather people will should be able to get out and enjoy the autumn colours
High pressure has been building and is set to dominate across the UK in the coming days.
This is in stark contrast to last week which saw areas buffeted by a cluster of storms developed by a powerful Atlantic jet stream.
The jet stream, still running close to the UK, with the building area of high pressure bringing us much quieter weather.
Whilst Storms Austen and Boelo provided some short-term hydrological benefit, 82% of England remains in drought status according to the Environment Agency.

The area of high pressure will stay over or close to the UK for at least ten days as a result of a 'diffluent blocking pattern' forming in the Atlantic jet stream across the UK and western Europe, which will prevent weather systems reaching our shores.

It means we are heading into a long stretch of mostly dry weather. There could still be some patches of low cloud and drizzle associated with early morning mist and fog, however, rainfall amounts will be negligible.
A blocked jet stream pattern creates a near-stationary area of high pressure next week
With no storms on the horizon any time soon, it is likely to be a while before we see the arrival of Chloe, the next name on this year's storm list.
In the short-term this lack of rainfall will raise concerns about the drought and low water levels in England's reservoirs.

Following the latest meeting of the National Drought Group, water companies are being urged to speed up the fixing of leaks and members of the public to take shorter showers and turn off the tap when brushing their teeth.
The Environment Agency (EA) says that 20% more rain than average is needed over the next six months, external for the drought to end.
Philip Duffy, Chief Executive of the Environment Agency, said: "The recent rain is welcome, but the drought isn't over. A few wet days cannot reverse months of hot, dry weather.
"Our rivers, reservoirs and groundwater need sustained rainfall to recover, and the effects on nature can last much longer."

El Niño has been linked to wetter and stormier weather in late autumn and early winter. The current three month outlook from the Met Office forecasts that there is double the chance of it being wetter than normal.

items.title: Attenborough-backed appeal secures £30m estate
paragraphs: Conservationists have completed the purchase of a huge upland estate following a two-year £30m public appeal backed by the likes of Sir David Attenborough.

The Wildlife Trusts - a federation of 47 conservation charities - and Northumberland Wildlife Trust (NWT) plan to "enhance the rich natural heritage" of the Rothbury Estate, a 9,500-acre stretch of former grouse moor, woodland and farmland - having headed off fears it could be split among multiple owners.
Broadcaster Sir David described it as an opportunity "to create something very special for generations to come".
Not everyone supported the campaign, though, with some local farmers having warned the purchase would be "a folly".

Owned by Lord Max Percy, the Duke of Northumberland's youngest son, the estate had been in the family for about 700 years and was understood to be the largest area of land put up for sale in England in decades.

Worried public access could become more difficult if it was divided between owners, the wildlife organisations bought an initial tract in 2024 covering the Simonside Hills and a mixture of lowland, woods, riverside and farmland.

That also saw them strike a deal to purchase the remainder of the estate if they could raise the £30m in two years with ambitions for it to become a 40-mile (64km) "wild" corridor, stretching from the North East coast to Kielder and the Scottish border.

It has now been announced they have taken out a "low-interest loan to bridge the short-term funding gap between pledged monies still to be received and the fundraising target, ensuring completion of the entire estate".
The plan was not universally popular though.
Chris Armstrong, a tenant farmer overseeing 1,000 acres close to the site, was among those questioning it.
He told the BBC earlier this year the community was split over the issue: "The most recent strapline seems to be 'time is running out to save the Rothbury Estate'.
"The Rothbury Estate doesn't need saving. Saving from what?"
"I would put it very much akin to the Brexit vote, I would think it would be that finely split.
"I think the majority of the farming community see this as a folly."
Meanwhile, Defra's contribution has come under fire from Councillor Guy Renner-Thompson, chairman of Northumberland Conservatives.
He said the pledge showed the government "has its priorities wrong" in light of difficulties people across the country have faced securing sustainable farming incentive (SFI) funding.
"Farmers were left scrambling in an application window that opened and closed the same day," Renner-Thompson said.
"Yet ministers can find nearly £2m to help a charity buy an estate."

In response, Nature Minister Jenny Riddell-Carpenter said the government was "stepping in to help" having seen thousands of members of the public give their support for a "once-in-a-generation opportunity".
Follow BBC North East on X, external, Facebook, external, Nextdoor and Instagram, external and listen to Radio Newcastle on BBC Sounds.

items.title: Largest woodland bat survey a 'nice story of AI for good'
paragraphs: The red-listed Barbastelle is one of the rarest bat species in England
ByClara BullockSomerset and Harriet Bradshaw
Britain's largest ever woodland survey of bats would "simply not have been feasible" without AI, scientists say.
Researchers left devices on poles among the trees of 310 woodlands across Britain, recording 98 million bat calls over three years, which would have taken more than 30 years to analyse without AI.
Some of Britain's rarest and most threatened bats, including the red-listed Barbastelle, have been recorded in the south-west of England, including Somerset, Devon, Cornwall and Dorset.
Kate Jones, from University College London, said: "AI has fundamentally changed the scale at which we can monitor wildlife." She added the survey was a "nice story of AI for good".
Jones added: "Previously, analysing this volume of acoustic data would simply not have been feasible.
"These efficient open-source AI tools allow us to identify millions of bat calls across thousands of nights of recordings, identify patterns and flag species at a national scale."
The Barbastelle roams ancient forests but its elusive nature has made it challenging to track.
Hotspots of Barbastelle activity detected in the survey were concentrated across the South West.
The Barbastelle was mostly found in the south-west of England
Lia Gilmour, of the Bat Conservation Trust, which was involved in the survey alongside Forest Research, said the project was "unprecedented".
"We're getting some really good bat activity in the south-west area of Somerset," Gilmour said.
"Somerset is generally a really good stronghold for the bat species we have across the UK.
"It's been quite exciting some of the rarest species popping up in Somerset as part of the survey.
"In biodiversity monitoring, we view AI as a powerful tool," Gilmour added.
"We were looking at huge volumes of data and 90,000 hours of recording, there was no way we would be able to do this manually."

items.title: Syrians struggle with soaring prices as crisis challenges post-Assad recovery
paragraphs: Last month, protests erupted in squares and streets across Syria. People burned tyres, blocked roads and chanted slogans, angry at the government's decision to raise fuel prices again. It was the largest show of discontent yet since President Ahmed al-Sharaa came to power two years ago.

Speaking on a Syrian TV channel, a man said he still supported the authorities but that his situation had deteriorated to the point where he could no longer afford to buy bread. "Honestly," another said, "we have begun to fear what kind of new decision each morning will bring".

The increase was the latest in a series of measures people blame for a growing cost-of-living crisis. For many Syrians, life, financially, has worsened since rebels led by Sharaa ousted President Bashar al-Assad, ending five decades of his family's brutal rule and more than 13 years of a devastating civil war.
Catapulted to the presidency, Sharaa has, since then, led Syria's transition and efforts to revive a broken economy after a long period of mismanagement, isolation and conflict.

There was never any doubt about how challenging this would be. But as they celebrated Assad's overthrow and their new freedoms, Syrians, perhaps unrealistically, hoped things would quickly improve. That, however, has not materialised, and the handling of the economy has frustrated many here.
From essential bills to basic items, the cost of virtually everything has gone up. And many saw a further and unexpected rise in fuel prices as a sign of a government out of touch with its country.
"We don't want roundabouts. Every day they build a new roundabout. People stood by you and are still with you," another protester said, addressing Sharaa, "but this will [make] things explode".
Days later, amid calls for further demonstrations, the increase was revoked.
In a suburb of Damascus, I joined Fatima Saleh Eid at an open-air market for her weekly shop. At 50, she works as a cleaner to help support her family.

"We've suffered a lot," she said. Her husband had recently been hired by a ceramic factory after a year unemployed. He is among the lucky ones, as many are struggling to find work. In some streets, men gather in the hope of meeting someone offering a day job; often, they wait in vain.

Since coming to power, the government has slashed long-held subsidies as part of an austerity drive. The price of bread, a Syrian staple, has increased tenfold. Fuel prices are now in line with the international average, which has put pressure on farmers and made transportation more expensive, while the cost of electricity has gone up several hundred per cent for some.
The authorities, in response, have adjusted public sector wages, including pensions; unsurprisingly, the effect of the additional pay for people has been lost as prices keep rising.
"We eat more sparingly now. We can't afford chicken anymore nor meat. We only eat vegetables but even [that is] expensive," Fatima said. "Inshallah [God willing] things will get cheaper."

As she spoke, around a dozen people, of all ages, gathered around us. Nobody disagreed. One elderly man also said he had stopped eating meat. Another, in his 20s, told me his family were no longer able to pay the medicine for his father, who had a heart condition. One young woman said she and her four children could only afford to have a proper meal every two days.
Marwan Bashour, a 68-year-old pensioner, said his monthly pay was around $90 (£70), which is the public sector minimum wage. "It's not enough at all," he said.
The United Nations Development Programme said 90% of Syrians were in poverty last year.
"Sometimes I borrow money, sometimes I sell things from my house," he said, "like an old pot or plates that we never used, gifts that were given to us. I've even had to sell furniture".

There have been other pressures too. Like many Syrians, Marwan used to rely on help from aid agencies. But, for him, that has stopped, as organisations have been forced to cut back services because of funding cuts.
Sharaa has, of course, scored some important gains.
International sanctions imposed in the Assad-era have been lifted, and the US has removed the country from its list of state sponsors of terrorism.
Security remains volatile and a source of concern, but the country feels more stable.

And the president continues to consolidate his power and, earlier this year, retook the resource-rich north-east from a Kurdish-led militia. (The Druze still control areas in the south, where they want to create an autonomous state; Israel occupies parts of the south-west.)
But real economic recovery is yet to happen. Large parts of Syria remain in ruins after a war that killed half a million people and displaced half of the population.

Unable to afford rent, many families live in partially destroyed buildings. The World Bank says reconstruction costs are estimated at $216bn and, without foreign help and investment, it will be impossible for Syrians to rebuild.

Samir Aita, a Syrian economist who heads the Circle of Arab Economists, a Paris-based independent think-tank, said the crisis was a "combination of policies with the [government] not managing expectations and creating unrealistic hopes".
When I asked him about how he felt about the future, he said: "It's unsustainable. If they don't change, I fear chaos."
Exhausted after years of conflict, Syrians, left with almost no choice, remain hopeful.
Abu Mahmoud, a cab driver, told me: "They inherited the country bankrupt, so people need to be patient. Things don't happen overnight."
Additional reporting by Lana Antaki, Samantha Granville and Neha Sharma

items.title: Al-Jawad Pike refreshes Aesop store with terracotta-tiled counter evoking ancient Persia
paragraphs: Local studio Al-Jawad Pike has given skincare brand Aesop’s shop in London department store Harrods a revamp, centred on a terracotta-clad counter designed to have “the qualities of a miniature building”.

Aesop has had a counter in Harrods for over a decade. For this revamp, Al-Jawad Pike, which is a long-term collaborator of Aesop’s, aimed to take the design further than a regular beauty-brand counter.

“We were interested in giving the counter the qualities of a miniature building, with suggestions of apertures, openings and floor levels: something designed with the architectural ambition of a building but the care of a cabinet,” Al-Jawad Pike co-founder Jessam Al-Jawad told Dezeen.
“Through carved alcoves we also wanted to recall the architecture of ancient Persia – the highly literate civilisation that developed liquid perfumery.”
The studio drew on Harrods’ easily recognisable red brick facade when designing the central counter, which is clad in terracotta tiles from Italy that were chosen for their ability to hold scents.

“We chose glazed terracotta early on in the process because of its connection to traditional fragrance production, but also because of its strong association with Harrods’ iconic facade,” Al-Jawad explained.
The counter is decorated with an alchemist-style design piece, described by Aesop as an “olfactory sculpture.”
Glass vessels filled with fragrances hang from a copper stand, with copper cones that let visitors experience the different scents.
“The olfactory sculpture is something that Aesop has been independently developing in different forms across a number of their projects,” Al-Jawad Pike explained.
“Our take on this was to create a delicate but organised structure of copper piping and blown glass, through which fragrance-infused air is pushed to scent funnels for customers to interact with.”
The colour palette of the Aesop store complements the monolithic terracotta counter, with brushed copper brought in as a tactile contrast.
“The colour palette was chosen in collaboration with the team at Aesop for its intensity and richness, which we felt resonated with the olfactory experience of fragrance,” Al-Jawad said.
“We paired this with matte, brushed copper because of its connection to fragrance creation and distillation.”

Earlier this year, Aesop launched its first lighting collection at Milan design week. Previous Aesop stores featured on Dezeen include a Barcelona shop by Mesura that won the 2024 Dezeen Award for best interior.

items.title: The Dunu Vitruvian promises DaVinci’s JM-1 warmth, trading low end for top-end sparkle
paragraphs: Earphone manufacturer Dunu has just released the DaVinci Vitruvian, a follow-up to one of the most talked-about in-ear monitors (IEMs) of recent years. For the same price as the original ($299.99), it promises a cleaner, more balanced take on the DaVinci sound, and I for one am excited to hear it.

The DaVinci was one of the early high-profile IEMs associated with the JM-1 target and the “New Meta” tuning trend. In terms a normal human can understand, that means a broadly balanced sound, with a generous dollop of extra bass and a relatively relaxed treble. In practice, many people loved its warm, full-bodied sound, but others found the bass overdone and the treble a little too subdued. Still, some of the best representatives of this sound are featured on my list of the best IEMs under $500 for a reason. You'll also find them on my list of the best budget IEMs too.

On paper, the Vitruvian looks like Dunu’s answer to those critics, and suggests the brand is moving in the same direction as much of the industry: towards a more natural, neutral sound. Let's dig into what we can expect...
Interestingly, Vitruvian started life as the DaVinci 2, and the first prototype essentially turned everything up: the same big bass, extra treble drivers and even a bone-conduction driver.
But then, in response to feedback at the Shenzhen International Audio Show, the brand changed tack. Consequently, it reduced the bass, boosted vocal clarity and dropped the bone-conduction driver.

The new name – inspired by Leonardo da Vinci's Vitruvian Man; a naked male figure in two overlapping poses – reflects that shift towards balance. The design pairs two dynamic drivers, one for deep sub-bass and one for bass, with five balanced armatures handling mids and treble.

That’s one more than the DaVinci, and Dunu says the extra treble driver brings smooth, open highs with more air and no harshness. It also promises the bass hits harder and faster than before, even though there’s less of it.
In the box, you get a modular cable with swappable 3.5mm and 4.4mm plugs and 13 pairs of ear tips. The earpieces themselves sport vintage-inspired faceplates with precision gear details.
For years, the Harman target, with its boosted bass and bright upper mids, has shaped how most headphones and IEMs sound. Lately, though, brands seem to be going for something more natural.

Sennheiser’s HD 480 Pro is a great example. In our review, we called them the best closed-back headphones we’ve heard due to their neutral, balanced sound, with just a touch of bass warmth. As for IEMs, the CrinEar Reference tops our guide to the best IEMs under $500 thanks to its balanced tuning.

The Vitruvian probably won't go that far: Dunu talks up its “enveloping warmth” and “deep bass presence”, making it sound more like a nudge towards neutral than a leap. That said, for anyone who found the DaVinci’s low end overwhelming, that nudge could make all the difference.

Tom May is an award-winning journalist specialising in art, design, photography and technology. He is the author of the books The 50 Greatest Designers (Arcturus) and Great TED Talks: Creativity (Pavilion). Tom was previously editor of Professional Photography magazine, associate editor at Creative Bloq, and deputy editor at net magazine.

items.title: Gruffalo illustrator considering legal action against AI firms
paragraphs: The Gruffalo has been a staple of children's bookshelves since 1999

The illustrator behind the popular children's book The Gruffalo has told BBC London he is "seriously considering" launching legal action against artificial intelligence (AI) firms he says breach copyright in reproducing his work.
Axel Scheffler, whose illustrations have captivated children since 1999, said he wanted AI companies to stop using artists' work without permission.
The Gruffalo, written by London-born children's author Julia Donaldson, tells the story of a mouse who outsmarts a beast.
"I've been in touch with a lawyer in Germany," Scheffler said.
"There have been illustrators taking legal action against AI companies and I'm seriously considering it. I just want them to stop."
The south London-based artist did not name a company his legal team would consider pursuing.
AI firms have previously argued that using copyrighted material to train their models does not necessarily constitute copyright infringement.
Axel Scheffler says he wants better protection for creative works

Scheffler, who does not own a smartphone, said he tried to ignore AI until someone showed him how his most famous creations had been digitally recreated in locations such as Silicon Valley and Oktoberfest.
"I was quite shocked. It's clearly my mouse, my Gruffalo, as close as they can do it, but the rest of the image is completely created - it's a clear theft of copyright," he told the BBC.
Scheffler is considering launching the legal action in Germany because he believes the European Union is more creator-friendly.
Nick Buckland, an intellectual property lawyer at London firm Lewis Silkin, agreed that Germany could offer a route for creators seeking to protect their work.

"There have been two cases in Germany where music collecting societies have been able to win against AI companies by showing that those AI companies have copied lyrics of songs verbatim and have presented them," he told the BBC.
But proving copyright infringement could be difficult, he said.
While having a distinctive character such as the Gruffalo could help Scheffler's case, he would need to establish that his copyright had been infringed.
"Generative AI doesn't copy, it trains," Buckland explained.
"This is what AI companies say means that they're not infringing someone's copyright.
"For example, if someone wants a picture of a dog, what the AI machine does is it scans everything it's trained on, millions of pictures of dogs, and then one gets presented to the user."
Nick Buckland said proving copyright infringement would not be straightforward
OpenAI, the company behind ChatGPT, is already being sued by German publishing group Penguin Random House, together with author and illustrator Ingo Siegner.
The allegation is that OpenAI copied the children's book character The Little Dragon Coconut (Der kleine Drache Kokosnuss)
Whether the AI company has breached copyright law will be decided by the Munich Regional Court in spring 2027.

Carina Mathern, children's and young adult books publisher and member of the management board of Penguin Random House publishing group, said: "Through this lawsuit, we... want to help ensure that copyright remains effectively protected in the age of artificial intelligence and that fair conditions are secured for creative professionals."

An OpenAI spokesperson said: "We're having productive conversations with rightsholders around the world about supporting creativity, including fan art, while protecting intellectual property and taking appropriate action in response to copyright complaints."
The California-based firm said its models were trained in various sources and that copyright holders could submit disputes directly with them.
Penguin Random House is suing OpenAI over AI created-images of Coconut the Little Dragon, like this example on the left. The original cover is on the right
For Scheffler, the issue goes beyond the work of an established illustrator whose Gruffalo books have sold more than 18 million copies worldwide.
He said any legal action would not be about compensation, but about protecting creators now and in the future.
Other artists also fear the possible impact of AI on their livelihoods.
Ivy Deng, who is doing a master's degree in painting at the Royal College of Art, said: "In terms of regulations, I don't feel protected about the fair use of my art."

"In terms of the art industry and the people who support art, I have faith that they understand that there is a difference between the process and the perspiration behind developing an art practice and creating something by hand and replicating something in one moment," she added.
Ivy Deng says she has faith people will see the value of human-produced art
Prof James Coupe, head of the college's Artificial Intelligence & Digital Art programme, welcomed Scheffler's contribution to the debate.

"We tend to frame this debate as a choice between embracing AI and rejecting it, but that misses the more important question of who gets to shape these technologies and whose interests they serve," he said.

"Art has a vital role here, not because artists should become technology developers, but because artistic practice should challenge the assumptions, values and forms of power that technology often asks us to take for granted."
Last June, the UK government announced £2bn of investment in AI by 2030 "to harness the transformative potential".
Buckland said the government needed to strike a balance between protecting creative industries and allowing AI to develop.
"It seems pretty clear that in order for the AI investment to be maximised, you need to open those floodgates," he said.
"The government has a difficult choice to make. It's trying to find a middle ground."
Scheffler encouraged artists to continue "drawing by hand and being old-fashioned"
The government said it did not accept that backing the creative industries and supporting the AI sector were mutually exclusive.
A Department for Culture, Media and Sport spokesperson said: "We have engaged extensively with creatives, AI firms, industry bodies, unions, academics and AI adopters.
"Copyright laws must protect the UK's position as a creative powerhouse while unlocking the extraordinary potential of AI-driven innovation to grow the economy and improve British lives."
Even so, Scheffler and his publishers are still discussing the possibility of legal action in his native Germany.
For the illustrator, the value of the work itself remains central to the debate.
"AI can never replace the hand-drawn image," he said.
"There's always something lacking. I recommend drawing by hand and being old-fashioned, and hopefully that will be more appreciated when AI takes over."
Listen to the best of BBC Radio London on Sounds and follow BBC London on Facebook, external, X, external and Instagram, external. Send your story ideas to hello.bbclondon@bbc.co.uk, external

items.title: Former Sydney childcare worker Ashley Paul Griffith hit with 202 more abuse charges
paragraphs: One of Australia’s most notorious paedophiles is facing hundreds more child abuse charges, including for the alleged rape of children as young as one.

Days after being extradited from Queensland to New South Wales, Ashley Paul Griffith was hit with 202 charges dating from between 2014 and 2017, with police labelling the allegations “deeply disturbing”.
The Queensland man was working at a childcare centre in Sydney’s inner west at the time of the alleged offending, which included dozens of alleged rapes against children between one and five.
Griffith, 48, was jailed for life in Queensland in November 2024 after he pleaded guilty to more than 300 child sexual offences against nearly 70 victims.
The fresh charges from NSW include 68 counts of rape of a child aged less than 10 and 42 counts of aggravated rape of a child aged less than 10 who was under his authority.
Other charges include 69 counts of aggravated indecent assault and 23 charges of producing child abuse material.
Police said the charges pertained to 23 alleged victims aged between one and five.
He was charged while being held in Silverwater Correctional Complex in Sydney.
NSW Det Supt Linda Howlett said charging Griffith with further alleged offending could help potential victims.
“There’s no other word for it, it’s actually horrific,” she said in relation to the allegations.
The child abuse squad commander thanked witnesses, alleged victims and detectives for their work in preparing the challenging but “airtight” case.
Police are extending every assistance to those involved, Howlett said.
Griffith did not apply for bail in a brief court appearance on Friday.
The NSW police assistant commissioner Brett Greentree said the lengthy investigation included collaboration with police across the nation.
“The allegations before the court are deeply disturbing and involve some of the most vulnerable members of our community,” he said.

“Every child deserves to be safe and protected from harm. NSW Police is committed to ensuring those who exploit positions of trust to offend against children are identified, investigated and brought before the courts.”
In Queensland, he admitted to assaulting and filming young girls over the course of years while working at childcare centres.
His transfer was approved by a Brisbane magistrate earlier in the month, where the alleged victims’ supporters yelled insults at the rapist as he stood in the dock for the decision.

In Australia, children, young adults, parents and teachers can contact the Kids helpline on 1800 55 1800, or Bravehearts on 1800 272 831, and adult survivors can contact Blue Knot Foundation on 1300 657 380. Other international helplines can be found at befrienders.org

items.title: Crypto exchange Binance freezes billions in funds amid potential $6.3bn security breach
paragraphs: The world’s largest cryptocurrency exchange has been hit by an industry-record $6.3bn (£4.6bn) hack, with experts identifying North Korea as the likely culprit.

Binance has scrambled to freeze the affected assets, with about $3bn located so far. The company gave no update on the other $3.3bn as Binance’s co-founder Yi He said the company would cover “all hacking losses”.

Analysts attributed the attack to North Korean state-backed hackers. North Korea has a history of crypto hacking and was behind the theft of approximately $1.5bn in virtual assets from a Tokyo cryptocurrency exchange last year, according to the FBI, in what was the previous record crypto heist.

TRM, a crypto analysis firm, blamed the attack with “high confidence” on TraderTraitor, North Korea’s elite hacking unit. Chainalysis, another analysis outfit, also attributed the heist to TraderTraitor.

Binance did not explicitly confirm that funds had been stolen, although TRM and Chainalysis claimed more than $6bn had been taken. The company said its teams were “working around the clock” to resolve the problem.

An initial investigation suggested the breach may have started with a hacked laptop belonging to one of its engineers, which let an attacker gain access to one of its systems and ⁠make unauthorised withdrawals, Binance said.
Binance, which allows users to buy, sell and trade digital assets, has 335 million registered users globally and had about $162.8bn in assets under custody as of the exchange’s 2025 annual report.
“Bottom line - your money is safe, and we’re covering every loss,” said Richard Teng, the co-chief executive of Binance.

The company said in a statement: “As a precaution, all deposits and withdrawals are temporarily suspended while our security teams conduct checks, secure wallet infrastructure, and trace affected assets, with the close support of our law enforcement and industry partners.”

Markets reacted immediately in early Asian trading on Friday, and bitcoin – the most popular crypto asset by far - dropped more than 3% to a six-week low of $76,368. Shares in the crypto exchange Coinbase Global slid 4.8%, while those of the bitcoin buyer Strategy fell nearly 6% in extended US trading.

Binance was founded in 2017 by Changpeng Zhao, who in 2023 pleaded guilty to a felony related to his failure to prevent money laundering on the platform and stepped down as CEO. Donald Trump pardoned him in 2025.

Zhao posted to X on Thursday that “User funds are safe!” but added that the incident “does look like a hack on Binance”. He added that while he doesn’t manage Binance any more, “as a shareholder, I expect all user funds will be fully covered”.

If confirmed, the incident could be the world’s biggest crypto ​heist, according to Chainalysis and other industry experts. “It’s the biggest hack in history,” said Aravind ‌Srinivasan, the head of the large crypto market maker GSR’s systematic ‌OTC business.

Beyond the potential loss of assets, the security breach was likely to have wider ramifications for crypto, which had already been under pressure lately because of higher US interest rates and softer demand from ‌exchange-traded fund buyers, analysts said.

“It may further dampen risk appetite and prompt investors to reassess the safety of assets held on centralised exchanges, as well as counterparty, solvency and liquidity risks,” said Tim Sun, a senior researcher at HashKey Group, based in Hong Kong.
Binance runs a secure asset fund for users, which is a reserve held entirely in ‌bitcoin that is intended to protect user assets in cases of security breaches, according to its website.

“It’s becoming very hard to counter hacks as AI can find vulnerabilities faster than you can fix them,” said Bernardo Brites, the CEO of Trace Finance, a payments and stablecoin infrastructure company.
“My view is that users will move away from smaller ​and medium-sized exchanges, [as it is] becoming too risky to park your money somewhere that couldn’t cover a hack of meaningful size.”
The stablecoin issuer Tether said it had frozen nearly $1.57bn in assets linked to the incident, while Circle froze more than $800m.

World Liberty Financial, a crypto company linked to Trump and his family, said on Thursday it had worked with the cryptocurrency custodian BitGo to freeze funds stolen in what it described as a Binance hack. Binance’s Yi said $27m in stablecoins and about $2m worth of World Liberty tokens had been frozen.

The incident adds to a string of crypto thefts. Last year attackers stole $2.9bn worth of cryptocurrency across nearly 150 attacks, according to researchers ​at TRM Labs. In September the cryptocurrency exchange Bitget ‌said roughly $350m in crypto had ​been stolen from its platform, underscoring the industry’s vulnerability ​to hackers.
Authorities have warned that organised crime groups are increasingly using cryptocurrencies to move funds across borders outside the traditional financial system.
Binance.US, a separate cryptocurrency exchange, said it was not affected by the security incident.
Coinbase said it was unaffected and was monitoring the situation.

In an unrelated incident earlier on Thursday, prediction market operator Polymarket temporarily halted trading after a security incident involving a third-party provider. It later resumed trading and said it would fully reimburse affected traders.

items.title: Electrocutions, disease and no pay: how workers risk exploitation in Europe’s datacentres
paragraphs: Sandu* checked his watch. He was winding down the last 15 minutes of his shift at a vast Google datacentre site in Saint-Ghislain, Belgium, in March, when the call came in. The 34-year-old electrical tester had already worked almost 10 hours, but says such last-minute jobs were normal: “I had no choice. People have been fired after saying no.”

The task was one Sandu had done many times before and involved a series of tests measuring the safety and integrity of the electrical wiring. A protective suit was locked away in an equipment room. The round trip would have added another 15 minutes to the job, he says, and people were waiting, so he decided not to retrieve the suit.

Once in the voltage room, Sandu says the managers confirmed the lines had been de-energised. In the first round, everything went as planned. Then, on the second test, while holding insulated tongs, he linked the cables. But this time, the lines were live.

The blast was immediate and catastrophic. In milliseconds, 400 volts and 12,000 amps hit Sandu’s face and across the right side of his body. “I went completely blind,” he says. When doctors received him in the Grand Hôpital de Charleroi, he says he was placed in an induced coma for five days.

Hospital records seen by the Guardian and Investigate Europe show that the arc flash electrocution had burned 12% of Sandu’s body, with second-degree burns to the face and neck, as well as third-degree burns across his right shoulder and fingers.

When Sandu woke from surgery in the intensive care unit a week later, his wife was at his bedside. He says his entire body felt like a “white-hot blister … It was so much pain. The human heart cannot comprehend it.”

Sandu says the regional director of Google, along with a representative from Dornan Engineering, an Irish company that oversaw his contractor, and his recruiter, came to visit. While he lay bandaged in the hospital bed, he says the Google director told him he was lucky to be alive.
To date, no company or contractor appears to have been found liable for the accident. The local labour inspectorate closed its investigation in late October and found no wrongdoing.

A spokesperson for Dornan Engineering said it was “committed to maintaining safe working conditions, complying with applicable labour laws and continually learning to help prevent incidents like this from happening again”.

Sandu’s electrocution appears brutal and harrowing, but far from unique, according to a five-month investigation by Investigate Europe and the Guardian into conditions for migrant workers on datacentre sites across Sweden, Norway, Belgium and the Netherlands.

Europe is in the midst of a datacentre boom, the largest infrastructure surge the continent has seen in decades, with more than 2,300 datacentres rapidly altering the physical and energy landscape of Europe (at least 500 of them in the UK) and hundreds more under construction.
But unions say the push for tech sovereignty in Europe is becoming increasingly reliant on the exploitation of migrant workers.
In dozens of interviews we found evidence of debilitating injuries, squalid living conditions, an unreported infectious outbreak, unpaid wages and exploitative employment practices.

In the UK, a general contractor died while working on a datacentre site last year, while another fatality was reported in 2024 at an electrical substation being built for a Microsoft datacentre. Serious accidents have also been recorded this year at projects in Italy, Sweden, Norway and Belgium, and exploitative labour practices have been found at projects around the world, including in Brazil.

On the outskirts of Gävle, a city two hours north of Stockholm, past timber-framed cottages and dense pine forests, lies a smooth road leading to one such site. The remote clearing is part of a 130-hectare, €3bn expansion plan begun in June 2024 to scale up Microsoft’s AI datacentre infrastructure.
One subcontractor at the site is the Irish-owned construction company BenBau. It is among 148 firms working under Collen Construction at the Gävle site, including 28 direct subcontractors.

For months, there has been a growing sense of outrage among Adrian*, 45, and his colleagues working for BenBau on the Microsoft site. They showed evidence of crowded living quarters – 24 people to a kitchen, 14 men to a single bathroom – and say they have reported vermin infestations, broken ventilation systems and lack of heating during the sub-zero Swedish winters, but the problems remain.

Such conditions can make the transmission of disease more likely. In February this year, one Romanian worker tested positive for active tuberculosis, medical records show. Shortly after, others living in the same shared housing showed similar symptoms. BenBau initially informed only a few men who shared close quarters with the infected worker and then told the men that testing was optional, according to workers. After the first worker who contracted the disease had left for hospital, Benbau moved another worker into his bedroom.
Freedom of information requests made to Sweden’s national work authorities and its Public Health Agency say no outbreak had been reported.

The living and working conditions form only part of the story. More than 30 workers have shown hundreds of payslips to the Guardian and Investigate Europe that appear to show some of them working up to 50 or 60 hours a week with no overtime pay and missed holiday pay. With many foreign workers unfamiliar with the laws, unions say inequity can arise quickly.

Days before publication of this investigation, the union Solidariska Byggare, representing the 70 Romanian workers at Microsoft’s site in Gävle, brokered a settlement with BenBau, which it says will give workers back pay and allow unions access to sites.

A spokesperson for BenBau said the company “takes all concerns regarding the welfare, health and safety of our people extremely seriously” and has “stringent procedures for reporting, investigating and addressing workplace concerns”.

Since 2021, Sweden’s Work Environment Authority (AV) has opened 50 cases into working conditions at datacentre sites involving Microsoft and a number of Irish firms, according to a freedom of information request.

Earlier this month, a contractor fell through a roof hatch while carrying out maintenance work on a ventilation system at the Microsoft site in Gävle, according to freedom of information request to AV.

In October 2021, a forklift allegedly ran over the foot of a supervisor working for Collen at the site. The worker subsequently needed surgery. An incident report submitted by Collen to work authorities says that the wrong machine had been used, the driver had no formal certificate for it and the lift plan was incomplete. Still, it had been signed off. The Work Environment Authority saw no grounds to report the employer to prosecutors.

A spokesperson for Collen said: “We are committed to ensuring that every Collen site is a safe, healthy and respectful place to work, where everyone is treated with dignity and their fundamental human rights are protected. We expect the same throughout our supply chain and have zero tolerance for any conduct inconsistent with these principles.

“Our projects are subject to rigorous compliance with our own mandatory policies and procedures, our clients’ requirements, all applicable laws and regulations, and recognised industry standards in every jurisdiction in which we operate.”

A similar pattern is found throughout Europe, says James McCabe from Unite the Union, an Irish-UK group representing more than 1.2 million workers. “Everywhere we’ve encountered Irish datacentre contractors at tech-giant datacentre sites we’ve learned of lack of normal and meaningful union access … as well as serious concerns of labour crimes and exploitation of workers,” he says.

Johan Danielsson, a European parliament rapporteur in charge of regulating subcontracting chains, says: “If people let these big American multinationals come here and import their anti-union business models, then it becomes a problem. Because behind the fence they are abusing workers, and they don’t want anyone to know it.”

A spokesperson for Google said: “Our supplier code of conduct and contracts require all suppliers to comply with local labour laws and uphold safe, healthy working conditions. We maintain active dialogue with union leaders and trade groups, and are committed to providing transparent information about our workplace.”

A spokesperson for Microsoft said: “In our datacentre construction, we work with contractors and suppliers, with whom we set clear requirements on health and safety, working conditions, and the freedom of association and right to collective bargaining. To ensure our contractors’ compliance with Microsoft’s human rights and fair labour policies, we have robust processes in place, including audits.”

This investigation is led by Investigate Europe, a cross-border team of investigative journalists: Lorenzo Buzzoni, Jan Daalder, Pascal Hansens, Ella Joyner, Chris Matthews, Nico Schmidt and Astri Thunold.

items.title: Sinkholes, scarred land and scapegoats: the scourge of illegal gold mining in Johannesburg
paragraphs: Cora Bailey has been encountering illegal miners ever since she first started treating injured animals in the townships around Roodepoort, west of Johannesburg, in 1991. But as the price of gold has soared, so too has activity in the abandoned mine shafts that mark the area.

In late September, dozens of zama zamas – the name given to illegal miners in South Africa, meaning roughly “to take a chance” in Zulu – arrived to dig for gold across the dirt road from her charity, Claw (Community Led Animal Welfare).

Soon, they were taking water for their panning and processing from the organisation’s two 25,000-litre water tanks, which are filled irregularly by the city government for the 100 or so rescued and injured animals on site.

“We’ve asked them really nicely and haven’t ever refused them water to drink … But, for the first time ever, we closed the gate at 12 [midday], because we literally had about two buckets of water left,” Bailey said in mid-October.

Police told her that the scale of the illegal mining was too big for them to do anything about, she said at the time. About a week later, officers sheared away the grass that had partly hidden the zama zamas. But within a few days a smaller group had returned, although Bailey said they were now taking Claw’s water only for drinking.
South Africa’s police regularly trumpet their success in tackling illegal mining. On 19 October, they said they had arrested 71 suspected zama zamas across the country in the previous week.

However, researchers put the number of illegal miners in the tens of thousands. In 2019, Marcena Hunter, a researcher at the Global Initiative against Transnational Organised Crime, estimated that a tenth of South Africa’s gold production, worth about $1bn, was being exported illegally.
Police operations have also led to tragedy. In 2025, 93 bodies were pulled from a mine shaft in Stilfontein, after officers blocked food and water from being delivered underground.

Meanwhile, there is no end in sight to the dynamics driving illegal mining, including the high price of gold, poverty, unemployment, corrupt politicians and police profiting, and the failure of mining companies to fulfil their legal obligation to seal mining shafts when they cease operating.

South Africa’s modern history is tied to mining. In 1884, gold was found on a farm, sparking a gold rush that led to the creation of Johannesburg. Gold production peaked in the 1970s, but South Africa was the world’s largest producer, a title it held for more than a century, until 2007.

In 2009, Morris Viljoen, a geology professor at the University of the Witwatersrand, estimated that the reef that gave the university its name had produced more than a third of the gold ever mined globally. Claw is housed in the old offices of the Durban Deep mine, which shut at the turn of the century, having once lent its name to an Elton John song.
The city government claims there is still 40,000 tonnes of gold underground in the region. But, with the remainder lying ever deeper, the costs of recovering it have risen.

Mining companies are supposed to seal up old mine shafts and rehabilitate the environment around them. However, in 2025 there were “6,100 derelict and ownerless mines and 1,170 unsafe mine openings”, the mining minister, Gwede Mantashe, said in response to a parliamentary question.

Zama zamas have stepped into those voids left in the earth. While there is no comprehensive data on them, experts agree that a majority are from neighbouring countries, principally Lesotho, Mozambique and Zimbabwe.
The skyline south of Johannesburg is punctuated by the pale yellow ridges of mine dumps. Increasingly, the ground is also caving open.

For politicians seeking votes in local elections on 4 November, the culprit is clear: illegal miners. In May, Kenny Kunene, the Johannesburg council member responsible for transport, took journalists on a tour of sinkholes that he claimed were the fault of zama zamas, including a section of Wemmer Pan Road that had completely collapsed.

The road was once the main artery linking the city’s central business district to the south-eastern suburbs. In one section it has completely disappeared, now raw earth pitted with the holes where illegal miners have been digging.
However, when it comes to sinkholes, experts say zama zamas are being scapegoated.

Rosalind Morris, an anthropology professor at Columbia University, who has worked extensively with illegal miners, noted that the porous dolomitic rock to Johannesburg’s south and west becomes unstable when water is removed.
“The biggest culprit of sinkholes in South Africa is formal industrial mining, which dewaters at a scale of hundreds of millions of gallons of water removed from underground every day,” she said.

“There are areas where there is a lot of residual gold, which are being very intensely mined by zama zamas, and some of that definitely causes structural collapse, there’s no doubt about it. But the idea that this was invented or caused for the first time by zama zamas is completely fallacious.”

Zama zamas are also frequently blamed for violence in mining areas, including a September mass shooting in Wedela township, west of Johannesburg. However, David van Wyk, the lead researcher at Bench Marks Foundation, said culpability laid with the often-feuding gangs that controlled access to the shafts.
“The guys working in the mine are actually super-exploited cheap labour … The guys with the guns are the guys who take the gold,” he said. “They don’t go underground.”

In Khutsong, about 50 miles (80km) west of Johannesburg, illegal miners, local and foreign, kept the township afloat, said Vusi Cele, the youth secretary for the local branch of Mining Affected Communities United in Action, a campaign group that advocates for “artisanal miners” to be granted mining licences. “Without those rents, it’s a ghost town,” he said.

While Cele, 33, currently hustles above ground selling mobile phone covers and screen protectors, he said he too would mine if he could get a licence. “On the surface there’s peanuts,” he said. “Underground there’s money.”

items.title: Sudanese diaspora and human rights groups denounce UAE nominee for UN top job
paragraphs: Members of the Sudanese diaspora and international human rights monitors have denounced the candidature of an Emirati diplomat for the top job at the UN, citing her denial of accusations that the United Arab Emirates is fuelling the war in Sudan by supporting the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces.
The UAE nominated Lana Nusseibeh last week to replace the UN secretary general, António Guterres, as he finishes his second five-year term ⁠this year, upending a race that had become gridlocked.

Rights groups and others have for years documented evidence of UAE support for the RSF, which has been accused of atrocities during the course of its war against the Sudanese army, including an attack on the city of El Fasher in October 2025 that the UN said had “hallmarks of genocide”.
Nusseibeh, the UAE’s representative to the UN until 2024, has repeatedly reflected the UAE’s blanket denials of the accusations.

The Sudanese pro-democracy and women’s rights activist Hala al-Karib, the regional director of the Strategic Initiative for Women in the Horn of Africa, said Nusseibeh had “no track record of acting independently of her country’s role in Sudan” and that endorsement by the security council would amount “essentially [to] a denial of the genocidal acts committed in El Fasher by the RSF”.
There was also strong criticism of Nusseibeh’s candidature at a virtual briefing by the Avaaz human rights advocacy group on Tuesday.

Ibrahim Alduma, who grew up in El Fasher and is the co-founder of the human rights organisation Sudan Action Hub, told the briefing that success for Nusseibeh would result in people losing faith in the UN.

“If this candidate [succeeds], how would we tell people on the ground that the United Nations is not an obstruction of the [rights of] the people of Sudan?” said Alduma. “How could the people – not only in Sudan, but other victims of wars and international criminals – trust that the UN will achieve some kind of justice?”

Husam Mahjoub, a Sudanese advocate and co-founder of independent media Sudan Bukra TV, said: “Electing [the UAE’s] senior diplomat as secretary general would hand leadership of (UN) institutions to that government’s chief defender, at the very moment Sudanese civilians most need the ‌UN to hold powerful states accountable.”

Kenneth Roth, a former executive director of Human Rights Watch, told the briefing: “She has been asked about the UAE’s role in arming and supporting the RSF, and she just blatantly denies it without regard to the facts. That is not what we need as UN secretary-general.”

On Wednesday, Bruno Stagno Ugarte, the chief advocacy officer at Human Rights Watch, said Nusseibeh’s dismissal of UN reports documenting the UAE’s links to the RSF had “seriously undermined justice and accountability for the victims”.

In a statement on Tuesday Nusseibeh said that if she got the top UN job she would support the work of UN fact-finding missions for accountability and transitional justice over the war in Sudan, and described the RSF’s crimes as “atrocious”.

She added that she had taken a leave of absence from her ministerial post in the UAE government to be “mindful of the obligations of independence” the UN role would entail, adding that “the horrific conflict in Sudan will be the litmus test of the success of an incoming secretary general”.

To become the next UN security general, a candidate must secure a minimum of nine affirmative votes out of the 15 security council members, and avoid a veto from the US, the UK, China, France or Russia, its permanent members.

An ​informal security council poll earlier his month had ‌placed the former Costa Rican vice-president ​Rebeca Grynspan as the narrow frontrunner in ​the race. But she and all other candidates received two or more opposing votes from the permanent council members. The next straw poll could take place as soon as Friday, but the format and exact timing are still being negotiated by the diplomats.

At Tuesday’s briefing, Roth said: “It’s fair to say the RSF would not have been able to be nearly as successful militarily as it was and has been without that support from the UAE. And with that support, it didn’t just fight the Sudan armed forces. This wasn’t just a civil war. It committed mass atrocities.”
He added: “It amazes me that she’s being put forward. This is a completely unsuitable candidate.”

Kate Ferguson, co-founder and co-executive director of Protection Approaches, a charity working to prevent identity-based violence, said at the briefing: “There is not, as far as I have seen, sufficient evidence that this candidate is independent from the state from which she comes. And we must not be naive nor hide behind the pretence of naivety.
“This is autocratic capture of our most significant multilateral institution.”

items.title: Lighting design a "strategic economic investment" says Signify's Sameer Sodhi
paragraphs: According to business leader of entertainment and colour kinetics at lighting brand Signify, Sameer Sodhi, lit-up architecture and public installations can encourage interaction, strengthen local identity and support overall wellbeing.

Sodhi explained that for decades, the value of a building has been measured by appearance, energy performance, return on investment and construction costs. A building’s lighting design is one of the most influential factors but is often overlooked and seen as a “finishing touch”.
He added that well-designed lighting can shape the experience of places, support local economies and strengthen communities.
“The question is no longer whether lighting matters,” Sodhi said. “But whether we can accurately measure the (overlooked) value it creates.”

Sodhi points to a recent study by lighting brand Colour Kinetics that examined four illuminated spaces across the United States and found that lighting generated social, economic, and cultural benefits “well beyond the initial investment”.

“The report assesses lighting through a broader framework that includes community engagement, tourism, economic development, media visibility, partnerships, sustainability and health and wellbeing,” Sodhi explained.
“Rather than viewing lighting as an isolated building system, it recognised it as infrastructure capable of influencing how cities function and how communities connect,” he added.

Sodhi cites the lighting of Daniel Hoan Memorial Bridge in Milwaukee, Wisconsin, as an example, which has transformed the infrastructure into a “dynamic visual icon” that reflects the city’s identity and connects residents and visitors to the waterfront.
“The bridge now hosts community and civic events, causes and initiatives and annual festivals, while serving as a canvas for civic celebrations throughout the year,” he said.
According to Sodhi, architectural lighting also creates economic value. For example, the thoughtful lighting design of West Sacramento’s Barns in California has supported the area’s placemaking.

Although the venue was originally conceived as an event and dining venue, the strategic lighting design has helped establish it as the focal point for the surrounding mixed-use district, which includes spaces for hosting concerts, festivals, community activities and sporting events.

Sodhi explained that, because of the building’s lit-up impact, approximately ten residential developments have since been built or are under construction nearby, highlighting the role “quality public spaces” can play in wider regeneration.

“Importantly, the value created extends beyond construction economics,” added Sodhi. “Visitors stay longer, businesses benefit from increased footfall, and the location develops an identity that encourages repeat visits and investment.”

According to Sodhi, lighting can also serve as a form of public communication. For example, Philadelphia City Hall’s lighting is programmed to respond to national celebrations, charitable campaigns and civic events, “transforming a historic landmark into a dynamic expression of the city’s identity”.
“Whether celebrating sporting victories or marking important social causes, the building becomes an active participant in public life rather than simply a backdrop,” added Sodhi.

This also applies to Nashville’s illuminated installation, Loqui, Sodhi explained. The artwork includes words and stories from more than 400 local residents and demonstrates how illuminated public art can amplify local voices and bring a community together.
“Rather than lighting serving the artwork, the lighting becomes integral to the experience itself,” he added.
“These projects suggest that good lighting is no longer simply about visibility. It is about participation.”
Sodhi added that buildings are also assessed by how efficiently they operate, but also how effectively they create meaningful experiences.

“Architectural lighting is uniquely positioned to support that ambition,” he explained. “It can extend the usability of spaces after dark, strengthen local identity, encourage social interaction and help transform ordinary infrastructure into memorable landmarks.”

“When thoughtfully integrated from the earliest stages of design, lighting becomes a strategic investment rather than an aesthetic upgrade,” he added. “Perhaps this is the real measure of good design.”
