items.title: Sir Patrick Stewart: A life in pictures
paragraphs: Watch: The life of legendary actor Sir Patrick Stewart

Legendary actor Sir Patrick Stewart rose from humble beginnings in his native Yorkshire to become a global superstar whose work became immortalised portraying characters on some of the most popular sci-fi franchises in history.
Baby Patrick seen being held by his Aunt Dolly. He is seen with his mother (right) and brothers Trevor (left) and Geoff
He grew up poor, and later spoke to journalists about witnessing his mother being abused by his father.
Stewart (right) pictured with his brother Trevor and his mother, circa 1945
Young Patrick's love of drama came at school when one of his teachers introduced him to Shakespeare and encouraged him to perform.
Stewart played Launce for Robin Phillips' production of 'Two Gentlemen Of Verona' in London in 1970
He threw himself enthusiastically into the flourishing local theatre. "I used to recite Shakespeare from memory," he said. "I just learned all these big speeches."

He went on to star in countless Shakespeare plays. One of his earliest breakout roles was in 1970's Two Gentlemen of Verona, which also featured his rescue dog, Blackie, playing the role of the dog Crab.
Stewart played Sejanus in the 1976 BBC historical drama series I, Claudius
His expertise in Shakespeare led to play a major role in the 1976 BBC television series I, Claudius.
In 1981, he was featured in 1981 fantasy film Excalibur, bringing him one step closer to his future sci-fi career.
Stewart (far right) played Leondegrance in the film Excalibur
Sir Patrick has won numerous awards, including a Grammy and two Laurence Olivier Awards. He was also nominated for a Tony, along with multiple Golden Globes and Emmys over the years.
His iconic voice and facial expressions saw him star in both the Star Trek and X-Men franchises, helping to spawn a generation of global sci-fi fans.
Stewart played Jean-Luc Picard, the commanding officer of the Federation starship USS Enterprise, on Star Trek
In 1987, he took on the role of Jean-Luc Picard on popular TV series Star Trek: The Next Generation. Tapping into Star Trek fandom earned him millions of adoring fans around the world.
Star Trek: The Next Generation started airing in 1987 and spanned 178 episodes over seven seasons.
Sir Patrick starred in a 2008 Broadway performance of Shakespeare's Macbeth
Queen Elizabeth II knighted Sir Patrick at Buckingham Palace in 2010
Sir Patrick poses with his knighthood medal
His scores of sci-fi fans reached new heights with his starring role as Professor Charles Xavier in the X-Men film series, which began in 2000.
He reprised the role multiple times over decades through the Marvel Cinematic Universe, including in 2026 in Avengers: Doomsday.
Stewart gained scores of new fans with his portrayal of Professor X in X-Men
Stewart appeared alongside X-Men co-stars Hugh Jackman (left) and Ian McKellen (right)
Stewart continued to reprise his role even after X-Men was re-booted with a younger cast in a prequel series
Watch: "A big loss" - Fans react to death of Sir Patrick Stewart

items.title: Feral deer will become Australia’s next feral pig problem without prompt action, report warns
paragraphs: An unpublished government report on feral deer shows Australia is failing in its efforts to stop the spread of what one advocate warns could become “Australia’s next feral pig”.

The five years from 2020-2025 over which the national feral deer action plan was assessed covers a period in which the famously elusive species has increasingly encroached upon major cities, leading to more frequent encounters – including a memorable occasion in which two men in various degrees of undress were fined after becoming lost in the bush when they were spooked by deer while nude sunbathing.

The report says deer, one of the country’s “most rapidly increasing invasive pests”, have both increased in numbers and spread in territory, costing more than $91m in production loss and management time every year.
Deakin University’s Prof Euan Ritchie, president of the Australian Mammal Society, said he was “not at all” surprised by this year’s national vertebrate pest management report card.

“This report shows that governments are failing miserably to invest enough to control deer populations and the severe impacts that they can have on agriculture, native wildlife and the environment, road safety and culturally significant sites,” Ritchie said.
“This is what sustained failure to act sufficiently results in.”

Six species of feral deer are established in Australia – chital, fallow, hog, red, rusa and sambar – with well-established populations across south-eastern Australia, where densities are highest. There are smaller, more localised populations in South and Western Australia and the Northern Territory.

The report card, produced by the National Vertebrate Pest Coordinators, shows every state and territory is failing or floundering in their efforts to control feral deer – with one notable exception. South Australia, which launched an ambitious statewide eradication plan in 2022, received a green in all four categories assessed under the traffic light system of marking. The report showed – with high confidence – that the state had decreased the abundance, distribution and environmental and agricultural impacts of deer.
New South Wales and Tasmania were given reds in all four categories, while Queensland and the ACT both received three reds and a yellow. No jurisdiction but SA received a single green pass mark.

Invasive Species Council advocacy manager Reece Pianta said the report confirmed what land managers had been seeing on the ground for some years. In May 2025, the council released footage and images that it said showed the Gold Coast “under feral deer siege”.

Pianta said the report, leaked to his organisation, points to “a long-term systemic underfunding of deer control”. He said deer did not have the recognition of other more notorious invasives, but controlling them was every bit as necessary.
“Deer are the next feral pig,” he said. “The difference with deer is that an intervention now could make a significant difference to the population numbers and contain, or even reverse, that spread.”

While Pianta said deer “probably can’t be eradicated” from the entire continent, he said South Australia’s “A+” report score showed it was possible to do so in some states and territories, while others would require a long-term effort to contain the spread of deer and mitigate their impacts.
Adelaide University Environment Institute director Prof Andrew Lowe said the report was a “good news story” for his state that rang true with what he was seeing on the ground.

Lowe, who is also member of the Hills and Fleurieu Landscape Board, which is involved in managing deer, said SA grappled with its “massive problem with deer” in earnest from 2022, after an agricultural impact estimate showed the $36m worth of damage done every year by deer there was set to increase to $241m by 2031.

But although deer had “massively declined” in the few years since a $4m eradication program began, Lowe said deer were seeking refuge on the fringes of urban areas, where culling was more expensive. He said functional eradication of deer from SA would take about another $10m over 10 years.
The cost of inaction, though, was of a different magnitude.
“If we don’t do that, then the population will go up again and we’re going to be in the same situation,” Lowe said. “So $10m versus $240m – do the math.”

items.title: China expels a record number from Communist party amid Xi’s intensified purges of top officials
paragraphs: China expelled a record number of officials from the Chinese Communist party (CCP) as it concluded a major political gathering, which saw an unprecedented number of empty seats indicating the scale of the purges under Xi Jinping.
A record 33 members were expelled at this week’s fifth plenum, a gathering of top officials that takes place roughly once a year.

Just 279 of the full and alternate members of the CCP’s Central Committee attended this week’s gathering, compared with the 376 originally named as members in 2022. That means that more than 25% of the original cohort were absent, many due to purges. It is the highest number of “empty chairs” at the plenum in modern Chinese history.

The confirmed expulsions included Zhang Youxia, the former second-in-command to China’s leader in the military hierarchy, and Ma Xingrui, the former party secretary for Xinjiang. Other absences were unexplained.
“More empty seats underscores the plenum’s focus on Xi’s vision of strict internal discipline,” said Neil Thomas, a senior fellow at the Asia Society thinktank, in a post on X.

The theme for this week’s plenum was party governance. Since coming to power in 2012 Xi has focused on stamping out corruption in the party. But in recent years the campaign has intensified, taking out officials in the highest ranks of the party and the military, raising questions about if the campaign is also a tool to remove political rivals or punish disloyalty.

Xi appears to have grown increasingly frustrated with what he sees as a lack of discipline in the ranks of the party that wields absolute authority over the state and society in China. Earlier this year he said that the party must uproot “sick trees” and that the fight against corruption was a “never-ending journey”.

A series of purges has gutted the seven-man Central Military Commission, the ruling body of China’s People’s Liberation Army. There are now just two members left: Xi himself, and the military’s anti-graft tsar, Zhang Shengmin.
Zhang was promoted to the politburo of the CCP this week, the highest ruling body in the party. Zhang is now the only military member of the senior leadership body.

The plenum also laid the groundwork for the 21st Party congress, an event which happens every five years and is expected to next be held in the second half of 2027. Xi is expected to secure a fourth term as leader of the party, making him the longest ruler of Communist China since Mao Zedong.

The ranks of the Central Committee and the politburo will be refreshed at next year’s congress, but many analysts believe that recent purges have been so wide-ranging that there are few suitable candidates to be promoted.

items.title: Sam Wood to remain in custody after another failed bail bid over domestic violence charges
paragraphs: Former Bachelor star Sam Wood will remain in custody while he awaits trial on domestic violence charges, after he was refused bail for a second time.
Wood, 46, from Melbourne, has been held in custody since his arrest on 4 October at Noosa.

On Friday supreme court justice Patrick McCafferty said Wood posed “an unacceptable risk” of further offending, meaning he will remain in the high-security Wolston correctional centre until his trial, which the court heard might not take place until 2028.
Wood was previously remanded over allegations he choked and assaulted his wife, Snezana Wood, while the family was holidaying on the Sunshine Coast.
He is charged with two domestic violence offences: assault occasioning bodily harm and strangulation in a domestic setting.
His legal team have indicated he will fight the charges and he has not yet entered a plea.
During an initial bail hearing, a court heard Snezana was supportive of the charges, that she was allegedly choked and that “there was a cessation of breath”.

“She articulates [in a video-recorded statement] the banging of her head on the floor. She couldn’t breathe,” police prosecutor Jeanette Grigoris told the earlier hearing. “She thought she was going to die.”

The more serious charge, related to strangulation, placed him in a “show cause” position where there is a presumption against bail unless he can demonstrate he does not pose a risk of re-offending. McCafferty said that Wood had not satisfied him that proposed conditions could ameliorate that risk.

During Friday’s bail hearing, the Supreme Court heard claims that Wood used drugs and alcohol, engaged in a “party lifestyle” and that he “struggles with anger”. On Friday Wood’s lawyer, Paula Morreau KC, said that there was no suggestion Wood “suffered from addiction” despite crown submissions that he used drugs and alcohol use and engaged in a “party lifestyle”.

Morreau said that if granted bail, Wood proposed to reside in Tasmania, where his father lives, and that he would agree to the condition “to not enter Victoria” where Snezana lives. At the earlier application, Wood had sought bail to reside in Melbourne.
Morreau said Wood had been suffering “significant stressors” and that he “struggles with anger” but that in such situations “he usually leaves and takes time”.
“He shows he has the capacity for self-control,” she said.
Wood’s legal team proposed he undergo a “men’s behavioural change” course if released on bail.
Crown prosecutor Jessica Guy said there were “serious features” to allegations that Wood assaulted and strangled his wife.
“[Wood] didn’t desist. [The] violence extended beyond the application of force to her neck, to the banging of her head to the floor of the skirting boards.
“[It occurred] in the presence of an adult witness and the close proximity of young children.
Wood is now being held at the high-security Wolston correctional centre near Brisbane. He was not brought to the court for the hearing on Friday.

items.title: Democrats have an identity crisis - it won't be an easy fix
paragraphs: James Stevens calls himself a democratic socialist. The 24-year-old film student is the type of Democrat who recalls watching the provocative left-wing internet commentator Hasan Piker six years ago, "before he became relevant in politics". Last year, James flew up from his home in Georgia to New York City to canvass for Zohran Mamdani's mayoral campaign.

His mother, Tamara, 56, is a loyal Democrat too. But of a different ilk. She grew up Republican then switched to the Democratic Party after seeing Barack Obama on Oprah. These days, she's a loyal party woman, championing reproductive rights, attending campaign rallies and donating to local candidates.
Both mother and son want Democrats to win control of Congress at next Tuesday's midterm elections, but they don't entirely agree on what they want their Democratic Party to be.

"I'm very sick of how compromising Democrats are to Republican policies that don't benefit a large group of people," James told me, as his mother looked on. "There needs to be a bold vision for the Democrats," he says, arguing that the party should adopt policies affiliated with the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA), a left-wing splinter group. In his view, that means anti-Zionism, getting corporate money out of politics, and government-run free healthcare.
The conventional wisdom in Washington is that Democrats are well-positioned to take control of the House, and possibly even the Senate, after the vote next week.

Underlying conditions are in Democrats' favour – Republican US President Donald Trump's approval rating is at a record low for a president heading into a midterm, comparable to George W Bush in his final term in 2006; the Iran war still isn't over and it's proving unpopular with American voters; and this has led to higher gas prices, which are frustrating an electorate that is already worried about the cost of living. Traditionally, the midterms are a referendum on a sitting president. In 18 of the last 20 US midterm elections, the party in power has lost seats in the House.

I've covered every national US election in the past dozen years and this is an unusual one. When I was out interviewing voters ahead of the 2018 midterms during Donald Trump's first term, I was struck by how united many Democratic voters were in their opposition to the president. This time, I've noticed that under the facade of unity, there's a brewing fight.

There are persistent questions about what the Democratic Party stands for, and these divides erupted during the primaries this midterm cycle. "The identity of the party is pretty cloudy," said Ruy Teixeira, a senior fellow at the American Enterprise Institute, a centre-right think tank. "It's all centred on reaction to the Trump administration and taking advantage of what is a thermostatic reaction against the administration... Beyond that, there's all these different factions in the party."

Part of the reason for this Democratic infighting is that the party never had a chance to have this fight during the 2024 presidential race, with the sudden departure of Joe Biden months before the election and nomination of Kamala Harris.

Analysts agree that if Democrats make big wins on election night, it still won't answer deeper, unresolved questions as they try to keep their big tent together to corral votes in Congress or eye the 2028 presidency.

In simplistic terms, the divide is between the centrist, more moderate wing of the party and its left flank. But operatives and analysts say it's also a divide between institutionalists and those who want to completely upend the existing institution. Both feel they have a better read on what voters genuinely want.

Usamah Andrabi, of the Justice Democrats, a prominent left-wing group, blames the Democratic establishment for ushering in a Republican Congress and president. "And so I think the people who led us into this mess are simply not gonna be the ones who lead us out of it," he told me.

"The affordability crisis… is a massive one, and it's not going to be resolved by tinkering at the margins," he added. Instead, he insists, it'll be solved through policies like universal healthcare and childcare, and redistributing money by cutting the Pentagon's budget to stop "endless wars". His organisation sprang up in 2017 to recruit and support the congressional members who became known as "the Squad", the furthest-left faction in the House, which includes members such as Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez and Ilhan Omar.
Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez has been consistently popular among progressives

Healthcare will be one of the main arenas in which this fight is likely to play out, says Carrie Dann, managing editor of the Cook Political Report, a nonpartisan newsletter that forecasts the competitiveness of races.

"There is a lot of appetite for, at the very least, more transparency, more understanding of why healthcare costs are so high," said Dann. " Take a bad step, break your leg, and a huge swathe of Americans would see their worlds turned upside down by that because of the healthcare system as it is."

Several Democratic candidates this election cycle have outlined ideas to lower "out-of-pocket" costs for those who already have health insurance - being hit with additional costs on top of regular insurance payments is a common feature of the American healthcare system. But there's another flank of the party that is fed up with incremental changes and wants a national healthcare system that is free at the point of use - Medicare for All.
Recent polling suggests a majority of Democrats favour this kind of healthcare system, but a majority of Republicans oppose it.
But some Democrats say there's nuance in the issue.

"People want to have universal healthcare, and they also want to be able to keep their health insurance," says Neera Tanden, Joe Biden's former domestic policy adviser, now CEO of the Center for American Progress, a liberal think tank.

Mainstream establishment Democrats acknowledge that many people see healthcare as a right, but they insist that others strongly oppose a fully government-run programme, fearing lower standards of care, and insist on having the option of keeping their private health insurance.

Healthcare costs have gone up across the board - health insurance and out-of-pocket healthcare expenses, hospital expenses and prescription drug costs have all surged in recent years, rising faster than the rate of inflation. As medical expenses have increased, polls suggest the idea of universal healthcare isn't as outlandish as it once seemed, and this campaign cycle has shown that it's far less taboo for politicians to openly call for it.
Back in Georgia, it's an issue on which Tamara and James agree - they want universal healthcare.
But their most fundamental disagreement is over Israel. Tamara calls herself a Zionist. "My kids get mad at me for saying that," she said.
And they're hardly the only Democrats having this debate.
Abdul El-Sayed's race is being seen as a bellwether

Dann, from the Cook Political Report, says one of the biggest lessons from this election cycle is that Democratic voters weren't just looking for candidates willing to fight Trump, but candidates willing to take on the establishment. Dann points to the key swing state of Michigan, where in the primary, Abdul El-Sayed - a fierce critic of Israel and its actions in Gaza - came out on top over the objections of the Democratic establishment.

"I think one reason for that was that he was not only talking about taking on Donald Trump, but taking on the Democratic establishment… the establishment in Washington writ large," she said. And part of that anti-establishment attitude is about US support for Israel.
Some who left the party in 2024 because they believe Biden was too supportive of Israel's actions in Gaza are now returning, energised by El-Sayed's tough tone.
"My red line has been Gaza," said Samraa Luqman, an Arab-American activist in Michigan who voted for Trump in the last presidential election, feeling betrayed by Democrats that year.

"2023 and 2024 have really taught this community a lesson that we are no longer going to be wishy-washy about the issue. It's Gaza or bust," she told me. "If you're not good on Gaza, on Israel, on Palestine, then we don't need you. We don't need you in office, and we don't need to vote for you, no matter what your party affiliation is."
Support for Israel has become a core issue within the party

But as El-Sayed has energised voters, he's also alienated others, particularly some who see support for Israel as connected to Jewish safety in the US and feel that antisemitism in their party has grown after the deadly Hamas attacks of October 7.
Zach Nessel is one of those Democrats. And he's increasingly worried about becoming politically homeless.

"We have people who don't think Zionists should have a place in our party, that they should be removed from the party," Nessel told me. "And as a proud Zionist, I don't want to be removed from the Democratic coalition just over this one issue in the Middle East."

Support for Israel became a litmus test in some Democratic primaries this season, leading to mounting resistance to the American Israel Public Affairs Committee, the longtime influential lobbying group.
But Dann tells me that it's not just Israel that's a litmus test, it's El-Sayed's race itself.

"Abdul El-Sayed's theory of the case is that he can run as an unabashed progressive in a purple state [a state that swings between the 'red' Republican party and 'blue' Democrats] and win because progressive ideas are not only popular if they're communicated correctly, but also activate voters who are not necessarily a normal part of the political process, particularly young people," she said.

If he wins, left-wing candidates will see it as a model, she adds. And if he loses, Democrats in the more centrist wing of the party will see it as evidence that left-wing ideas are out of touch with mainstream voters.

But there are others, like Jim Kessler with Third Way, a centrist think tank, who think Michigan shouldn't be the focus. He pointed out that if Democrats take control of the Senate it'll be because of more centrist candidates: Roy Cooper in North Carolina, Mary Peltola in Alaska, James Talarico in Texas, Josh Turek in Iowa, Adam Hamilton in Kansas. They, he said, are the ones expanding Democrats' odds this cycle. " So the bigger the Democratic victory, the more it seems like the centrist Democrats came through, not the DSA candidates," he said.
DSA-endorsed candidates made gains during the primaries this election cycle, but their ideas are still controversial to many.

" I don't think… the vast majority of working-class people in America are kind of mini socialists," Tanden told me, pointing to reporting that suggests the majority of people who support the DSA are college-educated voters.
" Working-class people are pretty moderate on issues like crime and immigration," she added.
Nonetheless, if Democrats gain the majority, their congressional leaders will have to navigate a group of Democrats in which there will likely be an increase in the loudest and most left-wing voices.

" The Democrats' biggest challenge is to figure out how to actually deliver on running the economy better and making things more affordable, because they've said over and over again and very loudly that's what they're going to do," said Teixeira.
In all likelihood, people will start thinking seriously about the next presidential candidate the day after the midterms.
So, who actually has the momentum: the left flank or the centre?

"I think after the election we'll see a lot of fighting between the factions to claim credit," Teixeira said. " And that will of course feed into the jostling for the presidential nomination for 2028."
Back in Georgia, Tamara and James may disagree on some things, but they both want Democrats to win big on Tuesday.
"I'm a very pragmatic person when it comes to progressive politics," James said. He wants to make it clear he doesn't agree with everything DSA members espouse.
So much of this midterm cycle has also come down to candidate quality - not just the message but the messenger. So I asked both mother and son who their "ideal" Democrat is.
Tamara instantly answered Jon Ossoff, the Democratic senator running for re-election in Georgia.
Jon Ossoff is being watched closely in Georgia
It's a point of agreement. They both really like their Georgia senator.

Ossoff is seen by many as a rising star of his party. The seat he is contesting is characterised by the Cook Political Report as "likely Democratic" - considered by analysts to be an impressive achievement in a swing state that voted for Trump in 2024.
"He knows how to speak to moderate Republicans, moderate Democrats, and members of the DSA," Tamara said. "He's not afraid to pull any punches… I appreciate how much he talks about corruption."
On Wednesday night, she joined thousands of people just outside Atlanta for a rally to cheer on the senator as former President Barack Obama campaigned for Democrats.
And when Ossoff took the mic, he spoke at length about what he sees as "corruption" in the Trump administration and in American politics, healthcare and corporate money.
And I heard this concern from voters in Georgia this past week, not just at the campaign rally, but at early voting sites in both Republican and Democratic counties.

"We have a corruption crisis," said Richard Schosky as he walked out of the voting booth in north Atlanta, after casting his ballot early. It's an issue that seems to be resonating deeply with voters, although the White House has repeatedly denied any allegations of wrongdoing.
In fact, Dann with the Cook Political Report says "corruption has become one of the central issues of this election".
Still, she added, "Democrats would be foolish to believe that a very good night for them in November is a mandate for the Democratic Party," said Dann.
"They are as almost as unpopular as Republicans and the president."

items.title: El Niño-driven drought in Papua New Guinea a ‘national crisis’ as rivers dry up and local farms fail
paragraphs: Extreme drought driven by an historic El Niño is affecting as many as 8 million people in Papua New Guinea, causing a cascade of issues from shortages of food and water, to electricity scarcity and schooling disruption.

An influential coalition that includes churches, trade unions and business groups has said the Pacific nation is in the midst of a “national crisis”, but there appears to be “no coordinated plan to protect vulnerable communities from the worsening impacts of El Niño.”

Residents and community leaders have told the Guardian that rivers and creeks have dried up and family food gardens – a vital source of food and income for many – have shrivelled. Schools and health facilities are being forced to close early because they lack sufficient water to provide basic services.

Emilly Meren, humanitarian projects manager at CARE International in PNG, said in rural highland areas families were rationing food to one meal a day – while food insecurity was leading to localised disputes between families.
“For women and girls, they are expected to do more to support their families,” she said, yet they were “the last to eat because they have to serve others first”.

“They have to travel three to four hours to source water and food and are exposed to a heightened risk of harassment. We are hearing stories of transactional sex happening in the community – exchanging sex for money or for food.”
The El Niño climate pattern is gaining strength in the tropical Pacific with forecasts suggesting it will be the strongest ever recorded with its impacts worsened by global heating.
Some parts of PNG have had less than a quarter of their usual rainfall since August.

The PNG National Weather Service declared the onset of El Niño in June but Kasis Inape, the service’s assistant director, said at that point, much of the country was already in drought and about 8 million people had been affected.
Inape said PNG was one of the wettest places in the world with rain fed by warm tropical waters, but the El Niño had seen those waters shift east “and we’re starved of rain”.
“Because we’re a rain-fed country, a lot of our people are subsistence farmers and they depend just on rainfall to survive and to feed themselves,” he said.
PNG’s wet season is between November and April and Inape said while some short term relief was forecasted, there were concerns El Niño would shorten the season.
“The place is so dry – just two months of rain is not enough to allow crops to grow and water levels to be comfortable,” Inape said.
In Morobe province’s Bulolo district, smaller rivers have dried up leaving families without access to water for drinking, cooking and washing.
Resident Theophil Zarack said many schools and health centres were operating for only half a day, with some clinics no longer accepting inpatients due to a lack of available water.

Martha Zureno, a resident in Leklu village, said: “All our rivers have dried up, including the one behind my house. Now, my children and I have to walk for miles every afternoon to fetch water for cooking and drinking from the other side.
“We have a well that we dug ourselves, but we only use that water for washing. All the crops in our gardens have dried up and died, and we cannot grow anything now.”
Zureno said that most of the local residents depend on panning for gold to earn an income, but without water, “even that has become increasingly difficult”.

Meanwhile, a destructive hailstorm in parts of Enga province earlier this month – not blamed directly on El Niño – buried sweet potatoes under ice, exacerbating the food scarcity issue, according to George Iki, president of the Sambe Unity Development Association.

In the capital Port Moresby, PNG Power has begun planned electricity blackouts after falling dam levels cut hydropower generation and said disruptions could continue for up to 10 months. The company was working to manage dam releases to protect the city’s water supply.

Peter Aitsi, a prominent PNG business figure and co-chair of the Community Coalition Against Corruption, said the government needed to carry out “proper assessments” of the unfurling impacts, particularly on rural communities.

Last month the group called the drought situation a “national crisis”, but according to Aitsi, urban centres have been mostly shielded from the impacts. That could change, however, with electricity blackouts and a shortage of fresh food from drought-stricken areas, he said.
Aitsi said the capital had been covered in a smoke haze in the past week from fires elsewhere on the island, and in Indonesia to the west, that scientists say have been fuelled by El Niño.

Prime minister James Marape has directed provincial and district authorities to prepare for a prolonged dry season, saying his government was examining financial arrangements to support disaster responses.

“Cabinet is looking at tailoring provisions of our financial instructions to make sure that districts and provinces are assisted to respond to disasters as they happen where appropriate,” Marape said.

items.title: Crypto worth billions frozen after suspected Binance hack
paragraphs: Cryptocurrency giant Binance said on Thursday that it has frozen digital assets worth around $3bn (£2.24bn) to prevent them from being stolen while it investigates a security issue.
The company said as part of a series of alerts online that all deposits and withdrawals are temporarily suspended while its teams conduct security checks and that the firm will "cover all losses".
"It does look like a hack on Binance," said Binance's former boss Changpeng Zhao, who remains a majority shareholder of the firm.
Two other major crypto platforms, Tether and Circle, said they have also frozen a total of about $2.4bn of assets in response to the potential Binance hack.
Binance said the amount of funds frozen may continue to increase as its teams work closely with law enforcement and other partners to trace and seize additional assets.

"We are working around the clock and will share a full post-mortem once the investigation is complete. Please rely only on official Binance channels for updates," the firm said, adding that users' funds are safe.
Binance is the world's largest crypto exchange by daily trading volumes.
Bitcoin dropped by around 5% following the alerts. The price of other major cryptocurrencies including Ethereum and Solana also fell sharply.

Circle chief executive Jeremy Allaire said his firm is "closely tracking reports of a potential exploit involving Binance" and that his company has frozen more than $800m in assets linked to the incident.
Circle is the issuer and co-creator of the USDC, one of the world's largest US dollar-backed cryptocurrencies.
Tether CEO Paolo Ardoino said his firm has frozen around $1.6bn "related to a potential Binance exchange hack."
"Protecting the industry and our partners is our main priority," said Ardoino, whose company issues a cryptocurrency known as USDT.
Several crypto industry observers had flagged concerns about a potential hack on Binance hours before the exchange confirmed the attack.
The scale of the attack is still unclear.
In 2025, hackers stole $1.5bn in crypto from the Dubai-based cryptocurrency exchange Bybit. The record-breaking incident has been attributed to hackers linked with North Korea.

items.title: 'A big loss' - Fans react to death of Sir Patrick Stewart
paragraphs: Admirers of the Star Trek actor gathered at his Hollywood Walk of Fame Star in Los Angeles to pay tribute to his life and acting career.

items.title: We went on holiday with our neighbours and swapped families - it tore us apart
paragraphs: Rachel and Ian had initially been delighted when a new family moved in next door. "We instantly hit it off, all four of us." They were thrilled to be going on holiday together.
Rachel remembers two caravans parked side-by-side and a trip up Mount Snowdon.
But when it was time to go home, everything was mixed up - people were getting in the wrong cars.

Rachel remembers her mum leaning back from the passenger seat, saying: "'We're going to have a new family. We're going to be living in number eight with Eddie and Alison. Alison's going to be your new sister.
"And your dad and brother are still going to live in number 10. And Auntie Irene and Dawn are going to live there. And Dawn's going to be your brother's new sister."
Rachel immediately felt "very panicked and afraid and upset" and says she started to cry.
As the car rumbled along, she felt "bewildered, but also a little bit excited". She liked Alison and had always wanted a sister.
That night, Alison let her sleep on her top bunk and the next morning the adults switched belongings between the houses in the Isle of Sheppey where they lived.
Rachel says she felt very confused. "You can't help but think that it's your fault."
Life at number 8, where Rachel now lived, was very different to number 10. Her old house had been clean, whereas this house had "dog hair, greasy things, car things".
She describes her mum as "firm but fair" and very practical.
Her stepdad Eddie "was never horrible to me, but I never called him dad. I wasn't his girl."
She also missed Ian desperately. "I was very proud of him. He was my big brother.
"I used to wait in the front garden for him to come home from school when I was a toddler."

items.title: I didn't know I was lacking in vitamin D until I collapsed at work
paragraphs: Twenty-three-year-old Saskia Reeves-Priestley was at work when she suddenly collapsed.
"I just felt really dizzy, really nauseous, was having heart palpitations and was really hot," she says.
There had been no prior warning. Saskia, a special educational needs teacher, was a keen goalkeeper who played football four times a week and felt fit and healthy.
She would later be diagnosed as vitamin D-deficient – blood tests showed her levels were "next to nothing".
In the UK, low vitamin rates are increasing in some age groups, external - particularly in girls and young women.
According to data from the National Diet and Nutrition Survey, last year nearly a quarter of 11- to 18-year-olds were classed as deficient.
Vitamin D can come from our diet, in foods such as oily fish and meat, or supplements.

But most is made by our body when UV light in sunlight hits the skin. Lower levels of sunlight - depending on where in the world you live or the time of year - decrease the body's ability to produce it.
Covering parts of the body and wearing sunscreen also has an impact - despite their protective advantages.
Those with darker skin need exposure to stronger light to produce the same amount of vitamin D as lighter skin.
Doctors don't routinely offer blood tests to check for vitamin D deficiency, but will offer a supplement if a patient is concerned they might be high risk.

items.title: Bombshell confession in The Traitors as faithfuls finally turn the screw
paragraphs: Spoiler warning: This article reveals details from episode nine of The Celebrity Traitors, series two.
With the traitors still riding high following last Friday's episode, could they really just walk it to the final? It was time to find out.

Having been bestowed with the almighty power of the double dagger - well, metaphorically speaking, at least - King Kenny held all the cards, choosing to use his special power of a double vote to send another faithful packing.
As cliffhangers go, it wasn't hugely thrilling for viewers at home, given that the pair up for banishment - Sharon Rooney and Joanne McNally - were both faithfuls.
Nevertheless, it left a big impact on the faithful crew as they realised they had let the traitors land yet another blow ahead of Friday's final.
"We've got to pull something out of the bag," said frustrated faithful Michael Sheen later. He wasn't wrong.
Joanne got teary as she departed and joked "she was premenstrual," before revealing she was "a hardcore faithful".

Maya described her as a "ball of fun", while Kenny put on his best acting skills in the aftermath by pretending to be struggling with having the deciding vote, even comforting poor Sharon. Give that man an Oscar.
Meanwhile, James Blunt was on the hunt for whiskey like a teenager at the end of a house party: "Where do they keep the stiff stuff?" he asked himself, finding only a tray of empty glasses.
Murder was soon on the minds of the traitors again as the dastardly trio of Kenny, Maya and James A trudged up to the turret.

"The life of a traitor... it's not for everyone," said Maya. And that probably includes James A, although to be fair, he has shown a bit more enthusiasm for some pantomime villainy in the last couple of episodes. More on him later.
"Let's have faith," said King Kenny without a hint of irony.
As ever, James B was as far off the pace as me in the year 11 cross-country race.

When Leigh-Anne Pinnock, probably the most astute faithful of the series, brought up James A being a potential traitor over breakfast, James B sarcastically replied: "I think that's a good theory to start banishing the most innocent."

Sharon - aka Poundland Poirot - failed to appear in the dining room, having been chosen for the chopping block so soon after escaping banishment, throwing all the faithfuls into more confusion. She was getting a bit stressed, so it was probably for the best.
Michael had a warning for the traitors though, giving his most rousing oratory since his motivational speech for the Welsh football team ahead of the 2022 World Cup.
"Traitors... today is going to be a living hell for you, I am going to push and push and push and you are going to suffer today. This is the apocalypse.

Theories were soon flying left right and centre, with Bash throwing the spotlight on "the head of the round table" Michael, Kenny putting suspicion on James B, while Romesh pointed the finger at actual traitor Maya, shock, horror.
And the obsession with the peacock perfume wasn't going anywhere.
Finally Michael 'Vengeful Daddy' Sheen seemed to be on to something, telling a shell-shocked Maya in the kitchen: "I think you could be a brilliant traitor, and if you and Kenny paired up, amazing."
She was probably relieved when the jeeps turned up for another day trip, and Romesh was all of us with his hilarious reaction to news of yet another insane mission.

On being told by host Claudia Winkleman that they had to find the severed heads of some of the murdered celebrities and reunite them with the head of the buried body, he got the giggles: "It's just so ridiculous. I love it though!"

James B tried to get one group in the Frankenstein-style lab to sing his hit Beautiful - which had Leigh-Ann and Michael bopping along but by the puzzled look on Kenny's face, he had clearly never heard it. Awks.

This mission was a bit of a rehash of the wailing in the well challenge from the first Celebrity Traitors series, with Claudia going full headteacher and cheering - or should we say, shouting - the teams on.
Digital versions of the dead celebs in bell jars had to be matched to the correct gravestone in the castle gardens.
"Seeing Ross's face when he was alive was enough to give a man pause, let alone when his dismembered head is looking out at you from a pickle jar," quipped Michael.
Watch on iPlayer with new episodes every Thursday and Friday
The latest banished and murdered celebs have their say in Uncloaked
Back at the castle, it seemed that Michael wasn't the only one starting to turn up the heat on Maya.
Romesh and Bash decided she had gone under the radar long enough: "One of the greatest gliders in the game. Maybe Olympic level gliding," mused Bash. And King Kenny was also in their sights.
And so to the penultimate round table. (A shout out to Claudia's sequin-tastic midnight blue trouser suit).
Michael was under the spotlight first due to his presence, intelligence and status as "the father of the table."
In turn, he first went back to his previous suspicion of Leigh-Anne on the night of the murder in plain sight, accusing her again of using her Big Mix dance with Miranda as a distraction.
Romesh put heat on James B due to his vocal accusations, which were often wrong.

The quiet ones - traitors James A and Maya - were then questioned by Michael and James B, who soon honed in on the murder in plain sight, working out that Maya, Kenny and James A were in the library at the end of the night when Ross was killed.
Vengeful Daddy was indeed in the house, and James B was on the money for once. Credit where it's due.
Then the bombshell of the series - something that has never happened before in the history of the show.
James A, who failed dismally to defend himself against Michael's accusations, clearly couldn't take any more and confessed he was a traitor at the table.
"I was made a traitor without wanting to be," he revealed, as the others gasped.
"I've had a unique experience on this that no-one has had before, I wanted to be a faithful and that's all I wanted to be. But I couldn't just say 'guys, vote for me.'"
At least no-one had to explain their decision when they all wrote his name down on the boards.
And as Michael and Maya stood round the firepit before heading to bed - or the turret in Maya's case - she looked like a dead woman walking. And DSI Sheen is on her case.

items.title: From workshops to the catwalk - why mended clothes are going mainstream
paragraphs: Alice Brown uses felt animals to cover holes and stains on her clothes
If Alice Brown is browsing in second-hand shops and finds a jumper with a hole, that won't stop her buying it.
"I see it as challenge," says the 27-year-old forest ranger from Lincolnshire.
She is a champion of the growing fashion for eye-catching repairs.
Over the last year she has developed her own unique style, needle-felting cute animals and insects to cover moth holes, stains and other imperfections, winning her a huge following online.
"The natural place for decoration is in the centre at the front. If the hole is under the arm or on the shoulder, it forces you to think about the design," she says.
Often dubbed "visible mending" the trend is spreading from hobby crafters and community workshops, even drawing in fast-fashion brands and reaching the designer catwalks this year.
Some mends are designed to be eye-catching
At one Saturday morning workshop in Brighton, Jayne Eagle shows her students how to attach a patch of fabric behind a tear so the cat-face design peeps through.

Then she instructs them in stitching techniques inspired by the traditional Japanese methods Boro and Sashiko. Instead of matching the thread colour to the garment, they make the mend highly decorative using geometric patterns in large white stitching.
She also offers classes in darning using contrasting vibrant colours that celebrate, rather than disguise, the repair.
Jayne Eagle sees repair as an "act of rebellion" against fast fashion

One student, Nicola, has already used her newfound skills to stitch over sunscreen marks on a T-shirt "making a feature of it" and is now delighted that people "stop seeing the stains and just see the decoration".
Another student, Lisa, says her mother's generation would never have wanted the mends to show. "Now part of it is being proud of what you've done," she says.
Lisa bought a second-hand jacket online, but snipped the fabric with the scissors when she was opening the package. She managed to patch it in a way that "looks intentional".
"I was actually pointing it out to people," she laughs.
Lisa says she's so proud of her mends she wants people to notice them
In the past mending was primarily about saving money, by wearing clothes for longer, rather than buying new. But visible mending is about celebrating that choice.
The trend took off about six years ago, Jayne says, and has boomed since.
An era of "throwaway" fast fashion from the 1980s onwards undermined the tradition of looking after and mending your clothes and people lost the skills, she says.
The revival of interest feels to her like a backlash against overproduction in the fashion industry and the damage it causes: the pollution, carbon emissions, water use, and poor labour conditions.

So perhaps it is surprising just how popular mended style is proving among retailers, with brands from Ralph Lauren to ultra-fast-fashion firm Shein currently selling stitched and patched garments, albeit in both of those cases brand new off the peg.
Other High Street chains are adopting a more authentic approach, offering in-house repairs and workshops.
"We want to give customers practical ways to extend the life of the clothes they already love, rather than simply replacing them," says Uniqlo's head of sustainability, Maria Ledous.
Uniqlo offers decorative mending using Sashiko techniques, in keeping with the brand's Japanese heritage
Primark, often seen as a fast-fashion retailer due to its lower prices, has also joined the trend.
"We don't think that affordability and durability should be opposites," says Vicki Swain, the brand's longevity lead.

Outdoor brand Finisterre says around a fifth of the mends it provides for customers are designed to be eye-catching, while premium artisan clothing store Toast says around a third of customers go for that option.
Part of the "magic" is that customers can bring in a garment and "choose what they'd like it to become next", says Toast chief executive Suzie de Rohan Willner.
Toast has a team of 14 in-house "repair artists" providing a range of creative mends
Toast's repair services are free, but off-the-peg "renewed" pieces fetch higher prices than the originals to reflect their unique character.
Levi's, which boasts probably the longest tradition of being fixed up by its fans using anything from rhinestones to fringed cuffs, is rolling out a workshop programme this year.
The firm says its research shows younger customers in particular want to repair more but don't know how.

For now, Levi's' workshops focus on traditional mending skills, such as sewing on a button and hemming, rather than visible mends, and at a recent launch event in London, that seemed to be what its Gen Z participants were looking for.
"I'm from East London. If you have holes in your clothes people are like 'Ha ha! You're poor!'," says 16-year-old school student Bianca.
At a workshop run by Levi's, Nicholas (r) says he prefers mending not to show, while Bianca (centre) says people still see it as a sign of poverty
Theo, 19, says he'd rather learn how to mend without it showing.
"I would want [the jeans] to look how I originally bought them," he says.
He has a side hustle selling clothes at car boot sales and thinks traditional repair skills would make it more lucrative.
His friend Nicholas, also 19, says most people want to look "fresh".
"No-one wants to look like they came out of a dumpster," he says.
Still, Paul Dillinger, Levi's head of global design innovation, thinks more creative repairs will win them over as they pick up more skills.
"No-one has time for that perfect 'straight from the shop' thing. That's not cool.
"People crave agency," he says. "Mending is a demonstration of humanity: it's not a mustard stain, it's a memory of a great day in the ballpark."

items.title: What makes this golden eagle chick so important?
paragraphs: Beaky Junior is seen as a symbol of the co-operation between landowners, gamekeepers and a project to boost golden eagle numbers
A golden eagle chick has become the first to fledge from a nest on a managed grouse moor in the south of Scotland.
The bird - Beaky Junior - hatched in a nest in a secret location in the Moffat Hills, at a site used for recreational gamebird shooting.
It comes after a Royal Society for the Protection of Birds (RSPB) report revealed that two-thirds of UK persecution incidents involving birds of prey had occurred at similar sites.
And it is being considered a "hugely significant milestone" by those running a project to boost golden eagle numbers in the region.
Dr Cat Barlow, chief executive of Restoring Upland Nature (Run) which is behind the scheme, said they had received "incredible support" from landowners and gamekeepers.
Beaky Junior marks golden eagle milestone in south of Scotland
The project to relocate birds from the Highlands to a secret location in the Moffat Hills started in the summer of 2018.
Numbers in the south of Scotland had fallen to a handful of breeding pairs but they are now at a record level of more than 50 - despite some setbacks.

Birds have been shot at or killed and that is why the birth of Beaky Junior - one of five golden eagle chicks successfully fledged in the area this year - is being seen as so significant, since it happened on a managed grouse moor.
Earlier this year, the RSPB report highlighted 182 confirmed persecution incidents involving birds of prey in Scotland over a 10-year period.
It said they were widely scattered across the country but the majority - 64.3% - had occurred on land managed for gamebird shooting.
Against that backdrop, the efforts in southern Scotland to encourage estates and conservationists to work together are seen as particularly important.
Beaky Junior was even named by local gamekeepers in recognition of the "key role" they have played in helping golden eagles thrive.
Dr Cat Barlow said the fledging of five young birds was a "hugely significant milestone"

Barlow explained: "It is wonderful to see a golden eagle hatch, fledge and fly freely from the newly-established nest of a translocated golden eagle that has made its home on a managed grouse moor in the Southern Uplands.

"This reflects the incredible support we have had from landowners and gamekeepers – from translocations in the Highlands, to continued monitoring and protection of birds and eyries on their lands and estates.
"Indeed their support has been absolutely vital to our success in restoring the population of golden eagles to record numbers."
She said the fledging of five chicks from the nests of birds they had translocated to southern Scotland was a "hugely significant milestone".

Barlow added that it gave "genuine hope" in the battle to reverse biodiversity decline and ensure future generations across Scotland, England and Wales could experience the "incredible sense of awe" when seeing a golden eagle.
Beaky Junior was named after its mother, Beaky
Michael Clarke, who chairs Run, said individuals from "all walks of life" had helped the birds to thrive.
He added that they would continue to monitor the impact of the golden eagles on the area "with support of land managers, gamekeepers, farmers and the wider community".
The chief executive of landowner body Scottish Land and Estates, Sarah-Jane Laing, said it was thrilled to hear gamekeepers had named the chick.

"Beaky Junior's arrival serves as a powerful example of what can be achieved when land managers and conservationists unite behind a shared vision, grounded in trust and genuine partnership," she said.
"Seeing this magnificent species return to and flourish in these landscapes is something we can all take pride in."
What stories would you like BBC News to cover from the south of Scotland?
The gamekeepers involved asked to remain anonymous in order to protect the location of the bird.

Speaking on their behalf, Mark Ewart, regional co-ordinator at the Southern Uplands Moorlands Group, added: "It is incredibly rewarding to see gamekeepers celebrated for the important role they have played in the success of Run's South of Scotland Golden Eagle Project.
"Monitoring and providing the right habitats for golden eagles and other species to flourish is an important part of what gamekeepers do on a day-to-day basis.
"To encounter golden eagles daily is the ultimate indicator of the success of the project-gamekeeper partnership."

items.title: More than half of Victorian lawyers use AI – but only a quarter have cut client fees as a result
paragraphs: More than half of Victoria’s lawyers have reported using AI in their work, according to a new study, but just over a quarter say they have reduced fees as a result of efficiency gains.
They also say clients seeking advice from chatbots have added to their workload, forcing them to correct errors made by AI.

The 2026 census of 2,221 of the state’s lawyers, conducted by the Victorian Legal Services Board and Commissioner’s legal services research centre, found a big increase in lawyers using AI in their practices, rising from 37% to 55% in the last year.
While the 2025 report found AI use was highest among those under 30 years of age, in 2026 this disparity had largely disappeared, although usage remained low for those aged 60 and over.

AI use was most common in trade practices (85%), banking and finance (78%) and information technology and telecommunications (78%), while it was used much less in criminal law (29%), family law (45%) and administrative law (46%).

While there are AI tools designed specifically for legal services, 79% of lawyers reported using consumer chatbots such as ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini or Copilot. Legal-specific tools alone were used by 22% of respondents.
The increased use in AI has not translated to a reduction in fees for most, the survey found, with just 26% of lawyers responding that their use of AI had resulted in lower client fees.
Reduced fees were more likely to be reported by those working for business clients (34%) compared with individual fee-paying clients (23%).
Some reported AI had enabled them to take on work that would have previously been uneconomical (18%).

The principal researcher and report co-author, Dr Georgie Rychner, said fee reductions in corporate and big firms could be attributed to the fact clients in those settings were repeat users of legal services.

“They have a high level of legal capability,” she said. “They also are perhaps using AI in their own work, so they have a better understanding and are able to advocate for lower prices … whereas we’re not seeing that as much in the community legal system sector.”

Rychner said the efficiency gains of using AI were not as high as expected, but that in 2025 the survey found 89% of practitioners said they had taken steps to verify the accuracy of AI output, which might have negated the gains.

In 2026 there had been a rise in clients using AI for their own legal research, she said, with 46% of lawyers reporting their clients were arriving with inaccurate or misleading information, and 41% presenting AI-generated documents that required correction.
Nearly half of lawyers said there was an increase in time and effort required if their clients used AI, compared with 19% who said it led to a reduction in time and effort.

“What we are hearing is that clients are more frequently arriving with misleading or inaccurate information about their legal problems, more so than they’re arriving with a better understanding of legal problems,” she said, adding that more research was needed to understand client perspectives.
Courts and legal practitioner bodies across Australia have been grappling with the rise in AI use among lawyers and the public since 2023.

A Victorian lawyer last year was the first in the country to face sanctions for false citations discovered, being stripped of his ability to practise as a principal lawyer. Investigations were also launched by regulatory bodies in Western Australia and New South Wales in similar cases.

The federal court in April issued new rules around using generative AI, while the chief justice of the high court, Stephen Gageler, said last year the use of AI-generated content in legal cases had reached an “unsustainable phase”.

items.title: White House official to VOA: Trump keeps ‘all options on the table’ to deny Iran acquiring nuclear weapons
paragraphs: Editor's note: this story was translated from the original VOA Persian article.

President Donald Trump is keeping “all options on the table” to prevent Iran from acquiring nuclear weapons, a White House official told VOA following reports that the U.S. military has drawn up options for potential new strikes against Iran after the midterm election.

The official was responding to a VOA inquiry seeking a response to reports by The Wall Street Journal about the possibility of a new wave of strikes targeting Iran's missile and drone infrastructure as well as the regime's nuclear facilities.
Iran warned against escalation in the region and said it was open to diplomatic resolution to the conflict.
Trump this week said the U.S. is weighing options on whether to "finish it off" or reach a deal with Iran. He previously ruled out military action before the U.S. midterms elections next Tuesday.

"We do not comment on sensitive military plans that may or may not exist," the White House official said in response to a question that that the administration has reached out to U.S. allies in the Gulf about the potential military campaign.
VOA also asked for comment on whether military options were still on the table after the mid-term elections.
"President Trump keeps all options on the table to ensure that Iran can never have a nuclear weapon," the official said.

Trump repeatedly said that Iran would have used a nuclear weapon if it had one. The president this week said the U.S. is monitoring the situation of Iran's underground nuclear facility at Pickaxe Mountain.
"We know exactly what is going on at Pickaxe Mountain, we know the other three are obliterated ... we watch, we have entrances on every one of those that we blew up,” he told Fox News on Sunday.
Iran said its nuclear program is "peaceful"
Iran’s permanent representative to the U.N. Amir Saeid Iravani speaking to the Council claimed that his country's nuclear program has not posed a threat to international peace and security.

The head of the International Atomic Energy Agency Rafael Grossi this week told the U.N. Security Council that despite request from the agency, Iran has not provided information and access so that the IAEA can verify previously declared nuclear material at Iran’s facilities under safeguards.
