items.title: Brazil’s victory for the planet and democracy: seven lessons from Lula’s win
paragraphs: Thank you, Brazil, for demonstrating how the far right can be trounced while protection for the Amazon is strengthened. In a world where nature and democracy appeared to be bleeding out in tandem, voters and forest defenders in this global south powerhouse have shown it is possible to staunch the flow. This should provide much needed inspiration and, more practically, a playbook for social and environmental movements in other countries facing elections, including the US, Spain and France.

The astonishing comeback victory of Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva in Sunday’s presidential runoff against his extreme right challenger Flavío Bolsonaro has brought oceans of rapturous supporters on to the streets, while also thrilling conservationists, climate activists and social justice campaigners across the world.

Coming just weeks after the Lula administration announced a record fall in Amazon and Cerrado destruction, they hope Brazil can now go on to achieve its target of zero deforestation by 2030 and continue to support a global transition away from fossil fuels. That would provide a huge boost to flagging global efforts to stabilise the climate and protect degraded ecosystems. It would also set a remarkable example of leadership by the global south.

Big battles lie ahead. In the Amazon region itself, far-right members of Bolsonaro’s party have won the governorships of seven of the nine states and a large number of municipal mayorships. Brazil’s congress is now dominated by agribusiness and mining interests that have set the political agenda in recent years, and will push hard to allow more extractivist industries in indigenous lands, expand road-building, privatise rivers, weaken environmental protections and possibly attempt to impeach the president.

In the regional sphere, Lula, alone among the leaders of main South American nations in not aligning with Donald Trump’s so-called Shield of the Americas, will face pressure from Washington to channel critical minerals and other natural resources to the US, rather than selling to China or Europe, or leaving them in the ground. And, on the planetary level, Brazil faces the threat of accelerating global heating, which is pushing the Amazon ever closer to the point of no return.

So although Sunday’s result will hopefully provide a little breathing space for the Amazon and other crucially important biomes, the joy and hope that Brazil has gifted the world will quickly fade unless it inspires political change in other countries. In that sense, the biggest environmental impact of Lula’s victory may be the lessons it provides for campaigners elsewhere. Here are some initial takeaways:

1 Politics matter. There is no higher environmental priority than defeating the far right, which is a Trojan horse for extractivist – and often criminal – groups to capture states and erode protections for people, democracy and the environment. Just look at the 59.5% surge of Amazon deforestation under the 2019-2022 term of Jair Bolsonaro – the highest level of any four-year presidency in Brazil. Compare that with the 71.2% fall during the Lula administration. Over the past year, forest loss was 3,335 sq km, the lowest level since the start of satellite measurements in 1988. And Lula is not, by any means, an environmentalist. He has approved several destructive projects himself, but he is a people person who listens to the voice of social movements.

2 Don’t give up. Lula was largely written off by the markets and some polls after his first-round defeat. No first-round loser had ever previously come back to win the runoff. Lula was able to do so by securing an extra 10m votes over three weeks. The energy for this came from the streets and the forests. Social movements organised giant rallies in cities. In the Amazon, indigenous, riverine and quilombola groups travelled by hours – sometimes days – to reach polling stations by boats or buses.

3 Mobilise a campaign army. The first round of Lula’s campaign had been stodgy, old-fashioned and defensive – three traits that are also often applicable to environmental campaigns. This was transformed during the runoff, when federal deputy André Janones launched a “Lula’s Army” WhatsApp group that used humorous memes, live streams and algorithmic outreach to seize digital territory that had long been dominated by the right. By voting day, this army had 10m “soldiers”, about 8% of the electorate. Volunteers devoted hours posting stories and spreading messages across social media, speeding up the Lula campaign’s response time and emotional impact. Everyone was instructed not to share or respond to posts by the opposition camp.

4 Go on the offensive against US tech giants. Lula’s campaign accused Meta, which runs the Facebook, WhatsApp and Instagram social media platforms, of political favouritism towards Bolsonaro in its algorithms and AI tools. Meta denied bias but acknowledged technical failures. Brazil’s electoral court ordered corrective action. Among the most popular chants of Lula supporters was “Hey Meta, vai tomar no cu!” (Hey Meta, take it up the arse!). Many on the left have blamed US social media platforms for spreading rightwing disinformation and fearmongering, causing recent electoral defeats in Colombia, Chile and Peru. Lula made clear that would not be allowed in Brazil: “We had to overcome foreign interference through digital platforms, which we will have to regulate. We cannot have a monstrously large corporation earning millions and billions paying no taxes to this country and trying to steer our election results.”

5 Reclaim the flag. Brazil’s green, yellow and blue national colours had been associated with Bolsonaro’s movement in previous elections. This time, Lula seized it back by posing in a national football team strip while his “army” launched a campaign called “The green and yellow is ours”. Before voting day, millions of people across Brazil and the world – from Indigenous leaders in the Amazon to Hollywood celebrities and European football stars – flooded social networks with images of themselves in Brazil colours making an L (for Lula) sign with their thumb and little finger extended.

6 Increase social spending. Amazon protection may have galvanised conservationists, but the far greater motivations for many Lula voters were record low unemployment, robust wage growth, a 15% increase in “bolsa familia” poverty relief payments and a promise to raise the minimum wage. The importance of combining social justice with climate and nature action is widely recognised by Brazilian environmental groups. Without it, elections are lost and protests can erupt in the streets – as the world learned from France during the violent gilets jaunes (yellow vests) demonstrations of 2018.

7 Defend sovereignty, democracy and sustainability. Lula and his army called out the interlinked threats posed by the Bolsonaro family’s fealty to Donald Trump (now doubly confirmed by Flávio’s post-election flight to the US). They highlighted the interlinked threats posed by the obsequience to Trump, Bolsonaro’s desire to change the constitution and his promise to open up exploration of the Amazon and other biomes. This reflects a global phenomenon. Now that seven of the planetary boundaries essential for the flourishing of life have been breached, more and more people are affected by business activities that make the situation worse by destabilising the climate, damaging ecosystems and polluting the air, soil and rivers. This makes it harder for extractive companies to secure a social mandate so they become more inclined to either break the law or support extreme politics that override democracy.

The former environment minister Marina Silva pulled these threads together during the victory celebrations, saying Brazil had come together against these threats: “Long live the people who emerged from every corner of Brazil to sow hope for a future that is socially just, sovereign, democratic and sustainable.”
Brazil has given the world a remarkable example of hope through action. Now it needs others to follow.

items.title: Meta discussed ‘whisper strategy’ against social media critic Jonathan Haidt, files show
paragraphs: Meta staff discussed deploying a “whisper strategy” to undermine the influential US academic whose work has inspired a global social media crackdown, according to court documents.

Employees at the parent group of Facebook and Instagram sought to discredit Jonathan Haidt, the social psychologist and author of The Anxious Generation, a book that helped tip the debate about online safety towards more stringent measures such as the under-16 ban in Australia.
Minutes of internal meetings contained in a recent legal filing in the US showed that staff discussed how to “get the academic community to disavow Haidt”.

They appear in a document titled “Well-being Meeting Sound-check Notes”, which refers to discussions of how Meta could “turn other academics against Haidt” and to a “whisper strategy” aimed at achieving that goal. It also mentions “debunking” his work.

Minutes from a meeting on 8 March 2023 mention “Curtiss”, an apparent reference to Meta’s then vice-president of research, Curtiss Cobb. It states: “Curtiss’s goal for this work: how do we get the academic community to disavow Haidt. Can’t co-opt them, so how do we enrage them … so the media finds him not credible.”
It then adds: “Not thinking about this as a loud strategy. A below-the-line campaign.”

It suggests getting someone called “Gellman” to write “a takedown piece”. The “Gellman” figure is not identified in the document but Andrew Gelman, a professor of statistics and political science at Columbia University who has been critical of Haidt’s work, wrote in a blogpost this week that he was “never hired by Facebook to do a hit job on Jonathan Haidt”.
Gelman said he had received money from Mark Zuckerberg’s company in the past on a “no-strings” basis but had never been asked by Meta to look at social media’s impact on teenagers’ health.
Haidt’s book The Anxious Generation argued that widespread use of smartphones has caused a mental health crisis for young people.

The academic has become a persuasive advocate for strict regulation of digital media and devices, including bans on social media for under-16s and on smartphones in schools. Early this year the then health secretary, Wes Streeting, asked Haidt to address officials on a possible social media ban for under-16s in the UK.

The minutes were produced before Haidt published his book in 2024 and discuss responding to a Substack post written by the academic in which he reviews “a bunch of articles”. It is not clear whether Meta acted on the ideas outlined in the minutes.

In statement to the tech news website The Verge, Haidt said he was “not surprised” by the discussions, which were revealed in a court filing as part of a litigation brought by school districts suing the company.
“When companies can’t dispute the evidence, they go after the messenger,” he said.

items.title: US calls for an immediate end to Taliban violations of Afghan women’s rights
paragraphs: Editor's note: this story was translated from the original VOA Pashto article.
The United States says the Taliban’s violations of Afghan women’s rights are “unacceptable” and must stop immediately.

Speaking Tuesday during the annual open debate on women, peace and security at the U.N. Security Council, U.S. Deputy Representative to the United Nations Tammy Bruce said, “Over the past five years, the Taliban have systematically reversed decades of hard-won progress on women’s participation in peace and security... These practices are unacceptable and must cease immediately.”
Bruce went on to say that the Taliban have continued to bar women from education, training and employment.
After returning to power in August 2021, the Taliban rolled back two decades of progress made by Afghan women.

The group imposed repressive restrictions on women, barring them from secondary and university education, working in government agencies and non-government organizations, going to public parks, beauty salons and gyms, and traveling long distances without a close male relative.
Human Rights Watch in August reported that the Taliban’s ‘draconian’ policies made Afghanistan “one of the world’s gravest human rights crises, particularly for women and girls.”
The group has issued more than 100 decrees that curb women’s and girls’ rights and freedoms, including their right to get an education.
Tamana Zaryab Paryani, Afghan human rights activist, told the U.N. Security Council that the international community has failed Afghan women.

“Every day that passes, another generation of women and girls loses opportunities, dreams and futures. This is not only Afghanistan's crisis. Violations do not stop at borders. They spread when they are tolerated. They grew when they are ignored,” she said.
The Taliban have not changed their position on girls’ education and women’s rights despite the international pressure on the group.
Kate Foster, UK Deputy Permanent Representative to the U.N., said that women’s rights should be central to Afghanistan’s future.
“Peace cannot be sustainable while half the population is shut out of shaping it,” she added.
Zainab Razai, an Afghan women’s rights activist, told VOA that the international community should take concrete steps to end the violations of women’s rights in Afghanistan.

She said that the international community should “put more diplomatic pressure on the Taliban and support women in their efforts to secure their rights, reopen schools and universities to women and protect their freedoms.”
“Peace without women’s participation is no real peace,” Razai added.

items.title: Apple’s touchscreen MacBook Pro makes more sense than you might think
paragraphs: ”It doesn't work. Touch surfaces don't want to be vertical. After a short period of time you start to fatigue, and after an extended period of time your arm wants to fall off. It doesn't work, it's ergonomically terrible."

That’s what Steve Jobs said about the idea of a touchscreen MacBook in 2010. Those comments have been dredged up far and wide across the internet this week, as Apple yesterday launched, yes, the first ever touchscreen MacBook Pro. Clearly Apple thought the moment had finally come to give the concept a chance. And after testing it at the launch event in LA, I think the company might just be right.

But even before touching the device, I was intrigued by Apple’s marketing of it. The name, MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display, makes no mention of touch (although ‘PROLED’ is up there with ‘Apple Intelligence’ as an example of the company’s hilarious penchant for ‘brandifying’ existing words and phrases). Right from the bat, it seems Apple isn’t trying to pitch touch as the laptop’s headline feature. Indeed, judging by the cheer in the room, you’d think the return of the illuminated Apple logo was the biggest update.

When viewed as a bonus, an additional input option to sit alongside the traditional trackpad and keyboard, touch starts to make sense on the Mac. It’s useful for certain tasks, such as scrubbing through the timeline in Final Cut Pro, playing a virtual keyboard in Logic Pro, or pinching to zoom in on photos or maps. But it’s clear that, unlike the iPad, the Mac simply isn’t a touch-first device. But for creatives, a brand new input option can only be a good thing.

It helps that Apple has got the hardware and software just right. The PROLED display is absolutely stunning, and the touch super responsive (I experienced no latency when testing the aforementioned Logic Pro keyboard). And small software touches, such as the way the close/minimise window buttons enlarge when touched, make the experience much less fiddly than you might expect.

But it isn’t perfect. Apple claims that it has strengthened the hinge to reduce wobble when touching the upright screen, but I still noticed a fair amount of rebound. And while testing Final Cut, there were times when I found the trackpad more accurate.

Simply put, it’s a nice-to-have. And it’s a nicer-to-have than I expected. Had Apple gone ahead and called this the ’MacBook Ultra’, my eyebrows may have raised considerably more. Because on a notebook-style laptop, a touch screen is never going to feel like an ‘Ultra’ feature. In this case, though, it’s a delightfully well-executed bonus feature.
The MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display is available to pre-order now, starting at $2899.

Daniel John is Design Editor at Creative Bloq. He reports on the worlds of design, branding and lifestyle tech, and has covered several industry events including Milan Design Week, OFFF Barcelona and Adobe Max in Los Angeles. He has interviewed leaders and designers at brands including Apple, Microsoft and Adobe. Daniel's debut book of short stories and poems was published in 2018, and his comedy newsletter is a Substack Bestseller.

items.title: Herzog & de Meuron and Field Operations release visuals of Eames Institute of Infinite Curiosity
paragraphs: Master plan designs for the Eames Institute of Infinite Curiosity museum in California have been released, showing galleries connected via a bridge in an adapted 1960s warehouse and a landscape designed by Field Operations.

The updated design for the property in Navato, California, includes the 400-foot-long Great Hall, which the studios said will be “one of the largest single-span spaces for art installations in the country”, a 275-seat theatre, a Japanese-inspired garden and children’s play spaces.

The Eames Institute of Infinite Curiosity (the Eames Institute) bought the 88.5-acre property in 2025 to establish a public exhibition space and museum for its collection of furniture and other objects designed by architects Charles and Ray Eames.

The site includes a sawtooth-roofed warehouse and office building designed by architects Jan Lubicz-Nycz and John Savage Bolles, which were originally built for the McGraw-Hill publishing company in 1965.
Shoe company Birkenstock USA operated out of the site until 2019. The Eames Institute now plans to adapt the landscape and buildings for the project.

Architecture studios Herzog & de Meuron and EHDD were signed onto the project when it was first announced last year, and with this most recent update, Field Operations has been announced as the landscape designer.
“What makes this place so extraordinary is the relationship between its remarkable architecture and the landscape of Marin County,” said Field Operations partner Richard Kennedy.
“We imagined the grounds as a living extension of the museum. The idea is simple: ten landscapes, hundreds of places, and infinite journeys.”
According to the team, the warehouse will contain galleries, maker spaces, a theatre and a cafe, while the former office building will be converted into a pavilion for events.
Visitors will enter the warehouse building past a fountain, into a “warm, wood-clad space” containing admissions and the museum shop.

A grand stair will lead to a 120-foot polished stainless-steel bridge that traverses the gallery spaces below. The renders show the spaces as largely open-plan, with the enormous concrete bevels of the roof exposed above.

Other spaces, such as wood and ceramic workshops, will be distributed throughout the building. According to the team, the material palette will primarily consist of colour-stained plywood and plaster, and aluminium windows to “create a dialogue between old and new”.

For the landscape, Field Operations looked to an original plan by landscape architect Tito Patri, which used berms to help bury the buildings into their surroundings, buffering them from a highway which runs directly in front of the site.
The design includes a reconfigured parking and arrival sequence, gardens to the north and south of the warehouse, native stormwater gardens and custom furniture designed by the studio.
Overall, the masterplan will “transform what was once a private, truck-oriented industrial campus into a public cultural destination”, according to the team.

“For my grandparents, design was always grounded in curiosity and intention – looking closely, asking questions, embracing constraints, and finding beauty in the practical and the functional,” said Eames Institute co-founder Llisa Demetrios.

“The museum carries that spirit forward, and it feels especially meaningful to do so in a building that asked us to do the same: work within a remarkable existing structure to imagine what else it can become,” she continued.
Groundbreaking is expected for 2028, with openings projected to begin in 2030.
The project has garnered some criticism for being backed by Airbnb co-founder Joe Gebbia, who was appointed America’s first Chief Design Officer in 2025 under President Donald Trump.
Dezeen spoke to Gebbia about the appointment in 2025.
The Eames Institute was founded in 2023 and opened a California headquarters in 2024. San Francisco-based design agency Manual created its current brand identity and logo around the same time.

items.title: The new Atelico AI Engine gives game NPCs memories
paragraphs: When artists and game developers hear the term 'gen AI', they often assume it means cheaper concept art and character designs, and fewer people hired to make them. Studio Atelico is behind something else: AI that changes what happens while you play.

The independent studio has opened Early Access, by request, to the Atelico AI Engine, a toolkit for adding language models, image generation, speech systems and AI-driven character behaviour to games. It works with Unreal Engine, Unity, and Godot, and runs on players’ own hardware rather than cloud servers.

Atelico says developers can give NPCs personalities, motivations, relationships, and memories that shape their later actions, so a character could react to something you did hours earlier instead of following a fixed dialogue tree. In a video released today, it shows some rough ideas of how this works, with the player character offering an amount for a sword and the shopkeeper 'remembering' the day before the same player offered more coins, and so he ups the price. The release doesn’t name a game that uses this system yet.
Studio Atelico - AI Engine Debut - YouTube

Games have remembered player decisions for decades, though. Branching dialogue and reputation systems are hardly new, so the question is whether generative AI makes them more convincing, less memory-intensive, or just less predictable. An NPC that remembers you betrayed them sounds good, but if the game only gives them a different line of dialogue, that’s not much of a leap.

What matters is whether developers use those memories to change how a character behaves, so your choices feel like they count without driving the game down dead ends; after all, that shopkeeper could keep raising prices or even decide you don't have good credit, and any kingdom-saving shenanigans are over because one guy wouldn't sell you a sword.

Atelico's AI Engine idea differs from simply prompting an algorithm to vibe a game or asset. Most of the backlash against AI in creative industries has centred on how it produces work. Artists have objected to models trained on their work without permission, and developers worry studios will use generative tools to cut costs and jobs. In the 2026 Game Developers Conference survey, 52% of industry professionals said generative AI was bad for the industry, up from 30% the year before.

Generating a background texture or creating a 3D model from a sketch or text, as Maxon's AI announcement is teasing, and managing an NPC’s memories are different propositions. The first can replace an asset an artist might have been paid to make. The second is a gameplay system, and could give designers new ways to build interactive stories.

The two do overlap. The AI Engine also generates images, and Atelico’s debut game, Bobium Brawlers, lets players describe a creature in plain language and get a portrait and playable deck on their phone.

Several questions remain open. Atelico says the engine supports open-source language models and uses its own image-generation technology, but it doesn't say how any of those models were trained. It's also unclear how much control developers have over output, or what happens when an NPC says something that undermines the story. The studio says the engine has safeguards to keep output aligned with a game’s creative direction, including a safety pipeline that rewrites problematic outputs instead of blocking them. Those claims will need testing in real games.

Running on-device means, in Atelico’s account, no recurring server costs, no network latency and player data staying on the player’s hardware. It doesn’t answer the training question, and local inference still strains players’ devices, though Atelico has the ethical agreement ARC, the Artist Rights Contract, a creator-agreement framework that proposes upfront compensation and consent for how its AI is implemented.

I'm interested in developments like the AI Engine and Nvidia's similar ACE platform for gen-AI NPCs, because they could lead to new gameplay ideas and ways to interact with game worlds where choice matters. An NPC that remembers what you’ve done could make a game feel personal, or at least offer choices that matter, not the illusion of choice.

Ian Dean is Editor, Digital Arts & 3D at Creative Bloq, and the former editor of many leading magazines. These titles included ImagineFX, 3D World and video game titles Play and Official PlayStation Magazine. Ian launched Xbox magazine X360 and edited PlayStation World. For Creative Bloq, Ian combines his experiences to bring the latest news on digital art, VFX and video games and tech, and in his spare time he doodles in Procreate, ArtRage, and Rebelle while finding time to play Xbox and PS5.

items.title: Pakistan, Afghan Taliban trade accusations over ‘unprovoked’ attacks
paragraphs: Editor's note: this story was translated from the original VOA Dari article.
Pakistani officials and the Afghan Taliban blamed each other this week for what they described as “unprovoked” attacks at a border crossing.

A Pakistani official in South Waziristan Lower, in northwestern Khyber Pakhtunkhwa province, said Tuesday that one person was killed and five others were injured when a mortar fired by the Taliban struck civilian homes and shops in the border town of Angoor Adda.
Calling the Taliban attack "unprovoked," the local official said in a post on X that Pakistani forces responded, “effectively and heavily.”

The Afghan Taliban said that Pakistani forces, however, carried out four drone strikes in the southeastern Afghan province of Paktika “without any provocation” in Angoor Adda and the provincial commissioner’s office.
Angoor Adda is an important town that serves as a trade and transit crossing between Afghanistan and Pakistan.

The crossing has been closed since October 2025, after Pakistani forces and the Afghan Taliban clashed along the border. Because of the border closure, crossings between Afghanistan and Pakistan and trade between the two countries has declined by some 95% in the past year.
The United Nations Mission in Afghanistan said in September that it had documented more than 1,100 civilian deaths and injuries from cross-border attacks in Afghanistan so far in 2026.
Pakistan accuses the Taliban of sheltering the militant group Tehrik-e-Taliban Pakistan, or TTP, which has taken responsibility for attacks inside Pakistan.
The Afghan Taliban publicly deny harboring any militant group, but a U.N. report, released in August, said that the Taliban continue to support TTP.
A spokesperson for the U.S. State Department told VOA in an email statement in July that Pakistan has the “right to defend against terrorist attacks.”
“The Pakistani people have suffered greatly at the hands of terrorists,” the unnamed spokesperson said at the time.
The U.N. said that the Pakistani Taliban’s attacks inside Pakistan have increased.
Pakistan has said that the attacks inside Pakistan have resulted in more than 3,500 casualties so far in 2026.
Ismail Khan, an editor at Pakistan’s Dawn newspaper, told VOA that relations between the two countries have deteriorated.

He said that although China, Turkey and Qatar tried to mediate between Pakistan and the Afghan Taliban, their efforts have not yielded results, and that tensions between the two countries are likely to remain high.

items.title: The perfect closed-back wired headphones just got a $40 discount
paragraphs: Closed-back headphones are notoriously difficult to tune properly. Without open grilles allowing drivers to breathe, internal cup reflections and low-end buildup can muddy the sound or result in a hollow, clinical presentation. But Sennheiser managed to crack that formula with the HD 480 Pro. Now, the upgraded bundle – the HD 480 Pro Plus (which is the same headphone, but with a cool hard carry case) – has had $40 knocked off over at Amazon.

For full details on why I think this is the best closed-back headphone, head over to my detailed HD 480 Pro review. It's my top overall pick in my list of the best-sounding wired headphones of any price.

Usually retailing at $439, the HD 480 Pro Plus package is down to $399, matching the list price of the base model while bundling Sennheiser’s dedicated protective travel case and premium accessories at no extra cost. In short: you get the best closed-back headphone out there, and a free hard travel case!
For me, the Sennheiser HD 480 Pro is simply the finest closed-back pair I've tested, setting a fresh benchmark in a slightly compromised category.

Any manufacturer can tune cans to sound exciting, with booming mid-bass and ear-piercing treble spikes. Sennheiser took the far more difficult route of making everything sound fundamentally correct. It's basically the most exciting 'boring' set I've ever heard.

Instead of the boomy, loose bass that plagues most closed-back sets, the HD 480 delivers low frequencies with speed, detail, and grip. It avoids encroaching on the lower midrange (for the most part), ensuring vocal clarity remains intact. Those vocals and acoustic instruments sound lifelike, avoiding the scooped or honky timbre common in studio tracking headphones.

Lower highs are smooth and relaxed without sacrificing detail or a sense of space, giving high-frequency elements actual body rather than harsh sizzle. I can totally understand if someone wants more treble than the 480 Pro gives, but sibilant treble is fatiguing. You don't get that issue here.

At just 272 grams, the chassis avoids the heavy clamping force associated with traditional tracking cans. The modular architecture with washable, replaceable components also means you'll be able to hang on to yours for decades of daily listening.
Subscribe to the Creative Bloq newsletter for details of expert-curated offers, bringing the tools you need to create – and products perfect for the design-obsessed.

Beren cut his teeth as Staff Writer on digital art magazine ImagineFX, and has since worked on and edited several creative titles, including Paint & Draw and Computer Arts. As Ecom Editor on Creative Bloq, when he's not reviewing the latest audiophile headphones or evaluating the best designed ergonomic office chairs, he’s testing laptops, TVs and monitors, all so he can find the best tech deals for Creative Bloq’s digital professional audience.

items.title: Mass Effect 5 art director says it's “truly heartbreaking” we'll never play his team's game
paragraphs: When EA announced last week that it was closing BioWare, the studio behind Mass Effect and Dragon Age, gamers worldwide howled in protest, mourning the games they'll never get to play. When footage, info, and visuals behind the cancelled Mass Effect 5, now also known as Mass Effect Universe, came to light, fans were even more distraught.

At Creative Bloq, we also felt for the artists who'll never get to build these games or see their Mass Effect 5 work seen widely. Now one of those artists has just added his voice to the chorus in quite an unexpected way.

On X, Sparth revealed that from April until last week, he'd quietly been working as art director of the Mass Effect franchise. In other words, he was responsible for what the next Mass Effect would look like. Yet now, nobody will ever see it.

in light of last week’s news about BioWare’s closure, I felt it was time to share something I haven’t talked about publicly: from April until last week, I was the art director of the Mass Effect franchise.October 27, 2026

It's a story every creative will recognise: a talented team doing some of the best work of their careers, only for it to vanish into nothing because of decisions made by people way above their pay grade.

In case you haven't been paying attention, here's a quick recap. Founded in Canada in 1995, BioWare made role-playing games where you play a character whose choices shape the story. Its Mass Effect trilogy (2007-12) became one of gaming’s most celebrated series, but recent releases disappointed, and its umbrella company EA, now carrying around $20bn of debt after a Saudi-led buyout, has cut 400 jobs and closed the studio.

Now, here's the skinny on Sparth. Real name Nicolas Bouvier, he's worked as a concept artist in video games since 1996, with credits including Prince of Persia: Warrior Within, the original Assassin's Creed, Halo 4, Halo 5: Guardians, and Halo Infinite.

Outside gaming, he's painted more than 100 sci-fi and fantasy book covers and authored the Structura series of art books. He's been a regular presence on Creative Bloq and our sister title ImagineFX over the years, sharing everything from his custom Photoshop brushes to VR sculpting experiments.

In his X thread, he says it was "a privilege to work alongside such a talented team, with the shared ambition of exploring new creative territories while staying true to the legacy and spirit of the Mass Effect trilogy."

Next comes the sucker punch. "Knowing that this work will never see the light of day is truly heartbreaking. We were good at this. We really were. I'm thinking about the team, the talent, what we could have achieved."

And then, perhaps the most telling line of all: "In nearly 30 years in this industry, I've rarely seen a group so tightly knit, so experienced, and so good at working together. And I feel extremely honored to have been part of it."

As for his own future, Sparth is candid in saying: "I simply don't know. For now, I'll take some time before figuring out next steps. In the meantime, I wish everyone affected all the very best for what lies ahead."

So why is this such a big deal? Well, it's largely because of who Sparth was replacing. Derek Watts was Mass Effect's long-time art director, and the man most responsible for the trilogy's distinctive look. He retired before work on the new game was complete, and replacing him would never be easy.

Mike Gamble, BioWare's project director on Mass Effect, makes that clear in a reply to Sparth's thread. "Nic, you were incredible," he writes. "There are few people on the planet I would have chosen to replace Mr Watts after he retired, and I'm glad we got to work together." Sparth's response is characteristically modest. "Derek's legacy was everything. I was humbly an extremely dedicated participant to an amazing human adventure, thanks to you, him, and the team."
On paper, this appointment was inspired and looked set for great things. In practice, we may never see Sparth's work on the project, which EA owns.

Agonisingly, though, we've learned a fair bit about what the team was building. An internal trailer has leaked online, reportedly revealing the title "Mass Effect: Universe", and YouTuber Dantics, who sat on a panel of fans BioWare consulted during development, has shared details that IGN says it has verified.
I Worked With BioWare on the Next Mass Effect - Here's What They Were Making - YouTube

According to Dantics, the game is set more than 600 years after the original trilogy, in a galaxy split into three rival power blocs, more like an interstellar cold war than another apocalyptic invasion. One of those, the Geth (a race of sentient machines from the original games), had become a superpower that built huge megastructures.

Players would have taken the role of a customisable secret agent, a James Bond type with experimental implants that let you see through walls and hack your surroundings. Missions would have been handcrafted, but with lots of freedom in how you tackled them, and fan-favourite character Liara was set to return.

Dantics says it "looked incredible", and the responses to Sparth's thread suggest that many fans agree. "I have to say the artistic vision was/is phenomenal," writes one. "I can only imagine what else there could have been."

It'd be great if EA released some of the Mass Effect concept art one day. It would be a small but meaningful way to honour the BioWare staff who've lost their jobs. In the meantime, whatever Sparth does next, I'm sure we'll be featuring his work on Creative Bloq again soon.

Tom May is an award-winning journalist specialising in art, design, photography and technology. He is the author of the books The 50 Greatest Designers (Arcturus) and Great TED Talks: Creativity (Pavilion). Tom was previously editor of Professional Photography magazine, associate editor at Creative Bloq, and deputy editor at net magazine.

items.title: Nvidia CEO reportedly targeted by Chinese spy
paragraphs: US intelligence agencies believe the Nvidia chief executive, Jensen Huang, has been targeted by a Chinese spy who had done business with him, according to a new report by the New York Times.

Alice Huang or Huang Le, of no relation to the Nvidia CEO, is an executive at a Singapore-based datacenter company called Megaspeed. She had previously been suspected of smuggling Nvidia chips to China, prompting American officials to surveil and monitor her. Those officials have determined that she was acting as a Chinese intelligence asset, passing commercial information to Beijing, the New York Times reported, citing unnamed sources.

In the course of their surveillance, American officials determined that Alice Huang developed a close relationship with Nvidia’s CEO, according to the Times. Nvidia’s powerful chips serve as a cornerstone of the AI boom and have vaulted Jensen Huang into one of the most influential leadership positions in the industry. In that position, he has developed a close partnership with Donald Trump as the US government attempts to defend its position as a leader in AI development.
White House officials are reportedly alarmed by Alice Huang’s access to the head of Nvidia precisely because of the close relationship he’s developed with Trump, according to the New York Times.

The Trump administration has imposed restrictions on exports of advanced AI chips to China as a matter of national security. Megaspeed’s Huang was suspected to have been helping the government get around those restrictions.
In a statement to the New York Times, Nvidia said there was nothing out of the ordinary about the Nvidia CEO’s interactions with Alice Huang.

“Meetings with customers are part of a CEO’s job; Jensen talks with thousands of customer executives every year,” the spokesperson said in a statement. Megaspeed and customers like it “receive ordinary business information – not sensitive Nvidia trade secrets – and zero information relevant to national security”.

items.title: What is it like to work when your co-workers are AI agents?
paragraphs: On an average workday, Dhruv Amin chats with dozens of colleagues to get things done at his AI startup Anything. He might ask Gwen, his executive assistant, to schedule a meeting, then troubleshoot a technical problem with Cody, his coding partner. Then he might check in with Betsy for search engine optimization, or Juno for onboarding customers. If the office runs out of snacks, he sends a Slack message to Justin, the office manager charged with stocking the kitchen.

But none of these co-workers are people. They’re artificial intelligence agents, software that handles tasks without human intervention. Anything is one of several startups building them, and betting on a future where workplaces will increasingly turn over their sales, marketing, coding and other tasks to semi-autonomous AI. At Anything, there are 15 human employees and roughly 150 agents – a ratio that Amin believes will soon be the norm.
“I think in a year, every company will have more AI co-workers than human co-workers,” he said.

In the San Francisco tech scene, agents have quickly become a new status symbol, showing that a company can do more with less, several startup employees said. It’s common for workers to brag about how well their agents can handle common office drudgery like answering emails or help with essential business operations such as giving sales pitches.

But agents are also creating tension. They are alienating customers and colleagues who seek human interaction, eliminating roles and forcing employees to become overnight managers of the bots that often make mistakes.

While startup techies such as Amin are some of the early adopters, corporate America may not be far behind. About 40% of large organizations used AI agents in some capacity between May 2025 and June 2026, up from 27% the year before, according to McKinsey’s State of AI Global Survey. Companies also expect to scale back their workforce by 10% to 15% over the next few years as they delegate more work to AI, a recent report from Boston Consulting Group found. In the present moment, companies are not seeing major productivity gains from AI, MIT research shows.
A wave of startups and big tech companies are fueling the push toward AI agents, selling companies on automated co-workers.

There’s Viktor, a company that lets companies create their own “AI chief of staff”, and Lindy, which makes customizable agents for sales, customer support or admin work. OpenAI’s Dots, Anthropic’s Claude Cowork and Microsoft’s Scout can each integrate with thousands of other tools to handle projects after employees leave for the day.

Each of these products promises companies the tantalizing dream of cranking out new co-workers, who never clock out, complain or cause human resource problems. Delegating to an agent is also cheaper than hiring a human, making a large ratio of agents to humans a point of pride among startups.
“That’s the status symbol,” said Rafael López Muñoz, chief of staff at Wordware, a San Francisco-based startup that makes AI tools. Outsourcing parts of the job to agents is “an extreme time saver”.

Lindy, for example, used to have almost 50 employees. Now, after laying off one-third of its staff, the company says it has about 20 and has filled many of its open roles with AI agents instead. It’s still hiring people for some positions.

“People are constrained by having two hands and 24 hours in a day,” said Haneen Azhar, Lindy’s senior growth marketing manager. “Now, that constraint has gone away, because your one laptop screen can be divided into 16 different agents that are running in parallel. These tools make you feel so powerful.”

Azhar says she has outsourced a long list of tasks to agents, from managing her calendar to testing how well customers respond to different marketing taglines to generating brand images. She worries about her role in eliminating jobs as she offloads work to agents. Azhar says that Lindy’s agents now handle product announcements, social media posts and marketing videos, work that used to be handled by about 100 people in its creator program, for example.
She also worries about how the shift will affect the next generation of workers. “If I was trying to get my foot in the door right now, I’d be worse off than I was a year ago,” she said.

In some cases, agents have stepped in to cover for missing staff. Jay Blumenfield runs a production company in Los Angeles that creates vertical microdramas – short, scripted series meant to be viewed on your phone. The production schedules are tight, and so are budgets. So when he had to fire an assistant director on a recent shoot, he decided to try using an AI agent instead of hiring a replacement at the last minute.

Blumenfield uploaded the script and prompted the agent to do everything the assistant director would have done. The agent produced the schedule, call sheet and day’s script, and then sent the materials to the cast and crew. The result? Everyone got their work done.
“It would have been an unmitigated disaster, but this kind of saved us,” he said.
Now, Blumenfield and his partner, Tony Marsh, run the company alone with a suite of agents. “We don’t even have an assistant anymore,” he said.

AI agents handle everything from reading scripts, running social media and planning travel. He created an agent called Shirley to act as his chief of staff, and another that scouts and books locations needed for upcoming shoots. Normally, he would have to hire two to three people to work on these tasks for two or three weeks, he said. Now, it happens within hours.

Still, it does feel a little taboo to use so many agents instead of hiring people, Blumenfield said. But the economics of filmmaking had changed enough that he felt he simply didn’t have a choice. By using agents, he can afford to make the microdramas that star actual people – at least, for now.

“The game in Hollywood is that you’re not allowed to talk about using AI,” he said, reflecting industry fears that it could end creative work. “I don’t want it to replace people. But we should be honest about how it is helping us.”

Several workers who regularly rely on agents are adamant that the tech can’t replace the human workforce entirely. But agents are changing the kinds of skills and workers needed to manage them. Agents can code, making routine programming skills less valuable, but they still require humans to prompt them thoughtfully and judge the results. They also require a fair amount of oversight.

López Muñoz said that after he let AI agents run his startup’s recruiting, he spent most of his time undoing agents’ mistakes, such as mixing up candidates with similar names or hallucinating parts of a résumé.
“The qualities we’re looking for are changing,” Azhar said about new hires, adding that he now prioritizes the ability to coordinate and delegate over years of experience.
Tarek Abillama, founder of River, which makes an AI agent for sales calls, said workers now are required to constantly check AI’s work and give it feedback.

“We all became managers,” Abillama said. “We have to be great at multitasking, because now you’re running six agents who are doing different tasks.” Abillama’s first agent, a clone of himself, gave sales demos of River’s product. Later, he replaced it with an agent called Liv, a female persona that researches customers and their companies, demos the product and handles the sale process in any language, at any time of day.

Even though River tells customers that Liv is an AI agent, Abillama said people seem to anthropomorphize the experience. He’s seen transcripts from calls with Liv where customers appear to flirt with it. Customers have also tried to push the agent to go off-script and get bigger discounts.

Founder Brooke Hopkins said while her San Francisco-based AI voice startup Coval uses agents to speed up tasks, she views the tech as tools, not colleagues. She’s also banned her company from using agents to communicate with customers, suggesting that it’s lazy and sends the wrong message.
“I can immediately look at an email and know whether or not it was written by AI,” she said. “If I get an email and it feels like a human, then I usually will read it.”
The loss of human interaction has become a point of tension, Hopkins said. Using an agent to handle a company’s sales demos or recruiting process might save time, but at what cost?
Duncan McClure, who evaluates AI models as a contractor, said he had recently been hounded with emails and phone calls from AI agents seeking to hire him.

“The message it sends is that we don’t care enough to actually put in any effort,” he said, adding that he was turned off from working with those employers. Recruiters may save hours by using agents, “but it’s my time that they’re wasting”.

Though AI can automate the time-consuming and costly parts of people’s jobs, that doesn’t always mean working less, several startup employees said. Amin, for example, said he gets more done with agents. Still, he hasn’t stopped working on weekends.

items.title: Puddlesuits, movie nights and daytime baths: how to survive rainy days with small kids
paragraphs: Before becoming a mum, I never appreciated quite how complicated getting out the front door would be with kids in tow. But in my four and a half years of parenting two small people, I can confidently say it’s nothing compared with the challenge of a day spent inside when outside is off-limits. Whether because of endless rain or illnesses you don’t want to pass on, I panic at the thought of filling the hours spent indoors.

Being outside is profoundly helpful for my mental health, and it comes with its own built-in entertainment for small children: a bus ride becomes a sensory experience, a trip to the doctor’s an opportunity to pick up role-play ideas.

But what to do when leaving the house really isn’t possible? Over the years, I have developed a list of ideas for keeping my children (and me) sane indoors, and the products that have helped us muddle through (and dare I say, enjoy) those days. I’ve also recommended some gear to help you brave the wet weather.
How have you been keeping the kids – and yourself – entertained during the rainy days? Let us know by emailing us at thefilter@theguardian.com
An unexpectedly popular item in our house came from one of the kids’ many generous aunties and uncles: a play tent. My initial thoughts? “How big! How intrusive! How unnecessary!” How wrong I was.

Kids of all ages seem to gravitate towards it – perhaps owing to the illusion of privacy it offers (as well as being a very non-obvious place to scarper when playing hide-and-seek, wink wink). When ours was played with so much and broke beyond repair, I didn’t think twice about replacing it with this lovely, bright Djeco one. We chose it because of its colourful design, but I’d also seen one at a play cafe from the same brand and admired how sturdy it was. It’s a great place for us all to get cosy and read, and somewhere for my four-year-old to take a minute when his little brother is destroying his beautiful Magna-Tiles creations.

That brings me nicely to Magna-Tiles. Parents seem to enjoy these almost as much as their kids do, and they’re popular with older children too. We don’t have it, but I just know this Rail Racers set would be an absolute hit in this house. There are imitation brands, but we invested in the official Magna-Tiles, which have lasted really well and endured being lobbed around by our toddler – who may or may not end up being a bowler in later life, given how much he likes to throw. Friends with cheaper knock-offs say you get what you pay for in this case.

Look, I don’t really understand why, but my children were given this car toy by another auntie for Christmas last year, and every single child who has crossed the threshold of our house since then, big and small, has been obsessed with it. Not only does it play really earwormy songs, which they love, but it has a roller beneath a screen that shows a road unfolding in front of you as you “drive” with the steering wheel. You can also just push it around like any other toy car. So many friends have gone on to buy one too, but sorry in advance for the noise of the songs and for the fact it is, essentially, a big lump of plastic.

Our kids have a higgledy-piggledy medley of millions of different craft bits and pieces that their mother has bought for herself, used once and discarded. A visit to a craft shop such as Hobbycraft is probably the cheapest option for this, but there are a few nice premade kits out there too, like the Djeco one below. Another wildly popular craft activity in our house – also from a clever auntie – is this foil sticker set from Galt. It’s easy to use with minimal mess, so it ticks all my boxes.

Before I became a mum, I used to say I would be vigilant in rotating toys to maintain interest (putting some into storage and bringing others out from time to time), then I actually became a mum and, well, that never happened. But then I discovered Lovevery.

At first, I was a bit confused about why our kids might need new toys every few months, but after a few boxes, the value became evident. Those who sign up get a new set of toys (often sustainably made) every two to three months that are focused at their current age. It’s not cheap, but we’ve bought one or two boxes over the years or asked family to (as well as being sent some samples as press gifts in the past). There are favourites in every kit that have been thrown into the routine toy circulation, and saving them for a time stuck indoors has been a total salvation when I’m low on ideas.

The toys are good quality, often wooden, and a one-off box makes a great present for grandparents to give when they’re looking for new ideas. The newborn Looker play kit is especially valuable, chiefly owing to the wooden mobile I hung above the changing table, which helped entertain them while I was committing the grave offence of cleaning their bottoms.

When our eldest was given one of these as a toddler, I struggled to see the value. But then came baby number two: a future rock-climbing tornado who makes it his business to scale any piece of furniture that crosses his path. Pikler triangles can be added to with other products to make little indoor climbing frames, and ours has a slide, which our toddler spends his life climbing up and throwing himself down, especially on days when the park is off limits.

We have a wide array of Ravensburger puzzles, gifted by a very keen nanna. The brand makes a wide range of puzzles for different ages, so it’s worth investing in a couple. Hits in our house include the Hey Duggee one for younger kids and the current obsession: Spidey & His Amazing Friends (Ghost Spider specifically – IYKYK).

No imagination-based toy has been more used in our house than this ice-cream shop, made mostly of wood, by American brand Melissa & Doug. My friend’s children, seven and nine, still won’t part with theirs, which in my book is the sign of a good toy.
Melissa & Doug Scoop and Serve ice-cream counter

I have seen these Speed Track car-racing tracks pop up in living rooms and birthday parties, with little kids, teenagers and even adults getting in on the action. It works with most small car toys you probably already own, and it’s easy to roll up and put away.

A relatively new phenomenon, “play sofas” (modular sofas that can be rearranged to spark kids’ imagination) are fast becoming a go-to for parents of active children. Ours is from the Irish brand Baby Elegance, and has become a castle, a train, a spaceship, a cave, a house, a shop and many other things, all in the first few months. It has a foam core covered in hard-wearing corduroy fabric and doubles as a very comfortable bed for fans of what I like to call lying-down parenting (favoured by those with early-rising offspring, who have difficulties sitting up or who may have just had one too many the night before).
Suitable for: 1+ (with adult supervision)

I first came across Stapelstein stepping stones at a local play cafe, and initially had no idea what the appeal was. Doubly so when I found out the price. Nonetheless, I have been blown away by just how many hours of fun my two have had playing with them, especially when friends come over. They’re made from high-density foamed plastic, making them lightweight and easy to pick up, but sturdy enough to support up to 180kg in weight, so they’re perfect for stacking, climbing on, using as hats or making seats from.

They are great for mobility and practising balance, and they spark my kids’ imagination like nothing else I’ve seen. Visiting older kids have been just as obsessed with these, suggesting it may be a toy for the long haul, too.
Suitable for: 1+ (with adult supervision)

The Yoto player is a screen-free audio player that’s a reliable all-rounder for both my kids. We listen to stories and songs, and grandparents and other relatives have recorded their own cards of them reading stories or singing for the kids to listen to. Cards can be targeted to a specific age, too. Our two-year-old loves the nursery rhymes and our four-year-old listens to stories, and both get a real kick out of “being in control” of the content, without realising that it’s actually their father and me who oversee it all. The smartphone app means we can stop and start playback from our phones, and we have recently discovered the software is available on Android Auto, meaning we can listen to our cards when in the car.

Bad weather always leaves me jealous of friends who have projectors ready to turn their living rooms into home cinemas. A friend recommended this Samsung one, and it’s on my “if we ever have spare money” list.

Friends with older kids rave about the Nintendo Switch their families got for Christmas. It can be played alone or as a family, with plenty of games for everyone. In their case, the console is kept in the living room, and children can swap TV time for console time on weekends. Mario Kart and Just Dance are good for getting the whole family together.
The Switch 2 is the latest, but the original Switch has a huge library of games and is now cheaper thanks to the arrival of its successor.

I bought this fairly extensive colour palette of food dyes from Amazon, and the kids love being able to pick which shade they will play with that day. I use this recipe, but there are loads out there. One thing to be aware of is these playdoughs are more likely to stain than the shop-bought stuff, so are best limited to the kitchen.

When all else fails, I chuck my kids into the bath and let them have an extended play session they wouldn’t ordinarily have in the evening. If I’m feeling generous, I throw in a Munchkin ColourMix bath bomb, which my kids adore, even if the yellow shade does often make me think they may have had an accident.

I found a pile of costumes in my kids’ sizes on Vinted for days when we just need a little extra inspiration. I spent about £6 and got a huge range for whoever they feel like being on that particular day.
A timeless classic that is still a favourite for a reason. All you need is some chairs and bed sheets. For extra pizzazz, I sometimes add fairy lights, but this is not at all necessary.
We also often play the floor is lava (with the very annoying song you can find on Spotify), hide-and-seek or Bluey-style “keepy uppy” with a balloon and accompanying soundtrack music.

We live in the rainy south-west, so to have a fighting chance of leaving the house between November and April, good waterproofs for the kids are a must. For smaller ones, many friends have recommended these Muddy Puddles suits with a removable warm inner layer for adapting them to fluctuating temperatures.

For older kids, I love shell trousers because they really do keep kids dry. I am a huge Mini Rodini fan and, though they are expensive, their sizes span 1.5 to 2 years generally, so on average, can be worn for two winters. I also know many fans of Polarn O Pyret, which offers more reasonably priced options for toddlers through to 12-year-olds.

A good pair of wellies is essential, and my kids have always liked their colour-changing ones from Grass & Air. Put their little tootsies in some merino wool socks like these from Polarn O Pyret and job’s a good’un.
One final tip I must add is not to buy fur-lined wellies. I know they look cute, but trust me, they get wet quickly, and then your kid is essentially walking around in soggy socks.

Don’t buy anything until you’ve read the Filter, the Guardian’s home for truly independent product reviews and recommendations. Whether you’re after rigorous tests or shopping inspiration, affordable gifts or advice on how to make your belongings last longer, we’re here to help you make smarter, more sustainable choices.
The Filter is packed with trustworthy buying advice on everything from coffee machines to hiking boots, mascara to secateurs. So visit us today and start buying better and smarter, and wasting less.
For more, read the best wellies for everyone and the best umbrellas
Rose Stokes is a Bath-based journalist who balances writing about women’s health and parenting two small humans

items.title: 'The internet's a less whimsical place' - YouTuber Jacksepticeye branches out
paragraphs: Seán McLoughlin, aka Jacksepticeye, has been taking on more voice acting roles
ByAndrew Rogers and Tom RichardsonBBC Newsbeat
The world's changed a lot since Seán McLoughlin, better known to 31 million subscribers as Jacksepticeye, began making YouTube videos.
He started uploading in 2012, in what many people consider to be the platform's "golden age" when vlogging, video game playthroughs and comedy escapism were all the rage.
Like many in the content creation space, he's been branching out in recent years, taking more acting jobs and getting involved in film production.
BBC Newsbeat caught up with McLoughlin to talk about his new role, his work on bringing one of his favourite video games to the big screen and why he misses the "whimsical" days of the internet.
McLoughlin plays influencer Finnvictus in the latest Hitman mission
McLoughlin got famous playing video games, and these days there's a good chance you'll see - or hear - him in one.
After a role in the 2025 superhero adventure Dispatch, McLoughlin's got a new role in Hitman, the successful "assassination simulator" from Danish studio IO Interactive.
He plays controversial content creator Finn Colton, known as Finnvictus.
Although the fictional character shares McLoughlin's likeness and voice, he says the "manosphere-adjacent influencer" is not based on him.
As the name of the game suggests, players aren't there to collab with him.
He's one of the celebrity "elusive targets" Hitman's developers occasionally place in the game to encourage returning fans.
"If you love me it'll be funny to play and you'll get to kill me in different ways," says McLoughlin.
"If you hate me maybe that's even more fun to play."
It's not the first time McLoughlin's worked with IO - he appeared, briefly, in their James Bond game 007: First Light earlier this year.
He'd hoped to watch other streamers react to the blink-and-you'll-miss-it cameo, but says many of his friends missed it.
"This time you're forced to interact with me," he says, even if that does involve thinking of imaginative ways to kill him off.
Bloodborne, originally released on PlayStation 4, is considered an all-time classic
Earlier this year, McLoughlin was also unveiled as a producer on an animated movie version of Bloodborne, one of the highest-rated video games of all time.
Some parts of its passionate fan base reacted negatively to the announcement, questioning the YouTuber's credentials.
McLoughlin reassured them he's a huge fan of the games and has a tattoo of a Hunter's Mark - one of the game's key items - to prove it.
He's described himself as a "vibe-checker" and sees it as his responsibility to make sure the adaptation is done properly.
"If it feels off, especially with something like Bloodborne, people can feel it immediately, even if they don't know what they're pointing towards," he says.
"They know the game so well that if the atmosphere, or the world, or the vibe feels off, they'll pick up on it pretty fast."
McLoughlin says he's been trying to pick people for the project who have ideally played Bloodborne and "have a feeling" for what it's all about.
"I feel like I have good instincts on what works and what doesn't and what I like and what I don't like," he says.
"So the producing side of it fits a lot more naturally for me right now."
Screen adaptations are a big trend in video games at the moment, but they're not the only thing seizing the industry.
Hitman's new mission lands just weeks before the launch of the hugely-anticipated Grand Theft Auto 6.
It won't be released on disc at launch, a move that's arguably accelerated the game industry's move towards digital-only games.
McLoughlin, who fondly remembers PlayStation cases on a bedroom shelf and getting new games for Christmas, says "it would suck to see physical games disappear completely".
"Just in terms of the humanity behind it all, I think it would be a shame to see that stuff disappear because it's a magical experience," he says.
The use of generative artificial intelligence (AI) in video game development is another hot topic at the moment.
Earlier this month, Epic Games, makers of Fortnite, announced a "pivot" towards using AI as a primary development tool.
Like many players, McLoughlin's opposed to its use.
So no chance of seeing a Jacksepticeye Fortnite skin any time soon?
"I think the chances of that happening were already zero before anything related to that even happened," he says.
"But now it's definitely, definitely unlikely."
McLoughlin also appeared as reformed villain Punch Up in superhero adventure game Dispatch
Physical games, GenAI and content creators' career moves are sure to generate discourse, and conversations online are another thing McLoughlin thinks have changed since he started out.
He says there's been a "rise of anti-communities", where people will "rush to condemn a film or game before it's even been released".
"I'm just sad that the internet is such an angry place these days," he says.
"It's just zero to a thousand immediately. I think we're just not there in terms of having nuanced discussions about anything.
"But I think that's just endemic of the internet in general."
McLoughlin thinks that could be linked to people's real life worries.
"Right now, it's just people are angry in general, just at the world," he says.
"So it's harder to interact with stuff online these days.
"It's a less whimsical space. But hopefully that's something that can change."
McLoughlin's doing his bit to bring people together in December with his annual Thankmas event.
The fundraiser took a break last year but its returning to raise money for the Make-A-Wish Foundation.
"I think it's a nice little pinprick of light in the middle of everything else going on," he says.
And while he's not afraid to speak his mind, he says he is mindful of letting others do the talking sometimes.
"I'm trying to get better about not giving an opinion about absolutely everything any more," he says.
"Because I think there's too much of that in the world."
