items.title: Family row over George Michael items up for auction - including Faith guitar
paragraphs: A family row has broken out over an auction of George Michael memorabilia taking place on Thursday.
The guitar played by the singer-songwriter in the Faith music video is one of several items being auctioned by Sworders from the collection of Siobhan Bailey, Michael's long-time personal assistant.
Siobhan died in 2014 and the items are being sold by her estranged husband Ian Belcher, who inherited them after her death.

Gerard Bailey, Siobhan's brother, told the BBC she "would be horrified at the prospect of the auction being held in her name and that her personal, cherished possessions are being sold off to the highest bidder". Both Sworders and Belcher declined to comment.
Sworders describes the 32 lots as a "remarkable group of memorabilia from the collection of Siobhan Bailey, George Michael's long-time personal assistant and trusted confidante".

Michael grew up in Hertfordshire and shot to fame alongside Andrew Ridgeley in pop duo Wham! He went on to enjoy solo success with hits such as Faith, Careless Whisper, Father Figure, Outside and Fastlove. He died in 2016.
Siobhan was in the process of divorcing Belcher when she died, but was legally still married to him. She did not leave a will.
Her brother claimed she had started to draw up a will shortly before she died, which would have left the items to her nieces and nephews, but it was not registered.
There is no suggestion that Belcher does not have the right to sell the items, because her estate legally passed to him when she died.
Bailey said if his sister had lived a few weeks longer, the items would not have passed to Belcher because he would not have been considered her next of kin.

In a letter to the auction house seen by the BBC, Bailey said the rest of the family considers the auction a "breach of [Siobhan's] privacy", adding that the use of her name is "disingenuous" and "wholly unethical".
He told the auction house that Belcher's "misuse of my sister's name" is "frankly dishonourable", and profiteering from the items was "egregiously shameful".
Bailey has asked that the auction should not go ahead, or, if it does, that it be in Belcher's name rather than Siobhan's.
Bailey began working as Michael's personal assistant in 1984, joining him in the year Wham! had their first number-one hit with Wake Me Up Before You Go-Go.
She remained his PA for 20 years, and her brother told BBC News she avoided the limelight and guarded the pop star's privacy, despite the attention of tabloid journalists hoping for stories.
"I think she was one of the few people George trusted and whose opinion he valued," Bailey said.
"She was always honest and straight with him. I guess that's why she stayed working for him for so long through the very, very good and not so good times."
The guitar now going under the hammer was "a gift" to his sister because the singer "thought so much of her", he said.
The instrument had a key role to play in Michael's reinvention from teen pop idol to serious solo artist.

In the 1987 video for Faith, Michael - in ripped blue Levi's jeans, white T-shirt and black leather biker jacket - strummed the vintage acoustic guitar that he reportedly picked up in a shop in Los Angeles shortly beforehand.
Guitarist magazine recently billed it as "arguably the most famous Gretsch Synchromatic in the world".
It has an estimated price tag of between £60,000 and £120,000. Other less significant but more personal items have already exceeded their estimates.
A Filofax from the 1988 Faith tour with Siobhan's handwritten notes and annotations had a guide price of up to £600 and a current bid of £1,750.

Other items include a note written "with love and admiration" from Michael and Ridgeley, an official Wham! photograph signed "To Siobhan (Special...)", and an invitation to Ridgeley's 21st birthday party.
The auction also includes the gold disc and platinum CD presented to her for sales milestones achieved by Michael's music.
"I know she was proud of the various personalised gold and platinum discs she got, though she was very modest about it all," Bailey said.
He said "she would never have consented" to the sale of these items, adding that the auction "breaks my heart".
"I think she'd be devastated that something as personal as her Filofax and notes from George are up for grabs. It's just so tawdry and contrary to how she was," he said.
Siobhan died suddenly and unexpectedly of natural causes at the age of 56. According to her brother, she wanted the possessions to "have remained with her family and we would never have sold".
He accused Belcher of deciding "12 years after my sister's death to cash in".
Bailey acknowledged that Belcher has a legal right to sell the items but called it "disingenuous" that the sale was being promoted in her name.

items.title: Investors turn on Google owner Alphabet after profit miss, ad slowdown and high spending
paragraphs: Shares in Google parent Alphabet fell more than 10% in after-hours trading Wednesday, erasing tens of billions of dollars in stock market value from the $4tn tech giant. The company had reported lower-than-expected profit and a slowdown in its advertising business while it maintained big spending on AI.
Net profit slid 25% from a year earlier to $26.2bn in the July-to-September period, or $2.12 a share, well short of expectations by analysts surveyed by FactSet.
Alphabet booked an $8.7bn loss on its equity investments, which it attributed to its stake in SpaceX, the Elon Musk-led company where shares have struggled since going public in June.
Revenue, however, rose 25% to an enormous $127.6bn. The figure was slightly below the roughly $128bn analysts had forecast.

Advertising revenue grew 11% to $82bn, short of expectations. Revenue from Google’s search business, still the company’s largest source of income, rose 12% to $63.4bn, slowing from 17% growth in the previous quarter.

YouTube, now the most-watched content provider on American TV screens, saw advertising revenue grow 9% to $11.2bn, down from 13% growth in the previous quarter. YouTube Music and Premium passed 150 million subscribers worldwide, including trials.
Google Cloud, which rents computing power and AI tools to businesses, saw revenue jump 103% to $30.7bn, ahead of analyst expectations.
The company said sales of its in-house AI chips, known as TPUs, contributed significantly to that growth. Operating income for the unit tripled to $11.1bn.
Google is also selling its TPU chips to outside companies, in a growing challenge to market leader Nvidia. OpenAI reportedly plans to buy some of the chips.
Alphabet’s “Other Bets” division, which includes robotaxi company Waymo, posted revenue of $372m and an operating loss of $2bn.
Waymo now provides more than 500,000 paid rides per week across 15 US metropolitan areas and aims to reach 1m weekly rides by the end of the year.
Alphabet spent $51.4bn on capital expenditures during the quarter, mostly on datacenters and AI chips, more than double the $24bn a year earlier.
Its latest forecast for capex spending is between $195bn to $205bn in spending for 2026.
The company said it would continue to increase capex spending significantly in 2027.
“I would broadly think of all of this as a long-range planning process, not a short-term allocation exercise,” Sundar Pichai, the Google CEO, told analysts of the company’s investment splurge.
The company’s spending, which included a fine paid to the European Union, outstripped the cash generated by Alphabet’s businesses for a second straight quarter, leaving a $9.1bn gap.
During the quarter Alphabet raised $28.7bn by selling bonds and $12.4bn by issuing new shares to help pay for its AI ambitions.
Google has stepped up the pace of its AI releases since a delay to a flagship model in July raised questions about whether it was falling behind rivals OpenAI and Anthropic.
It launched Gemini 4 at the end of September and later released a version focused on cybersecurity.
The Gemini app has reached 1bn users. Google’s AI models now process nearly 32bn tokens, or units of text, per minute, more than four times the level of a year ago, the company said.
Anthropic, the maker of the Claude chatbot, is also one of Google’s largest cloud customers. It has committed to using up to one million Google AI chips.
In September, a US judge declined to order Google to sell off parts of its advertising technology business, imposing restrictions on how it operates instead.

items.title: Building boom puts 300,000 people in the path of potential Himalayan disasters
paragraphs: Construction of tourism and housing facilities has surged in parts of Nepal and India's Uttarakhand
Environmental correspondent, BBC World Service
At least 300,000 people in parts of the Himalayan region could now be living in the path of potential disasters, a new study suggests.
Researchers found that the amount of built-up land in high-risk zones in northern Nepal, parts of south-eastern Tibet and a corner of India's Uttarakhand had grown by about 45% between 2016 and 2023.

In areas particularly threatened by flooding from glacial lakes, development increased even faster, rising by almost 78% over the same period, according to the peer-reviewed study published in Scientific Reports.
The team of scientists behind it said the true number of people under threat could be much higher, as they only analysed a specific territory and not neighbouring areas which face similar risks.

The study was carried out before August's devastating mass floods which left more than 1,400 dead and thousands missing in Nepal. More recently there have been several smaller incidents, including flooding along the Budhi Gandaki river on 11 October that damaged 200 houses, swept away five bridges and left five people missing.
The major tourist hub of Pokhara has seen major development in recent years
Nine researchers from the UK, Nepal and India looked at areas up to 50km (30 miles) downstream from Himalayan rivers, as well as around 1,360 glacial lakes.
They found significant development in these areas - including an expansion of tourism facilities, infrastructure development and real estate.
It's clear in Pokhara, a major tourism hub at the foot of the Himalayas that's grown significantly in the past 30 years to cater for a massive increase in visitors.

Mayor Dhana Raj Acharya says it's a huge challenge to deal with the risk posed by the Seti Gandaki River, which stems from the Annapurna mountain range and flows right through the city. Many old buildings are just 5m (16ft) from river banks, he says, despite new rules requiring them to be further away.
"Where we move them, and how we do that, is the real challenge."
To the north is the world-renowned Annapurna trekking region that has also seen a major increase in settlements along river banks - some hit by recent floods and landslides.

Phurpa Chhiring Lama, who runs a homestay there, feels helpless. Normally all of his 20 rooms are occupied at this time of year - the peak trekking season - but now only five are. "We have been doing this business for more than 40 years, but we've never seen this kind of disaster."

Krishna Gauchan, whose hotel is close to the glacier-fed Modi river, is worried too. "This river can flood if the glacier collapses or if the glacial lake bursts out and we are living in constant fear."

Tourism investors promote some of these spots as destinations without factoring in the risks, suggests Khagendra Poudel, a geographer at a local campus of Tribhuvan University. It's similar to what's happening in parts of north India's Himalayan valleys which host major pilgrimages.
The president of the Hotel Association Pokhara admits tourism businesses have expanded "without any proper planning" in the region and been promoted "haphazardly".
"By the time disasters hit, it is too late," says Laxman Subedi. "As a professional body we are trying to create awareness among tourism entrepreneurs and investors."
Moment buildings are swept away as flash flood hits Nepal's Budhi Gandaki river
But it's not just tourism. The regions surrounding the Bhotekoshi and Trishuli rivers have seen a significant rise in the construction of hydropower plants.

"As river valleys become increasingly populated, development decisions being made today will shape disaster risk for decades to come," warns the study's lead author, University of Leeds glaciologist C Scott Watson.
And even more buildings may be under threat than those identified by the researchers.
The study categorised buildings at risk as all those that were within 50 vertical metres (164ft) of a river or glacial lake's surface.

But during the catastrophic flooding on 26 August, locals in Rasuwa district say the river level had risen by 70m (230ft) at some points - so even buildings that were relatively far from the river banks were hit and buried by debris-sludge.
Two months after the devastating August floods, these buildings in Trishuli Bazar remain devastated

The risks in all of these areas are largely driven by warming in the Himalayan region, which scientists say is happening at twice the global rate. This has sped up the melting of glaciers, icefields, snowpacks, and ground that's normally frozen all year.
This can, in turn, destabilize mountain slopes which are also frequently shaken by earthquakes, unleashing devastating disasters downstream.
The rapid melting is also filling up and expanding glacial lakes until they burst, causing deadly floods. Nepal alone has documented around 30 of these events since 1940.
Another issue is that rising temperatures cause rain to reach high altitudes where it used to only snow, leading to slope failures, rock and ice falls, and other disasters.

Nepal's Prime Minister Balendra Shah raised the dangers of climate change at his recent UN General Assembly speech, where he said his country was paying a "colossal price" for a crisis it did not create.
"Every major disaster threatens to erase years of development. And it forces a poor country to borrow money to repair damage it did not cause."

Alton Byers, a mountain geographer at the University of Colorado who was not involved in the study, says it should serve as a "springboard" to bring about more effective early-warning systems and other precautionary measures.
But achieving that will be a challenge. Campaigners say building regulations aren't implemented on the ground and through the years, development has been haphazard in too many places.

Roads, hydropower projects, hotels and market towns have expanded on the low, flat land along rivers, which is accessible and buildable, says Prof Surya Raj Acharya, an urban planning expert and registrar at the University of Nepal.
Those responsible have often ignored safeguards including keeping off the river bank, he adds.
"A fragile ecosystem like the Himalaya demands stricter planning and building regulations than elsewhere, yet these rules have been weak and poorly enforced."

Authorities in Nepal say they are working to address these issues. Settlements within 15m (49ft) of the riverbank along the recently devastated Rasuwa-Bhotekoshi corridor will soon be banned, according to the national disaster agency. Similar rules are being introduced in other river corridors soon.
"It is a challenging job because people in many places have sentimental attachments with their land and property but we cannot ignore the increasing risks," says chief executive Dharam Raj Uprety.
There has been "rampant construction" in the Indian state of Uttarakhand in areas at risk from flooding, activists say

A similar story has unfolded across Nepal's western border in India's Uttarakhand state, where maximum tourism limits and environmental regulations have been bypassed in the name of economic growth, claims activist Anoop Nautiyal.
On paper there are zoning rules prohibiting the construction of houses and infrastructure too close to river banks, "but on the ground we see no implementation of such rules.
"You can see rampant construction all over."

The Uttarakhand government on 12 October approved new floodplain zoning rules to regulate land use and development. "Its objective is to protect life, property and important infrastructure from possible flood damage while maintaining the natural flow of flood waters," the state's cabinet decision read.
But Basanta Raj Adhikari, director of the Centre for Disaster Studies at Tribuvan University, thinks it will not be possible to mitigate such threats completely.

Insurance grades, he suggests, could be another way to encourage people to build in less risky areas. If authorities were to map places as high, moderate and low risk, he believes insurance coverage would "follow accordingly" ensuring people who build homes in safer areas get better protection.
But for now, the pace of construction across the region shows no signs of slowing.

items.title: Details of thousands of US immigration agents leaked in major hack
paragraphs: Details of more than 41,000 personnel working for the US Department of Homeland Security (DHS), including thousands involved in immigration enforcement, have been leaked to the public.

The leak includes names, work addresses, and phone numbers of DHS staff, including agents working with Immigration and Customs Enforcement and Customs and Border Protection, along with descriptions of the work that they do for each agency.
Wednesday's leak marks the third time in recent weeks that a government agency has been targeted in leaks or hacks.
A representative of the DHS did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
The seemingly unprecedented breach of employee information was put online on Wednesday by a group called the Department of Peace alongside cybersecurity researcher and hacker maia crimew.
The information was put in a database named Icepick and shared through a website hosted by Distributed Denial of Secrets.

The groups wrote in an online statement that the goal of the leak was not meant to be a directory of every DHS agent. Rather the aim was to replace "anonymity with accountability", according to Emma Best, a co founder of DDoSecrets.

"The leak is extraordinary but deceptive in it's simplicity as it identifies the officials responsible for overseeing covert and undercover operations, the government's hunt for leakers and the failed BlueLeaks investigation - along with key personnel in DHS's ever-escalating rendition and deportation programs," Best added.
The Department of Peace said on Wednesday that it accessed the DHS agent profiles through a single sign-on service called Okta.
Okta is a popular online security tool that organisations use to ensure that only people with access to internal platforms are logging on to them.
A spokeswoman for Okta said the company is aware of the claims being made, but said: "Okta is secure, and we have no evidence our data or systems were compromised."
Last month, the FBI was hacked with a group called ShinyHunters taking personal information about thousands of agents.
In recent days, the Federal Election Commission, which makes public political campaign donation data, was taken offline because of a suspected hacking attempt.

items.title: Mbappé, Real Madrid forced to apologize over 'dictator' comment about China's Mao Zedong
paragraphs: Editor's note: this story was translated from the original VOA Mandarin article.
France and Real Madrid soccer star Kylian Mbappé is facing a backlash in China after commercial sponsors cut ties with him over comments he made about China's founding leader Mao Zedong.
In a recent interview Mbappé described finding a meme—which photoshopped him onto an image resembling that of Mao and referred to it as a "Chinese dictator."
Mbappé has since issued a public apology for his comments as Chinese brands dropped Mbappe and a broadcaster suspended broadcasting Spain's La Liga matches.

In an apology issued on Tuesday in both Chinese and French, Mbappé said that his comment during a recent interview was “ill-judged”, adding that he now understands that it hurt "many people in China and in Chinese communities around the world."
A U.S. congressional committee on China said Mbappé should not have apologized for calling Mao Zedong a "dictator."

The U.S. House Select Committee on China posted a statement on X, saying that Mao Zedong "was indeed a dictator, and the harm he inflicted upon the Chinese people was far more severe than anything a soccer player might say."

The committee, chaired by Congressman John Moolenaar (R-MI), followed up with a repost of a video it recently created about the Cultural Revolution, which Mao launched 60 years ago, calling it “one of the darkest chapters in Chinese history”.
Former Turkish American basketball player and rights activist Enes Kanter Freedom also suggested he disagreed with Mbappe's apology.

“I'm not here to judge Mbappe for apologizing. I don't know what pressure he faced,” Freedom told VOA Tuesday. “But you know, when athletes feel they have to choose between their principles and their careers, we have a serious problem. So that's why I think it's a shame that he came out and apologized because Mao Zedong is a dictator.”

A video clip from an interview with Mbappé on the French show The Bridge has been circulating on social media platforms since Monday. When asked which meme featuring his likeness is the funniest, Mbappé mentioned one where his face is superimposed onto an image of a "Chinese dictator."

Mbappé did not name the character by name, but the show’s post-production team inserted an image of his face superimposed onto a portrait of Mao, implying that he was referring to Mao, triggering the backlash in China.

The following day, several Chinese enterprises—including beverage company Dongpeng, dairy producer Mengniu, and cheese maker Milkground, moved to terminate all partnerships with Mbappé, saying they had "zero-tolerance" policy toward "words and actions that hurt the feelings of the Chinese people". The official China Central Television (CCTV) began suspending all broadcasts related to the Spanish football league LALIGA and matches involving Mbappé, and all advertisements featuring him have been pulled.

Mbappé, the 2026 World Cup Golden Boot winner currently plays for Real Madrid in Spain. He helped France win the 2018 World Cup and scored a hattrick in the 2022 World Cup final. Mbappé is considered one of the most influential and commercially valuable soccer players in the world today. Until this week's incident, he had multiple lucrative sponsorship deals with Chinese companies.
Spain's premier league football known as La Liga has issued an official apology to China over Mbappé’s comment on Tuesday. Real Madrid issued a similar apology Wednesday.
Asked about Mbappe's apology during a regular press briefing in Beijing Wednesday, Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesperson Guo Jiakun said: "We take seriously the apology that the person has made."

Mao Zedong who led China from 1949 until his death in 1976 is revered in China as the “Great Leader” and the main founder of the Chinese Communist Party (CCP) and the People’s Republic China. In the 1980’s, Chinese authorities, in their attempt to launch reforms and break away from the Cultural Revolution era, once acknowledged some “serious mistakes” made by Mao. However, the current leader Xi Jinping has publicly expressed his admiration for Mao and called him a "great patriot and national hero of China in modern times."

Mao’s critics in China and abroad view him as one of the deadliest dictators in human history. In its X post, the U.S. House Select Committee on China alleged that Mao's "dictatorship and disastrous policies killed tens of millions of Chinese people in the Cultural Revolution, the Great Famine, and other atrocities.”

The committee’s post added: “The real disgrace in this news story is the companies rushing to apologize so they can continue to do business in China. The CCP is the largest oppressor of the Chinese people and their human rights, and those businesses that work with the CCP help normalize its crushing brutality.”
Mbappé is not the first sports figure to face varying degrees of censorship or boycotts in China due to their public comments.

Ironically, it was a former Real Madrid and Arsenal star, Mesut Özil who, through social media post, criticized Chinese government policies and the detention of Uyghurs in Xinjiang in December 2019. Özil left Arsenal in 2021 to joint Turkish club Fenerbahçe though it's unclear whether it was related to the comments he made about China.

Freedom himself faced similar problems when he criticized Chinse communist party in October 2021. After making remarks on social media and during games that were critical of Chinese actions in Tibet, Xinjiang, and Taiwan, broadcasts of games featuring his then-team, the Boston Celtics, were halted in China. Chinse platforms such as Tencent Sports also scrubbed all videos and merchandise related to him.

Chinese companies also suspended broadcasting NBA games after two NBA-related incidents involving the former General Manager of the NBA’s Houston Rockets, Daryl Morey, and former LA Lakers star Dwight Howard in 2019 and in 2023. The suspensions cost the NBA millions of dollars in revenue from broadcasting rights.
VOA Mandarin’s Stella Hsu contributed to this article.

items.title: Former Russian detainee’s sister says Stephen Hubbard ‘escaped hell’
paragraphs: Editor's note: this story was translated from the original VOA Russian article.

The sister of former Russian detainee Stephen Hubbard says her brother's condition is better than the family expected. The 74-year-old American was released from Russia after more than four years in detention and returned to the United States last week.

"It was incredible. I don’t even know how to describe it. It’s simply unbelievable to realize that he is free and has escaped the hell he spent nearly five years in," his sister, Patricia Hubbard, said in a recent interview with VOA.
"He underwent all the examinations and tests. Now he needs to rebuild his muscles and regain his strength," she said.

Russian forces detained Stephen Hubbard in the Russian occupied-Ukrainian town of Izium in April of 2022, where he had lived and taught English since 2014. Russia convicted him of being a mercenary and sentenced him to six to 10 years in a penal colony in October of 2024. Patricia Hubbard says her brother was never a mercenary.
"That was just a pretext to take his property," she told VOA, adding that her brother had absolutely no intention of joining the Ukrainian military or taking part in the Russia-Ukraine war.

"He hated the war. He was against it. Stephen was never a military man. Yes, he served in the U.S. Air Force, but that was not during wartime," she said. "As a child, he never got into fights. He wasn’t one of those boys who was always getting into trouble. He was a good, quiet child who took part in the [Boy] Scouts and read a great deal. He always loved books."
Patricia Hubbard told VOA that she heard of her brother's possible release about two days before it happened.

"I was told that everything could change at the last minute," she said. "They [U.S. officials] did say, expect anything to happen at the last minute because that's happened before when a country will say they're going to let someone out, then they like to torture you by not letting them out [until the] last minute."
She noted that the moment she saw her brother was special.
"We just hugged. We kept telling each other, “I love you,” over and over again. We hugged for a long time," Patricia Hubbard said.

Stephen Hubbard spent the first days in the U.S. under medical evaluation. His sister says after a medical assessment, he was sent home with a new set of clothes, new medical records, a new passport, and identification.
"When someone is taken hostage, they lose everything. Everything is stripped from them," she told VOA.
Patricia, who holds a master's in psychological counseling, said she chose not to talk to her brother about his experience in the Russian jail, where she said he was tortured.
"Some of the guards who knew only a few words in English would shout, 'Die, American, die!' while beating him," she said.

"Psychologically, he is doing much better than expected," Hubbard said. "His faith has helped him enormously. Psychologically, he has been through a great deal. But he did say one thing. He said, 'I want to be around people I know and who love me.' He said there is no love in that place. No love at all. Only darkness."
While in the Russian jail, Patricia says her brother Stephen spent most of his time in complete isolation.

"And even when someone else was nearby, they didn’t speak the same language," she told VOA. "There was no television or radio. He had no sense of time. He had absolutely no idea how much the world had changed over the past five years. All of it is a shock to him. It’s as if you had fallen into a coma and then woken up.”

items.title: Death of US actress Hayden Panettiere ruled accidental, ending local police probe
paragraphs: The death of US actress Hayden Panettiere has been ruled accidental, ending a local probe into her death, police in South Carolina have said.
The Heroes and Nashville star died in August from the toxic effects of fentanyl, Xanax and several other drugs in her system, at the age of 36.
Citing the medical examiner's report last month that found Panettiere died from a drug overdose, the Greenville Police Department said it had "concluded its investigation" into her death.
The US Drug Enforcement Agency (DEA) reportedly joined a local police probe. It is unclear if that investigation has also concluded. The BBC has contacted the DEA for comment.
"Based on the Medical Examiner's determination and the findings of the investigation, Hayden Panettiere's death has been ruled accidental," police said in a statement.
Authorities, including the DEA, were reportedly investigating the circumstances of Panettiere's death, according to the BBC's US media partner CBS News.

items.title: Elon Musk is a 'real genius', Putin says after satellite talks with SpaceX boss
paragraphs: Elon Musk is a "real genius", Russian President Vladimir Putin said on Wednesday after revealing the two are in "close" contact about satellite technology.

The remarks came during the Russia-Africa Summit in Moscow, during which Putin discussed Russia's own satellite internet project Rassvet, which provides internet connections to people from satellites.
"He's a genius, a real genius," Putin said of Musk, according to a translation of his remarks by the BBC. "We are in close contact with our American partners, including Mr. Musk."
Starlink is part of Musk's company SpaceX. The company did not respond to a request for comment.
Putin added that it was important for Russia to be in contact with Musk so Rassvet and Starlink satellites do not "interfere with each other in orbit".
"We and our American partners value this mutually, and despite all the political questions, we are working hard," he said.

Starlink has launched roughly 13,000 of its satellites, according to the company. By contrast there are only a couple of dozen Rassvet satellites currently in orbit, according to online satellite trackers.
The Russian Embassy in South Africa said on Wednesday Rassvet is "Russia's Starlink alternative" and "marks only the country's first steps in this field".
"Russia maintains close contacts with the US on space, including with Elon Musk," the embassy wrote.
Putin's comments about Rassvet and Starlink were made as the US and Russia appear to be growing closer, even as it approaches five years since Putin's full-scale invasion of Ukraine.

Ukraine relied on Starlink internet in its efforts to keep Russia's forces at bay. But its military last week suddenly suffered Starlink connectivity problems, something Musk has admitted SpaceX did intentionally.
US President Donald Trump earlier this month said he'd struck a deal with Russia to import diesel in an effort to lower gas prices that have skyrocketed due to the US war with Iran.
Then Trump waived certain sanctions against Russia that were set to take effect.
Not long after, a US citizen was released from Russian custody, with US envoy Steve Witkoff referring to Putin as a "humanitarian".

Musk was born in South Africa and then immigrated to Canada before settling in the US. All of his business ventures, including Tesla, SpaceX and Starlink, are based in America, with most operating out of California and Texas.
The billionaire, and off and on again trillionaire, has been one of the biggest political allies and financiers of Trump and other Republican US politicians.

items.title: Renowned Iranian Filmmaker Sentenced to Prison, Asset Confiscation
paragraphs: Editor's note: this story was translated from the original VOA Persian article.

The Tehran Revolutionary Court has sentenced Jafar Panahi, the renowned Iranian director and filmmaker, to five years and one month in prison. The court also ordered the total confiscation of all his property, a two-year ban on social media activity, and a two-year travel ban.

Panahi’s defense attorney, Mostafa Nili disclosed the verdict to the news website Emtedad, revealing the sentence was issued in absentia and "without scheduling a court hearing" by Branch 26 of the Tehran Revolutionary Court.

Explaining how they learned of the sentence, Nili added: "Last week, we noticed that Mr. Panahi’s bank accounts had been frozen. Upon visiting the sentence execution branch of the Culture and Media Prosecutor’s Office, we learned of his new sentence."

Jafar Panahi, director of It Was Just An Accident and winner of the Palme d’Or at the Cannes Film Festival, returned to Iran via land border crossing in late March 2026, following the Oscar campaign for his film.

Panahi’s return to Iran came after he had previously been sentenced in absentia to one year in prison, a two-year travel ban, and a two-year prohibition from joining political or social organizations on charges of "propaganda against the state" - citing allegations of "making subversive underground films against the government," supporting political prisoners and protests, and backing the "Woman, Life, Freedom" movement.

The U.S. Department of State has previously cited the restrictions imposed on Jafar Panahi in its human rights reports on Iran, highlighting his travel ban and prosecution on charges of "propaganda against the Islamic Republic" as prominent examples of the suppression of freedom of expression and artistic activity in the country.

The State Department also noted that the Islamic Republic imposes widespread restrictions on cultural and artistic freedoms through strict oversight of film production and screening, censorship of cinematic works, and the prosecution of critical filmmakers.

Additionally, the U.S. Department of the Treasury previously sanctioned two Revolutionary Court judges, Abolghasem Salavati and Mohammad Moghiseh, for their roles in penalizing citizens for exercising their rights to freedom of expression and assembly.

When announcing those sanctions in December 2019, the Treasury Department emphasized that Iranian artists, including filmmakers and poets, have been prosecuted on charges such as "propaganda against the state" and "assembly and collusion against national security" solely due to the content of their creative work.

Acclaimed Iranian filmmaker Jafar Panahi is one of the few directors in cinema history to win top honors at the world’s major European film festivals, having earned the Golden Lion at Venice, the Golden Bear at Berlin, the Golden Leopard at Locarno, and both Palme d’Or and the Caméra d'Or at Cannes

items.title: They did it! Sennheiser HD 480 Pro are the best closed-back headphones I’ve heard (and it's not even close)
paragraphs: The Sennheiser HD 480 Pro is the new benchmark in closed-back sound quality, offering a balanced, neutral sound profile with a touch of added bass warmth. It's rich and detailed mids are exceptional, and its smooth treble will be enjoyed by the maximum number of people. Critics will think it lacks the excitement of some audiophile headphones, but if you want correct-sounding headphones that will present your favourite music in the absolute best light, you can't do better than the Sennheiser HD 480 Pro.
Why you can trust Creative Bloq Our expert reviewers spend hours testing and comparing products and services so you can choose the best for you. Find out more about how we test.
I first fell in love with audiophile headphones because they offered so much more clarity, technicalities, resolution, and other words that basically mean perceived detail.

Price: $399 / £339 (just headphone); $439 / £369 (with hard case)Release: April 2026Driver & housing: 38 mm dynamic driver; closed-backMaterial: Matte composite body, metal headband slider, washable velour/fabric acoustic ear padsCable: Detachable single-sided cable connecting via a 4-pin mini-XLR port (pluggable to either ear cup); 3.5 mm straight jack with screw-on 6.3 mm adapterImpedance: 130 Ω (at 1 kHz)Sensitivity: 107 dB SPL (1 kHz / 1 Vrms) / 98 dB SPL (1 kHz / 1 mW)Weight: 272 g

The pair that first opened my eyes was the Sennheiser HD 550, and they blew me away because their neutral/bright sound profile encouraged me to focus on higher frequency detail that I otherwise wouldn’t have noticed. The HD 550 also offers an excellent midrange with natural timbre, but it was the exciting treble that I fixated on.

The $400 Sennheiser HD 480 Pro isn’t here to excite you. Made for studio pros, specifically for tracking and mixing, the 480 Pro isn’t made for audiophiles, so instead of throwing fireworks at you, it paints a neutral, balanced, correct-sounding sound profile.
The result is the best closed-back pair of headphones that I’ve yet heard, and my new go-to recommendation if you’re looking for a set of the best-sounding headphones on sale today.

Overall, Bass and treble are gloriously well balanced without overshadowing the midrange. That’s a feat for any type of headphone – including the more forgiving open or Bluetooth sets – let alone a closed-back pair. The overall sound is correct-sounding with a touch of warmth. Nothing is out of place, and listening to music I’ve been familiar with for several decades, it all just sounds as it should.

The only negative aspects to the 480 Pro are preference-based, as opposed to glaring tuning errors. For example, you might prefer a different approach to treble than the 480 Pro – yet the 480 Pro’s treble is the best version of its approach that I’ve heard. All together, this is an exceptional-sounding headphone, and the best closed-back I’ve ever used.

Bass: This bass is full with plenty of detail and slam, putting a focus on sub bass yet still offering plenty of mid-bass punch. I find this presentation detailed, with some nice ‘grip’ to it. If I’m nit-picking, I can totally see it being too much bass for audiophiles searching perfect neutral, yet what’s on offer here doesn’t step on the toes of the midrange. It does, however, lend a warmth to things that some might not like (it’s definitely my jam).

You can get bigger bass in the far less expensive $160 FiiO FT1. However, you don’t hear bass in a vacuum, and where the FT1’s midrange’s clarity is hit by the wads of (wonderfully executed) low range, the 480 Pro’s overall balance remains faultless.

Playing Parliament’s Give Up The Funk, I love the fullness of the mid bass of Bootsy Collins in the intro. It has body and slam, backed up with a substantial sub bass that grounds the whole thing. On lesser sets that simply ramp up the bass, lower frequency details get lost easily, and listening to familiar music becomes frustrating – you can't hear the detail you know is there. That’s not the case with the 480 Pro. I get quality and quantity, and let there be no doubt, there’s plenty of quantity here!

Midrange: There’s more focus on the mid and upper mids, and less on the lower mids here. That makes the bass and lower mids seem more distinct, which is a presentation some people will love, and some will feel lacks cohesion. For me, the 480 Pro has the best of both worlds here, with the mid-bass being distinct enough from the mids so it hits hard, but not so much that the lower mids sound lean.

The ear gain region – the bane of many a headphone tuner – is exceptionally well done. I hear a little dip just before an elevation around 2.45kHz then again at 2.9-3.5kHz, followed by a noticeable dip around 4kHz. The former elevations are never too much, and serve as extra seasoning on male and female vocals.

4kHz is actually an area which usually gives me issues, so I tend to headphones that make a plateau around 2-4kHz instead of putting a spotlight on that area. The HD 480 Pro isn’t shy in this region, but it still doesn’t come across as shouty or grating. Instead, everything in the midrange comes across as timbrally correct. That’s basically the hardest thing to do with audio – any chump can make headphones sound ‘exciting’. The HD 480 Pro makes instruments and vocals sound correct, all balanced with each other. And when you put on a beautifully-produced track, the results are ‘right’.

For this review, I played through the Luxsin X8 DAC/Amp and the Mojo 2 by Chord. These pairings provided ample power delivery and headroom for the headphones, maintaining a transparent, uncoloured signal path from source to transducer. Music streamed via Spotify Lossless.

Treble: To my ears, there’s a generally relaxed approach to the lower treble that I initially read as dark. However, the more I listened to the 480 Pro the more I found Sennheiser’s approach to the treble was purposeful and in accordance with the balanced approach of the bass and mids.

I get a little spice around 6.6-7kHz, a dip around 8kHz, and then a little bit more around 9kHz. But as with the ear gain region, these slight peaks give added dimension to the sound, rather than sounding piercing or sibilant. In fact, this is the smoothest detailed treble I’ve heard, whether open- or closed-back. Michael Jackson’s remarkably bright Billie Jean has all its stabbing peaks rounded off, and Lucinda Williams’ jarringly sibilant Sweet Old World blends in rather than stands out. That never happens!

Of course, as I've said, a subtle, smooth, balanced treble isn’t everyone’s idea of audiophile-grade audio (Grado still sell headphones, after all). I happen to love the HiFiMan HE1000, with its comparably elevated treble profile. I love that it, along with its incredibly open ear cups, gives me a sense of crisp detail – it’s what I think of when I think ‘audiophile’. And yet, the HE1000 isn’t a practical set for everyday use. It’s a specialised headphone for specific moments. With its balanced sound, the Sennheiser is both an every-day set for YouTube doom scrolling and a specialised set for critical listening. It’s a rare bird in that it excels in every area, so that it may appear unexceptional. That's far from the case.

At $399/£339, the Sennheiser HD 480 Pro is in a competitive price bracket. It's also in a tricky spot for budget-conscious creatives who may look to the cheaper workhorse classic the Beyerdynamic DT 770 Pro ($200).

The value proposition here, however, is undeniable and convincing. Where the Pro DT 770 Pro offers bucket-loads of perceived detail with its incredibly elevated, sibilant treble, the 480 Pro offers unparalleled neutrality that can be enjoyed for hours on end without fatigue.

Closed-backs notoriously struggle with boomy bass, due to internal acoustic reflections and resonant standing waves trapped inside the sealed ear cup. But Sennheiser tames low-end clutter without muddying the mix. This is really very rare. Factor in the featherlight 272g build and washable components, and it’s a brilliant, durable investment. For me, at $400, this represents excellent value. After all, it's one of the best headphones I've heard, and it will last many, many years.
The HD 480 Pro slams just as much as the notorious Focal Azurys in the bass, but it's cleaner and clearer, without reverting to the overly-bright approach of the Focal set.
The Azurys is a very comfortable, cool-looking pair of headphones, but it offers more of a V-shape sound profile than the perfectly-balanced HD 480.

The upside of that is that the Azurys is a more exciting, dynamic pair of headphones. More bass and more treble mean more contrast. The midrange is really good with the Azurys as well. Yet it's not the star, as it's slightly overshadowed by all the excitement. You get none of these compromises with the HD 480 Pro.

For me, the smoothness of treble in the HD 480 allows everything to pull focus, whereas the comparatively sharper Azurys can sound almost hollow in comparison. And I think this is largely down to treble, as both cans sound very similar in the midrange (and certainly graph so).

The Focal Azurys retail for $599, though you can currently (and frequently) get them for more like $449 over at Amazon, and though I'd recommend them to certain people, I'd recommend the HD 480 Pro to everyone.

I have a soft spot for the FiiO FT1 – and not just because they are one of the best value pair of closed-back headphones in existence, at $165 over at Amazon. They sound fantastic, with their vaguely absurd levels of bass, which is plenty detailed and only messes with the lower mids a bit (coping much?!)

But A/B testing the FT1 with the HD 480 Pro, I still think it holds up... kind of. Sure it offers a more dynamic V-shape sound profile to the Sennheiser cans, but just like the Azurys, it does exciting well. The bass is definitely the boss here, but the midrange isn't just bullied around as is the case with so many bass cannons.

However, when comparing the treble responses, it's like comparing a scalpel to a sledgehammer. The HD 480 Pro walks a fine line between detail and sibilance. Going between the two with the glitchy, treble showcase that is K-Lone's slk, and where the FT1 ramps up the highs, shouting the detail to you, the 480 Pro seems to convey all the same high frequency detail, but with more body. I know that might sound weird, to refer to treble having body, but the 480 Pro just offers a fuller picture.
The Sennheiser HD 480 PRO is relatively easy to drive despite its 130 Ω impedance, because its sensitivity is reasonably high at 107 dB SPL (1 Vrms) or 98 dB SPL (1 mW).
What that means in practise is an M-chipped MacBook or modern PC will drive the HD 480 PRO effortlessly with ample headroom.

For music listening, a $9 Apple dongle will give you all the clean power you actually need. The only real limitation would be maximum volume if you're working with quiet, uncompressed studio recordings. Which I don't!
Bottom line: for the majority of music fans thinking about buying the HD 480 Pro, as long as you have a $9 Apple dongle, you're golden.
Build and comfort are big wins for the Sennheiser HD 480 Pro. Although it may look like a lot of other headphones, this set really is amongst the most comfortable out there.

It's the combination of light plastic, stainless spring steel, and soft velour ear cups that make this a durable, lightweight headphone that doesn't register even after hours of use. And with that steel, you know this headphone is going to retain its shape, no matter how it's treated.

This level of comfort is rare on a single headband headphone (ie, not headphones with dedicated comfort straps to distribute the weight on your head). I've previously had to add an additional Capra strap to make most single-band headphones bearable – such as the FiiO FT1, or the HEDD D1. And all these super light materials are replaceable – the detachable headband padding is even washable!

The width and depth of the ear cups is such that my average-sized ears never touch the driver housing, and the depth and soft materials of the cups means that the passive isolation is excellent. This is actually one of the highlights for me, as I work in a home office with my beautiful (noisy!) wife and a an equally beautifully noisy gaming PC. With the 480 Pro, I get to immerse myself in great sound, and not be distracted by either.

This is a well-designed headphone that's not built for show, but is built to last a very long time. For $400, this should be the standard – if I'm going to spend $400 on headphones, I want to be listening to them in 20 years time. And there's no reason that won't be the case with the HD 480 Pro.
I've given this pair of headphones a full five stars, so the answer is obviously, 'yes, yes, yes – of course you should buy it'. But that doesn't mean they're for everyone.

So, who is this headphone not for? I think any audiophile who wants a detail monster set that offers high-treble sizzle excitement and accompanying hearing loss, should give the 480 Pro a miss. Instead, pick up a HiFiMan instead (my current favourite is the HiFiMan HE1000 Stealth).

The Sennheiser 480 Pro doesn't get in the way of the music. It presents it honestly and clearly. It lacks the fireworks of the more exciting sets out there, but this is a pair of headphones that you can use all day every day with absolutely no issues – in sound or comfort.
If you want timbral accuracy, supreme comfort, and the passive isolation benefits of a closed-back, there is currently no better option than the Sennheiser 480 Pro.

Beren cut his teeth as Staff Writer on digital art magazine ImagineFX, and has since worked on and edited several creative titles, including Paint & Draw and Computer Arts. As Ecom Editor on Creative Bloq, when he's not reviewing the latest audiophile headphones or evaluating the best designed ergonomic office chairs, he’s testing laptops, TVs and monitors, all so he can find the best tech deals for Creative Bloq’s digital professional audience.

items.title: Skulls, bulls and someone peeing in her own eye: four great exhibitions to see for free
paragraphs: Andy Warhol’s skull leers at Francisco de Zurbarán’s trussed-up little lamb from across the length of the gallery. Separated by hundreds of years – Warhol’s painting from the 1970s, Zurbarán’s from the 1630s – it’s an intergenerational conversation about still life’s staying power, and the inevitability of death.

This brilliant little show brings together still life paintings from way back in the past right up to the present day. There’s a gorgeous 1610-19 Dutch flower painting by Osaias Beert the Elder, and a vast vision of meats and cheeses with a pair of animal lungs hung grossly on a hook behind by Giovanni Battista Recco from the 1650s. There are piles of 19th-century French apples, vases of undulating 18th-century flowers. And then that little Zurbarán lamb – one of six he painted – glassy-eyed and morose, so laden with religious symbolism.

When we hit the modern era, there’s a lovely Pierre Bonnard painting of grapes and apples in sickly yellow and orange, a genuinely amazing Nicolas de Staël composition of stark, blocky bottles, lumps of pink rock by Philip Guston that look like cheese. Ignore the crap Picasso and the lumpen Juan Gris, and you get to come face to face with Warhol’s grim, grinning neon orange skull.

The whole show reinforces the idea that still life painting is terribly named. Because it’s not about life at all, it’s about death. Every fruit and vegetable in these works is about to rot, every flower is wilting, every animal carcass is about to go fetid. These are paintings of life’s fragility and precariousness. This is about how time is fleeting, how life is temporary. Mortality is written into every brush stroke.

Is this the greatest still life show ever put on? Does it have a tight curatorial concept? Does it tell an important story about the history and evolution of the genre? No, no and no. It’s just a bunch of really good, historic paintings. See, still life isn’t all just flowers and fruit. And even when it is, it’s pretty good.

Panting, his grey tongue hanging out, blood streaming down his back, the bull is on the verge of death. Paul Pfeiffer’s newest film captures the moment a matador plunges a sword into that bull’s back, but with no fanfare, no drama, no judgment. This is a film about ritual and spectacle, not about animal cruelty or cultural violence.

This isn’t Pfeiffer at his most attractive or impressive. Instead, this long, awkward, often ugly piece of art cinema zooms in on the faces of the crowd at a corrida, the hands of the saxophone players in the band, the colours of the walls, the patterns on the matadors’ clothing. It’s all the tiny details of this spectacle, the intricacies that make it tick.

It is, essentially, a film about how humanity creates spectacles to lose ourselves in, and how we repeat actions, sounds and movements to create some kind of meaning. The film is outwardly about bullfighting, but more widely about all rituals, religious or cultural. Is the corrida any different from going to church or a concert or a football match? In the end, we’re all just trying to find meaning by taking part, by belonging, by coming together and cheering as one. Throughout the film, people cheer, drink and eat, the band plays, a bull dies. That’s life, I guess. Joy and sorrow with some snacks in between.
Thomas Dane Gallery, London, until 19 December
Ebecho Muslimova has gone through the looking-glass, and what she has found on the other side is more worrying and uncomfortable than any kind of horror fantasy land. She’s found reality.

In every painting and installation here, Muslimova’s cartoon alter ego Fatebe is navigating a world turned upside down, spun on its head and inverted. Fatebe is a lewd, rude, nude comic book character, her naked body able to twist and contort, her face always plastered with a grin and her orifices always on display. One painting finds multiple Fatebes bent over, gleefully scrubbing parquet floors (a nod to a Gustave Caillebotte painting, this show is drowning in art history references) while another Fatebe makes a paper chain out of fabric she’s yoinking out of her nethers. Yet another work sees hundreds of Fatebes filing up the stairs of the gallery itself, but the plaster is crumbling and the print is peeling.

Fatebe is trapped under a glass like a spider, or she’s turned herself into the legs of a table. In one drawing she has grown two heads, one peeing into the other’s eye, the other defecating back in return.

All this gross-out weirdness and art historical density isn’t about fantasy and escape though. I think it’s about feeling pulled in endless directions, it’s about being stuck between the place you came from and the place you’re in now, it’s about discomfort and alienation. Or it’s about being able to wee in your own eye. Who knows, really. Either way, it works.

Back in 2013, a Palestinian fisherman found an ancient Greek statue of Apollo poking out of the sand. Thinking it was gold, they cut off a finger, but it was just beautiful, mottled green bronze. They tried to sell it on eBay, posting pictures of the sculpture laid carefully on Smurf bedsheets, but the authorities stepped in and confiscated the sculpture. No one knows where it is now, but Rosalind Nashashibi has painted it here, preserving its strange, almost magical history in hazy visions of green limbs on cartoon-covered sheets.

Not all the works are good, and the images of nudes and landscapes feel either like a distraction or filler. But the Apollo images are great. They’re like paintings of an autopsy, stark and unsettling. They’re filled with narratives – a clash of ancient art and modern cartoon, a beleaguered people finding hope of salvation in a gift from the gods, an act of care as those people gently try to preserve this sculpture on their softest bedsheets. Hope and despair, history and the present, all colliding in some often beautiful, washed-out painting.

items.title: China-Russia defense ties move upstream as Beijing gains Russian know-how
paragraphs: Editor's note: this story was translated from the original VOA Mandarin article.

Russian defense-linked companies are beginning to embed production inside China, acquire Chinese intellectual property and use Chinese equipment to sustain manufacturing at home, according to Washington-based research organization Center for Advanced Defense Studies (C4ADS).
A newly published report from the group notes that this marks a shift from arms sales toward semiconductors, machine tools, designs, testing, and scientific research.

“What’s changing is the nature of that support,” C4ADS analyst Allen Maggard said. “It’s not just China sending dual-use technology to Russia. It’s Beijing tolerating Russian defense industry contractors setting up production inside China.”
The relationship is not new: many links predate the 2022 invasion of Ukraine, and some expanded after 2014. But Maggard says upstream defense-industrial cooperation has accelerated since 2022.

Element, a sanctioned Russian microelectronics holding, reported that it had begun assembling chipsets in China and incorporated at least four Chinese subsidiaries in 2025. In April 2026, Element reportedly acquired power-electronics intellectual property from Shijiazhuang Tonhe Electronics. Ten days later, one of Element’s Chinese subsidiaries acquired a Chinese company from which Element had bought unspecified equipment.

On September 30, Russian news outlet CNews reported that an Element-controlled company had delivered more than 100 pieces of semiconductor-production equipment in Russia and opened a subsidiary in China to oversee logistics and quality control. Neither source establishes that Element is producing military-grade chips in China or that the equipment is going to military customers.
China supplied more than 90 percent of Russia’s imports of goods that Western governments classify as high-priority dual-use items in 2023, according to data cited by C4ADS.
The report says Moscow receives an immediate industrial lifeline while Beijing gains designs, testing capacity and scientific expertise.

“In terms of short-term gain, Russia is gaining a lot,” Maggard stated. He said Chinese equipment, and Western equipment routed through China, helps Russia sustain wartime production and could support rebuilding its military after the war.
Henry Ziemer, a fellow with the Americas Program at the Center for Strategic and International Studies, said Moscow’s need is becoming acute.

“Russia in particular simply cannot do without support from China in the military-technical domain as war and sanctions erode its industrial base," Ziemer said. He added that the partnership remains significant despite its limited institutional structure.

China’s potential benefit is longer-term. Its reliance on imported weapons fell 72 percent between 2016–2020 and 2021–2025, according to SIPRI data cited in the report. C4ADS says Beijing increasingly seeks the knowledge behind Russian weapons rather than just its finished systems.

Russian trade records analyzed by C4ADS show that the Rubin submarine-design bureau sent 12 shipments worth more than $80 million to Chinese recipients linked to military procurement and state-owned shipbuilding between 2015 and 2023. The descriptions appear to involve submarine concepts and testing documentation.
“When you look at the long-term trajectory of Chinese Russian military-technical cooperation, China is going to come out on top,” Maggard said.

Maggard expects more Russian defense-linked production to move to China if the United States and its allies impose no additional costs. He said Russian companies could establish facilities, acquire stakes in Chinese firms and buy their intellectual property.

Lyle Goldstein, Asia Program director at Washington-based think tank Defense Priorities, expects collaboration in 2027 and beyond to encompass “drone warfare, drone defense, air and missile defense, electronic warfare, and undersea warfare.”
“Absent U.S. and European pressure, I expect China-Russia collaboration to increase going into 2027,” Ziemer said.

The relationship still has limits. China reportedly restricted Russian access to advanced Chinese chips and precision machinery when sales might expose Chinese companies to Western sanctions, while Russia has prosecuted scientists accused of sharing sensitive information with China.
C4ADS recommends coordinated sanctions and export controls, stronger enforcement, investment in Western innovation and separate diplomacy with Beijing and Moscow.
Ziemer said Washington and its allies “should seek to raise the costs of collaboration for China and Russia,” including through selective pressure on Chinese research links and exports.
Goldstein was more skeptical. “I do not think sanctions make much difference now,” he said, citing Russia’s existing sanctions burden and Chinese countermeasures.

Analyst Maggard said no single policy can force the two countries to stop cooperating. The more realistic goal, the report suggests, is to raise costs, slow sensitive transfers and exploit the partnership’s internal tensions.

items.title: KPF completes Texas' tallest skyscraper in Austin
paragraphs: New York architecture studio KPF has completed Waterline in Austin, Texas, a supertall skyscraper with a mixed-use programme that slopes away from Lady Bird Lake as it rises. It has a form that resembles a “cowboy boot”, according to its designers.
KPF, which is known for its skyscrapers around the world, was not originally meant to design the 1,025-foot-tall (312-metre-tall) structure.
The building’s original developer was the coworking real estate company WeWork, which selected a design by its collaborator, architecture studio BIG, through a competition.
However, after WeWork’s failed IPO in 2019 and governance scandals, KPF was brought back in to take up the mantle on the project, which had already begun its early construction.

KPF president James von Klemperer told Dezeen that the concept of a “we-building” or a mixed-use building with overlapping functions remained part of the DNA of the building as the project was awarded to KPF by its new development team.

“Space isn’t as proprietary,” said von Klemperer of the project and concept. “No, it weaves together with other things, and with the spaces that are shared at the rooftop of the base of the building.”

The structure features hotel and office programmes at the bottom, with luxury residences at the top. Double-height exterior floorplates supported by massive columns mark changes in the programme from the exterior, and the whole building slopes up and away from Lady Bird Lake, a wide section of the Colorado River that flows through Austin.

Deference to the waterway was one of the main goals of the project, as were nods to the regional heritage, and a desire not to “strangle” the low-lying historic Rainey District to the southeast of the site.
It was originally supposed to be multiple towers, but the studio decided that shoring its density into a single tower allowed for these goals to be achieved.
“The project grew into the design, if you will, the way it inclines down like a cowboy boot at the base,” said von Klemperer
“It inflects towards Lady Bird Lake, and I think that was a powerful profile in everybody’s estimation, because it says something about a vertical structure becoming a piece of landscape or geology.”

Von Klemperer also contrasted the skyscraper, with its wide-grid facade and columns, with black-glass skyscrapers with wide bodies that block urban view corridors, referencing recent skyscraper construction in New York.

“It’s not often or always that a tall building is also seen as a kind of supple building that is good for the community,” he said, adding that Waterline’s facade, which features rust-coloured details to reference Texas geology, is “lacy” and full of moments “where your eye can see through or see some depth or see pattern”.
“We hoped to make a beautiful little piece of waterway facade.”
Working closely with landscape architecture studio TPG Partners, the structure steps up from the creek, with massive columns meeting the ground plane.
These columns form what von Klemperer compared to an amphitheatre of sorts, adding “urban drama”.
“Cities should have places that support urban drama, and I think already this has shown it really works,” he said.
At the centre of the structure’s stepped podium is a paseo from the city to the water that is lined with stone and makes the lower part of the structure, mostly retail and parking, more porous.
On top of the podium, amenity spaces serve the 1 Hotel, which is taking over the middle part of the programme.
The columns at the base and at the breaks were designed with oak trees in mind.
The studio included some V-shaped columns to add to this character, but also to structurally aid the building as the floorplates changed to accommodate the programme shifts.

“From an office grid to the residential grid, those misalignments along the perimeter were actually beneficial for getting a better column placement in the residential above,” said KPF design director Andrew Klare.
At the top of the building is a sky lounge, and the bulkhead has a slight angle that echoes the slope of the skyscraper.
Von Klemperer said both the shifts in the facade and the tilted top of the skyscraper were subtle nods to the city’s slogan – Keep Austin Weird.

“It’s not an exceedingly weird gesture that interrupts the skyline, but it’s a bit of whimsy, which is in character with the rest of the skyscraper’s geometries,” he said. “It destabilises the conventional grid of the world.”
The mixed-use programme also came to pass during the Covid-19 pandemic, which was a period of doubt in the feasibility of downtown cores.
This didn’t stop the project, but intensified the studio’s desire to create an open building with multiple uses and to “multiply” the uses of the podium.
“It restores your faith in the urban agenda of development – to make such a mixed-use project with levels of shared use throughout,” said von Klemperer.
Other recent skyscrapers by KPF include a “beaux-arts” supertall in New York that is nearing completion and a pair of skyscrapers in Istanbul.
