items.title: Africa’s ‘unprecedented’ Ebola outbreak could reach UK, says top health official
paragraphs: The “unprecedented” spread of the Ebola outbreak means it could reach the UK and other countries, according to one of Africa’s top health officials.

As the current outbreak reached 10,000 cases, with almost 5,000 deaths, Dr Jean Kaseya, director general of the Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), compared the outbreak to the Covid pandemic, which first took hold in China before spreading to countries across the world, claiming millions of lives, and ravaging health systems and economies.
“We want all countries to know that they are not safe if they don’t take appropriate measures,” he said.
“Each country, not only in the African region, but all continents, must now increase the preparedness level and the possibility for treatment.
“It is the first time three African regions have been affected [by Ebola]. The geographic extension of this outbreak is unprecedented,” he said.

Kaseya said leaders around the world should realise that although the brunt of the health crisis is affecting Africa at the moment, the situation could change. “We shouldn’t forget that at the beginning of Covid, many countries said there was zero risk of being affected, but a few months later, they became the hotspot,” he said. “We don’t want to see the UK and other countries become the hotspot.”
This outbreak, the 17th in the Democratic Republic of the Congo since Ebola was identified, was caused by the Bundibugyo virus and has become the largest and deadliest in the country’s history.

Ebola is a highly contagious, severe, and often fatal illness. It is spread through direct contact with body fluids such as the blood or vomit of infected people, or dead bodies, such as during funeral preparations.

On 15 May, DR Congo’s health ministry declared an outbreak in Ituri province, though sequencing shows it had begun in February. It has now spread to Kenya and Uganda in east Africa, while last week, in west Africa, Nigeria confirmed a case in the capital, Abuja, after a woman who arrived from Uganda tested positive for the virus.
France is the only non-African country to have confirmed a case of Ebola so far – a doctor who had returned from DR Congo – in June.
The Bundibugyo virus has no approved treatment, though vaccine trials are under way. The results should be available in three to six months, said Kaseya.
Of the total 10,091 cases, 10,060 have occurred in DR Congo, with 4,887 deaths. Two people have died in Uganda, and two in Kenya.

The response to the crisis has been hampered by inadequate protective equipment and unpaid health worker wages, leading to strikes. Conflict in DR Congo as well as mistrust towards officials in affected areas, misinformation and global aid cuts have further complicated the situation.

Kaseya will convene a meeting of African health ministers on Wednesday to urge greater cross-border cooperation. He wants governments to introduce screening and testing for people coming from affected regions at points of entry and exit.
“The main message to ministers is that they have to understand they could be affected, and we don’t want them to be surprised by what could happen,” he said.

At a meeting in November with African heads of state, Kaseya will call for a “corridor of peace” in conflict areas. “Currently, we have colleagues in Ituri who want to go and support the population, but they cannot because of insecurity,” he said. “I have to say to leaders, this outbreak is not for rebels, it’s not for the official army, it’s for everyone. Ebola can affect everyone … We need to come together to have a kind of agreement on how to protect each other.”

Kaseya called for a global effort to fund the response. He said governments had pledged $3bn (£2.3bn), but that more than $2bn was still outstanding. African countries had committed $120m, he said, while the rest is meant to come from international donors including the US, the UK and the EU.

“We need this money now,” he said. “We must understand that failure to provide funding now to African countries [will result in more being spent] because the outbreak will continue to move. If we have other countries affected we’ll be talking about trillions of dollars because it will require a lot of support to stop this outbreak.”

items.title: How a lifelong Republican came to lead the data center battle in Ohio
paragraphs: Nick Owens, an attorney in Brown County, Ohio, stands at the edge of a Mt. Orab neighborhood next to farmland that has been sold to a data center developer. Owens is leading an effort to halt the buildout of hyperscale data centers in communities like this one. Andrea Hsu/NPR hide caption
Stay up to date with our Politics newsletter, sent weekly.
MT. ORAB, Ohio — The data center mystery in this rural exurb of Cincinnati has consumed Nick Owens.

The lifelong Republican and self-described small-town attorney has spent countless hours trying to figure out what's going on with 1,000 acres of farmland and trees that property records show were sold to a data center developer in 2024 and 2025.
In a few spots, the data center property runs right up against beautiful two-story homes.
"This is the Ohio that people brag about. This is the Ohio people love. This is the small town charm," he says. "Living in the rural area, but getting the benefits of a nice, lovely neighborhood."
Some of the most coordinated opposition to data centers anywhere in the country grew out of what happened in secrecy in this village of 4,300 people, a short drive up a country road from Owens' home.

Nondisclosure agreements have stymied Owens' efforts to learn more. But along his quest, he crossed paths with another local attorney and a real estate agent who were equally alarmed. Together, they mobilized a network of volunteers in nearly all 88 counties in the state. They are Democrats, Republicans and Independents. They called themselves Conserve Ohio.

"We all share the same ethos and the same passion for preserving our way of life, preserving the future of Ohio, frankly, from the hyperscale data center invasion," says Owens. "It's really beautiful."

This fall, the group is behind ballot initiatives in 10 communities that would amend local charters to prohibit the construction of large-scale data centers — the kind used to power artificial intelligence. It's an effort that goes beyond the temporary pauses that hundreds of municipal and county governments have embraced.
"All too often you hear from the politicians, 'Well, the community should have a say,'" says Owens. "We're going to find out in ten communities whether or not the communities want them."

Meanwhile, the grassroots group is working on a more ambitious undertaking: a petition for an amendment to the state constitution that would ban large-scale data centers statewide. Their goal is to put that to Ohio's voters in 2027.

It's been more than a decade since tech companies first came to Ohio, drawn by the state's inexpensive and abundant land, its energy infrastructure and its generous tax breaks. That combination paved the way for some of the fastest data center growth in the country.

Now, despite the economic benefits — considerable tax revenue, money for schools, numerous construction jobs and a smaller number of permanent jobs — no one seems to want a computing campus in their backyard, especially one shrouded in secrecy.
Signs opposing data centers outnumber campaign signs in a neighborhood in Mt. Orab, Ohio. Andrea Hsu/NPR hide caption

"Should the school have extra money or the local government have extra money so we have a constant hum and ridiculous amounts of emissions and pollution?" Owens says, pointing out that hyperscale data centers will require new power plants. "Our community is not for sale."
Pressed to consider whether the state should forgo all opportunities, Owens says he'd entertain the idea of putting data centers on old industrial sites, where they'd be buffered from people.

"If we're going to have data centers, those are the prime places," he says, while acknowledging that it'd be cheaper and easier for a developer to build on pristine farmland than on an old coal site. "I don't know if there are enough brownfield sites, but shouldn't we start with those first?"

In recent months, candidates running for statewide office in Ohio have been trying to convince voters that they hear their concerns — even as they stop short of backing the kind of sweeping moratorium data center opponents are seeking.
Until recently, data center projects weren't all that controversial, in part because they were smaller and weren't being built for AI.

But as the issue has gained traction, it's become a hot topic in the midterms, including in the tight race to fill a U.S. Senate seat. Former Democratic Senator Sherrod Brown has cast his opponent, the incumbent Republican Senator Jon Husted, as "the face of data centers." Brown has been reminding voters that as lieutenant governor, Husted welcomed tech companies to Ohio and championed their data center investments.
Meanwhile, Husted has accused Brown of hypocrisy, pointing to Brown's past support for data centers.

Husted has also introduced his own solution, pushing a bill in Congress aimed at getting data centers to pay for power grid upgrades and other costs associated with their massive energy use. Senate Democrats have blocked the bill, calling it toothless, prompting Husted to accuse the Democrats of not caring or helping.

These political gestures have not persuaded Linda Moodie, an independent who's been volunteering with Conserve Ohio. She doesn't trust that any of the candidates running for statewide office "will do the right thing" if elected, which is to give the people a say in the data center buildout.
"It's really something that I think a lot of us didn't see coming, and all of a sudden there's just an influx of them," she says.

Linda Moodie (right), a volunteer with Conserve Ohio, collects signatures for a petition to ban large-scale data centers statewide at a Halloween event in Fairfield, Ohio, on Oct. 22, 2026. Andrea Hsu/NPR hide caption
Between now and election day, she's seizing every opportunity to collect signatures to get the statewide ban on the ballot next year.

On a recent evening, she set up a booth at the "Halloween on the Green" celebration in the Cincinnati suburb of Fairfield. She handed out candy to kids and clipboards with the petition to parents. Both were enthusiastically received.
"The closer it hits to home, the more people that are going to want to do something," says Moodie.

Two years ago, Owens served as a Trump delegate at the Republican National Convention. He won't say how he's voting this fall, but he says no doubt the data center issue, along with $6 diesel, have dampened Republican enthusiasm.
Throughout Mt. Orab, the absence of campaign yard signs is notable.
"Two years ago you would have seen Donald Trump signs left and right," says Owens.
This county, like much of rural Ohio, voted 80% for President Trump in 2024.

"You always have depressed votes in the midterms," says Owens. "But I think the enthusiasm gap for Republicans in particularly rural areas is going to be a lot more pronounced… than any type of enthusiasm gap for Democrats in the cities."
Trump's belittling of data center opponents isn't helping, he says, citing recent comments the president posted to his social media platform Truth Social.

"The only reason that communities throughout the U.S.A. should not want Data Centers is if they want to end up being backwards and poor. If they want to be successful and rich, with far lower taxes and jobs all over the place, let Data Reign," Trump wrote. "If we kill the Golden Goose, you will only have yourselves to blame."
Owens calls the president's statements "tone deaf."
"I mean, no one wants to be poor or backwards," he says. "I want our regular way of life."
Construction at the Mt. Orab site hasn't yet begun. It's not clear when it will. Owens says because of nondisclosure agreements, people who live here know nothing.
For now, standing at the edge of the data center property on a crisp fall day, it's nearly silent but for the birds.

items.title: US and China share a love of "new things and innovation" says Ma Yansong
paragraphs: Chinese architect Ma Yansong has completed one of the highest-profile US buildings of 2026 – the Lucas Museum of Narrative Art, in California. In this interview, he explains his architecture’s international appeal as a “bridge between imagination and reality”.

Speaking over video call on the occasion of the Lucas Museum’s opening, Ma told Dezeen that the building has acted as a stable point in a rapidly changing world, with trade wars, AI races and a US federal government that has enshrined classical architecture as a national norm.
“This project took 12 years, across two countries, and the world changed around it. The building didn’t,” he said.
The long-anticipated project, funded by Star Wars creator George Lucas, was first planned for San Francisco, then Chicago, before landing in Los Angeles.
“What made it possible is that George and I come from different roots, but both love the same kind of thing – stories that belong to ordinary people, not to high culture,” said Ma.

Ma believes this shared tendency toward exploration between himself and the American filmmaker applies more widely, and the 51-year-old architect spoke positively about the potential for architecture to illuminate the similarities between China and the United States.
“I see a lot in common between the two countries,” he said. “They both like innovation and new things, and they focus on young people, on education.”
“I think architecture is a bridge between the imagination and reality”
His own life mirrors this outlook. Attracted by innovation as a youth in Beijing, he travelled to Yale, where he graduated with a master’s degree in 2002.
At Yale, Ma became interested in Zaha Hadid’s parametric architecture and eventually worked at her firm in London.
Despite teaching and working mostly in the United States and Europe, Hadid cultivated her signature parametric style working in China’s early 2000s building boom.

The completion of the Lucas Museum represents a Chinese architect taking these principles abroad, a full-circle moment as Ma moved from the US to the UK, back to China, where he has completed dozens of projects, bringing his honed sensibility to California.

Buildings created in the parametric style, or design based on the specific geometries allowed by computer calculations, have been criticised for their lack of relation to sites, and for being self-referential.
The museum’s curved exterior is covered in thousands of white polymer panels, giving it a futuristic look.

Nevertheless, Ma pushes back on Dezeen’s description of the building as “spaceship-like”. Instead, he compares it to a cloud, as an enduring symbol for the imagination – an aspect of consciousness that the architect hopes is provoked by his buildings.

He worked with landscape studio SLA to design an expansive park to serve as an extension of the museum, and the building itself, according to him, features organic curves. He called the effect of these combined elements “surreal nature” and said he aims to bring the natural into the urban environment.
The suggestion of the surreal also points to his aim of provoking the imagination in his design – something the architect said he shares with Lucas and science fiction storytelling.
“I think architecture is a bridge between the imagination and reality,” he said, adding that he hopes the Lucas Museum functions like the narrative art that it holds.
The relationship between Ma and Lucas developed around the question of narrative art since the filmmaker first tapped the architect for the project in 2014.
Ma had actually referenced a scene from Star Wars in his bulbous 2005 museum for Ordos, though he didn’t advertise the influence in his early meetings with Lucas.
“On the personal level, me and George have very easy communication,” said Ma, who famously wanted to become a science fiction director before his career in architecture.

“[George and I] are always talking about ideas, and he’s always supportive. We were constantly discussing what is narrative art,” he continued, adding that the question has led Ma to ask a question that has helped clarify his own practice – “what is narrative architecture?”
Ma said that the project has allowed him to “kind of achieve my goal as a movie maker”.
“You create a dream,” said Ma. “That’s important.”
“It’s why I like science fiction movies – because you put your imagination on the screen, and when people watch it, they believe in something.”

For Ma, this narrative approach to architecture is about opening up to different perspectives, and like science fiction and fantasy, this bridge to the imagination requires a certain suspension of disbelief.
“I’m not interested in everyone receiving the same message,” he said. “I think good public space lets everyone reflect their own experience or knowledge or thinking and share with other people.”
“So I’ve had to find a balance between abstraction and emotion.”

At the Lucas Museum, this intersection of abstraction and emotion is most evident in the massive open-air dome, where visitors can stand on the ground and look up through the panelled apex at the sky.
The space has almost a cathedral-like quality in its grandeur, but it is without ornament and other traditional figurative elements of storytelling in architecture, such as statues or text.
“The architectural space is a trigger for different people to have their own stories. I think that’s a little different from the classic buildings.”

“When you frame it and bring the light into the space, people start to look up, and they will see this connection between individuals and the universe beyond the building, so I think that’s something narrative to me.”
“I like the future, but not the cold future”
The building was also designed to evoke well-proportioned natural elements and bring nature into the city, literally in the case of the green roofs and surrounding park.
Other projects by Ma’s studio have had similar ambitions, such as the Shenzhen Bay Culture Square and One River North in Denver.
And if his architecture is futuristic, Ma hopes that a greener version of the city is the future it evokes, he said.
“I like the future, but not the cold future,” said Ma. “It’s more important that the building is warm and welcoming.”
Ma hopes that Lucas Museum will be inspiring to people, just as his younger self was inspired by the innovative architecture coming out of Yale when he was starting.
“When people see a building that’s so idealistic, that is pushing the boundary, everyone will be encouraged,” he said.

If you enjoy reading Dezeen’s interviews, opinions and features, subscribe to Dezeen In Depth. Sent on the last Friday of each month, this newsletter provides a single place to read about the design and architecture stories behind the headlines.

items.title: This 3D artist achieves incredible realism to breath life into striking character designs
paragraphs: Tom Newbury is a 3D artist based in Australia who has been working commercially for 15 years. He's worked across many feature films, game cinematics and series, and he's passionate about realism and bringing 3D characters to life.

He creates his art using Maya, ZBrush, Mari, Marvelous Designer and Blender (see our guides to the best 3D modelling software and the best laptops for 3D modelling). Below, he talks us through four examples of his work.

“This piece was the subject for a tutorial I made for the Think Tank Training Centre. I had to choose a concept and present my workflow from start to finish. This subject is a bit more stylised than the work I usually do, but I had a vision of how it would work with my detailed style.”

“I created this piece after seeing an illustration by the artist Vetarmora. When I see a design which really inspires me I begin to visualise it in my own style. Through my work, I enjoy breathing a level of realism into the character.”
“Inspired by the work Weta did on The Planet of the Apes series, I wanted to see how far I could push my skills to create my own realistic chimpanzee.”
“Based on a painting by Vetarmora. I just loved the use of light in this piece, the earring design being the focal point, paired with the deep dark shiny eyes.”

items.title: Anthropic is preparing to go public. A look at the company's plan
paragraphs: NPR's Steve Inskeep asks Machine Gods host Casey Newton about the reaction to Anthropic's preparations to become a publicly traded company.

We're going to try to understand the business plan for Anthropic. The AI company that produces Claude is preparing to go public, selling shares on the stock market. They released a prospectus this week, trying to explain how it could make sense for a company that has made billions of dollars to be worth trillions of dollars. Casey Newton is the co-host of the new NPR podcast Machine Gods, all about AI. So we've called him in. Hi there, Casey.
CASEY NEWTON, BYLINE: Hey, Steve. Thanks for having me.
INSKEEP: OK. So when we talk about a company that might be worth well north of $1 trillion, what does Anthropic say they plan to do that would make that pay off?

NEWTON: Yeah. So what Anthropic does is they sell intelligence. So far, that intelligence is mostly going toward writing software to writing code, and Anthropic has been able to sell intelligence for those two jobs quite successfully. The question and the sort of investor bet is can you expand that intelligence to many other sectors of the economy, and could you maybe even eventually start to automate away some entire jobs? Because if you can do that, then I think there will be a plausible argument that Anthropic would be worth trillions of dollars.

INSKEEP: I want to talk through the mechanics of that, though. As everybody is learning, you have to build data centers in order to have the compute - the computing power to do more and more with artificial intelligence, and that is costing trillions of dollars. What's on the line here?

NEWTON: Yeah. Well, as you note, you do need data centers to run AI models, and those have become very unpopular politically. At the same time, there are enough of them that now have already been built, and there seem to be enough in construction that there will be a really healthy amount of compute for the next few years.

And one of the things that we learn in the Anthropic prospectus is just that they've been able to sell that compute at a really good gross margin. You know, for every dollar worth of Claude they're selling, they're keeping about 85% of that. So if that remains the case, you know, they may be able to keep their books balanced and earn a healthy profit.

INSKEEP: Oh. You just told me some news here because there've been a lot of stories over the past year or so about how that compute was getting more and more expensive, to the point where people wondered if it would even be worth it for some tasks.

NEWTON: That's right. And many observers, I was reading this week, have been surprised at just how good the margins Anthropic has been able to make are. Now, where I would say there is some room for worry is that the reason that Anthropic has been able to sell at such a great margin is that it has arguably had the best model for most of the past year or two. There are many competitors in this market, and their models are getting better continuously.

INSKEEP: There, nevertheless, are some mind-blowing phrases in this prospectus. I was reading the letter by the founders at the top of it, and they admit in the letter - they say in the letter, we're going to spend money. We're going to invest money in such enormous amounts that it will seem, quote, "irresponsibly large at first glance." Wow.

NEWTON: Yeah. It's - you know, it's a really crazy thing about the AI business is that you have to buy compute many years in advance - those data centers that you just mentioned. They're ungodly expensive. They take a long time to build. And you're buying them assuming that demand will be there, but, of course, you know, you can't guarantee that in the moment that you're buying it. So I think that was a signal to shareholders, like, hey, if you want to buy our stock, you need to be in for a kind of long ride here because we are going to have to make that calculation.
INSKEEP: Meaning that if there's a bubble, if things go down, there could be some pain along the way here.

NEWTON: Absolutely. And, you know, the CEO of Anthropic, Dario Amodei, has talked about that because, you know, believe it or not, the company was getting criticized at the start of the year for not buying even more compute. And one of the things that Dario said was, look, like, if I had made that bet and been wrong about the amount of demand for what we make, we would be bankrupt right now.
INSKEEP: OK. I want to ask about another phrase in this letter from Amodei and others. They say that if everything works out, they could usher in, quote, "an age of miracles."
NEWTON: (Laughter) Wouldn't that be nice?
INSKEEP: Yeah. But, like, what if it only turns out to be a really good business and not an age of miracles? Is everybody going to lose their shirt?
NEWTON: (Laughter) Then I think there will be a lot of disappointed shareholders, yeah, and people selling their stock, among other things.
INSKEEP: Casey Newton is the co-host of the NPR podcast Machine Gods. Thanks.
And a disclosure - Casey Newton is engaged to marry a person who works at Anthropic.

items.title: ‘Emotional intimacy’ from AI chatbots would be banned under Australia’s digital duty of care laws
paragraphs: The federal government wants to ban AI chatbots which seek to create “emotional intimacy” after prime minister Anthony Albanese raised the alarm in a heartfelt speech about children treating these agents as their “best friend”.

But Labor is coming under increasing pressure to empower the telecommunications ombudsman to become a watchdog for social media and AI to give Australians an external complaints mechanism and allow the “naming and shaming” of big tech.

The digital duty of care bill passed the House of Representatives on Wednesday and will be debated by the Senate in coming weeks. The government hopes to pass the bill by the end of 2026, but its pathway through the upper house remains unclear. The Greens support the bill, while the Coalition has said it will not vote for it, though Labor still appears keen to win the opposition’s support and remains open to amendments.

The planned framework would apply new online safety standards to social media, games, apps and chatbots. Labor said it would place “an overarching obligation” on tech platforms “to provide a safe online environment for all Australians” and replace a range of existing online codes and standards with a broader duty-of-care requirement to protect users from certain “harmful” content. It would also require social media platforms to offer an “opt-out” feature for its algorithm and suggested content.

The communications minister, Anika Wells, has suggested content that that promotes misogyny, terrorism, suicide, self-harm and eating disorders would be captured by the laws. On Wednesday, the government accepted amendments from crossbencher Kate Chaney which would add certain AI chatbot activity to the list of harms, requiring platforms to ban “material or conduct that simulates emotional intimacy and encourages or fosters a child’s dependence on it in place of human relationships”.

In an emotional address on Tuesday night, where he again implored the Coalition to consider voting for the bill, Albanese said: “the stories we hear about people identifying a chatbot, a non-person as their best friend, should be a huge wake up call for every member of this parliament to be prepared to act.”

The opposition voted against the bill in the House, alongside One Nation. Political opponents have accused Labor of an “Orwellian” system of “censorship” and of seeking to influence conversations online – claims Wells strongly denied.
“If they really care, the test is simple here, they should bring an amendment, not a slogan to ‘kill the bill’,” Wells told ABC radio on Wednesday.

Another Chaney amendment accepted by Labor would require the algorithm opt-out features to be “accessible, easy to use” and “prominently available” on platforms, amid concerns that social media firms may offer only small or hard-to-find features.

The bill now moves to the Senate, where the Greens have set up an inquiry to probe the laws due to report back in late November. Senator Sarah Hanson-Young backed a digital duty of care, calling for the government’s legislation to be strengthened. The Greens want Australians to have the right to pursue private legal action against platforms and for penalties to be increased.
“Australians also need an external complaints pathway, free from the profit-driven whims of big tech’s content moderation,” she said.

Independent MP Sophie Scamps had proposed changes to the bill to expand the remit of the telecommunications industry ombudsman. She said such a watchdog – which does not currently exist for big tech – would allow ordinary social media users to seek remedies to their accounts being hacked or inaccessible, including compensation, and investigate broader issues to name and shame companies behaving badly.
Labor did not accept this amendment in the lower house and Wells declined to voice support for such an idea, but the Greens will push for such a reform in their Senate negotiations.

The telecommunications industry ombudsman, Cynthia Gebert, said her office would be well placed to carry out such a role for big tech. She said such roles were funded by the industries they regulate and that expanding its remit could be financed by big tech.

“There are some real strengths in the DDOC [digital duty of care] because it’s putting the onus on platforms to make things safe … but I think the area that needs to be strengthened is giving people somewhere to go if they can’t get their complaints resolved with the platform,” Gebert said.
“It risks leaving Australians in the safe place they are now, where they get automated responses or escalation procedures that don’t go anywhere.”
Gebert said the government should make it mandatory for big tech to be part of an ombudsman scheme, saying it would “hold industry to account and drive system improvement”.
“[The telecommunications industry ombudsman] can help with your Telstra account, but we can’t help with your Gmail account. Consumers come to us sometimes and ask, ‘why this, not that?’,” she said.
“We want to help but don’t have the powers to do so now.”

items.title: 'An annoying buzz': The search for stealthier drones
paragraphs: Schmidt is one of a growing number of people living with the noise of drones dispatched by companies including Amazon and Walmart as they seek to speed up home deliveries.
Delivery drone services, not long ago a novelty, are becoming part of everyday life for many people in the US.

Among them, Amazon Prime Air is in the process of expanding deliveries to nearly 500 cities and towns, delivering items that fit into a space the size of a shoe box. It has also launched to customers in and around Darlington in the north of England.
Smaller drone delivery services are popping up too: in some US cities, customers can order flying treats from their local pizza joint or ice cream parlour.
Even in cities where noise is already a steady part of life, the sound of drones seems to irk in a particular way.
While the steady passing of traffic might blend into the background, the sudden whine of a drone's rotors can pierce the everyday hum.

The sound tends to be "particularly noticeable, even when overall sound levels are relatively low," says Antonio Torija Martinez, professor in acoustic engineering and psychoacoustics at the University of Salford.
Unlike planes, drones operate at low altitudes and may fly directly over residential areas.
"They can expose communities that have not previously experienced significant aircraft noise, and who may therefore be more sensitive to changes in their local soundscape," says Torija Martinez.

He points to research showing that people respond strongly to a noise when they consider the source to be "novel, intrusive or frequent". People who benefit from a drone delivery service, for example, may be less bothered by the noise.

However, complaints about the sound of drones are likely to grow, he warns: "At the moment we are seeing some of these problems localised in some areas, but… as the drone sector expands, more and more of these complaints will happen."

In the US, the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) regulates commercial drones, but it has come under fire for allowing noisy drone delivery operations. The FAA says operators and local community leaders have primary responsibility for addressing any community concerns.
Might better technology muffle the irritating buzz?
One startup, Greenjets, set out to tackle both "noise level and the frequency of that noise," as Darren James, future technologies lead at the company, puts it.
The London-based business has designed a propulsion system it claims can reduce drone noise by at least two thirds.

While standard drones use spinning propellers that slice through open air, creating that high-pitched buzz, Greenjets encloses spinning blades inside a pod, to muffle the sound and direct the noise away from the ground.
Its system also quietens things down through slower rotor speed and by using materials that reduce vibration noise.
Making quieter drones isn't just about keeping the noise down for neighbours who are already sick of airborne deliveries.

Greenjets' low-noise tech has been used by police and harbour security teams in Germany. It has also helped conservationists in Africa, who are seeking to track poachers from above without being detected.
Battlefield drone operators also have good reason to keep the noise down, to avoid alerting the enemy of the approach of their unmanned vehicles.

"There are some efforts to reduce the sound of drones. The US Special Forces are interested, at an experimental stage," says Robert Tollast, a research fellow at Whitehall think tank The Royal United Services Institute (RUSI).

But he stresses that drone speed, rather than stealthiness, tends to come first for larger drones used in the war between Russia and Ukraine. "Make it faster, not less quiet, seems to be the approach," says Tollast.
For Detroit-based entrepreneur, Greg Sharrow, it was the challenge of broadcasting a classical music performance back in 2012 that set him on the path to quieter drone design.
He needed to film a violinist from a tricky angle and a drone seemed the only solution – expect that it would be far too noisy.

As a starting point, "I knew that most of the noise from the drone was coming from the propeller, not the motor," he says. Specifically, it was the tips of the blades that he realised were creating the noise as they swiped through the air.
"I asked myself a very simple question, what would a tipless propeller look like and how would it function?"
The result was to create a propeller with twisted loop-shaped blades with no points.

It turned out it was easier to test his propeller in water than it was to repeatedly fly a drone, which led Sharrow to initially develop a less noisy boat propeller. Now, however, his company, Sharrow Engineering, is focusing on developing "ultra-quiet" drone rotors.
"We have validated that the technology works in drone applications and that it is dramatically quieter," says Sharrow.

Companies at the forefront of drone deliveries say they are also working to reduce the noise of their fleets. A spokesperson for Amazon says it has made "measurable sound improvements" to its drones and its latest designs use custom-designed propellers "that produce almost half the perceived sound of the prior generation, with a milder tone".

Drone maker Wing, which provides its vehicles for Walmart deliveries, says its propellers are designed to minimise noise. It also varies its flight paths to prevent repeated overflights over any single home or neighbourhood.

For Schmidt, fed up with the noise of drones, the only truly satisfactory solution would be to halt drone deliveries in her area. "I would like them to completely stop until they figure out how their services stop being a nuisance," she says.

items.title: UN official says North Korea’s human rights situation has not improved over past decade
paragraphs: Editor's note: this story was translated from the original VOA Korean article.

North Korea’s human rights situation has not improved over the past decade and has deteriorated significantly in some key areas, including the use of the death penalty, a senior U.N. human rights official told VOA.

James Heenan, representative of the U.N. Human Rights Office in Seoul, said concerns persist over political prison camps, restrictions on movement, and access to food and health care. “Our assessment is that the situation, particularly over the last decade, has overall not improved,” Heenan said during an October 22 interview in Washington. “In some key respects, it’s degraded significantly.”
He pointed to increases in both executions and the number of offenses punishable by death as a major concern.

Heenan also stressed the urgency of resolving longstanding enforced disappearance cases involving South Koreans, Japanese and citizens of other countries. Victims, relatives and alleged perpetrators are aging, narrowing the time available to establish what happened and pursue justice, he said.

He noted some anecdotal indications of reduced ill-treatment in detention, including accounts that central authorities had instructed personnel not to beat detainees. But he cautioned that such limited signs of improvement did not change the broader assessment.
Heenan also warned that repeatedly publishing the identities of the two North Korean prisoners of war held in Ukraine could increase risks to them and their relatives.
Even if they have been revealed before, it doesn’t allow people to reveal them again,” he said.
In North Korea, people perceived as having broken the law can face harsh punishment and that can extend to their families, Heenan said.
Asked about reports that the prisoners had been transferred from Ukraine to South Korea, Heenan said his office did not know the terms of the transfer agreement and had no access to the men.
“What I’ve said is based on public press reports,” he said.
He called for privacy protections and appropriate assistance, including mental health and psychosocial support.
“Their well-being needs to be the center of the story,” he said.

Heenan also spoke to VOA about the issue of North Koreans who have escaped to China and are being forcibly returned to North Korea. He said authorities must first assess whether anyone repatriated could risk abuse or torture upon returning to North Korea.

The U.N. Convention Against Torture, which China ratified forbids returning anyone to a country where they could face a risk of torture. The rule is called "non-refoulement." China considers North Koreans who cross its border as economic migrants and returns them as part of an agreement with Pyongyang. Critics say this allows China to ignore its legal obligations against refoulment.
U.N. reporting has documented particularly severe punishment for returnees who expressed interest in reaching South Korea, embraced Christianity or had contact with Christian pastors.
Heenan said tighter border controls had reduced departures from North Korea, making conditions inside the country more difficult to assess.

He also raised concerns about South Koreans detained in North Korea, citing cases where they are denied consular access. He said there are also concerns about judicial fairness and the methods used to obtain evidence supporting convictions.

Heenan said that going forward it is necessary to set up a system that will hold North Korean officials accountable for abuses. He said that should include criminal trials and civil proceedings, as well as recognition of victims, truth-telling, compensation, and psychological support.

His office maintains a central repository database containing thousands of potential crimes in North Korea that could someday be used as evidence in future trials. Some information could be shared with countries that have appropriate jurisdiction over crimes committed abroad, he said.
Until those trials can happen, Hennan said the work of collecting and preserving evidence must continue. “It is laborious work,” he said. “But it’s a long-term goal.”

items.title: UN: Large-scale return of Afghan refugees strains Afghan economy
paragraphs: Editor's note: this story was translated from the original VOA Dari article.
The return of millions of Afghan refugees from Iran and Pakistan has put pressure on the Afghan economy, according to the United Nations.
The United Nations Development Program in Afghanistan said Tuesday in a post on X that the large-scale return of Afghans has added “pressure on jobs, essential services and infrastructure.”
The U.N. said that nearly 1.3 million Afghans have returned, including those deported, from Pakistan and Iran, the two countries hosting most of Afghan refugees, to Afghanistan, so far in 2026.
UNDP adds that between 2023 and 2025, about 4.9 million Afghans returned to the country.

Even with the millions of returns, the U.N. says that 4.4 million Afghans are still living in Iran, including 1.4 million undocumented Afghans. About 1.6 million Afghans live in Pakistan including an estimated 159 thousand undocumented Afghans.
The U.N. said that “policy changes and economic pressures” in host countries have led to large-scale deportations and returns of Afghans.
The returns have further burdened vulnerable communities and essential services, according to the U.N.
The World Food Program said about 19.2 million people face acute food insecurity, while 4 million women and children are expected to suffer from malnutrition in 2027.

Afghan returnees are “with few or no resources, leaving them to settle in remote mountainous areas far from major roads and essential services. They live in makeshift shelters, often just tents under the scorching sun or on bare stones, with no access to clean water, food, or even basic shelter,” said the UNHCR. “Healthcare is out of reach, and many lack even the simplest identification documents, leaving them vulnerable and invisible in the margins of society.

Mohammad Bashir Doodyal, a former economics professor at Kabul University, told VOA that poverty, a lack of job opportunities and presence of diseases could pose major challenges to the integration of returnees into Afghan society.
“It is the responsibility of governments to plan ... to address these issues,” said Doodyal, adding that “it looks there are no such plans in place.”
He added that Afghanistan would need to improve its relations with neighboring countries and the international community to attract domestic and foreign investment needed to strengthen the economy.
“Afghanistan must emerge from isolation and have a government that the international community can trust and work with,” Doodyal said.

Khan Jan Alokozay, president of the Afghan chapter of the Pakistan-Afghanistan Joint Chamber of Commerce and Industry, told VOA that neither the government nor the private sector has the capacity to absorb millions of Afghans at once.

items.title: The Museum of the American Revolution in Philadelphia now speaks Ukrainian
paragraphs: Editor's note: this story was translated from the original VOA Ukrainian article.
The Museum of the American Revolution in Philadelphia has become the fifth institution in the United States to introduce Ukrainian-language audio guides.

"The Museum of the American Revolution allows people from around the world in 2026 to understand and connect with the people and events of 1776 during the American Revolution, and delivers narratives about the immense complexity, diversity, and uncertainty that the Revolutionary generation faced," said Tyler Putman, senior manager of gallery interpretation.

"To be able to offer Ukrainians and Ukrainian speakers a resource in their own language in order to explore The Declaration's Journey, and the chance to better understand how independence movements across time and space inform each other and connect people from disparate corners of the world, is a great honor for our institution," added Putman during the official presentation of the audio guide, held at the museum on October 22.

The exhibition The Declaration’s Journey, which explores the influence of the U.S. Declaration of Independence on historical events over the past 250 years, includes Ukraine’s Declaration of Independence, displayed alongside declarations from other nations.

This was part of the initiative launched in 2019 by Ukraine’s first lady, Olena Zelenska, who continues to introduce Ukrainian-language audio guides at leading cultural and historical landmarks around the world.

“For Ukrainians living far from home, hearing their native language in a place like this museum is a meaningful connection to their roots. The Ukrainian language is also a way for us to engage as equals through culture, art, and history,” said Denys Sienik, Ukraine’s chargé d’affaires in the United States, during his remarks at the museum.

“The Ukrainian language is an essential part of our national identity and a powerful expression of our resilience, dignity, and freedom. For centuries, Russia has sought to suppress our language and erase our cultural identity. Preserving our language and sharing our history are essential to protecting Ukraine’s identity,” he said.
Iryna Mazur, honorary consul of Ukraine in Philadelphia, and president of the Ukrainian Federation of America, helped bring the audio guide to the Museum of the American Revolution.

Such guides are now available in 59 countries worldwide. Visitors can hear Ukrainian at such renowned sites as the Palace of Versailles, the Colosseum, the Tower of London, and the Metropolitan Museum of Art in New York City.

items.title: ACOTAR fans put real life on hold for latest release
paragraphs: As I arrive at Waterstones in York shortly before 08:00, there is already a queue forming outside the bookshop.
Fans of Sarah J Maas's bestselling A Court of Thorns and Roses (ACOTAR) series are waiting eagerly to get their hands on the latest instalment.
Among them is Olivia Bray, 28, who has spent more than a decade immersed in the American author's fantasy world.
For Bray, the appeal goes beyond magic, romance and fantastical kingdoms. It is the feminism running through Maas's books that has kept her coming back.

And with the release of A Court of Splintered Harmony, Bray is prepared to put real life on hold, having booked an entire week off work to give herself time to recover from whatever awaits her between the covers.
"I'll be done [with reading] by tomorrow," she said. "I've just got the whole week off in case it's traumatising."
Set in the fictional world of Prythian, the series has amassed millions of fans across the world.
The series follows Feyre Archeron, a young huntress drawn into the dangerous world of the fae, where she navigates political intrigue, war and romance.

There have been five books so far, A Court of Thorns and Roses (2015), A Court of Mist and Fury (2016), A Court of Wings and Ruin (2017), A Court of Frost and Starlight (2018), and A Court of Silver Flames (2021).
A Court of Splintered Harmony, the sixth book in the best-selling series, was released on Tuesday - five years after fans last heard from the characters.
Another ACOTAR fan, 22-year-old Abigail Wright, hoped to finish the book on release day, which coincided with her day off, before returning to work.
She said the books were her "gateway back into reading" aged 19.
Like Bray, Wright believed the recurring theme of female empowerment was a key part of its appeal.
"I think it's so popular because, yes, the romantic side of it is very good, but the strong women you see in the books are just a way to make other young women feel really empowered," said Wright.

"It just gives them a sense of power and [makes them] see you can start from nothing, like Feyre does, and just make your way up… you don't need a man to do all these things for you, you have the power to do anything you want to do."

Gabriella Booth, 29, was introduced to the series in 2013, but attributes ACOTAR's explosion in popularity to both the pandemic and "BookTok" - a TikTok community dedicated to sharing what people are reading and writing.
"The characters in general are so easy to read about. You can relate in different parts to a lot of them, I find," said Booth.

"For me, I love the fantasy world - that's something I've loved reading growing up. So, to have that combined with the romance side of everything... there's something that's just so exciting to read about."
Booth has previously taken time off work to read new releases and plans to do so when the seventh ACOTAR book is published in January.
However, on this occasion, she hopes to finish A Court of Splintered Harmony after work.

Alice Boyce, a bookseller at Topping and Company Booksellers on Museum Street in York, said ACOTAR fans had made their way straight up to the science-fiction area of the store as soon as doors opened at 09:00.
"People are really enthusiastic; we've had emails saying, 'can you put a copy aside for me?', and last night we had people asking to put it on pre-order."
An ACOTAR fan herself, 26-year-old Boyce said she felt she could truly disconnect when she read the books.
"You can dive into books and just escape a little bit," she added.
Events were held across the UK, including in Wolverhampton and Northern Ireland, to mark the new book's release, with Waterstones on York's Coney Street hosting its first ever midnight release event.
Eighty ACOTAR fans, some of whom were dressed as their favourite characters, attended the event, while 100 members of the fandom flocked to a party in Wolverhampton.
Organiser Holly Fellows, from Redditch, told the BBC people were "ecstatic" when the book was finally released.
"The community was just lovely, it was so nice to see everybody come together and fan-girl over a book," Fellows said.
Fellows, who booked the day off work to read the book, said she was already through the first chapter.
"It sounds like it's going to be incredible", she said.

items.title: Will a new strategy help protect Northern Ireland's nature?
paragraphs: Agriculture and environment correspondent, BBC News NI
A new strategy to restore and enhance protection for nature in Northern Ireland has been launched by the agriculture and environment minister.
About 40% of the plants and animals in protected sites across Northern Ireland fall short of meeting the standard for "favourable condition".
And just one of 49 priority habitat types - like ancient and native woodlands, blanket bogs and species-rich grasslands - have favourable status.
The Nature Recovery Strategy sets out a long-term framework based on science for tackling biodiversity loss and restoring habitats.
The Nature Recovery Strategy sets out a long-term framework based on science for tackling biodiversity loss and restoring habitats
Minister Andrew Muir said supporting nature was "not just a nice thing to do", but "a moral obligation to future generations".
But the minister acknowledged that money would be needed to address the challenges.
And just one of 49 priority habitat types - like ancient and native woodlands, blanket bogs and species-rich grasslands - have favourable status
The strategy highlights the importance of nature as providing the food we eat, the water we drink and the air we breathe.
Muir said nature must be put "back at the heart of everything we do, because when nature thrives, people flourish.
"It is essential to a strong economy, healthier communities and a more resilient Northern Ireland.
"With so much of our natural world lost, we must protect what remains, restore what has been damaged and create new habitats at scale."
Many places in Northern Ireland support rare or threatened plants, animals and habitats.
They can be legally designated to help ensure better management and protection of those species.

There are hundreds of such designated sites across Northern Ireland, covering around 10% of the land and 38% of coastal waters - classed as Areas of Special Scientific Interest; Special Areas of Conservation (SACs) which have international biodiversity importance; Ramsar Sites which cover wetlands of international importance; Special Protection Areas (SPAs); and Marine Conservation Zones (MCZs).
That should lead to work to protect the species and habitats they have been designated for.
But the Office for Environmental Protection found not enough sites are being designated and the condition of those that have been is worsening.
The number of sites that were in favourable condition dropped from 61.7% in 2008, to 51.5% in 2024.
It is now investigating how those sites are being managed, external by the Department of Agriculture, Environment and Rural Affairs, after it found implementation of the designation fell short.
Northern Ireland is one of the most nature-depleted areas in the world, according to the 2023 State of Nature Report.
It found 12% of species here are under threat of extinction, and the number of flowering plants had declined by 14% since 1970.

The Nature Recovery Strategy identifies six external pressures affecting nature and biodiversity - invasive species; climate change; human impact through inappropriate development; land and sea-use change; increased intensive farming; pollution.
It says these must all be addressed effectively to allow nature to thrive.

items.title: This AI billboard might be too ballsy for its own good
paragraphs: Recently, billboard ads have been getting daring. From brands ditching their logos to wild guerrilla marketing, we've seen some real out-of-the-box thinking, but this latest ad from AI company Notion might be the most gutsy yet.

Placing itself shoulder to shoulder with the competition, Notion's confident ad proves that it stands out against its rivals. Dividing critics with its bold and minimalist billboard design, the ad proves that creative bravery is a priceless tool for standing out in a crowded market.
i can’t even tell who the billboard is for 😭 https://t.co/jclLv2cdtBOctober 26, 2026

The billboard in question features a lineup of AI logos including Claude, Perplexity, Grok Bot, ChatGPT and, of course, Notion front and centre. It might seem a little barmy to place yourself among the competition in your own ad, but it's this very confidence that makes Notion's ad shine.

"As much as I hate to admit it, this is a really great ad," a user on X wrote. "No words, just app icons. There’s mystery over who paid for it. There's controversy over why certain apps should be there. It's bold and makes a statement," they added. "Super cool and smart, or super dumb?" another added.

I, for one, am in the "super cool" camp. Given that most AI logos look the same, Notion's simple letterblock logo instantly stands out against the competition. The neutral ground of the logo lineup only helps Notion to emerge among its competitors, suggesting a certain edge against the competition.

While some have criticised the billboard for being too vague, I think that's where its strength emerges. The best adverts often spark conversation, and Notion's bold billboard is not only a symbol of confidence, but a conversation prompt about where the brand belongs in the AI sphere.

items.title: Rare dinosaur skeleton goes to auction in New York with £4.5m price tag
paragraphs: The mounted skeleton of a newly-identified dinosaur once mistaken for a young Tyrannosaurus rex is up for auction - with a price-tag of at least $6m (£4.5m).
Nicknamed "Jodi", the roughly 10-foot-tall (3m) skeleton will be auctioned by Sotheby's in New York. The sale comes a year after researchers confirmed that the skeleton belongs to a distinct genus.

The Late Cretaceous carnivore is expected to fetch up to $9m when it goes under the hammer on Tuesday. The auction comes after Sotheby's sold a Tyrannosaurus rex, dubbed "Gus", for a record $50.1m (£37.4m) in July.
The sales comes as some in the scientific community debate whether dinosaur remains should be sold privately.
Sotheby's described "Jodi" as an "excellent exhibition-ready" skeleton with about 191 fossil-bone elements and a "beautifully preserved, virtually complete skull".

The auction house added that the Nanotyrannus is "one of only three such skeletons known to science." The specimen is the first to come to market since the existence of the genus was confirmed by US researchers last October, Sotheby's said.

Megan Jenkins, a palaeontologist at the University of Portsmouth, told BBC Radio 4's Today programme on Tuesday that Nanotyrannus "was for a very long time believed to be sort of a teenager of T. rex".
"But it's a lot smaller and its a lot more gracile. So it's very sort-of sleek, slender, [with] blade-like teeth for slicing through meat," Jenkins said.
Tyrannosaurus rex and Nanotyrannus lived alongside one another during the same geological period approximately 67 million years ago.
"Jodi" was initially exhibited as a juvenile T. rex at London's Frieze Masters international art fair in October 2023, before the Nanotyrannus genus was classified.

The skeleton was discovered in the US state of Montana by rancher Jodi Pierson on her land in the Hall Creek Formation, a heavily studied geological site. It was later excavated by commercial palaeontologist Clayton Phipps.

Phipps also discovered the famous "Dueling Dinosaurs" fossil. That specimen, which shows the remains of a Nanotyrannus and Triceratops apparently in combat, was found eight miles (13km) away from "Jodi" in 2006.

The "Dueling Dinosaurs" discovery became crucial to the research published by Lindsay Zanno and James Napoli that classified Nanotyrannus as separate from T. rex. Their paper ended decades of debate over whether the dinosaurs were distinct from one another.
The auction of "Jodi" comes as some scientists warn that auctions could herald a new era in fossil collecting by the ultra-rich.
Researchers told the BBC after the sale of "Gus" that such remains should be exhibited in public spaces where they can be more freely studied.

Prof Steve Brusatte, a palaeontologist at the University of Edinburgh and consultant on the Jurassic Park films, told BBC World Service's What in the World programme in July that the T. rex's auction was "concerning".

"I don't know of any museum or university that can afford a price tag like that," he said. "Imagine if the Mona Lisa was just owned by a super-wealthy person and it wasn't on display and people couldn't see it, couldn't enjoy it."
He said that the time that he hoped such a sale didn't become a trend, adding it could adversely affect scientific research and public education.
Responding to today's auction, Brusatte called it "harrowing" that "Jodi" could disappear from public view.

"We've really just found out that Nanotyrannus is real, and now one of the best skeletons is about to be sold to the highest bidder, and it's harrowing to think it could disappear into the vaults of a collector rather than displayed on a museum where it can wow and inspire kids and families and the public at large," he told the BBC.
But Jenkins told the Today programme on Tuesday there were two sides to the debate, and that a lot of time, effort and money went into excavating the specimens.

"I don't begrudge the people involved for wanting to sell it for such a large amount of money," she said. "Although its a scary prospect, actually a lot of them have ended up in the public eye... these things without a doubt will end end up in a museum at some point."

items.title: Scotland's recycling rates fall to lowest level in five years
paragraphs: Waste experts have warned that landfill space in Scotland is rapidly running out
Scotland environment, energy and rural affairs correspondent
Scotland's recycling rate has fallen to its lowest level in five years, according to figures from the Scottish Environment Protection Agency (Sepa).
The Scottish government's environmental regulator says households recycled 42.8% of waste in 2025 - down from 44.3% the previous year.
According to a roadmap set by the Scottish government in 2010, recycling rates should have hit 70% last year but are falling well short.
The share of waste processed at an incinerator remained broadly the same at 82% but the amount being diverted to landfill fell by 10%.
Recycling rates vary massively by local authority. South Ayrshire's residents recycled 55% of their waste, compared to 26% in Glasgow.
The islands have the lowest rates, with Orkney recording a figure of just 18.2%.
A total of 2.31 million tonnes of waste was created by households in 2025, which represents a fall of just 1,500 tonnes.
Recycling rates have remained similar - at about 45% - for more than a decade.
The biggest change has been seen in the way black bag waste is treated.
A rapid growth in the construction of energy-from-waste plants, which generate electricity by burning rubbish, has seen a shift away from landfill.
But this has not happened quickly enough to meet a landfill ban which was due to come in at the start of the year. It has now been effectively delayed to 2028.
The figures do not reflect a disruption to Scotland's waste management by the long-term repairs being carried out to the incinerator at Polmadie in Glasgow.
The Glasgow Recycling and Renewable Energy Centre in Glasgow was shut down in April this year, with much of the waste being diverted to other incinerators or landfill.
The centre is operated, along with a facility at Dunbar, by Viridor.
Karen MacCormick from the company says waste incineration is a greener option than landfill because it can also generate electricity.
She added: "When it's in landfill you've got the landfill gasses, you've got methane, etc.

"This is a more sustainable way of dealing with the waste, coming through an energy recovery facility, and obviously we can create something at the end of it which is low carbon energy going straight to the grid."
A deposit return scheme for bottles and cans, which has seen recycling rates increase significantly in other countries, has been repeatedly delayed.
Experts have also suggested that the lack of consistency in what is collected by local authorities across the country makes it confusing for households.
While some councils take glass at the kerbside, for example, others are forced to drop them off at bottle banks.
Research from Zero Waste Scotland also suggests that more than half of the waste placed in black bins could be recycled.
Sepa's chief scientific officer, Dr Richard Allan, says the figures highlight an "ongoing challenge" with how waste is managed.
He added: "It's clear that where waste ends up is important, but we need to focus on preventing waste in the first place and recycling more of that material when it is produced."
Kim Pratt, senior circular economy campaigner at Friends of the Earth Scotland, said there had been a "shocking decline" in recycling rates.
She said this showed that Scotland had "lost its way", with households missing the 2025 target of 70% recycling "by a mile".

"Recycling levels have stalled in Scotland since the Scottish government encouraged a new generation of waste incinerators to be built, meaning that household waste which could have been recycled is being burned instead," she said.
"The Scottish government is expected to consult on new circular economy targets this year.
"If these are to be meaningful, it must learn the lessons from the past – setting targets is the easy part, meeting them requires real commitment and planning that puts people and nature first."
The Scottish government has been approached for comment.

items.title: What is Nasa's Artemis III mission? And what comes next?
paragraphs: Artemis III has been described by Nasa as the most complicated mission it's ever attempted.
It involves four astronauts, three rocket launches, three different spacecraft and two dockings. It will last for 14 days, although it could be extended to 17 days if needed.

The first rocket to launch will be Blue Origin's New Glenn rocket, blasting off from Florida. It will be carrying its prototype lander called Blue Moon. No astronauts will be on board and the lander will be placed into low Earth orbit.

Then Nasa's Space Launch System rocket will launch from the Kennedy Space Center in Florida, carrying four Artemis III astronauts in the Orion capsule. This is the same type of rocket and spacecraft used for the Artemis II mission, which saw astronauts fly around the Moon and back to Earth.
Orion will also be placed into orbit around the Earth, and the crew will spend two days checking out their spacecraft.
Then on day three of its flight, Orion will dock with the Blue Origin's Blue Moon. The crew will open the hatch and enter the lander, where they will spend two days checking out its systems.

On flight day six, SpaceX's huge Starship rocket will blast off, also from Florida. The upper stage of its rocket, called "the Ship" is the prototype lander (although it has not yet been fitted out as a lander and lacks life support systems) and this will be placed in low Earth orbit.

Nasa's Orion spacecraft and its crew will undock from the Blue Moon lander and then dock with the SpaceX Ship. This will be a shorter demonstration lasting for two hours, and the Artemis III crew will not enter the SpaceX lander.
Once undocked, the Orion crew will spend the rest of their mission carrying out additional tests of their capsule and carrying out science experiments, before returning home.

The overarching ambition behind Artemis is to establish a long-term human presence on the Moon. Nasa's Moon Base programme — unveiled in May 2026 by the agency's administrator, Jared Isaacman — sets out three phases:
Before 2029: robotic landers and hopping drones will survey the south polar region and deliver scientific instruments
From 2029 onwards: repeated crewed missions will expand the site
By the mid-2030s: Nasa envisages "semi-permanent" habitats with astronauts living on the Moon for extended stays

A working base would allow sustained scientific research, the testing of technology bound for future Mars missions, and the eventual extraction of lunar resources. It would also keep the United States ahead of China in a renewed space race.
Many in the field doubt that Nasa's timetable can be met.
Experts are concerned about the slow pace of the development of SpaceX;s Starship lunar lander and the absence of any in-orbit refuelling tests.
But the biggest set back was on 28 May 2026, when Blue Origin's only launch pad at Cape Canaveral was seriously damaged after a rocket exploded during an engine test.
Rebuilding the New Glenn launch pad is expected to take many months. When SpaceX lost a pad in 2016 it took 15 months to rebuild it — and SpaceX had other pads to fall back on.
Blue Origin does not, which calls into question the company's ability to provide the Blue Moon Mk2 needed for one of the lunar landings.

"It would not surprise me at all if China gets [to the moon] first," the Open University's Dr Simeon Barber told the BBC. The limiting step, he said, was the lander — the most challenging piece of the mission's technical architecture, and the one least under Nasa's direct control.

items.title: Polymarket has investigated 'dozens' of election-related cases
paragraphs: Prediction markets, like Polymarket and its main rival, Kalshi, have flourished in Trump's second term. Gabby Jones/AFP via Getty Images hide caption
Polymarket has investigated "dozens" of bets on its prediction markets related to the midterm election, according to the company's head of global intelligence and investigations, Shana Bautista.

At least two of these Polymarket investigations have been referred to its regulator, the U.S. Commodity Futures Trading Commission, according to a person who is familiar with the probes, but not authorized to speak publicly about them.

These investigations into election insider trading and manipulation come as prediction market Polymarket — and its chief competitor Kalshi — have exploded in popularity over the past year. But the fast-growing industry also faces significant legal challenges from states and political pushback from lawmakers who argue betting on the outcome of elections poses serious risks to the democratic process.

In April, Kalshi banned and fined a handful of political candidates from betting on themselves. A month later, NPR reported that campaign staffers had made "thousands" using insider polling information to bet on their own candidates on platforms like Polymarket and PredictIt.

Polymarket's Bautista — a former FBI official and cryptocurrency analyst — told NPR her team of 16 and a new election surveillance system are actively policing election bets ahead of the Nov. 3 midterms.

"If you have information that you have a duty to protect, don't trade on it," Bautista said. "It's explicitly against our terms of use on both platforms, but also is against the law. If you decide that you are smarter and can do it, we will find you."

Bautista joined Polymarket in June. She oversees information gathered from both the U.S.-regulated version of Polymarket, which requires users to provide their real identities, and its bigger brother, Polymarket International, which is essentially unregulated and where trading can be done anonymously and with cryptocurrency. Despite this, Bautista said crypto trades are rarely completely anonymous.
"There's never been a case that we work where we haven't been able to identify, potentially, who these people are," Bautista said.

She said her election surveillance system pulls in "gigabytes" of data on each user from social media, Federal Election Commission data, cryptocurrency companies, banking partners, statistical models and other public information sources. If a user hits a certain number of internally-defined red flags, Bautista gets an alert on her phone.
"We're getting hundreds of alerts a day," Bautista said.

When asked about the specific detection criteria and thresholds, Bautista did not comment citing system security. But she said insider trading and market manipulation all look the same regardless of the financial market.

"We're looking at threat vectors and risk areas that have existed for decades in traditional markets," Bautista said. "But we recognize, too, that when it comes to prediction markets, we're seeing some of the old tried and known tactics, but being applied to a new vector through prediction markets."

Back in May, Kalshi, Polymarket's top rival, announced its own election surveillance system that also uses FEC data. Their system purportedly blocks any campaign staffer listed by the FEC from betting on an election. In July, Kalshi said it had blocked "dozens" of staffers from trading on elections, though at least one staffer told NPR they got around this. The staffer shared records of their recent trades and spoke to NPR on the condition of anonymity for fear of consequences for their future employment.

Prediction markets for elections are uniquely vulnerable to market manipulation and insider trading, said Rajiv Sethi, an economics professor at Barnard College at Columbia University, who has studied prediction markets for decades.

"[Election prediction markets] have the possibility of being a self-fulfilling prophecy," Sethi said. "Elections have the property that what one believes is going to happen can actually affect what happens if a candidate is thought to be losing momentum or the campaign is flagging."
Bautista said her Polymarket team and surveillance system is learning from past cases and putting their feet in the shoes of would-be insider traders and market manipulators.

"If I was worried about somebody trying to materially move an election market to make it look like one option was more likely to happen than the other and I identify a pattern where they're opening several different accounts and they're doing that in short bursts and I see device IDs consistent across different trades placed in short succession with new wallets across five or four different accounts," Bautista said. "If I were to work that case and then action that, the findings of that tactic go back into the process to create the detections."

As prediction markets have exploded in popularity over the last two years, the industry's federal regulator, the CFTC, has done little to police these new financial markets, largely leaving that work to the companies themselves.

items.title: Our loos? They’re inspired by Milan’s Villa Necchi! The reborn planks-and-plasterboard theatre trouncing its flashy neighbours
paragraphs: Since the 2012 Olympics, the skyline of Hackney Wick in east London has bristled with cranes. The athletes may be long gone but the legacy of the sporting spectacle rolls on, as developers continue to extract profits from rising land values around the Olympic park. Across the canal, in this former industrial edgeland, there are more cranes than ever, busily hoisting prefabricated brick cladding panels into place, wrapping the latest loft-living concepts with a veneer of industrial chic. Where factories once stood, replicas of factories have risen, complete with sawtooth roofs and Crittall-esque windows, offering concierge-serviced views of the surrounding regeneration-scape.

But among all the crane towers, one is different from the rest. It stands still, now relieved of its duties, and encased in a silvery sheath of polycarbonate. Big red letters cling to the shimmering shaft, spelling out the new home of the Yard theatre. Once used to haul bits of buildings, the steel crane tower now serves as a beacon-cum-ventilation shaft, glowing by night while exhausting stale air from the theatre below.

It is one of many elements of this striking, low-budget building that have been cleverly reused and recycled, bringing economical pizzazz to the energetic young establishment. Founded in 2011 in a former printworks, the plucky warehouse theatre has come of age, with a £4m new building on the same site – and Ian McKellen set to star in the next show.

“We only expected it to last a few months,” says Jay Miller, founder and artistic director of the Yard, describing the theatre’s first incarnation. He cannily secured a cheap lease by pitching to the building’s owner that he could eliminate their security costs by occupying the vacant warehouse. He then hired the recent graduates of Practice Architecture to conjure an ad hoc auditorium on a shoestring. Their beguiling bricolage of butcher’s curtains, pink plasterboard and scavenged scaffolding planks lasted more than a decade and drew a loyal local crowd, staging shows that transferred to the National Theatre, became Bafta-winning television and won an Olivier award.

Miller, ever on the lookout for funding opportunities, saw a chance to expand when plans were mooted to redevelop the surrounding Queen’s Yard into a mixed-use district. That project never materialised, but Miller succeeded in leveraging £3m of CIL (Community Infrastructure Levy) from the London Legacy Development Corporation – the post-Olympic regeneration body – to fund the new theatre. In effect, the apartment blocks rising all around the Yard helped to pay for its existence.

The resulting project is far more than the usual “planning gain” token of community benefit. The work of Takero Shimazaki, a Tokyo-born Londoner who was shortlisted for the Stirling prize last year for an elegant timber and stone-roofed house, it is a tour de force of how to do a lot with a little. It reads like a collage of its context: a shed clad with corrugated fibre-cement sheeting, rising from graffiti-covered warehouse walls on one side and framed by a new brick gable end on the other. The bricks include subtle shades of blue, yellow and magenta, in a nod to the previous printworks, while the name of the theatre is spelt out in the brickwork, recalling the faded factory signs of the area. In keeping with the waste-not ethos, these K-Briqs, manufactured in Scotland, are unfired and made of 95% construction waste, recycling 16 tonnes of waste that would have otherwise gone to landfill and saving the equivalent of 3.5 tonnes of CO2 that regular bricks would have emitted.

There is a grandeur to the new theatre’s form. With its central tower and symmetrical pitch roof, Shimazaki says the Yard was inspired by Palladian churches to bring a sense of permanence, as if the building might have been here far longer than it has. “The Yard was interested in the idea of permanence in theatre, and fakery in architecture,” he says. “And how to build something grownup with not much money.” Mirrored panels in some of the windows bring a theatrical touch, while bright pink guttering and yellow coping blend with the local street art vernacular. Miraculously, for now, the new brickwork remains graffiti free.

Entering through big double doors – emblazoned with “open me up now” – you find a large open foyer and cafe, with walls and banquettes in rich shades of burgundy, while a glossy blue bar is framed with bands of teal and green, recalling a Josef Albers painting. Gold-painted columns add a touch of theatrical bling, which will be cranked up a notch next year when a vestibule is installed. Designed by artist Ed Atkins, it will usher theatregoers through a dramatic ruched silver curtain. The loos add further sparkle, inspired by the bathroom at the Villa Necchi Campiglio in Milan, with glossy black tiles, shiny brass fittings and coloured lino floors – “a little bit of economical opulence”, as Shimazaki puts it.

So what of the theatre itself? A central staircase leads up through a dark passage to the new auditorium, where the architects had to strike a tricky balance. “We wanted to retain what people loved about the old space,” says Miller, “and evolve what wasn’t as functional.” It has the same bare bones quality as before, with an exposed back wall built with bricks salvaged from the site, a concrete stage (actors’ knees won’t thank them), and curved, raked seating in the manner of an amphitheatre. The plastic cafe seats were upgraded for upholstered communal benches.

“Epic and intimate at the same time” was the brief, and Shimazaki has risen to the challenge, creating a 250-capacity space – more than double the previous theatre – that is at once cosy and grand. Continuing the fakery theme, the cast concrete-looking seating structure is actually cement particle board, while banks of radiators hidden below the seats keep bums warm while aiding the passive stack ventilation system. As before, what you see is what you get: there are no wings, no fly tower, nowhere for the actors to hide. “We wanted to amplify the sense of liveness,” says Miller. “After all, that’s what makes theatre unique.” It still feels raw – although performers now benefit from the luxury of dressing rooms, tucked beneath the seating, saving them from dashing to beat the audience to the loos in the interval.
