Around the other side of the building, the graffitied warehouse offices are being transformed into a youth hub by Jeremy Deller and architect educators Matt+Fiona, alongside local schoolchildren. It’s part of an Arts Council-funded series that has also seen an Antony Gormley figure appear on the roof – visible from the elevated platform of Hackney Wick station – with further commissions and community collaborations in the works.

The ad hoc ingenuity on show puts what is emerging across the other side of the park into sharp relief. One of the biggest components of the Olympic legacy is the “cultural quarter” of East Bank in Stratford, a £1.1bn colossus that houses branches of the V&A, Sadler’s Wells theatre, BBC studios, University of the Arts London and University College London, soon to be garnished with towers of unaffordable flats. The presence of these institutions is welcome – but despite the big budgets, top architects and endless design review panels, the results feel less than world class.

It is a cumbersome beast, designed by committee and airlifted in from on high, begat from the loins of mayors hungry for legacies. The Yard, by contrast, shows how a young, agile team with a fraction of the resources can achieve so much, building a project that feels truly grown from its place.

items.title: Apple says it will replace iPhone Duo handsets with screen problems
paragraphs: Apple says it will replace iPhone Duo handsets that have developed problems with their screens just days after the highly-anticipated smartphone went on sale.
Photos posted by social media users show lines that appeared on the screens of the technology giant's first ever foldable device, which has a starting price of £1,999 ($2,668) in the UK.
Apple said it is aware of "an issue impacting the inner display on a small number" of units and urged affected users to contact the company for a replacement.
The Duo's launch, which attracted long queues at Apple stores around the world last week, comes as the brand tries to reinvigorate its catalogue and challenge the foldable phones offered by rivals.
Some Duo owners also posted photos online showing cracks along the screen's centre crease, while others reported a crunching noise when opening the device.

An iPhone Duo user, Justin Lokos, posted an image of a device with lines across the right side of the display and later uploaded a picture of a new handset alongside the broken one, thanking an Apple store in New York for its help.
The extent of the issue remains unclear. Apple did not say how many devices were affected, while some images showing faulty devices may have been created using artificial intelligence.
The Duo's 7.6-inch (19.3cm) inner display is held together by a central hinge - a complex piece of engineering that has resulted in flaws in the folding devices made by some of Apple's competitors.
Samsung's first foldable phone, the Galaxy Fold, suffered an early setback in 2019 when reviewers reported broken screens on the devices.

items.title: New weather warnings as third storm set to hit Scotland
paragraphs: The Met Office said gusts of up to 65mph (105km/h) would hit coastal communities in the south-west on Monday evening and into the morning.
Forecasters added strong winds would be accompanied by heavy rain at certain points.
The latest weather system is unlikely to be as widely disruptive as Storm Boelo - or Storm Austen which came before it - and has so far not been named.
The next name on the storm list for the 2026/2027 season is Chloe.
Storm Boelo brought heavy flooding and wind gusts in some areas of up to 85mph (137km/h) on Monday.
A 60-year-old man died after being struck by a falling tree at Mid Kelton, near Castle Douglas, in Dumfries and Galloway on Sunday.
On Monday evening, Scottish and Southern Energy Networks (SSEN), which covers the north of Scotland, said work was ongoing to reconnect the supplies of about 15,000 homes that remained without power.

Meanwhile, Scottish Power Energy Networks (Spen) said all but a "very small number" of its 50,000 customers who lost power in Ayrshire and Dumfries and Galloway would have it restored by 02:00 on Tuesday.
Almost 100,000 homes had power restored in both areas across the weekend.
The Scottish Environment Protection Agency (Sepa) said it had put an amber risk of flooding in place for the northern and Western Isles and Caithness and Sutherland.
Sepa said areas of the southwest and Argyll, including the Solway Firth and Firth of Clyde, would experience volatile conditions, with large waves and strong winds.
They said flooding of low-lying land was likely.
Highland Council said flood gates on the mile-long Caol and Lochyside flood protection scheme, near Fort William, had been closed following a warning from Sepa.
Police Scotland said a high risk of disruption remained with poor weather conditions expected on Tuesday.

Police Scotland Assistant Chief Constable Mark Sutherland said that, although the amber weather warning was no longer in place, disruption was "likely well beyond that due to further poor weather, fallen trees and other damage caused by the storm".
Social Justice and Housing Secretary Shirley-Anne Somerville told BBC Scotland News there were "challenges ahead" due to the prolonged nature of the conditions.
She urged councils to review their readiness, adding authorities were working to ensure that "everything that can be done is being done".
Somerville also said that everyone can play a part by getting "households as resilient as we can, as well as looking after neighbours and friends".

items.title: Iraq's closure of Iran border crossing fuels protests
paragraphs: Editor's note: this story was translated from the original VOA Kurdi article.
Iraq's decision to close the al-Sheeb border crossing with Iran has triggered protests in the southern Maysan province and heightened tensions with Tehran.

The crossing was closed Wednesday, October 21, until further notice. Iraqi authorities cited technical and security concerns, but the decision has drawn growing opposition from influential Iran-aligned factions within Iraq's political establishment.
On Sunday, dozens of protesters blocked a main road leading to oil companies in Maysan, demanding the crossing reopen amid concerns about rising food prices and disrupted trade.

On Monday, an Iraqi court issued an arrest warrant for Mustafa Duair Abdulhassan, head of Maysan's provincial council, following a complaint from Iraqi Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidii's office regarding Abdulhassan’s threats of civil disobedience. The prime minister also ordered an investigation into his remarks.

Abdulhassan warned Sunday that residents would "resort to civil disobedience and cut Maysan off from the rest of Iraq" unless the crossing reopened. He is affiliated with Sadiqoun, the political wing of the Iran-aligned Asaib Ahl al-Haq militia led by Qais al-Khazali.

The Islamic Resistance in Iraq, an umbrella organization of Iran-aligned armed factions, separately accused Baghdad of yielding to American "dictates and pressure" over restrictions on border crossings and Iranian flights.
Iranian state media reported that Tehran had received no advance notice of the closure. Iranian Interior Ministry spokesman Ali Zeinivand said the matter was under review.
VOA has reached out to the White House and State Department for comment on allegations of U.S. involvement in the closure but had not yet received a response at the time of publication.
Speaking to VOA, Abdul Amir Ta'iban, an adviser to Zaidi, accused Iran of facilitating smuggling activities that have damaged Iraq's economy and society.

"Iran has caused great harm to Iraq through the smuggling of drugs and counterfeit money," Ta'iban said, warning that narcotics trafficking has devastated Iraqi youth and counterfeit currency undermined confidence in the dinar.

He said Baghdad should close crossings where violations persist but acknowledged that broader closures would require a political decision by the government, backed by the ruling Coordination Framework coalition.
Iran's Embassy in Baghdad rejected the smuggling allegations, describing them as false.
A State Department spokesperson told VOA earlier this month that Iran has long exploited Iraqi resources and supported armed groups threatening Iraq's sovereignty.

"Our goal remains a sovereign, secure, and prosperous Iraq that prevents attacks in and from its territory, delivers for its people and the region, and stands as a strong U.S. partner," the spokesperson said.

Safwan Qusay, an economist close to the prime minister's office, said Iranian exporters sometimes convert Iraqi dinar earnings into dollars through informal markets, complicating Baghdad's financial controls.
According to Qusay, Iraq is exploring a mechanism allowing payments for certain Iranian humanitarian imports through an account in Oman, subject to U.S. approval.
Jamal Kocher, a member of Iraq's parliamentary Finance Committee, also did not rule out a sanctions connection, citing efforts to combat weapons trafficking, narcotics and counterfeit currency.

items.title: Pentagon designates Confucius Institute in US as national security threat
paragraphs: Editor's note: this story was translated from the original VOA Mandarin article.
The Department of War has designated Chinese-funded Confucius Institutes on American university campuses as a national security threat.
China's Foreign Ministry responded Monday, saying it opposed what it called “smears and stigmatization” targeting the institutes.

In a video address Friday, Secretary of War Hegseth described Confucius Institutes as “Chinese government-backed propaganda cultural programs” that had infiltrated universities in nearly every U.S. state. He said Congress had banned the institutes several years ago, but they had returned in new forms under different names.

“It turns out that 80 new propaganda cells across 30 universities had popped up using different names and different charters, but with the same mission: to steal intellectual property and to infiltrate the minds of American students,” he said.

He said the Pentagon had added those organizations to its list of institutions threatening national security and had “systematically dismantled every single one of these organizations” over the past two months.
Hegseth did not identify a specific instance of intellectual property theft involving a Confucius Institute in his remarks.

Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesperson Guo Jiakun said at a news conference Monday that China opposed what he described as “smears and stigmatization targeting Confucius Institutes.”“Educational exchanges and cooperation between China and the United States help deepen mutual understanding between the peoples of both countries. They are two-way, mutually and win-win, and should not be disrupted or undermined,” he said.
Days before Hegseth’s remarks, the Department of War announced October 19 that it had successfully completed initial research security audits at 30 universities across the United States.

The Pentagon said all 30 universities covered by its initial audits had addressed identified relationships with foreign entities on the National Defense Authorization Act’s Section 1286 list of entities of concern.

According to the Department of War, the audits resulted in more than 80 “termination-related actions.” Those included ending relationships with listed entities, as well as precautionary terminations involving entities not specifically on the list

items.title: Pakistan defends attacks on Afghanistan, denies civilian casualties
paragraphs: Editor's note: this story was translated from the original VOA Pashto article.

Pakistan’s government has defended its attacks on Afghanistan as an act of “self-defense” and rejected killing Afghan civilians. Pakistan’s Foreign Affairs Ministry, in a statement Monday posted on X, said that its attacks are “directed against terrorists and their logistical support based in Afghanistan,” and rejected the civilian casualties “attributed” to the attacks.

Pakistani forces and the Afghan Taliban have recently clashed along the border, and Pakistan also has carried out airstrikes in Afghanistan. The Afghan Taliban called Pakistan’s airstrikes in Afghanistan “an act of aggression and crime in violation of all accepted principles.”
The United Nations Mission in Afghanistan said in September that it had documented more than 1,100 civilian deaths and injuries from cross-border attacks in Afghanistan so far in 2026.
Pakistan accuses the Taliban of sheltering the militant group Tehrik-e-Taliban Pakistan, or TTP, which has taken responsibility for attacks inside Pakistan.
The Afghan Taliban publicly deny harboring any militant group, but a U.N. report, released in August, said that the Taliban continue to support TTP.
A spokesperson for the U.S. State Department told VOA in an email statement in July that Pakistan has the “right to defend against terrorist attacks.”
“The Pakistani people have suffered greatly at the hands of terrorists,” the unnamed spokesperson said at the time.
The U.N. said that the Pakistani Taliban’s attacks inside Pakistan have increased.
Pakistan has said that the attacks inside Pakistan have resulted in more than 3,500 casualties so far in 2026.

Ismail Khan, an editor at Pakistan’s Dawn newspaper, told VOA that both sides blame each other, and relations between the two countries have deteriorated. “Borders are closed [between the two countries]. There is no trade and no negotiation is underway,” he said.
Khan added that some countries, including China, Turkey and Qatar, have tried to get Pakistan and the Afghan Taliban to resume negotiations, but those efforts have not yielded results.
“In the end, both countries have to negotiate and find a way out,” he said.
But Khan said the situation is likely to continue for now because both “Pakistan and Afghanistan are not ready to negotiate.”

items.title: Afghanistan sees drop in men’s university enrollment as women remain barred
paragraphs: Editor's note: this story was translated from the original VOA Dari article.

University enrollment among men in Afghanistan in 2026 has fallen nearly one-third from levels before the Taliban’s takeover, while women’s enrollment has remained at zero for the third consecutive year.

A new U.N. report says enrollment at public and private universities in Afghanistan totaled approximately 208,000 students, all men, in 2026, down from about 430,000 students, including 124,000 women, in 2020.

“Women remain excluded from formal participation, male enrollment is substantially lower than in 2019, the academic workforce has shrunk, and private institutions face continuing financial pressure,” the report said.
The Taliban barred women from university education in December 2022 and from medical training institutes, which offer diplomas in nursing, midwifery and other health fields December 2024.
Since seizing power in 2021, the Taliban have placed sweeping restrictions on women’s rights and freedom.

Under the Taliban, women and girls are not allowed to get an education beyond 6th grade. They are barred from working with government and non-government organizations, going to parks, gyms, public baths, and beauty salons.
The group has issued more than 100 decrees that curb women’s and girls’ rights and freedoms, including their right to get an education.

Meanwhile, the Taliban have tightened their control over men’s higher education by imposing numerous restrictions, such as conducting new oral exams on religious topics, dress codes, removing hundreds of books and other learning materials, and discontinuing over a dozen subjects related to human rights, democracy, gender, governance and other social science fields, according to the U.N.
Farid, a university student in Kabul, told VOA that students have few incentives to pursue higher education.
“There are only a few opportunities for graduates. This makes people not be motivated to continue their studies,” said Farid, who did not want his full name disclosed for security reasons.
He added that most of the students also face financial problems, forcing them to discontinue their studies.
“The economic situation has worsened. Students are not even able to pay for commuting to the university daily,” he said.
Farid added that students are also worried about their job prospects after graduation.
Mohammad Asif Nang, former deputy minister for education in Afghanistan, told VOA that the future of higher education in Afghanistan is uncertain.
“For example, a young man loses hope of a better future when he cannot find himself in a system based on competition, merit and professional qualifications,” he said.
“These trends affect not only higher education itself but also the future supply of qualified professionals across Afghanistan’s education, health and wider service sector,” the U.N. report said.

items.title: Surprising things we have learnt from Anthropic's blockbuster share listing
paragraphs: Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei has become a key figure in the current AI era.
Artificial intelligence (AI) firm Anthropic just released the required paperwork ahead of its long-anticipated debut on the US stock market.
The 335-page document included fresh details of how the Claude chatbot owner makes money, what it spends that money on and who it is controlled by.
Anthropic also detailed some of the the risks it claimed AI technology poses, including how it could take human lives. That information sat alongside the many purported benefits of the technology.
Here are five key points worth highlighting from the filing.
Every public company has to tell potential investors how things could go wrong.
Anthropic's "risk factors" were unique, also disclosing how the AI technology it is developing could doom humanity as a whole.

"Sufficiently advanced AI systems could, if not developed, deployed, and operated with appropriate safeguards, oversight, and security measures, pose catastrophic or existential risks to humanity," Anthropic said.

It noted that less than a year ago, a hacking group Anthropic believed to be sponsored by China "manipulated" Claude to successfully intrude on a number of institutions, including large technology companies, financial institutions, chemical manufacturing companies and government agencies.
But Anthropic said its success is dependent on its ability to constantly "develop, improve, and deploy the most advanced, capable, and useful AI models".

One of the most significant risks to that ability is Anthropic's access to infrastructure it needs, including computer chips and data centres, to build, train and operate the models that underpin its technology.
Anthropic has yet to disclose a target share price for its stock listing.

The company is widely expected to debut with a market valuation of $2 trillion or more, making it the largest stock listing in history. But the figure will be heavily influenced by its financial performance.
Anthropic lost $80.7bn (£60bn) in the first half of this year, double what it lost across 2025 altogether.
The company's overall revenue was $16.2bn billion for the six-month period. Revenues are rising rapidly, but the firm has a long way to go before it breaks even.

Troy Hooper, co-head of equity capital markets at Mergermarket, said Anthropic's revenue growth is "exceptional". But investors are "less forgiving" of tech companies promising huge future returns than they were even months ago, he added.
Anthropic's debt picture is also unclear given it has a huge amount of accounting charges related to certain forms of investment.
"As a result, investors do not yet have a clear view of Anthropic's underlying profitability or whether its rate of cash generation is sufficient to support the business as it scales," Hooper added.
Despite losing money, Anthropic has heaps of cash lying about.
At $131.6bn, almost all of its cash in hand is defined as "working capital", meaning it can use the money to fund its operations day-to-day.
Currently, Anthropic has more cash on hand than Meta and Google combined.
Anthropic's costs could rise as it faces fierce competition for top staff and computing power from other AI giants.
The leasing of data centres alone is costing the company $321.4bn so far this year.
Hooper said such large costs are expected to grow. Even with this kind of cash, it won't be enough to maintain its business growth.
Any investors in Anthropic "will be paying for future dominance, not present-day economics", he said.
Anthropic sees boundless ways it can sell its technology to customers.
A large portion of its current business comes from just 250 major enterprise customers, which it says have paid it at least $10mn in the past year.
An even smaller number, just five enterprise customers, make up a quarter of its current business.
Michael Monaghan, portfolio manager of Founder ETF, pointed out that "many top Anthropic customers have no long-term contract".
The company's level of business concentration leaves Anthropic dependent on a small fraction of its paying customers to support its growth, with no guarantee it will continue.

Anthropic also has enterprise relationships with the likes of Google and Amazon, both of which are also investors in the company "and competitors", creating potential business conflicts in the future, Monaghan noted.
Anthropic said its overall enterprise customer base has grown rapidly, going from roughly 1,500 customers last year to almost 12,000 this year.
Part of its growth strategy is offering Claude tools for free before working to "convert these users into paying customers over time".
The strategy has led to Claude seeing "the fastest enterprise adoption of any technology in history", the company claimed.
For all of the risks Anthropic has said AI poses, it also reiterated its claim AI will produce an "extraordinary" amount of good.
"Achieving our mission means the world gains the enormous benefits of frontier AI while mitigating the most significant risks," the company said.
That mission is defined as: "The responsible development and maintenance of advanced AI for the long-term benefit of humanity."
"We do not pursue projects based on commercial opportunity or research novelty alone; our efforts must advance our mission. "

Such hypothetical benefits include progress in healthcare, like the development of bespoke treatments for illnesses and improved disease detection, tailored education and legal advice and making more efficient power grids and batteries.
Decades of scientific progress could be condensed into years, accelerating drug discovery, disease detection, and the delivery of personalized therapy.

Anthropic said AI could provide individually tailored education and expert financial and legal advice, advance power grids and battery design for greater efficiency and reliability and help the "developing world" build more technological capabilities.
"Ultimately, we believe frontier AI will help drive global economic growth," the company said.

items.title: Two UN-sanctioned North Korean tankers spotted repeatedly off China
paragraphs: Editor's note: this story was translated from the original VOA Korean article.

Two North Korean oil tankers sanctioned by the United Nations Security Council have been repeatedly spotted off China’s coast, according to the public record by vessel-tracking Marine Traffic website, raising concerns that they may be circumventing sanctions while continuing to operate at sea.

The vessels, NAM SAN 8 and CHON MA SAN, have previously been suspected of engaging in prohibited ship-to-ship transfers, according to local media reports. A former member of a U.N. panel of experts on North Korea sanctions said their movements raise concerns that they could be using at-sea transfers to evade sanctions.

According to MarineTraffic, NAM SAN 8 was spotted on Oct. 24 near Xiaoqu Shan, in the Hangzhou Bay and Ningbo-Zhoushan area off eastern China. CHON MA SAN was also detected near Tang Yu on the same day, having moved south from its previously observed position.

Neil Watts, a former member of the U.N. Panel of Experts on North Korea sanctions, told VOA in an email on Oct. 23 that tracking images showed both vessels had spent time in territorial waters among the islands in the Ningbo-Zhoushan area, which he described as “an area synonymous with illicit ship-to-ship transfers of cargo from North Korean vessels.” Such transfers allow cargo to be moved between vessels at sea without entering a port, potentially making it more difficult to trace the cargo’s origin and destination.
Both the CHON MA SAN and NAM SAN 8 were added to the U.S.'s sanctions list in 2018 and are subject to port bans and asset freezes, Watts said.
“By not entering port and doing transfers at sea, they are using a ‘workaround’ tactic to create plausible deniability and thereby skirt around the consequences of their designation,” he said.
Both tankers are subject to an asset freeze and a ban on entering the ports of U.N. member states, including China.

Under Security Council Resolution 2397, member states must seize, inspect and impound vessels in their ports and may take similar measures against vessels in their territorial waters when there are reasonable grounds to believe they have been involved in prohibited activities or transported prohibited items. The U.S. Treasury Department’s Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) placed both ships on its Specially Designated Nationals List. That designation bars any American dealings with both craft.

“It is concerning that these tactics seemingly enable these vessels to escape the consequences of their designation and keep operating when the designations were intended to stop their illicit activities that are in violation of U.N. Security Council sanctions,” Watts added.
VOA requested comment from the Chinese government on the vessels’ activities and China’s enforcement of the relevant sanctions but received no response.

items.title: Political battle intensifies within Labour over Rosebank oil field
paragraphs: Scottish Secretary Douglas Alexander, Energy Secretary Miatta Fahnbulleh and Chancellor John Healey visited the St Fergus Gas Terminal on Wednesday
Scottish Labour leader Michael Marra is wading into the political battle which is intensifying over the Rosebank oil field.
He is making a direct appeal to Energy Secretary Miatta Fahnbulleh to approve the plans to allow production to begin in the North Atlantic.
Environmentalists have long campaigned against the proposals for drilling in the UK's largest untapped oil field, 80 miles north-west of Shetland.
That the debate is now taking place within the Labour Party is a sign of the UK's recent journey on the politics of energy.
When Labour came to power in 2024, it was with a manifesto pledge not to allow any new drilling for oil and gas in the North Sea.
Rosebank is the UK's largest untapped oil field
A legal challenge thrust the future of the Jackdaw and Rosebank developments into the hands of the then-Energy Secretary, Ed Miliband.

At that point, senior offshore industry figures didn't hold out much hope of getting the go-ahead, given Miliband's deep commitment to renewable energy and his close political ties to Prime Minister Keir Starmer.
All that was before the outbreak of the war between the US, Israel and Iran, which closed the Strait of Hormuz and made an ongoing cost of living crisis even worse.
A new government under Andy Burnham entered 10 Downing Street with greater political freedom on the issue - and a new energy secretary to make the decisions.
Strictly speaking, Jackdaw and Rosebank aren't applications for new drilling licences, just the adjudication of existing ones.
But in political terms, the change of tone within Labour has been clear.
What had been an article of faith on energy has become something much more flexible.

It's a shift that's also plain to see within the SNP, with the Scottish government that once favoured a presumption against new oil and gas drilling now issuing a careful welcome to the Jackdaw announcement.
Last week, Energy Secretary Miatta Fahnbulleh announced that production could begin on the Jackdaw gas field.
She said that over its expected 11-year lifespan, the project would support the UK's gas supply, protect hundreds of jobs and add £2.9bn to the economy.
Campaigners have called for the Rosebank plans to be rejected
Environmentalists said the decision would hamper efforts to tackle climate change and make "no meaningful difference" to UK energy security.
The UK government has always insisted that these decisions are part of a quasi-judicial process, judged on strict environmental criteria, not politics.
But as attention turns to Rosebank, the politics are seeping in.
Within hours of Jackdaw being granted approval, a briefing campaign began suggesting that Fahnbulleh was "minded" to reject Rosebank.
Now, in the week of the Budget, reports have suggested that Chancellor John Healey is in favour of approval.
Neither cabinet minister has given their view publicly, of course.
Fahnbulleh has insisted that the decision is "a regulatory process not a policy process," adding: "It sits heavy for such a big controversial decision because in the end only I can make it."
Even though she isn't looking for advice, the Scottish Labour leader is willing to offer it.
Marra is in Westminster meeting both Healey and Fahnbulleh in the run-up to the Budget on Wednesday.
Marra believes that on jobs and investment, the case for Rosebank is clear.
Michael Marra will be meeting both the chancellor and the energy secretary
"I supported Jackdaw and Rosebank because I think they're really crucial for the Scottish economy, for employment, and for the public finances as well," he told me.
"We need to make sure that we're a country that people feel they can invest in.
"You've seen what's happened with Jackdaw in recent days - a real boost to the morale and the investment climate in the north east of Scotland."
He's also arguing for increased levies on banks in the Budget, to contribute towards the cost of help on the cost of living.
That second request looks set to be granted - which is likely why Marra feels able to make it publicly.
On Rosebank, we still can't say for sure how things will go.
But the fact this debate is even being had is itself a symbol of our new energy reality.

items.title: LS Lowry review – matchstick men, or the broken denizens of a smog-filled hellscape?
paragraphs: While people queue at the British Museum to see the Battle of Hastings, this excellent survey of LS Lowry at the MK Gallery in Milton Keynes takes you back to another, maybe more decisive part of our past – the age when Britain was the most industrialised society on Earth. Laurence Lowry was born in 1887 and worked for 41 years as a rent collector, a job that took him all over his native Greater Manchester observing its people and places. He had the city’s grime and grind in his soul. The MK wants to show him as a fully rounded artist, to uncover the Lowry with a song in his heart, but it’s the misery of his urban hell that holds and harrows you.

In his 1930 painting Coming from the Mill it’s the end of the shift and scores of people emerge from a factory’s bleak yellow gatehouse as if leaving prison. Their daily captivity has left them broken and exhausted and the little abstracted figures hunch forwards as they walk without pausing to laugh or chat, going to their separate homes, each one withdrawn, wretched. They are not the painting’s protagonists – they are passive victims. The architecture of industry dominates the picture as it rules their lives. How can any of these little people, dwarfed by the mill that eats their time and energy, attain individuality? No wonder they all look the same except for minor variations in their drab clothes. They’ve been reduced by the Industrial Revolution to matchstick people.

Lowry is the Franz Kafka of industrial Britain. He is not a naive artist who painted crudely because that’s the best he could do. Nor is he a patient social realist laying bare the injustices of capitalism – although Friedrich Engels would surely have recognised his Manchester. He is a modern expressionist who finds his inner melancholy reflected in the industrial sublime. He drinks in its despair, feasts on its poetry of alienation. As you journey through Lowry’s North, you sink ever further into his personal slough of despond.

Slough of Despond would make a good alternative title for his 1924 drawing The River Irwell at the Adelphi. Heaps of mud and ash choke the slow-moving river that runs through Salford, its shores lined with decaying sheds and slums against a smoggy, chimney-lined sky. It’s Lowry at his purest as he depicts the stunning, crushing presence of the city itself. He draws and paints the black, gnarled spires of urban churches with as much relish as those monstrous mills. In the second world war he was a fire-watcher with a privileged view of the blitz: a drawing of freshly bombed buildings in Piccadilly, Manchester shows husks of charred brick still wreathed in smoke.

This show digs out other, less well known dimensions to his talent. But his paintings of the Lake District are even more chilling than his cities. Lake Landscape, painted in 1950, is a vista of low curving hills divided by silvery still water, receding in abstract, musical pulses of sadness. No people or animals inhabit this eerie world. When he paints people close up it’s even more disturbing: a young man with staring eyes, a father and sons who all seem equally desperate. He lightens up to paint his ideal woman with a simplified doll-like face apparently intended as his tribute to Pre-Raphaelite red-lipped beauties but the result is weirdly robotic. Her face is on the exhibition merchandise, perhaps because Halloween is coming.

The most bizarre painting, however, is his 1963 work In a Park. At first glance it’s another city crowd scene until you realise everyone in this fenced enclosure has something different about them. A one-eyed face screams while people walk around the white-earthed, empty space with spinal deformities, facial palsies, amputated limbs. The catalogue gets itself in knots – is Lowry mocking the disabled or questioning how we define disability?
But this painting is not about disability in a political sense at all. It uses it as an image of humanity in general: all people are broken and alone, misshapen in Lowry’s hopeless universe.

Lowry is a tricky customer. If it is pure snobbery to look down on him for being popular it is also patronising to see this troubled artist as a warmly sentimental nostalgist of the north. He is a painter of modern life in the age when that meant huge crowds staggering home in the shadow of smoking chimneys in cities blackened by carbon. At his best, Lowry is a great modern artist. His 1919 painting Pit Tragedy shows working-class people waiting for the worst news. They are statuesque, tragically posed in the grey dusty light. A woman turns towards us, her head veiled. Her pain is lost in the past but lives on here, observed and recorded by Lowry, visionary of the industrial age.
LS Lowry: The Theatre of Life is at MK Gallery, Milton Keynes until 28 February

items.title: UK sanctions Sudanese military leaders implicated in El Fasher ‘campaign of rape’
paragraphs: Senior Sudanese commanders implicated in a “campaign of rape” have been targeted by the UK on the first anniversary of a mass atrocity that saw tens of thousands of civilians killed over several days.

A year after the fall of El Fasher, the British government said it had sanctioned military leaders from both sides in the country’s ongoing conflict whom it suspected of sexual violence during the siege of the city.
A total of 15 commanders from the military groups – the Rapid Support Forces (RSF) and the Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF) – have been subjected to a travel ban and an asset freeze.
The Foreign Office said it hoped the action would ensure “the horrors that took place at El Fasher will be known to the world”.

During the RSF’s takeover of the city, up to 10,000 men, women and children are believed to have been slaughtered over two days – the fastest and largest massacre of civilians this century. Another 40,000 remain unaccounted for.
The killings came at the end of an 18-month starvation siege by the RSF, which was allegedly backed by the United Arab Emirates (UAE). The UAE continues to deny supporting the RSF.

Fewer than 70,000 people are believed to remain in El Fasher, compared with a prewar population of more than 1 million. Life inside the city continues to be horrendous, with testimony indicating routine detention, torture and unlawful killings.

Individuals targeted by the UK’s latest sanctions include Hussein Abu Jalak, an RSF colonel linked to atrocities during the siege, which forced hundreds of thousands of civilians to live off animal feed.
Another is Al-Nour Ahmed Adam – also known as “Al-Qubba” – who was identified as playing a prominent role in the attack on the city.
A Guardian investigation earlier this year revealed internal US and UK warnings were sidelined in the run-up to the RSF attack on El Fasher, and that action that might have saved lives was not taken.

A statement to mark the anniversary of the massacre from the Coalition on Atrocity Prevention and Justice for Sudan said: “The victims will not be forgotten, survivors will be heard, and we will continue to pursue accountability for those responsible.”
During the 12 months since the fall of El Fasher, Sudan’s ruinous conflict – which has forced 14 million people to flee their homes – has developed increasingly into a drone war.
The latest strikes saw the RSF causing mass power outages across east Sudan after targeting power stations with a coordinated drone attack.

items.title: AI giant Anthropic files for an IPO that could break records
paragraphs: Anthropic is taking a big step toward a blockbuster stock listing that would rank among the biggest IPOs ever. Patrick Sison/AP Photo hide caption

The artificial intelligence startup Anthropic, maker of the hugely popular Claude AI models, has taken a major step toward holding an initial public offering that analysts expect to be one of the biggest ever.
Anthropic filed final paperwork with regulators on Monday for an IPO under the ticker symbol ANT that reports have said could value the company at between $1.5 trillion and $2 trillion.

That would put it in league with Elon Musk's rocketry and AI company SpaceX, which was valued at around $1.8 trillion when it listed in June. Anthropic's listing prospectus did not say how many shares the company will offer or at what price range.

The filing of a public version of a registration statement called a Form S-1 with the Securities and Exchange Commission is a major milestone in Anthropic's meteoric rise. It was launched just five years ago by a breakaway group of OpenAI researchers, led by Dario Amodei, who were concerned that that company, run by Sam Altman, was not on a path to develop AI safely.

Anthropic has since become a juggernaut, and OpenAI's biggest competitor, with some of the most widely used AI models on the market. But the company has faced controversy, including a conflict with the Pentagon over how its models can be used and questions about Amodei's dire warnings on AI risks.

Still, the prospectus highlighted Anthropic's bullishness about the technology. "We believe this abundance of AI will rapidly transform every sector of the global economy in ways greater than the impact of industrialization, electricity, semiconductors, and the internet," it said.

In its prospectus, Anthropic highlighted breakneck growth — in revenue, income and losses. The company said its revenue in the first half of the year rose 1,300% at $16.3 billion, while its adjusted operating income — a measure of potential profitability — hit $1.6 billion during the period, vs. a loss of $1.8 billion the year before.
Anthropic has yet to turn an annual profit, and said it booked a loss of nearly $81 billion in the January to June period, up from $13 billion during the same six months last year.

In a statement emailed to NPR, Raj Joshi, senior vice president in the corporate finance group of Moody's, the ratings agency, called Anthropic's swing in adjusted operating income from negative to positive territory "a strong positive for the AI ecosystem."
U.S. stock indexes were up on Monday after Anthropic's early-morning announcement.

The filing comes at a volatile time in the stock market for AI-related companies, as investors waver between exuberance about the positive effects AI could have on the economy and concern about safety and the tsunami of investment in the technology.

The IPO, which could happen as soon as November, will be one of the most eagerly anticipated public share offerings in years. OpenAI, which makes ChatGPT, is also planning an IPO, but those plans are temporarily on ice, with Altman ruling out a listing this year as "ill-advised" in the face of swirling AI safety concerns.

"Going public has a lot of advantages. It brings in capital for growth. It makes it easier for you to raise additional capital elsewhere. And it makes it possible for your existing investors to cash out," said Jim Angel, an associate professor and markets specialist at Georgetown University.

But, he added, "there's concern that we may be in an AI bubble. We're in a very dynamic industry, to say the least, and we can expect a lot of volatility in the markets." Still, Angel said, it makes sense for Anthropic to "strike while the iron is hot" and list shares now to get as high a valuation as possible.

With SpaceX already trading publicly, Anthropic's IPO could test investor appetite for AI businesses at a time when markets are jittery about whether they can be profitable enough to justify the mind-boggling sums of money being invested in AI. SpaceX's shares soared briefly after the listing, but have come back down to around $150, where they started trading.
In May, at its last private fundraising round, Anthropic had a post-money valuation of $965 billion.

The balancing act for companies trying to ride the AI wave is real. The data center and infrastructure provider CoreWeave saw its share price plummet this month when investors got nervous about its ability to finance its expansion plans and its bond yields leaped. Other major players, including Intel, Meta and Nvidia, have also been buffeted by concerns and watched their share prices slide in recent weeks.

Debt financing has been a growing concern as AI-related companies scramble to raise money to meet demand at a time when interest rates are poised to keep rising as the Federal Reserve tries to douse stubborn inflation.

The S-1 filing that tees up the IPO flagged what Anthropic sees as the risks from AI — and to its business model. Among them are the risk that its AI models could develop faster than the company can keep them safe, or that they could be used to cause harm — or take harmful actions on their own. It also flagged the risk of heightened scrutiny or political backlash for the company's views on policy and regulation.

Amodei himself has issued some of the AI world's sharpest warnings about the possibility of AI spiraling out of control and causing harm, and urged AI companies to "pace the frontier," or to slow the development of their most capable models.

Anthropic has also clashed with the Pentagon this year over how the military can use its models. Amodei has drawn a line in the sand when it comes to using Anthropic's AI for autonomous weapons and mass surveillance of Americans.

In response, the Pentagon blacklisted Anthropic and designated it a "supply chain risk" — a label previously reserved for entities affiliated with U.S. adversaries. Anthropic has sued the Pentagon in two federal district courts. Those legal battles remain ongoing.
Editor's note: This story was updated to add additional information from Anthropic's prospectus. Oct. 26, 2026

items.title: An inside look at the massive data center tearing a Wisconsin community apart
paragraphs: Embed <iframe src="https://www.npr.org/player/embed/nx-s1-6011201/nx-s1-9977928" width="100%" height="290" frameborder="0" scrolling="no" title="NPR embedded audio player">

Workers continue construction on one of four main data center buildings at the Project Lighthouse complex in Port Washington, Wis. Thousands of contractors are working on the facility, bringing revenue to local businesses and traffic to city roads. Sacha Pfeiffer/NPR hide caption

Just north of Milwaukee, amid cornfields, rolling hills, barns and grain silos, there's a stunning sight: a massive data center under construction, covering two-and-a-half-million square feet of former farmland and stretching toward the horizon.

This emerging hyperscale complex in Port Washington, Wisconsin, has torn up the land and torn up this community. It's a local story that's also playing out nationally, as artificial intelligence companies race to build data centers to power their AI models – and people increasingly protest their construction.

NPR visited the site of the future Port Washington data center, called Project Lighthouse, and spoke with residents leading a crusade against it. We also met with the small city's mayor, who may be the data center's biggest champion.

Port Washington's gargantuan project has led to angry protests, multiple lawsuits, and opponents arrested for civil disobedience. Supporters say data centers will keep the United States competitive and could bring great wealth to places where they're built. But many residents feel frightened and helpless as they watch this rapid change, including 67-year-old Amanda Mueller.

"There should be a buffer zone around data centers, and it should be within at least a mile of a data center," she told NPR. "You should not have residents living anywhere near it. There has to be guardrails."
Port Washington Mayor Ted Neitzke says adequate guardrails have been put in place.
Ted Neitzke, mayor of the city of Port Washington, Wisconsin, believes the data center project will help his community by lowering taxes and generating new revenue. Sacha Pfeiffer/NPR hide caption
"Honestly, if you did your diligence, I don't understand why a community like ours, who grew up [with] an industrial base, would fight the fact that we would need this back again," Neitzke said.

But there are still many questions about Project Lighthouse, being built by Vantage Data Centers in partnership with Oracle and OpenAI – questions that even its strongest proponents aren't able to answer.
Listen to the full story by clicking the blue play button above.

items.title: When a teen posts a selfie, how much filter is 'too much' filter?
paragraphs: How much filter is too much filter for kids and teens posting selfies on social media?

That is the question state attorneys general across the country are grappling with following a landmark settlement with Meta this summer. As part of the agreement, the social media giant agreed to block some digital beauty filters for minors — specifically those mimicking extreme transformations like cosmetic procedures or heavy makeup.
Now, the burden falls on state officials to tell Meta where to draw the line. But defining where harmless fun ends and harmful manipulation begins is far from straightforward.

For teenagers navigating the digital landscape, the pressure of online perfection is a daily reality. Much of that pressure has been driven by online beauty trends like "Instagram face." Coined in 2019 by The New Yorker writer Jia Tolentino, the phrase refers to a look characterized by a small button nose, high cheekbones and pouty lips. While traditionally only achievable in real life through plastic surgery or extreme makeup, it can be applied instantly online using beauty filters.

Mia Lerner, a 17-year-old high school senior in California and a youth body image activist, knows the toll these digital tools can take. She told NPR experimenting with beauty filters contributed to her eating disorder and left her struggling with her self-image.

"I've even tried to fix my nose with AI," Lerner said. "My face looks a lot better, I think, in [the] photo that I manipulated with these beauty filters. But I'm still living with this nose that I see in the mirror."
Lerner welcomes the aspect of the Meta settlement that aims to restrict beauty filters for minors. "It's a very important step in the right direction," Lerner said.
However, the agreement reached in August between Meta and 47 U.S. states — plus Washington D.C. and three territories — does not institute a blanket ban on all digital effects.

Filters that transform users into playful characters, like elves or puppies, will remain available for young people. But so will filters offering subtle beautification effects — such as smoothing skin tone or adding a slight eye glow.
It is this category of relatively minor editing that particularly concerns Lerner.

"When I see something that has been so obviously AI-generated, it's very easy for me to logically say, 'Well, that's obviously been manipulated so I can't compare myself to that,'" Lerner said. "But when I see these videos of people who are just slightly edited, it's a lot easier for me to go down that comparison path."
Meta has previously implemented measures to manage beauty filters, which are increasingly powered by artificial intelligence.

The tech giant has already banned filters that explicitly promote cosmetic surgery, such as those overlaying pre-surgery marker lines onto skin. It has also shut down its platform for third-party creators of these tools, introduced mandatory labels for AI-generated content, and deployed automated AI detection systems. Despite these systems, harmful aesthetic filters and features that keep children trapped in an endless cycle of scrolling, clicking, and staying online persistently slipped past these guardrails, as a federal judge wrote in a summary judgement denying Meta's defense this summer.

Meta is not the only tech company grappling with teen access to beauty filters. TikTok also restricts users under the age of 18 from using them. Snapchat does not restrict teen access to filters. Neither company responded to NPR's request for comment. YouTube told NPR it does not have any filters. But there's nothing stopping users from posting images or videos made with third party filters to the platform — or onto TikTok and Instagram, for that matter.

Meanwhile, state attorneys general are reaching the end of a two-month window they set themselves to provide Meta with guidance in the form of a letter on what constitutes a bannable filter — and what does not.
They face a moving target, as digital beauty standards evolve rapidly.

"If the states want to define what is a beauty filter, they should define what is beauty," said Florencia Solari, a creative technologist who has spent years developing AI and augmented reality experiences for global brands.

Solari noted that trend cycles move quickly. "Instagram face" is already falling out of favor. "People are starting to move away from that because it's starting to look a bit clownish," Solari said. "Now it's going towards extreme thinness. So that's another problem."

As a result, the tools that are used to achieve the latest look are therefore also changing. So what might be branded by lawmakers as an "extreme" beauty filter in 2026 will likely be different in 2027.
While beauty standards are changing quickly, so is technology.

Instead of sitting in boardrooms debating pixel thresholds for cheekbones, Kelly Frasier, the co-author of a recent study highlighting the negative impacts of social media on body issues in adolescents, said legislators should consider the fact that teens will soon be able to use AI to create entire fake universes around themselves, not just change the way they look. So they should focus on broader AI regulation for minors.

"I think that legislators are asking the wrong question if they're asking where to draw the line for beauty filters," said Frasier. "And to be honest, filters will probably become completely obsolete within the next few years."

On top of the technological and cultural challenges, legal experts warn that individual states may struggle to reach a consensus on what does and does not constitute what the settlement agreement describes as a "cosmetic procedure filter."

"What we don't really have a sense of is what happens if the states disagree with each other?" said David Greene, senior counsel at the Electronic Frontier Foundation. "What if one state finds, you know, eyebrow lifting to be completely acceptable and another one thinks it's awful?"

NPR reached out to the attorneys general offices in all four plaintiff states that led the trial — California, Colorado, Kentucky, and New Jersey — for an update on the guidelines. But officials either declined to comment or did not respond.
Beyond the U.S., some international regulators are hoping to avoid discussions around beauty filter definitions entirely.
In Europe, the proposed KIDS Act — designed to regulate youth social media usage — takes a sweeping approach.

In that plan, "Beauty filters – not extreme beauty filters; beauty filters full stop – are forbidden for minors," said European Commission spokesperson Thomas Regnier. Regnier said EU legislators are closely watching the implementation of the U.S. settlement. "We want child-friendly services for our children. A beauty filter has nothing to do with a child-friendly service," Regnier said.
Meta says that it plans to enforce the ban on "cosmetic procedure filters" by early next year.

For youth activists like Lerner, the hope is that tech companies and regulators will include teens in these discussions. "So often it's just the government or these companies in these conversations," Lerner said. "The company should be asking us for our actual perspectives, like 'Are people actually using these extreme AI filters or is that not going to make a difference?' 'Do we need to target something else?'"
Meta said the company has partnered with teens over the years, but did not respond to NPR's question asking if it is doing so currently.

items.title: Musk says SpaceX restricted Ukraine's Starlink connection as service restored
paragraphs: Elon Musk has said his company SpaceX restricted Ukraine's Starlink internet service, after Ukrainian officials said connectivity issues appeared to have been resolved.

The tech billionaire accused Ukraine of violating its terms of service by using it for military activity - but denied being responsible for a simultaneous issue with its US-run, military-grade counterpart Starshield.
Kyiv has not officially commented on Musk's latest claim but Ukrainian presidential adviser Serhii Beskrestnov said his post was "very strange".
Musk had earlier denied deliberately throttling Ukraine's connection, which it says hampered its ability to conduct defensive operations for more than a week.
The issue first emerged last week during a broader row between Washington and Kyiv over Ukrainian strikes on Russian oil infrastructure.

Musk's latest comments, and the seeming restoration of the service, came after US President Donald Trump said he had told the Tesla and X owner to "put it back", having repeatedly denied instructing him to limit the service.
"Using Starlink, a civilian commercial service, for offensive drone strikes to kill people has never been allowed, nor should it be," Musk wrote on X on Saturday.
"Ukraine['s] military violated Starlink terms of service and used it for offensive drone strikes to kill people. That loophole was closed last week."

He went on to say that SpaceX had "done more to defend Ukraine than any private company on Earth" and reiterated his stipulation that Starshield was a different system and controlled by the US government, adding: "What they decide to do is up to them."
He added in a later post: "[Starlink] can be used for infrastructure that is military, but it cannot be used for unequivocally offensive strikes that make it fair game to be struck back."
Reacting to Musk's post, Beskrestnov wrote on Telegram that Starlink terminals operating in Ukraine have a speed restriction of 70-90km/h and do not work on Russian territory.
"Therefore, we physically cannot use commercial Starlink for deep strikes and medium-range strikes," he said.
"It is very strange that Elon Musk is not aware of Starlink restrictions in Ukraine."
There was no immediate comment from Ukraine's defence ministry.

Ukraine uses both the civilian service Starlink and the more secure Starshield, depending on what communications are needed, both of which run on networks of low Earth orbit satellites launched by SpaceX.

Starlink allows military units to co-ordinate, particularly in remote areas on the battlefield, while Starshield allows Ukrainian drone operators to see targets in real time, as well as operate interceptor drones.
Russia is not authorised to use Starlink, so when Ukraine sends long-range missiles or drones deep into Russia to hit oil refineries, the network does not work.

Ukraine's Defence Minister Yevhenii Khmara said earlier on Saturday that the military was now recording a "stable connection", with drones now able to reach speeds in excess of 400km/h (249mph). Kyiv previously said the connection would cut out above 161km/h.
"The speeds are now where they need to be," Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky wrote on Telegram.
Musk did not disclose in his post why SpaceX had chosen to make the change to its service last week, when Ukraine's extensive use of Starlink had been known for several years.
The connection issues coincided with a tense diplomatic standoff between Zelensky and Trump over Ukrainian strikes on oil infrastructure within Russia.
Trump said the strikes on Russian oil refineries, which Kyiv says are crucial to stemming the main revenue source for Moscow's war effort, have pushed global prices higher.
While the attacks have had an impact on global fuel prices, rises seen this year have primarily been due to the Iran war.

Faced with midterm elections next month and domestic displeasure with rising fuel prices, Trump has waived some sanctions on Russia and agreed a deal with Moscow - criticised by European allies as funding Russia's war machine - to supply Russian diesel to the US and the global market.

Zelensky initially agreed to cease strikes targeting Russian oil facilities on the proviso that Moscow cease striking Ukraine's energy infrastructure, before restarting the strikes after several instances of Russia disregarding this.

The Ukrainian leader said that, as well as seemingly limiting Starlink capability in Ukraine, the US had also threatened to withdraw intelligence sharing if the strikes did not stop, something Trump also denied.
Fighting and aerial attacks continue to be exchanged between Russia and Ukraine overnight.
Ukraine's emergency services said three people were killed and 15 others injured, including an 11-year-old girl, in attacks on the Dnipropetrovsk region, in the south east.
Another six people were injured when a Russian drone struck an apartment block in the central city of Vinnytsia, it said.

The Russian defence ministry said on Sunday that it had struck a cargo vessel it claimed was being used to supply the Ukrainian army while it was en route to the Black Sea port of Chornomorsk overnight.
It also said Russian forces hit a logistics centre, a distribution centre and a logistics terminal in the Ukrainian city of Kharkiv.

Ukraine's defence ministry earlier said it struck a facility in the Russian city of Oryol run by a sanctioned heavy machinery manufacturer. Russian authorities said three people were killed in the strike.

items.title: AI found the flaw. Hackers found the leak: The race to save 'PHP2SHELL'
paragraphs: AI discovered a vulnerability in part of the internet's architecture, called PHP2SHELL. Security researchers rushed to fix it, but news of the vulnerability leaked and hackers have swooped in.

items.title: Mobile internet tariffs in Iran rise by 40%
paragraphs: Editor's note: this story was translated from the original VOA Persian article.

Iranian mobile operators MCI and Irancell have announced increases of up to 40% in the tariffs for calls, text messages, and mobile internet packages, as the government continues to impose restrictions on internet access.
The companies said in separate statements on Friday that the new rates would take effect at midnight on October 23.
Irancell has also increased the prices of its fixed internet and fiber-optic services by the same amount.
According to the operators, internet packages purchased before the new rates took effect will remain valid at their original prices until their expiration dates.
The sharp increase in internet costs comes as the Iranian government continues to impose widespread censorship and restrictions on internet access.

In its annual Freedom on the Net 2026 report, U.S.-based nonprofit Freedom House gave Iran just 9 points out of 100, placing it alongside China and Myanmar among the world’s worst countries for internet freedom.
The report said Iran experienced the steepest decline in internet freedom among the 38 countries assessed.
During the suppression of nationwide protests in January 2026, Iran almost completely shut down internet access across the country for 20 days.

In February, coinciding with the start of the joint U.S. and Israeli military operation, the government imposed another nationwide restriction on internet access that lasted approximately 88 days. The measure was described as the longest nationwide internet shutdown in Iran’s history.

Freedom House also warned that the Iranian government has turned the country’s internet into a “two-tier” system in which most citizens are denied unrestricted access to the global internet, while a limited group retains that access.

The organization also cited disruptions to Starlink satellite communications, restrictions on virtual private networks (VPNs), and the arrest of internet users. It noted that internet freedom worldwide had declined for the 16th consecutive year.

Earlier, the deputy political commander of the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) claimed that if Iran's infrastructure were targeted, internet cables beneath the Strait of Hormuz would not be safe.

The International Cable Protection Committee said five active cable segments belonging to submarine cable systems pass through the strait, a route that carries less than 1% of the world’s international bandwidth.
According to the committee, damage to these cables would primarily disrupt regional communications.

items.title: Hammersmith Bridge is a symbol of our dysfunctional times. The money is there, the joined-up thinking isn’t | Simon Jenkins
paragraphs: London’s Hammersmith Bridge is a metaphor for all that is wrong with British government. Closed to motor traffic and inert for seven years, it is a victim of the anarchy that seeps into every tier of public administration. The bridge sits today on a sublime bend in the Thames, guarded by what looks like Checkpoint Charlie in iron curtain Berlin. With Albert Bridge also now closed, 37,000 extra vehicles seeking to cross the river have brought south London close to perpetual gridlock. No one cares.

London may be the richest, smartest, coolest place in Britain. Yet it is run like a high street vape shop. Its buses are ever slower, homeless people are ever more prevalent, waiting times in hospitals ever longer. No one can decide if they want an HS2 terminus or a Heathrow runway. A robotic Whitehall algorithm has just declared, ludicrously, that the borough of Kensington’s “housing target” must be 5,107 homes a year, up from a previous target of 1,381.

The first thing you notice about a city is its traffic. In other cities, it moves. In London, it crawls. Its congestion is officially rated the worst of any capital in the world. Efforts to improve the sclerotic traffic lights have failed. The recent installation of computer-assisted “smart” lights – the much-vaunted road time optimisers – has contrived to cut just 27 seconds off individual bus journeys. A Guardian investigation last month timed a series of trips, and found the average speed for a No 22 bus between between Putney Common and Oxford Circus was under 6mph, or 16% slower than a decade ago.

The principal reason for this appears to be London’s epidemic of roadworks. In most cities such infrastructure is subject to intense regulation and coordination. The reason is obvious: that the disruption can restrict movement and thus impose costs on third parties. There is no regulation worthy of the word in London.

In 2017 the Economist published what became a notorious map showing roadworks in Paris and London. The first had a scatter of sparse red dots; London’s map was a sea of blood. Estimates are that vehicles in London navigate 1,300 roadworks every day, with the total for 2024 at 490,893. There is no evidence of the slightest coordination of hold-ups.

The chief reason is that a quarter century of privatising utilities has given water and cabling companies virtually unlimited freedom to dig where and when they please. Streets in the most afflicted inner boroughs now awake each morning to what looks like an overnight blitz. A mass of road closures and detour signs have turned the London street into what looks like a permanent construction site. Seeing any work being done is rare and there is no sense of anyone being in charge.

Hammersmith Bridge is a tough case. It legally belongs to the local Hammersmith and Fulham council – not Richmond on the south bank – but it has decided it “cannot absorb” the cost of restoring its decaying structure, put at £300m. It merely allows pedestrians and cyclists to cross. Yet it claims to have spent £54m on it over seven years. Merely doing next to nothing costs millions of pounds a year.

The bridge’s predicament is serious. Built by Sir Joseph Bazalgette in 1887, it was one of the world’s first iron suspension bridges – and the iron’s life has expired. Repair could only be temporary, or over the longer term astronomical. As architecture it is a noble if rather ungainly structure, compared with graceful Albert Bridge downstream. A growing body of opinion is that it would be common sense to replace it.

Designing a new bridge should be a competitive challenge. It needs to respect the buildings and natural environment of Barnes and Hammersmith on either bank. A work of style and dignity should have nothing to do with the concrete gashes of the 20th century’s London and Waterloo bridges. It needs to be very special.

As for who should take the lead, in any other city a river crossing would be the responsibility of its mayor. British mayors spend their time trying for headlines or Downing Street. London’s Sadiq Khan appears to have no view on Hammersmith Bridge, any more than he does on the capital’s roadworks, building conservation or policy on tall buildings.

As for paying for a new bridge, there is an answer. The so-called City Bridge Foundation was formed in the middle ages to maintain London bridges and later City crossings. Its charter limits its responsibility to just five crossings: Tower, London, Southwark, Millennium, and Blackfriars bridges. However, its trustee, the City of London Corporation, could amend the charter so that it could reinvest in infrastructure. It is one of London’s richest charities – with assets in the order of £1.5bn. The foundation currently spends lavishly on causes that have nothing to do with bridges.

This needs changing. The City of London is an out-of-date relic of medieval local government. The legacy of London’s past wealth should be at the disposal of the whole metropolis. The money is there. A new Hammersmith Bridge should rise across the Thames’s most exquisite western reaches, and soon.

items.title: Is a job guarantee the solution to mass AI unemployment?
paragraphs: In a preface to his book Capitalism and Freedom, the American economist Milton Friedman famously observed that a crisis can propel once-fringe ideas into the political mainstream.

“Only a crisis – actual or perceived – produces real change. When that crisis occurs, the actions that are taken depend on the ideas that are lying around,” he wrote. The job of intellectuals, thinktanks and economists, he argued, is to refine the quality of these ambient ideas, so that good ones are ready when disaster strikes.

A chorus of influential voices is now predicting that AI may trigger crises of vast magnitude. Bill Gates has declared that AI will advance so rapidly that within a decade, humans will not be needed “for most things”. Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei has warned that the technology could cause widespread unemployment within one to five years, eliminating many positions in law, tech, finance and other white-collar professions. Even if these predictions are wrong, investors who bet heavily on the technology may conclude that AI is a bubble, and this in itself could cause a recession and widespread job loss.

Whether a crisis of mass AI-related job loss turns out to be actual or perceived, one policy idea that is attracting growing attention and support could directly mitigate this problem: a job guarantee.

In its most ambitious form, such a program would ensure that anyone who wants work is guaranteed a meaningful, decently paid job. By creating a public option for employment, its supporters argue, a job guarantee could protect millions of people from the financial and psychological damage of joblessness and mobilize a vast labor force to tackle urgent societal problems, from infrastructure and climate adaptation to elder care and childcare.

The concept of a job guarantee has a long history, both as an ideal and an actual policy. Article 23 of the 1948 Universal Declaration of Human Rights states: “Everyone has the right to work, to free choice of employment, to just and favourable conditions of work and to protection against unemployment.” During the Great Depression in the 1930s, Franklin D Roosevelt established the Works Progress Administration (WPA), which employed millions of Americans in ambitious public works projects that constructed roads, bridges, sewers, playing fields and much more. More recently, France, India and Argentina are among the countries that have launched versions of a job guarantee.

Though a job guarantee and universal basic income (UBI) are often grouped together, a recent global survey found greater support for job guarantees than UBIs. Polling of Americans by the Democratic strategist David Shor also shows the same pattern, with greater support for the creation of well-paid jobs than for direct income support. This makes sense, the venture capitalist and civic activist Nick Hanauer said, because “jobs represent so much more than income in human societies. They represent connection and dignity and enfranchisement and participation.”

Algernon Austin, director for race and economic justice at the Center for Economic and Policy Research, agreed: “A job guarantee is significantly preferable to UBI because work is more than just income. When you have a job, you gain work experience and you gain skills and you gain a network.”

Calculating the cost of a job guarantee depends on a holistic assessment of its impacts. During a US Senate hearing on affordability in June, John Kennedy, a Republican senator for Louisiana, suggested that a job guarantee would cost trillions of dollars and was impossible. When Dr Julie Margetta Morgan, president of the public policy thinktank the Century Foundation, told Kennedy that she supported a federal job guarantee, he replied: “Do you believe in the Easter bunny?”

Economists who study job guarantees see the calculation of costs and benefits differently. Max Kasy, a professor of economics at Oxford who has studied a recent job guarantee experiment in Austria, said that while the wages a job guarantee pays participants comprise a cost, such programs also save money in multiple ways.

“The cost saving comes from the fact that you don’t have to pay unemployment benefits, or maybe disability benefits or early retirement benefits. Then people who are working pay taxes and make social insurance contributions, so that’s additional revenue for the state. And then they hopefully do something that’s actually useful for society,” he said.

Participants in the job guarantee experiment in Austria also experienced social and psychological benefits. While the monetary value of greater wellbeing may be hard to quantify, such intangibles are crucial, according to Pavlina Tcherneva, a professor of economics at Bard College.

“Providing a good job to a person is absolutely transformative,” she said. Factoring in the costs of health problems that come from precarious unemployment and long-term unemployment, she added, makes the policy even more attractive, saying: “It’s not only affordable, it’s an investment.”

In September, the US representative Ayanna Pressley, a Democrat from Massachusetts, reintroduced a congressional resolution calling for the creation of a federal job guarantee, something she first proposed in 2021. Her proposal would create a federally funded but locally administered job guarantee that pays participants at least $25 an hour, with regular adjustments to reflect the rising cost of living. The jobs would include a range of sectors, such as emergency preparedness, relief and recovery after natural disasters, care for children and seniors, and public art projects modelled on the WPA’s popular Federal Art Project.

Another recent proposal would directly tax AI companies to fund a federal job guarantee. The plan, which is supported by Democratic US representatives Greg Casar of Texas, Valerie Foushee of North Carolina and Sara Jacobs of California, would tax large AI companies on whatever was higher: the value of their “tokens” – units of data used in AI models – or their revenue from AI products.

If the unemployment rate rose, the tax rate would increase. “AI CEOs are openly predicting their technology could put millions of Americans out of work, and our government is doing nothing to save jobs and protect working people,” Casar said in a written statement.

In Cleveland, Ohio, a non-profit called Universal Basic Employment (UBE) is launching a small pilot study with a cohort of five workers who drive vans at a transportation company. Rather than create new jobs from scratch, the program subsidizes the wages of existing private-sector jobs in a way that benefits both workers and employers, according to Devin Cotten, founder and CEO of UBE.

Cotten and his team wanted workers to make what they call an autonomous wage – the pay level at which people are no longer eligible for most social safety net benefits. In Cleveland, that was just over $27 per hour. At a cost of almost half a million dollars for one year, UBE’s pilot will split that $27 figure with employers. The drivers currently make about $15 an hour, so the employer will save money, and the workers will get a sizable raise.

The program is not meant to replace other forms of assistance such as housing vouchers, Cotten said. But workers receiving more money as wages, rather than as a siloed benefit, can build their credit, perhaps qualify for a mortgage and also keep dollars circulating in the local economy, helping to revitalize poor neighborhoods.

Such a model may even attract a broader base of political support. “Work is a shared value across political lines,” Cotten said. “I think crafting a solution based on work allows us to be a bipartisan solution.”

items.title: Apple Watch Ultra 4 review: longer battery life but still awaiting new features
paragraphs: As the Ultra enters its fourth year as Apple’s biggest and beefiest smartwatch it gets the best kind of spec upgrade – longer battery life – while waiting for something potentially more transformative.

That’s because several of the key features announced as part of Apple’s new smartwatch lineup for 2026 have yet to be enabled, awaiting updates towards the end of this year. That leaves the £749 (€899/$799/A$1,349) Apple Watch Ultra 4 the top dog, but basically the same as last year’s model.
The Ultra 4’s body, screen, colours and design are identical to the previous versions. It weighs about 1g more, but the bigger changes are on the back and inside.

Upgraded sensors on the back of the watch take heart rate (HR) readings every five seconds during the day, up from every five minutes on previous generation Apple Watches. They also enable the measurement of your heart rate variability (HRV) during the day, not only at night, which feeds into some new recovery metrics.

The Ultra 4 is the first Apple Watch in several generations to get a meaningfully faster chip with the new S11. The battery life for general use in my testing now stretches to 79 hours, too, meaning the watch lasted well into its third day between charges. Most will be able to charge it every third morning, or less if you use the low power modes, although that is far behind the week-plus stamina of top adventure watch rivals.
The new watch charges at 10W with its little magnetic puck, up from 5W of previous generations, and reached 82% in under an hour and 100% in less than 90 minutes.
Connectivity: Bluetooth 5.3, wifi 4, 5G RedCap/4G, UWB
Sensors: HR, ECG, spO2, temp, depth, dual-band GPS, compass, altimeter

The Apple Watch features some of the most comprehensive health tracking available on your wrist, which on the Ultra includes extremely accurate dual-band GPS tracking for exercise. The more frequent HR and HRV measurements enable a few new features for the Ultra 4. The Vitals app, which monitors your stats overnight, now works during the day giving you an assessment of your general health. It can let you know when your HR and HRV are outside your usual baseline, indicating strain or sickness that might be on the way.

The new readiness app adds a popular feature from sports watches, which looks at your activity, vitals and sleep and works out whether you have properly recovered from strenuous exercise or stressful days. It gives you a score out of 10 and some advice on how ready you are for exercise, which can be a useful tool for training for a race or goal.

The Ultra 4 runs watchOS 27, just like Apple Watches back to the Series 9 and Ultra 2, which includes Apple’s new Siri and improved AI tools, some of which are available now, while other exclusive features are awaiting updates planned for later this year.

The upgraded Siri is available to talk to and behaves very similarly to that on a modern iPhone, including the Siri app for reviewing previous interactions. The new Siri Modular watch face features the top timely widget, which has been surprisingly useful. It shows simple things such as the timer when you have one running, or the weather when it starts raining. It also puts your vitals front and centre in the morning, or your calendar if you have an upcoming event, replacing the need for multiple complications.

Shazam music recognition is now significantly faster, while the sound recognition accessibility feature, which listens out for certain sounds, such as a fire alarm, doorbell, car horn or baby crying, and sends an alert to your wrist could be very useful.

But the marquee “audio intelligence” features that could be transformative and controversial are not yet enabled, being expected in “late 2026”.
