Siri Recap promises to transcribe conversations all day before delivering them as an AI summary. It doesn’t record audio or keep full transcripts, just the text summaries, but the Live Rewind feature can show you a transcript of the last 15 seconds of a conversation so you can see what you missed.
Apple says the battery should last more than 1,000 full charge cycles with at least 80% of its original capacity and can be replaced for £95. Damage repairs cost £539.
The watch contains more than 45% recycled material, which is broken down in its environmental impact report. Apple offers trade-in and free recycling for devices.
The Apple Watch Ultra 4 comes in a choice of two colours and multiple bands costing from £749 (€899/$799/A$1,349).
For comparison, the Apple Watch Series 12 costs from £369, the Watch SE 3 costs £219 and the Garmin Fenix 9 costs from £860.

The Ultra 4 is the best smartwatch Apple makes. It has a great screen, rugged looks and all the trappings of other Apple Watches, including Apple Pay, comprehensive health tracking and full integration with an iPhone.

The faster charging and longer battery life are welcome, lasting about six hours more for general use than previous versions in testing. The more frequent heart rate readings and daytime heart rate variability monitoring are additive rather than revolutionary. The readiness and recovery monitoring add to the existing suite of training tools to close the gap to top-tier sports watches from Garmin and others.
Upgraded Siri is more useful on your wrist, and the new Siri Modular watch face was a surprisingly good addition. But the new audio intelligence features are not here yet.
That makes the Ultra 4 a great Apple Watch, just not a significant upgrade on those that came before.

Pros: great screen, rugged yet sophisticated design, hands-free gestures, three-plus-day battery life, 4G/5G and satellite SOS/messaging, comprehensive health tracking, great activity tracking with dual-band GPS, recovery/readiness tracking, better Siri, extra action button, 100-metre water resistance and 40-metre dive-ready, long software support.
Cons: no big upgrade on previous model, very expensive, only works with an iPhone, no third-party watch faces, shorter battery life than adventure watch rivals, marquee AI features not yet available.

items.title: Why has a crumbling bottle plant been rebuilt in Paris? The stunning show suggesting the future is Ghana-shaped
paragraphs: Ibrahim Mahama has dug through the ruins of post-colonial Ghana, sorted through the ashes of its ancient history, picked through the industrial detritus, the corporate waste, the piles of rubbish, and found something pretty unique: hope.

Sit on one of the Asante stools in his circular Parliament of Ghosts and you can almost feel a new future being worked out right in front of you. It’s the first installation in this huge exhibition at the Fondation Cartier in Paris, and it sums Mahama up pretty neatly. He’s looking at the collapse of the Ghanaian government in 1966, the way the hope of the post-colonial project was crushed in a military coup, and he’s looking at ancient Ghanaian history, at the empires that fell centuries ago and the way colonialism tore them to shreds. But he’s not lamenting any of them. He’s not mourning. Instead, he’s reclaiming them, asking how things can be rebuilt, how we can move forwards by learning from the past.

And he does it over and over. In 2024 he bought an old bottle factory – a symbol of industry and its collapse. He’s rebuilt it here, in the centre of Paris. Its steel roof beams, rusted and crumbling, reach up to the ceiling, its walls are lined with thousands of green bottles in Coca-Cola, Schweppes, Kool and Club Minerals crates. It’s a whole history of manufacturing, of commerce in West Africa post-independence. Not left to rot, but rebuilt and reconfigured into something new.
Nearby, he’s taken some of those bottles and piled them around a collection of local pottery. The industrial meets the artisanal, two lost arts creating a new one.

But this huge show isn’t really about Mahama, it’s about the people around him. Most of the work here is by nine other artists and collectives. Mahama runs three art centres near Tamale in Ghana, giving time, space and opportunities to local artists. Their work is given priority here, alongside art by his mentors and collaborators. He’s taken this massive exhibition opportunity and used it as a chance to celebrate his community. It’s almost as if he’s trying to make the rest of us feel bad.

Way up on the top floor, a long scroll of jute and bark by Dorothy Akpene Amenuke undulates across the floor. If it looks like Mahama’s work, it should: she was his art teacher back in 2013. Knowledge, and the past, gets reconfigured and reshaped once again.

Nearby, the wall of a farmhouse has been built by artist and architect Courage Dzidula Kpodo out of red earth clay, a material lost as modernism brought in concrete. Now, historic methods become a kind of resistance, a symbol of tradition’s ability to endure.

Those core ideas get repeated through pretty much every presentation here. Influential 97-year-old photographer James Barnor captures the communities around Mahama in large format, grainy Polaroids. Gideon Appah’s hazy, dream-like paintings imagine fictional Ghanaian youths staring out to sea, congregating on beaches in utopian, idealised visions of the country’s past. Some of the works are absolutely stunning, like Peter Doig and Noah Davis transported to Accra.

The best work, appropriately enough, isn’t by one artist but a collective. On the top floor, a bunch of lumpy, surreal sculptures of birds, bodies and men wrestling bulls is by the Congolese Plantation Workers Art League (CATPC). Each one is made of chocolate, sculpted in the DRC but poured into moulds in Amsterdam. Everything they make from selling the art goes towards buying back land confiscated in the early 20th century by the Lever Brothers, who we now know as Unilever. The work is a whole conversation about global trade taking place in sculptural form, an act of resistance and reclamation through chocolate.

This exhibition is essentially an ambitious, ultra-idealistic group show of West African art. It is art exhibition as political utopianism. Which is great, even if not everything in it is good. And the real draw is Mahama, with his archival approach to monumental installation art, and it’s a shame to not get a load more of it.

Mahama has sacrificed himself for the greater good, basically. But this collaborative approach is the point: he’s saying collective action, community, togetherness, that’s how we’ll build a future. It might sound a bit cloying and earnest, but then you see the results, you see the art and the ideas, you see the community and the hope and the idealism and you eventually say: “Get me a one-way ticket to Accra. I’m in.”

items.title: Why is Elon Musk plotting a mega-merger of SpaceX and Tesla?
paragraphs: Elon Musk has spent years building Tesla and SpaceX into a pair of trillion-dollar technology empires. Now, he is considering bringing them together.
Asked on Tuesday whether a merger would be a good idea, Musk was clear: "Yes."

The prospect is more than hypothetical. Musk said special committees have been formed to assess a potential deal, although he stressed that there is no guarantee a merger will happen and that nothing has been agreed.
With Tesla valued at roughly $1.5tn (£1.1tn) and SpaceX at $2tn (£1.5tn), a combination of the two companies would mark the largest merger ever.
Any deal would also need shareholder backing. But Musk said he saw "a lot to be gained" in bringing the businesses together.
"In my opinion, 100%. It's just a question of when," says David Nicholson, the Chief Technology Advisor at The Futurum Group, a market research company.

The unveiling of the Tesla Roadster last week - a futuristic electric car powered by SpaceX rocket thrusters - served as a "symbolic embodiment" hinting at the two Musk companies merging, Nicholson said.
Musk, the CEO of both SpaceX and Tesla, said bringing the firms together would be beneficial given the work each does around chips, artificial intelligence (AI) and other technology projects.
Specifically, the deal would combine Tesla's cars, robots and self-driving technology with SpaceX's rockets, data centres, satellites and telecommunications operations.
The move could be a step towards Musk's mission to build a self-sustaining city on Mars - a vision that has invited sceptics but also plenty of backers.
Over the past year, Musk has moved to consolidate his businesses, with SpaceX acquiring xAI and X, formerly Twitter, before going public this year.
Watch: Did Tesla really just unveil a flying car?

But the merger would ultimately be decided by shareholders, with half of Tesla's needed to back the deal, a threshold even Musk described as "quite a high hurdle". Musk, as CEO of both companies, cannot participate in shareholder discussions.
Even so, Musk, a key shareholder of Tesla, will likely get his way in the next few years, said investment analyst Dan Sheehan from Telos Wealth Advisors.
He believes shareholders will back the deal as the technology the companies develop complement each other, Sheehan said.
But the merger would mean that Tesla shareholders will likely hold a "smaller slice of a much larger and more complex business," he added.
"There's no real precedent for how a public company like Tesla gets priced in this," Sheehan said.
SpaceX shares rose 8% in after hours trading while shares of Tesla climbed by 1.5%.
Experts told the BBC that Tesla drivers are unlikely to see much drastic change in the near term, even if the two companies combine.
In fact, vehicles seem almost like "an afterthought", overshadowed by the potential to combine the Tesla and SpaceX's tech capabilities, Nicholson said.
Changes are already underway at Tesla. The carmaker said earlier this year that it would prioritise its best-selling Model Y and Model 3, shifting focus away from less popular models.
Tesla also started using a manufacturing plant in California to produce humanoid robots, known as Optimus.
Tesla's vehicle line-up includes the Cybertruck and Model 3
Pairing Tesla's self-driving technology and robotics with SpaceX's AI and satellite network could result in more capable vehicles, Sheehan said.
"The question is how much priority cars get inside a company increasingly driven by AI infrastructure," he added.
The recent Roadster showcase suggests SpaceX technology could be pulled into future Tesla products, which could attract more customers, said Tu Le, the founder of advisory firm Sino Auto Insights.
The Cybertruck-maker faces intense competition from Chinese carmakers like BYD, which overtook Tesla as the world's biggest EV maker in January.
The biggest winner is probably Musk - the world's richest man who also became the world's first trillionaire earlier this year.
The merger would give Musk greater voting control over the combined company than he currently has at Tesla, a factor the special committee assessing the deal would have to consider.
A single company makes it easier for Musk to run his AI strategy the way he wants, Sheehan said.
"The deal itself doesn't add to Musk's wealth, but it concentrates it further in one stock," he said.
However, the merger could attract scrutiny over Musk, already a polarising figure in the US, Nicholson said.
The move could also face more regulatory pressure if Democrats - many of whom have been critical of Musk - win more seats in the US midterm elections next month.
Shareholders have backed Musk's desires before. Last year, Tesla investors approved an unprecedented compensation package for Musk valued around $1tn.
"I honestly don't think Musk will be keeping track of what the merger will do for his wealth," Nicholson said.
The deal also brings Musk closer to what Nicholson says is "his mission in life": colonising Mars.

items.title: Labor and the Coalition are poised to take a reckless gamble on AI. Haven’t they realised community support has collapsed? | Edward Santow and Sarah Sacher
paragraphs: Australia’s major political parties are edging towards rare consensus. Labor and the Coalition increasingly want to take a major bet on artificial intelligence. Yet, just as the parties are coming together, the Australian community is running the other way.
Last year, only 30% of Australians believed the benefits of AI outweighed the risks. In 2026, community trust in AI appears to be falling even further.

It was an unusual step for our parliament to form a joint select committee on AI. It signalled that the decisions being made now on datacentres and how we adopt AI could define our economy, environment and society for generations.

As a fresh round of hearings starts this week, the committee members must confront the gulf between the politics of AI and the stark reality on the ground. Some parts of the business sector are urging us to prioritise innovation and AI adoption, which is often another way of saying: “Do a better job of selling the upside of AI.”

Whether you’re an AI optimist or a sceptic, this is a terrible idea. Sam Altman, Dario Amodei and the other titans of Silicon Valley have a golden megaphone to spruik the benefits of their technology. Australians don’t want our elected representatives to do the same thing – especially when the technology is already bringing both opportunity and harm.

This doesn’t mean being blind to the benefits of AI. On the contrary, Australia is among the highest users per capita of Anthropic’s Claude and other generative AI applications. But we must also be clear-eyed about potential risks. And, crucially, we don’t see a compelling response to our concerns from government or the AI companies themselves.

Take the impact of AI on work. Our community is asking practical questions. How will AI impact our jobs, and the jobs of our children? What is the government doing to ensure the AI systems used in Australian workplaces are safe?

Our new report, Drawing the Line, lays out how AI is propelling the rise of harmful tech-enabled worker surveillance. Often workers are unaware of the extent to which they are being monitored – including through their work devices and phones, and via software such as Microsoft Teams.

Unlike some of the hypothetical (and frankly terrifying) risks that the joint select committee on AI has already covered, such as AI-enabled biological weapons and engineered pandemics, this is happening today.

Australian supermarket workers are already being pushed to meet AI-generated productivity metrics that force them to work harder and faster under the threat of punitive repercussions – putting them at risk of injury and workplace accidents.

Remote workers are already being subjected to intrusive surveillance software capable of watching everything they do on their screen – including audio recording conversations they have with their families.

Rideshare drivers are already being penalised for road conditions and customer complaints that are unrelated to their performance, which can result in their account being deactivated and days of work lost.

Workers are being quietly crushed by commonplace AI-powered surveillance tools that have crept into our workplaces and home offices. And the impact is real. Think, for example, of the young woman who reported being sexually harassed by a boss that required her to be on video at all times. Or warehouse workers driven to suicidal ideation due to relentless micromanagement by machine.
Our workplace laws don’t protect workers from unreasonable surveillance. Nor do they give employers clarity about what types of monitoring are lawful.
Unlike existential risks from AI, which are outside the Australian government’s direct control, this problem could be addressed through straightforward law reform.

We urge the government to update the Fair Work Act to require any worker monitoring be “fair and reasonable”. This builds on the government’s commitment to require all personal information covered by the Privacy Act to be handled fairly and reasonably.
Australian workers expect the government to act to protect them from AI harms. There is a clear reform solution at hand. This is not a hypothetical future risk – let’s address it now.

items.title: I’m a CTO. AI still needs your human expertise | Madhu Shashanka
paragraphs: Autonomous cars, which may be the safest we have built, keep getting easily avoidable parking tickets. While Waymos crash far less often than human drivers over tens of millions of miles, they’re still terrible at performing basic tasks – keeping out of disabled parking spots and tow-away zones, or steering clear of a church garage during Sunday service, according to the Wall Street Journal.

That is the state of AI today: impressively capable at something complex, yet embarrassingly clumsy at something easy. And it has implications for what work will remain human and what will be automated by AI.

People expect AI to lead to fewer jobs in 34 of the 37 countries surveyed by the Pew Research Center. In wealthy countries like the US, Australia and South Korea, about seven in 10 expect job losses over the next 20 years. And across countries, concern among young people is rising. While fears focus on job numbers, the bigger change will be what jobs become.

The nature of human work will move towards judgment. Experts refer to AI as “jagged”, superhuman at certain tasks but weak at others, with no clear boundary between the two. AI rapidly improves where work can be automatically checked and examples are endless. But it’s shaky where no automated test can determine whether the answer is right. Even if AI is correct a majority of the time on a task, it often doesn’t tell you when it’s inaccurate. If you’ve used AI, you’ve probably experienced how it can be confidently wrong.
Some of these errors will solve themselves as models get better. But jaggedness is a symptom of how these models learn. I see this often as a technology leader building with these systems.

A smarter model still needs a right answer to learn from. When one gap is closed, it shows up somewhere else no one thought to check. But many business decisions don’t immediately have a clear right answer. Whether a choice is good depends on a future no one can see and data no one has. That’s where judgment comes in. So AI will keep mastering tasks that have checkable results but struggle where a person has to decide what a good outcome looks like.

As a result, a new type of work is starting to appear. Someone tests whether the output of AI is correct based on real work, not just on benchmarks. Someone sets limits on what AI is allowed to do before it runs, so the worst mistakes are avoided. Someone runs and manages several agents the way a shift manager runs a crew. Picture an airport control tower. Radar and software track flight paths, with humans judging the few that matter to avoid collisions. No one is manually watching every screen. That would never scale.

Setting AI’s limits is harder than it sounds. In a 2026 study, after an agent was told to protect a secret, it destroyed its own email server, deleting every single email. It was given a goal, without any limits on what it could do. The researchers described it as the right values paired with terrible judgment. Deciding what is off limits and what a mistake would cost takes someone who knows the work and will answer for the result.

Here is the good news for people worried about their own jobs. The people best suited for doing this new type of work aren’t computer programmers. They are the ones who know how the real work is done. Catching what a confident AI left out or got wrong takes someone who knows the complete answer. That knowledge is uncheckable, unwritten and takes the form of judgment honed over years of doing the task and watching it break.

Ford recently learned the value of human expertise. In recent years, it leaned hard on automating its quality control, cutting thousands of jobs. But earlier this year, it had to rehire 350 veteran engineers to oversee the process and hunt for failure points before a part reached the factory floor. They brought the judgment of watching parts fail over years. With humans at the helm, Ford’s quality ranking then hit first among mainstream brands for the first time since 2010.

But we are making a serious mistake with the jobs we’re eliminating due to AI: the entry-level, routine ones. That routine work is how judgment gets built over time. Junior employees work under the supervision of senior experts until their experience turns into instinct. AI eliminates the friction related to learning how to do the job. But the demand for judgment did not go away. We are just destroying the path to developing it.

The real question is not whether machines will take over our work. It is whether we will have the people who can tell when the machines are wrong. Right now, we are automating the training ground where judgment is learned. If you have hard-earned expertise about anything, the next few years will only make you more valuable. And if you are just starting out, the old apprenticeship model will not hand it to you. You have to go and earn it, deliberately, on tasks the machines cannot yet judge.
Madhu Shashanka is co-founder, chief scientist and chief technology officer at Concentric AI, a data security software company

items.title: Googlebook review: Google’s new laptops are woefully underbaked
paragraphs: Google’s attempt to create a new type of laptop to compete with Windows and macOS machines is finally here, combining the best of ChromeOS and Android into the new Googlebook. With advanced links to Android phones and the best of Google built in, can these Googlebooks really compete with a MacBook Air or Surface Laptop? I took two for a spin to find out.

For years, Chromebooks have been the boss of budget laptops, but Googlebooks take a different, far more premium approach. Made by a range of traditional PC makers, including Acer, Asus, Dell, HP and Lenovo, they start at £999 (€1,099/$899/A$2,299) – a far cry from the £160 Chromebooks.

While Google does not make these machines directly, it has set strict hardware quality standards that the laptops must reach. That includes backlit keyboards, haptic trackpads, fingerprint readers, crisp touchscreens, decent speakers and modern fast chips with at least 16GB of RAM.
It is a list of specs you should expect with a premium Windows PC, but those start at a much higher price, primarily thanks to RAMageddon.
As such, the Acer Googlebook 14 and the Asus Googlebook 14 I’ve been testing have excellent hardware with satisfying keyboards, great trackpads and quality screens.

The Acer is a convertible that allows the screen to fold over the back of the device turning into a tablet of sorts. It is 1.14kg and 13.9mm thick, with a glossy 14in 3K OLED screen and a smooth aluminium-magnesium body, costing £999.99.
The Asus is a traditional laptop with a matt 14in 3K OLED screen and a magnesium-alloy body that weighs just 0.99kg and is 11mm thick, costing £1,199.99.

Top quality hardware aside, anyone familiar with a Chromebook would be forgiven for thinking it was ChromeOS running on these machines. It has the familiar taskbar at the bottom, Chrome-based web apps and access to Android apps.

But the software is essentially Android underneath, which means getting it up and running is just like setting up an Android phone: scan the QR code with your phone, enter a passcode and transfer your apps and accounts. It is all done and dusted in about four minutes, which is faster than setting up a modern Windows 11 machine even if you know all the shortcuts.

Access to the full gamut of Android apps is the Googlebook’s biggest strength and its greatest weakness. Practically any app you have on your phone can be installed and run on the laptop. But almost all those phone apps are just that, mobile versions, with most not even aware that they are not installed on a phone.

Those that have at least some tailoring to the laptop form come in a few different types, categorised by Google broadly under “compatible with desktop”, which means they should support mouse and keyboard controls; “optimised for desktop”, which means they should scale properly to the laptop’s display; and “made for desktop”, which are a handful of Android apps redesigned with the laptop in mind.
Only the last category really seems to make any difference to the quality of the app, and even then most of them are still not of the same calibre as their equivalents found on Windows or macOS.
Even Google’s apps are a mixed bag. Google Calendar can only show one account at any one time, so you can’t see your personal, work and shared calendars on one screen like you can on Android.
Google Docs starts as its own app, but when you actually open a document it just becomes another Chrome window hidden behind the Chrome logo on the task bar, not the Docs logo.

The Files app shows your Google Drive files, but you can’t pin locations to the side bar to quickly access your commonly used folders, making it a time-consuming dig through endless folders to find things each time.

Even the Chrome browser is not quite up to par with its Windows or macOS counterpart, lacking features such as split-screen tabs, the auto-hiding vertical tab bar or the ability to have multiple profiles, such as a personal and work account.
Google has an app-gap problem and one that will only be solved if developers are convinced Googlebook OS is going to take off and be worth spending time and money making better apps for.

The other big selling point is deep integration with your Android phone. Google calls this “better together”, which is a collection of features that mirror capabilities of iPhones with Macs or Microsoft’s Link to Windows.

Some of the features are like magic. You can search the files on your phone straight from the Files app on the laptop without plugging it in, see your notifications from your phone, continue tasks on your laptop from your phone and even use apps cast from your phone.

As useful as these features sound, many are not up to scratch. Streaming apps from your phone is so slow that I feel as though I can type entire sentences before they appear on screen in chat apps, and it is restricted to one app at a time. If you click on a synced notification from your phone, it will open in a cast app, even if you have the full app installed on your Googlebook. Even viewing files on your phone from the laptop is irritatingly slow.
The only apps I’ve reliably managed to get to appear with the ability to continue from where I was are Google Docs and Chrome on the phone.
It also took me two hours of troubleshooting to get an up-to-date Google Pixel 11 Pro to actually connect with the Googlebooks, despite using the phone to set them up in the first place.

The other big selling point for Google is its Gemini integration into Googlebook OS. The Gemini app is just like it is on macOS and Windows. But it is the Magic Pointer feature, which appears when you wiggle the mouse to click or highlight something on your screen to send it to Gemini, that is the most novel.

You can use it to get Gemini to summarise text, explain something, search for things or generally chat. But I often hit a road block, such as Gemini refusing to generate images or saying it cannot add a date into my calendar in the mode Magic Cursor opens, which oddly isn’t within the desktop Gemini app. Sometimes it works, sometimes it doesn’t, and it is simply not joined up.

Magic Cue has been imported from Google’s Pixel phones, which is meant to pop up with helpful information such as calendar availability or a location in maps when you highlight a date or a place in a chat or email. But unlike on a Pixel phone, I have yet to get it to successfully activate in two weeks of testing.

Google’s super-charged voice dictation system called Rambler, also from the recent Pixels, does at least work as described. Press the dictation key and just speak naturally. Rambler will condense your speech into concise sentences removing filler words and errors.
Googlebooks are full of excellent ideas about how a modern laptop should work. The hardware of the Acer and Asus machines I’ve tested is top notch, but the software just isn’t ready for prime time.
When it works it’s great, but it is filled with limitations that might be acceptable on a super-cheap laptop but never on a £1,000 premium machine.

Chrome is not as good as it is on a Mac or Windows PC. Google’s various apps are generally better on an Android phone and the third-party app ecosystem is a mess of poorly optimised mobile apps. Even the best desktop-optimised Android apps pale by comparison to their counterparts on Windows or macOS.
The Android phone-linking system should be the killer feature, but it is partly broken or simply not up to scratch. Even the Gemini integration is flakey.
Most of the Google-specific issues and software bugs are eminently fixable. But the app gap will take serious time, effort and money to convince third-party developers to fix.
Unless you want to spend at least £1,000 to be a beta tester, your money is better spent elsewhere for now.

items.title: Light and Magic: The Birth of Art Photography review – a rhapsodic show to stop you in your tracks
paragraphs: I don’t remember the last time I saw such a well-researched and truly globally representative exhibition that doesn’t patronise but quietly makes its case unapologetically, fearlessly and through sheer quality. Apart from being the first retelling of the international, pluralistic pictorialism movement, Tate’s new show allows for some refreshing encounters with unknown works for British audiences – around half of the works included here have never been shown in the UK. The effect is to radically deepen and widen our understanding not only of art history but the human impulses that drive us to make images in the first place.

We move seamlessly from the sudden shock of colour in three-colour carbon prints of flowers in a London garden in the 1920s to works born of the photographic salons, circles and clubs of Sydney, Hong Kong and Brazil. Historical moments collide; the epic emerges from the everyday. A man rows home across the Norfolk Broads, another works on a construction site in Singapore. None of it feels out of place. It all belongs. It is all extremely, almost ecclesiastically, beautiful.

More than a few times, I stopped in my tracks. I could spend hours with Yip Cheong Fun’s 1940 Father’s Care, a cinematic image of a man holding one child with his hand extended to another, helping them down from the rocky crag they are walking over, on a journey across an open rural landscape somewhere. It’s a touching image of parenthood and the passage of time. Like this show overall, it’s about gestures rather than flashy declarations of feeling.

From this purist vision of love, we find a more ambiguous exploration in Lionel Wendt’s excruciatingly charged study of a young Sri Lankan man’s loincloth-clad body in the private intimacy of his Colombo studio, revealing hidden desires and truths the camera can’t conceal. It’s beauty as a kind of torture: the same medium that can expose the body to anthropological scrutiny transforms looking into something far more complicated.

I’m equally intrigued by a 1955 series by Han Youngsoo: small, noirish works of Korean street scenes that beg for narration from the viewer. Two 1925 bromide prints by Kate Smith show a woman in a flowing pre-Raphaelite style, pausing in a field dense with vegetation and foliage. Its title draws me closer: The Listener. What is she listening to, and what does this photograph want us to hear? It leaves me hovering between the visible and the imagined, its silence and stillness charged with the possibility.

Limb Eung-sik’s Feet 2 has a similarly ethereal atmosphere: flowing, diaphanous material folds around a dancer’s feet so that they dissolve into light and shadows. Nostalgia and sentimentality are dialled up, but it’s irresistible. If you’re attuned to it, these images suggest that anything – shells, shadows, a faucet, a wilting flower, a fishing net – can become magic, and these pictorialists teach us how to see the world that way.

This is not by any means a critical look at pictorialism. Mysteries are left intact, politics are largely left at the door. There’s no attempt to unravel the reductionist pitfalls of pursuing the fantasy of beauty. Some of the educational intrusions feel unnecessary – a timeline of photographic techniques is helpful and interesting but risks putting “art photography” back in the realm of craft, as does a full-scale recreation of a darkroom that you cannot enter. The magic of the darkroom is not that it is a dark room with a bunch of dirty aprons hanging outside. It is the transformation that happens within it: the strange alchemy of chemistry and light, which is already accounted for in abundance in the photographs.

But I can forgive these things. There’s genuine care and awe here. It’s a reminder that seeking moments of magic and breathtaking beauty is a human instinct, and we have a right to it. This is an exhibition about things that are universally shared and eternally human, that cannot be destroyed by the politics of a time or place, that survive and thrive. Light and Magic is as intelligent as it is beautiful, as whimsical as it is informative, as rhapsodic as it is real.

items.title: Wikipedia often gets taken for granted – but its history is fascinating, and its future is fragile
paragraphs: A few years ago, I was struck by the tension between how Wikipedia was used, and how it was talked about. Everyone was on it all the time, and yet its reputation had stalled at “don’t trust it”, because it was the “free encyclopedia that anyone can edit”.

Clearly people were trusting it, so much so it had become part of the fabric of everyday life since it was founded by Jimmy Wales and Larry Sanger in 2001. But despite the fact it now has been consulted trillions of times by billions of people (English Wikipedia alone is 5.2bn words long), it inspires an odd lack of curiosity. Even people donating to Wikipedia might say the money was “for the factcheckers”, though there aren’t any – not paid ones, anyway. Meanwhile, the internet in the social media era had begun to feel like a much uglier place, and some digital nostalgia was setting in: here was this holdover that had somehow survived; a website that functions – and even looks – much the same as it did 20 years ago.

You could say that I fell down a Wiki rabbit hole, especially when it came to the website’s early years. Almost everything important about the project came together quite quickly. Its amateurish, homegrown ethos was off-putting to a lot of writers and journalists, and that meant many questions about why it had worked had no answers. Most of the people seriously interested in Wikipedia were a handful of academics – so I decided to write a book about it.

I’m not a tech journalist. Instead, I have a background in the humanities. Wikipedia actually does, too: philosophy, and even off-piste disciplines like town planning and poetry, played a much bigger role in its inception than pure technology. Ward Cunningham, who invented the wiki in the 1990s – that’s a webpage anyone can edit, and the foundational tool of Wikipedia – thought very carefully about how the power of computers might be democratised. He drew on all sorts of oblique concepts for it, such as constructivism and the Zen concept of wabi-sabi – beauty in imperfection – and it’s remarkable how well the culture he created has persisted. Especially wabi-sabi – Wikipedia is, after all, always in a state of incompleteness.

Philosophy drew Wikipedia’s co-founders together as well. Though Wales worked in tech and finance, he corresponded with philosophers for years. And though Sanger was an academic philosopher, he spent lots of time arguing online – only “amateurs” seemed to share his sense that philosophy had life-and-death stakes. Lots of people in the dotcom boom started online encyclopedias, but Wales was the only one to hire a philosopher. In fact the only person he hired was a philosopher. It was such an unpredictable choice, and an important clue to what made Wikipedia work: it sprang out of this digital “republic of letters”, where all sorts of people were thinking about facts and why they were important.

Because Wikipedia is so massive, writing an “exhaustive” book on it is impossible, like trying to represent a mountain with a grain of sand. Instead, I concentrated on the human history – the small, sometimes very small, number of people who really influenced what Wikipedia became. Wikipedians can be difficult, and the most ornery get a bad wrap – even the Wikimedia Foundation’s leadership has made comments about their “Dorito-stained fingers”, or tendency to stay home on a Saturday night. But by the end of the process, I was in awe of them, and I still am.

Wales and Sanger are prominent, but many other important early Wikipedians are unknown. The first woman to edit Wikipedia, Gaytha Langlois, hasn’t had much attention. She wrote about two things dear to her: Rhode Island and standard poodles – small states and big dogs. Wikipedia has always had a gender imbalance, which has proved stubborn – Sandi Toksvig is only the latest in a long line of critics trying to address it. She is part of an effort to create a more balanced alternative to Wikipedia called Mappa Mundi, which has the potential to feed back into Wikipedia as well.

I became fascinated too with a little-known contributor who had the first biographical page for a woman on Wikipedia (today, it would be called a user page). Her name was Ruth Ifcher, and she was a very intelligent grammar pedant, with a PhD, who had been forced out of the workforce with severe agoraphobia. Wikipedia came along later in her life and opened a whole new avenue for creative and meaningful work.
Proust said that neurotics alone “composed our masterpieces” and that’s true here.

Neurodiversity is so central to Wikipedia that one former head of the Wikimedia Foundation told me the encyclopedia is a “city built by Asperger’s”. You can sense that energy in familiar topics – planes, trains and automobiles, comic books, weather, and all the rest. Often, Wikipedians are so prolific that they write too much, a phenomenon called “fancruft”. “Road geeks” (like trainspotters for roads) kept having their work about minor roads deleted, so a whole lot of them left in a huff, and started a separate online wiki encyclopedia for roads. That’s almost a microcosm of the inclusionists v deletionists debate, which is the biggest philosophical rift on Wikipedia – a rolling argument about what should be included, and what shouldn’t.

The co-founders had once believed that 100,000 articles would be “a reasonable size” for an encyclopedia, because that’s how big Britannica was. Today, Wikipedia has 68m, and Pew Research estimates that it served 1.9tn page views between 2015 and 2025. Because it is so monumental, I never expected Wikipedia to feel fragile or vulnerable – but as I was finishing the book, AI had begun to encroach on Wikipedia in an existential way by diminishing the web traffic it relies on, for instance, or by editors contributing huge volumes of poorly written AI-generated text. People ask me “is Wikipedia under threat?”, and it is, but so is everything from Hollywood to pure mathematics. I do think it will survive, but the quaking foundations made it feel urgent to say “we saw this made, and we won’t see anything like it again”.

The Last Best Place on the Internet: A Human History of Wikipedia by Richard Cooke is out now through Black Inc in Australia, and WW Norton in the US. It will be released in the UK on 5 November, via Granta

items.title: Apple AirPods 5 review: the best open-fit earbuds yet
paragraphs: Apple’s latest AirPods set a new standard for open-fit buds with upgraded noise cancelling that now rivals many plugged-in designs of the same price.

The AirPods 5 have the same design the popular AirPods 4 offering an option for those that do not like silicone ear tips used by most noise cancelling earbuds. They come in two versions, with or without a wireless charging case and swipe controls, costing from £119 (€149/$129/A$219) – £10 cheaper than the launch price of their predecessors.
The earbuds and case are almost indistinguishable from the AirPods 4, which makes the case very small and easy to pocket, fitting in the watch pocket of a pair of jeans.

The buds are some of the most comfortable open-fit designs available and stayed put when commuting, running for the train and generally going about the day. But for those that didn’t get on with the previous design of the AirPods, these are unlikely to change that, and they have no stability wings or similar to keep them in place for vigorous exercise.

The stalk has a pressure-sensitive panel you squeeze once, twice or thrice for playback controls. A squeeze and hold changes the noise cancelling mode or activates Siri. On the more expensive versions with a wireless charging case, the panel is also touch-sensitive for swipe volume controls – the same system used in the AirPods Pro to great effect.
Connectivity: Bluetooth 5.3, SBC, AAC, H2 chip
Battery life: four or five hours with ANC (22 hours with case)
Water resistance: IP57 (up to 1 metre for 30 minutes)
Charging case dimensions: 46.2 x 50.1 x 21.2mm
Case charging: USB-C or wireless (Qi or Watch)
The cheapest AirPods 5 have up to four hours playback with noise cancelling and a case that can charge them four times for a total of 20 hours playback.

The AirPods 5 with wireless charging case have longer battery life lasting slightly more than five hours of playback with noise cancelling with a total of 22 hours playback using charges in the case. That’s long enough for a week of commuting, but far behind the best in the business. A compromise for the design and super-compact case.

The new AirPods have noticeably improved noise cancelling and sound. They produce fairly detailed sound with good separation of tones and can handle complex and overlapping tracks very well. But it is the additional bass that helps them produce a fuller, more rounded sound that wipes the floor with most other open-fit rivals and compares well to many decent earbuds with silicone tips. They may not satisfy audiophiles but they are a great listen.

The noise cancelling is equally effective, managing to quiet busy roads, the drone of engines or fans, and dampen background chatter. It struggles with higher tones, such as loud keyboard clicks or the screeches from train wheels, but does as good a job as many similarly-priced noise cancelling earbuds with silicone tips and is miles ahead of the open-fit competition.
They suffer a little from wind noise and can’t rival the sound dampening of the best earbuds with tips from Sony, Bose or the AirPods Pro 3, but still do a solid job.

The transparency mode is first class, sounding almost exactly like not wearing them at all, which is great for awareness on the street. Call quality is equally good coming through loud and clear with only a hint of sudden background noise when passing something particularly loud.

The AirPods 5 support Apple’s various smart features with an iPhone, such as direct access to the new Siri, live translation, automatic volume adjustment, spatial audio, audio sharing, the ability to pause music when falling asleep and optimised battery charging to increase its longevity.

Batteries in earbuds typically maintain at least 80% of their original capacity for 500 charge cycles. Apple offers a battery service for £49 per earbud or case and replacements cost from £69. The specialists iFixit awarded the earbuds two out of 10 for repairability. The AirPods 5 are made with 40% recycled material, which the company breaks down in its environmental impact report. The company offers trade-in and free recycling schemes, including for non-Apple products.
The AirPods 5 cost £119 (€149/$129/A$219) or £139 (€169/$149/A$249) with a wireless charging case and touch controls.
For comparison, the AirPods Pro 3 cost £219, the AirPods Max 2 cost £499, the Google Pixel Buds 2a cost £129 and the Shokz OpenFit Air 2 cost £129.
The AirPods 5 take the comfortable open-fit design of their predecessors and upgrade the sound and noise cancelling to rival many plugged-in earbuds with silicone tips, which is quite a feat.

They provide a good amount of bass for a full, detailed sound that’s a great general listen and a step above most open-fit rivals. The noise cancelling is capable of dampening unwanted sound to tolerable levels, comparing well with better than average silicone-equipped earbuds. It can’t match the best plugged-in earbuds, but it is certainly good enough. Apple’s transparency mode and call quality are top-notch, and it’s hard to fault the earbuds for daily use with a compact design that’s easy to pocket.
The battery life is a little short, and while they work with any Bluetooth device, I wouldn’t recommend them to people who don’t have at least one iPhone, iPad or Mac.

There are few great open-fit earbuds, but if you didn’t get on with other AirPods, these won’t tip the balance. The extra money for swipe volume controls and longer battery life is worth it, if you’re considering them.

The fifth-generation earbuds are marginally more repairable than their predecessors, which opens up the possibility of replacing the batteries down the line, but otherwise they are just as disposable as most other earbuds.

Pros: comfortable open fit, good sound and noise cancelling, great case, great playback and volume controls, great connectivity, special features with Apple devices including spatial audio, great call quality.

Cons: battery life could be better, little passive noise isolation, lack of features when connected to non-Apple devices, no Bluetooth multipoint or higher quality audio format support, difficult to repair.

items.title: iPhone 18 Pro Max review: Apple’s biggest, heaviest and longest-lasting superphone
paragraphs: Apple’s largest Pro iPhone gets its biggest battery upgrade yet to make it a true two-day phone with new Siri AI and a variable aperture camera.

The iPhone 18 Pro Max is the supersized sibling of the regular 18 Pro and, though it is no longer Apple’s most expensive phone thanks to the £2,000 iPhone Duo, it has a similarly large price tag to match costing from £1,299 (€1,599/$1,299/A$2,299).

The 18 Pro Max follows the familiar formula of its Pro Max predecessors: take everything that’s great about the 18 Pro and supersize the screen and the battery. That means it has a first-class camera, the fastest performance and very long software support.

But it also means the 18 Pro Max is hard to use with one hand and pretty big to fit in a pocket. It weighs 249g, which is really heavy for even a very large smartphone, 23g more than its nearest rival, 38g more than its smaller sibling and heavier still than folding phones. It made my hand hurt after 10 days of use and is a two-handed phone needing some sort of handle or strap.

The 6.9in screen is a joy to behold. Super bright, crisp, smooth and with a very effective anti-glare coating it’s great for films, TV or games, and offers a similar level of real estate for video to most folding phones. It also has the new, smaller camera cut out and bigger dynamic island of the regular 18 Pro.
Screen: 6.9in Super Retina XDR (120Hz OLED) (460ppi)
Camera: 48MP + 48MP UW + 48MP 4x, 18MP front-facing
Connectivity: 5G, wifi 7, NFC, Bluetooth 6, Thread, USB-C, Satellite, UWB and GNSS
Water resistance: IP68 (6 metres for 30 mins)

The 18 Pro Max has the same new A20 Pro chip as the 18 Pro, which is one of the fastest chips you can get in a phone, plus a resigned cooling system that helps maintain peak performance during long gaming sessions.

It has the longest battery of any iPhone, lasting almost three days of light usage between charges, actively using the screen for seven hours for apps, browsing, messaging and photos. That is about four hours longer than its predecessor and almost a day longer than the 18 Pro. Even with heavy use, the 18 Pro Max still managed to end the day with about 50% left in the tank, meaning most people will have to charge it only every second or third day.

The 18 Pro Max runs the same iOS 27 as smartphones from the iPhone 11 onwards. The new software speeds up app launches and other parts of the system, refines the Liquid Glass redesign from last year and revamps Apple’s AI tools.

The new Siri AI chatbot is a significant step in the right direction, able to better understand you and perform tasks. It has its own app to review previous conversations and can see what is on your screen or through the camera. It can also suggest data from your various Apple apps, similar to Google’s proactive tools on the Pixels. But it relies on you using messages and mail, rather than third-party apps such as the WhatsApp or Gmail apps.

The battery will last in excess of 1,000 full-charge cycles with at least 80% of its original capacity, and it can be replaced for £119. Out-of-warranty screen repairs cost £389. The specialists iFixit awarded the phone seven out of 10 for repairability.

It contains more than 40% recycled material. The company breaks down the phone’s environmental impact in its report. Apple offers trade-in and free recycling schemes, including for non-Apple products.
The 18 Pro Max has the same camera system as its smaller sibling, which includes an 18 megapixel centre stage selfie camera in the screen and three 48MP cameras on the back.
The three rear cameras are some of the best on a phone, including a 4x/8x optical zoom and 0.5x ultra wide.

The big addition for the 18 Pro Max is a variable aperture on the main camera, allowing it to open wider than other iPhones for better low light performance or to narrow to preserve depth of field. But it also allows additional creative photography possibilities, including shooting starbursts.
The 18 Pro Max also has new AI-powered focus tracking, improved Photographic Styles for greater customisation, Apple’s new digital negative feature and automatic cinematic mode for video.
The iPhone 18 Pro Max costs from £1,299 (€1,599/$1,299/A$2,299).
For comparison, the iPhone 17 costs £899, the iPhone Air £1,099 and the iPhone 18 Pro £1,199; the Google Pixel 11 Pro costs £1,279 and the Samsung Galaxy S26 Ultra £1,359.
The iPhone 18 Pro Max is Apple’s biggest, longest-lasting and most expensive slab phone for 2026.

It takes what is great about the regular 18 Pro and supersizes the screen and battery, giving it a run time of up to three days, which is a good half day more than its smaller sibling. That places it shoulder to shoulder with some of the longest-lasting phones available on any platform.

But similar to superphones from Google and Samsung, the 18 Pro Max is too big to use one-handed and tricky to pocket. It is also too heavy and made my hand hurt without using a Popsocket or a similar handle attached to it.

Otherwise, it is a fairly iterative upgrade on the 17 Pro Max, with the same design and feel. The screen is still one of the very best on a phone, and the improved dynamic island is a useful upgrade. The A20 Pro chip is seriously quick, the cameras are some of the best you can get on a phone and the variable aperture on the main camera opens up some new creative opportunities, even if its impact on image quality is fairly minor.
Pros: fabulous 6.9in screen, better dynamic island, very long battery life, great cameras with variable aperture, USB-C, top performance, long software support, Face ID, better AI.
Cons: very expensive, very heavy, hard to use one-handed, small upgrade on last year, AI tools still lag top competitors.

items.title: Apple iPhone 18 Pro review: big changes for small differences
paragraphs: Apple’s smaller Pro iPhone gets the best kind of spec bump for 2026: longer battery life, faster chips and a fancy new variable aperture for the main camera.
The iPhone 18 Pro is one of a pair of slab phones launched alongside Apple’s first folding phone, the iPhone Duo, and is the cheapest of the new phones, with a regular iPhone 18 yet to be announced.
It isn’t exactly low cost, priced from £1,199 (€1,449/$1,199/A$2,099), with a £100 or equivalent rise over previous models courtesy of RAMageddon.

Having fully revamped the design of the body for the iPhone 17 Pro, the new model is a modest refinement. It is 7g heavier and the back glass now matches the colour of the aluminium body, which is available in a handful of new shades.

Apple has shrunk the amount of the screen taken up by the Face ID camera, allowing the dynamic island to show three continuing tasks, up from two on previous devices. It also now shows the 3/4/5G indicator next to the signal level when playing music, which is a most appreciated feature for public transport commuters sorely missed on previous models.

Otherwise, the 6.3in screen is one of the very best on a phone: super bright, crisp and smooth, while being big enough without making the phone enormous. An anti-glare coating makes it much easier to see outside, too.
Screen: 6.3in Super Retina XDR (120Hz OLED) (460ppi)
Camera: 48MP + 48MP UW + 48MP 4x, 18MP front-facing
Connectivity: 5G, wifi 7, NFC, Bluetooth 6, Thread, USB-C, Satellite, UWB and GNSS
Water resistance: IP68 (6 metres for 30 mins)

The 18 Pro has Apple’s new A20 Pro chip, which is about 27% faster than the A19 Pro in last year’s model, with about 45% faster graphics performance. Since the A19 Pro was no slouch, that’s quite the leap and puts it miles ahead of the competition, ready to handle anything.
The phone has a redesigned cooling system for longer peak performance, too, which is especially useful for running games on top settings.

The battery lasts a solid six hours longer than the iPhone 17 Pro, managing to stretch to about two days between charges with more than six hours of active screen use across apps, browsing, messaging and photos. Even with the heaviest of use while out and about, the 18 Pro managed to end the day with 40% left in the tank. Most people will only need to charge it every other day.

The 18 Pro ships running iOS 27, which was released for the rest of the iPhone line on 14 September. It refines the relatively controversial Liquid Glass redesign from last year and speeds up the system, including app launches. But the big new addition is Apple’s revamped Siri, backed by Google’s AI technologies.

Siri AI, as the new system is called, is significantly more capable of understanding and answering questions than previous iterations. It is a chatbot like most other AI assistants, but it is less chatty and sycophantic than others, being more likely to just get the job done. As well as a choice of voices, there are sliders to control how fast it talks and how expressive its responses are. It has its own app where you can review previous interactions, but it is accessible anywhere on the phone via the side button, is built into Spotlight search and can see what’s on your screen, including when using the camera.

It can also offer suggestions, such as adding an event to your calendar from the messages or mail apps, and attempts to display relevant information from your emails in the phone app when you call a business. But Siri can only do so if you use Apple’s apps, so if you use WhatsApp for texting and Gmail for your email, none of it works.

The battery will last more than 1,000 full-charge cycles with at least 80% of its original capacity and can be replaced for £119. Out-of-warranty screen repairs cost £349. The specialists iFixit awarded the phone a seven out of 10 for repairability.

It contains more than 40% recycled material. The company breaks down the phone’s environmental impact in its report. Apple offers trade-in and free recycling schemes, including for non-Apple products.
The 18 Pro has a similar camera system to last year’s 17 Pro with one big addition, a variable aperture for the main camera.
That means it has a very good 18MP centre stage selfie camera on the front and three 48MP cameras on the rear: main, 0.5x ultrawide and 4x telephoto.

The ultrawide is one of the best on a phone, handy for landscapes and group shots. The 4x telephoto is very good too, full of detail and manages lower light settings well. It shoots excellent photos with a crop zoom to reach 8x before digital zoom is required, which is a little behind rivals with 5x/10x telephoto zooms.

The variable aperture on the main camera can be left on automatic or controlled manually. It allows the camera to open wider than previous models for better low light performance, speeding up night mode shots and reducing unwanted motion blur.

But it also enables a number of creative uses, such as making starbursts by narrowing the aperture when shooting lights, which is very fun, or controlling the depth of field in your photo. However, because the iPhone’s camera is tiny compared with an APS-C or full-frame camera, the difference in depth of field – where the foreground and background of the image are either in focus or blown out for a nice bokeh effect – is pretty minor. When shooting something up close, manually closing the aperture to f/4.0 can bring things in the foreground or background into focus, but otherwise the difference for most shots is small.

The 18 Pro’s camera has a number of other useful upgrades. My favourite is AI-powered focus tracking that keeps a subject in focus as it moves about or into and out of the frame, which has been one of the best features of a Pixel camera for years and is extremely handy for fast-moving children or pets.

Apple has also added texture and grain control to its Photographic Styles feature to customise how the camera shoots photos beyond what was introduced with the iPhone 16 Pro, including film simulation. Finally, the new Apple Reference Image feature can sign an image for authenticity, on a per pixel level directly on the sensor, to help later prove a shot is not AI-generated, similar to a digital negative.

The camera shoots some of the very best video on a phone, too. New for this year is the ability to convert a regular video to a cinematic one after the fact, a bit like the excellent automatic portrait mode for photos.
The iPhone 18 Pro costs from £1,199 (€1,449/$1,199/A$2,099).
For comparison, the iPhone 17 costs £899, the iPhone Air costs £1,099, the iPhone 18 Pro Max costs £1,299, the Google Pixel 11 Pro costs £1,079 and the Samsung Galaxy S26 Ultra costs £1,359.
The iPhone 18 Pro is an iterative upgrade on an already great device from last year. Inside, it has some quite big changes, but their impact is fairly minor on the whole experience.

The new A20 Pro chip is super fast, but you can’t really notice the difference day to day, as previous iPhone chips have already been very quick. The extended battery life is great, but most people will still have to charge it every other day. The smaller camera cutout in the dynamic island now shows three continuing activities instead of two. Even the variable aperture in the main camera makes only a small difference to image quality unless you’re really trying to get creative.
The screen is fantastic and big enough. The aluminium body feels great to hold. The cameras are some of the best on a phone and even Siri is better now.

All of these things add up. The 18 Pro is without doubt the best iPhone ever made and at this size is one of the very best smaller phones available. It’s just not a transformative change unless you’re upgrading from a much older model and it now costs even more thanks to RAMageddon.
Pros: relatively compact, great screen, better dynamic island, longer battery life, great cameras, variable aperture, USB-C, top performance, long software support, Face ID, better AI.
Cons: small upgrade on last year, expensive, heavier than previous model, AI tools still lag behind top competitors.

items.title: ‘A saving gesture’: the art exhibition spotlighting US prisoners’ creations
paragraphs: With nearly 2 million people behind bars, America is the global leader in incarceration. When you look at it per capita, we have the highest rate of incarceration of any independent democracy and rank fourth overall in the world, just behind El Salvador, Cuba and Turkmenistan.

Despite these troubling numbers, mass imprisonment is largely invisible. “Our carceral system is something we as a society try to separate out from the everyday,” observes Terra Warren, an associate curator at Grand Rapids Art Museum, Michigan, who alongside curator Jennifer Wcisel brings audiences three solo shows from artists Julie Green, Gary Tyler and Ray Materson. They collectively aim to make us examine more closely just what prisons are doing to our society – and how art can prove transformative to those incarcerated.

In a major feat, Green’s show collects the artist’s work The Last Supper, rarely exhibited in full. This masterpiece took 22 years to complete and comprises nearly 1,000 plates, each depicting the final meal requested by an individual on death row before their execution. Poignantly, many of the plates are simply inscribed with the word “none”, indicating when an inmate opted not to eat a final meal. One imagines it would be hard to find an appetite under such conditions.

In centering breaking bread, a practice that’s a cornerstone of our shared humanity, The Last Supper forces audiences to reckon with the contradictions of a system that at once gives the pleasure of consuming a fine meal, yet also dehumanizes and even puts to death those within its grasp. Additionally, the piece opens space for compassion and understanding by giving us a window into the lives of those who are rarely represented in any meaningful way at all.

“There’s one in particular where a prisoner opted to eat vending machine food with their family,” Warren says, recalling plates that particularly stood put in her memory. “There’s another whose mother was allowed to come in and cook their last meal.”

Some of the plates also underscore the fact that the state will put to death individuals who are not even aware of what’s happening; one plate indicates that an inmate chose to save some of their last meal for later, not understanding that there would not be a chance to ever eat again. “One of the plates details that a person with an IQ of 61 was executed,” said Warren, indicating someone was put to death in spite of serious mental impairments.

Death row figures prominently in the life of Gary Tyler, an author and artist, who in 1974 was charged with the murder of a white teenager when Tyler was 16 years old. When he was convicted by an all-white jury and sentenced to death, he became the youngest person on death row in the United States. The case was marred by police misconduct, and Tyler is now widely considered to have been wrongfully imprisoned.

Although Tyler was never formally exonerated, he was freed in 2016 following the supreme court ruling in the 2012 Miller v Alabama case, where the court held that it was unconstitutional to adjudicate mandatory sentences of life imprisonment for juvenile defendants.

While serving four decades in the infamous Angola state prison – known as the Alcatraz of the south and currently the largest maximum-security prison in the United States – Tyler began to make quilts to comfort inmates dying in the prison’s hospice. At first reluctant to work with textiles, he soon saw just how valued his creations were. “I saw that I could help the men in the hospice, so it was something that I warmed up to,” Tyler said. “I realized we were doing something that would last for generations in the family. When our patients passed, the quilt was passed into their family, and it was really moving for me.”

As Tyler continued making quilts for dying inmates, he developed a perspective that would later inform his transition to making textile art, and that would help him be able to tell his own story through the intricate quilts that he had made for years as an artist. “You realize that that could be you, and it will be you eventually, you’re just as human as the individual you’re taking care of,” he says. “Being a hospital volunteer was one of the greatest things in my life. I never would have thought that I had the creative gene in me.”

Tyler’s quilts tend to be backgrounded by static colors shot through with rich texture and repeating motifs – flowers in one, abstract tear shapes in another. The scenes they depict are vivid and powerful: a bull smacking over a red table, a man literally struggling under the weight of the world, a child in shackles with their back turned to us.

One work that stands out in Tyler’s mind depicts a moment from the trial, when he was being led away from the courthouse in handcuffs by an escort of police, while a crowd of supporters cheered for him. “I got this surge of energy,” he says. “I wanted to raise my hands in a fist, but I had handcuffs on, with deputies holding my arms, but I still managed to show defiance, that despite what happened I would continue to fight.”

The Grand Rapids trio is rounded out by a comprehensive museum survey of Ray Materson, the outsider embroidery artist, who developed his signature technique of working with unraveled socks by necessity while serving seven years in prison due to drug addiction.

While boxer shorts and bedsheets could supply Materson with plenty of white thread, socks were of special importance to him, as they gave him the colors that he required in order to create intricate scenes. He would spend hours and hours simply getting the dearly needed materials. “Ray said to me one time: ‘Your biggest enemy in prison is the clock,’” said Warren. “For him to be able to spend days and days in this meditative act was such a saving gesture.”

Materson’s skills quickly became known to the other inmates, who soon began asking him to make embroidery of loved ones or items such as national flags with great symbolic meaning. These pieces gave Materson a purpose and allowed the men he created for to experience a sense of identity and selfhood in a profoundly dehumanizing environment.

Life in prison has stuck with Materson, who to this day sources vintage socks like the ones he used while in jail in the 1980s. “Their nylon has the stretchability that he needs in order to work,” explained Warren. His work tends to depict intense scenes, often derived from the likes of Shakespeare, Ibsen and Chekhov, as well as royalty like Queen Victoria and Catherine the Great. While small, often measuring just 2in x 3in, the works are filled with pathos and are a wonder to behold.

“This show brings a lot of shock at the facts of what’s the reality for a lot of people, but they also bring a lot of hope,” said Warren, sharing her hopes that the art on display can both humanize and inspire, as well as show audiences that artistic creation can be transformative for them too. “Ray was on a track of death through his addiction, but because of art his life turned around into something defined by creativity and giving.”

Julie Green: The Last Supper; Gary Tyler: Rebirth and Ray Materson: Metamorphosis are all at Grand Rapids Art Museum from 3 October 2026 until 24 October 2027 (Green) and 3 January 2027 (Tyler, Materson)
